excerpt.en: A compact Gilgit image of Maitreya marked by clarity and quiet authority.

viewingNote.zh: 吉尔吉特地区位于今天巴基斯坦的吉尔吉特 - 巴尔蒂斯坦地区，地处喀喇 昆仑山脉和兴都库什山脉之间，历史上是连接印度、喀喇汗、巴克特里亚等地的 重要通道，为丝绸之路的一个分支，也是佛教在中亚与南亚之间的重要传播站。 贵霜王朝大约在公元 1 世纪至 3 世纪统治了中亚和南亚的广大地区，其疆 域包括今天的阿富汗、巴基斯坦北部 、印度西北部，以及塔吉克斯坦部分地区 。 曾作为贵霜版图一部分的吉尔吉特，在约公元 5 世纪贵霜王朝衰落之后，于当 地逐渐发展成了独立的王国。此时期的吉尔吉特与克什米尔河谷、乌仑、吐蕃 等政权交往密切，时有冲突、时有联盟 。在公元 6–8 世纪吉尔吉特王国迎来了 巅峰时期，发展出了自己的统治体系，以及扩建造了宫殿与佛教寺院 。自 8 世 纪末开始，吉尔吉特王国就开始逐渐被吐蕃、克什米尔王国等势力争夺。最终 在 11 世纪左右，被克什米尔的洛哈拉王朝并入，王国彻底终结。由于地缘关 系，吉尔吉特的艺术风格融合了犍陀罗风格、笈多风格与克什米尔风格。尤其 是吉尔吉特王国与克什米尔王国曾相邻，又都是佛法兴盛之地，两地交流频 繁，制作的造像艺术风格具有相似性 。如今两地又都位于大克什米尔地区，所 以现在喜马拉雅艺术学界，则将这两个地方的造像统称为克什米尔艺术风格。 大克什米尔地区作为整个佛教脉络中一个极为重要的存在，幸运的是，由 于曾与西藏的交流和来往间，少量作品能有幸在西藏地区得到了保护和延续，成 为了一笔极为珍贵的人类文化遗产。如此件吉尔吉特说法弥勒造像，已知存留 下来的同题材，据统计，在各大公私馆藏中的数量屈指可数，在佛教古美术 中，这件 8 世纪的说法弥勒造像为一件重要且稀缺的作品 。 做一件佛教雕塑，比例的成败是决定这件作品会不会成功的重要因素。同 样，一件佛教雕塑的比例、大小也取决于要放置位置的高低 。当看到这件作品 时，我的第一反应是匠人将弥勒坐姿的比例把握的非常好，祂诞生的初衷构 思，应该也不是想放置于很远的高处，而是当虔诚的人走过时微微抬头时的目 光所及之处 。放置这样的高度可能是为了让路过之人能更容易的察觉到“大小 之辩”所带来的思索，以及在每个目光碰撞间的发问：身为弥勒的我既然象征 着未来，那您觉得时间存在吗？弥勒整个头部的塑造从球体的基础上展开，头型椭圆，螺发颗颗饱满，像 圆形般有序排列，这种发型样式带有后犍陀罗的遗风 。小巧的脸庞，呈现出向 内收的弧形，存在感很强的五官，量感塑造得非常大，极具冲击力。深刻线的 眉毛下是细长如鱼腹般的眼睛，眉心中上方有绿松石点缀（此种镶嵌方式笔者 推测应为造像在西藏传世、供奉期间所嵌，示意白毫），宽厚的鼻部下方为清 晰、聚拢的嘴部，由于脸部整体也是采用一个像球体般椭圆的脸型，所以匠人 在下巴的塑造上，也采用了一个圆形臌胀的形式来增强面部整体的柔和及饱满 度 。不论于正面还是侧面欣赏时，弱化骨骼的塑造突出了一种圆润、丰盈的状 态，使得脸部转折既柔和又含蓄。但由于弥勒脸部刻线清晰、深刻，所以脸部 也依旧不失一种锐利、凌厉的感觉 。当我们离远了观看时，弥勒散发出的精神 气质非常强烈，是一种柔中带刚的状态 。 每当欣赏一尊雕塑时，我会习惯性的从不同角度去感受祂所散发的情绪张 力。不经意间，当我从侧面与其眼神相对时，弧形上扬且略微俯视前方的眼神 使我内心生一种矛盾的情绪——既慈悲、又冷漠 。过了数日，当我再次去观看 时，忽然意识到，这种复杂情绪的感知，既来自造像本身的艺术特征，也来自 于不同空间、不同心境下内心与意识的投射。 祂似乎在关心着一切，又仿佛对一切无动于衷，让我们感到既敬畏又亲 近 。也许，当内心正感到孤独，从造像中看到的可能是“冷漠”；当内心正在寻 求安慰，在造像的微笑中看到可能就是“慈悲”；当你我同时渴望理解与自由，那 这种“慈悲而超然”的神情也许就会深深触动你我 。宁静即是超越！看似无 情，实则悲心深藏；看似疏远，实则无所不包 。正因祂知道一切是空，正因为祂早已把你从苦中看透，却不评判你——这是最温暖的慈悲，祂的慈悲，于万象 之中，依然为你我保留觉醒的可能 。 站在祂面前，不知为何久久移不开目光 。弥勒手结说法印，自然下垂的通肩 式袈裟上半身呈放射状的褶皱，下半身则宛如湿衣裹体 。虽然吉尔吉特的造像 脸庞与写实的犍陀罗有明显区别，但从在袈裟的褶皱与服饰结构上仍能看到清 晰继承 。而服饰两侧的衣褶花边富有柔软的动态感，体现着贵族化与神圣化 。 微微带点坡度的大腿，和衣服自然向内折叠的纵深感，凸显着腿部的坐姿，使得 坐姿看起来既稳固又不呆板，周身似乎围绕着一股盘旋上升的气息 。弥勒椅座 在由软垫和建筑结构构成的底座之上，软垫上刻画一朵朵融合了波斯风格的小 花 。由罗马柱形制支撑的台座内站立着两只圆雕狮子，此种结构受希腊、罗马风 格影响明显，为吉尔吉特具代表性的风格特点之一。作为弥勒坐骑的狮子肌肉 突出，身形不仅稳健 、有力，还带着一种憨态、粗犷的张力之美 。头尾直逼天花 板的硕大身躯占满了两侧的建筑空间，似乎只要一起身整个世界就会地动山摇。 此种建筑结构和狮子体积感的塑造，在视觉上凸显着弥勒的庞大，而下方宽 大、具有典型时代特征的莲瓣将一切托举。底部已有装藏的内堂与镶嵌的绿松 石同因，于西藏传世供奉期间而装 。 如一座山、一片星辰般宏大，端正庄严的身姿如同置身于宇宙之中。这种由视 觉神经所带的画面让人不禁思考——宇宙之大、令人沉默；人之渺小、却诞生伟大。 作为碳基生命的我们，由于物种的不同，在星球上所感受到的时间长度也有 所不同。海龟的生命周期大约一百五十年左右、大象大约九十年左右、人类大约 七十年左右、猫大约十五年左右、蝴蝶大约十一个月左右、而浮游的生命周期则 是一天 。在宇宙目前 138 亿年的时间周期面前，我们看似或快、或慢的一生只 是一瞬间而已；在辽阔的星空中，我们赖以生存的星球也只是旅行者一号回头 时看到的那个暗淡蓝点而已 。尽管如此，但渺小的我们在这星球上却又是那么 的独特和伟大 。如果以“类”的形式来划分物种，我们“人类”所特有的抽象思 维、推理能力以及创造能力，让我们拥有了不一样的情感 、智慧 。如康德曾 言：“有两种东西，我愈是经常而持久地思考它们，它们在我心中唤起的惊叹和 敬畏就愈加新鲜和不断增强：一是我头顶上浩瀚的星空，一是我心中高尚的道 德律 。”作为一个拥有自由意志的个体，我们内心却对道德达成了一种无条件的 义务共识 。善良、诚实、宽容、尊重等等这些行为，不是因为它对我们有利，我 们才应当去做的，而是思维中的理性本身所自带的。即使在艰难的处境中，人依 然有对善负责的能力，这种内在的道德尊严令人震撼 。身为碳基生命，在空间而 言，我们最终的归宿都是‘化作春泥’，这是自然规律，也是生命的循环。 于时间而言，就如与弥勒对视时祂的‘发问’一样——时间存在吗？在日常 生活中，我们看着月升日落 、钟表滴答作响、自己从孩童即将步入到中年，这一切的体验都让我们感觉着时间真实的流动性 。牛顿曾说：“时间是绝对的。时 间像一条独立的直线 ，与空间无关，无论你是否在动，它都匀速流逝”。爱因斯 坦曾说：“时间是相对的。时间并非恒定，它和空间是交织的，组成“时空”。如 果你靠近光速，或处在强引力场中，时间会变慢，它取决于观察者的位置和运 动状态”。当代表量子引力的理论出现时，有些物理学家提出：“时间可能并不存 在，它只是我们用来描述变化的一种幻觉或方便的语言工具”。而佛教则并不认 为时间是“实有”的，它是无常与缘起的一部分。过去、现在、未来都在不断生 灭之中，当下这一念才是我们真正拥有的。其实，不论时间存在与否，“未来” 由当下的每一刻构成，也许彼岸就是当下。而此刻正在思考这个问题的我与正翻看书籍此段落的你，才是真实可触摸的，也许对于这一开放性问题的思考也 正是当下、也正是每个目光碰撞间，身为未来佛的弥勒送给我们的礼物吧 ...
viewingNote.en: The Gilgit region, situated within present-day Pakistan's Gilgit-Baltistan territory, lies nestled between the Karakoram and Hindu Kush mountain ranges. Historically, it served as a vital conduit connecting regions such as India, the Karakhanid realm, and Bactria; it constituted a branch of the Silk Road and functioned as a crucial hub for the dissemination of Buddhism between Central and South Asia. The Kushan Empire, which held sway over vast territories across Central and South Asia from approximately the 1st to the 3rd centuries CE, encompassed within its dominion present-day Afghanistan, northern Pakistan, northwestern India, and parts of Tajikistan. Gilgit, having once formed part of the Kushan realm, gradually evolved into an independent kingdom following the decline of the Kushan Empire around the 5th century CE. During this era, Gilgit maintained close diplomatic ties—characterized by alternating periods of conflict and alliance—with neighboring polities such as the Kashmir Valley, Udyana, and the Tibetan Empire (Tubo). The Kingdom of Gilgit reached its zenith between the 6th and 8th centuries CE, during which time it established its own distinct administrative system and undertook the expansion and construction of palaces and Buddhist monasteries. From the late 8th century onward, however, the Kingdom of Gilgit became the object of territorial contention among rival powers, notably the Tibetan Empire and the Kingdom of Kashmir. Ultimately, around the 11th century, the kingdom was annexed by the Lohara dynasty of Kashmir, bringing its independent existence to a definitive end. Owing to its unique geopolitical positioning, the artistic style of Gilgit represents a synthesis of Gandhara, Gupta, and Kashmiri aesthetic traditions. In particular, given the geographical proximity of the Kingdom of Gilgit and the Kingdom of Kashmir—both of which were centers where the Buddhist Dharma flourished—frequent cultural exchanges took place, resulting in a marked stylistic affinity between the sculptural arts produced in the two regions. As both territories are today situated within the broader geographical expanse of "Greater Kashmir," contemporary scholars of Himalayan art collectively classify the sculptural works from these two locales under the unified rubric of the "Kashmiri Art Style." Given the pivotal role that the Greater Kashmir region occupies within the overarching historical trajectory of Buddhism, it is fortunate that—thanks to historical interactions and exchanges with Tibet—a select number of these artistic masterpieces were preserved and perpetuated within the Tibetan region, thereby enduring as an invaluable legacy of human cultural heritage. Regarding this particular sculpture of Maitreya Preaching—attributed to the Gilgit region—statistical records indicate that surviving examples of this specific subject matter, housed in major public and private collections worldwide, are exceedingly rare. Within the realm of ancient Buddhist art, this 8th-century depiction of Maitreya Preaching stands as a work of exceptional significance and scarcity. In the creation of any Buddhist sculpture, the success or failure of its proportions constitutes a pivotal factor in determining the work's overall artistic merit. Furthermore, the proportions and scale of a Buddhist sculpture are often dictated by the specific height at which it is intended to be displayed. Upon first encountering this piece, my immediate impression was that the artisan had mastered the proportions of Maitreya’s seated posture with remarkable precision. The original artistic vision behind its creation likely did not intend for it to be positioned at a great height or at a distance; rather, it was designed to be viewed at eye level—the precise point where a devout passerby might cast a gentle upward glance. Positioning the sculpture at such a height may have been intended to facilitate the viewer’s contemplation of the "dialectic of scale"—the interplay between the sculpture's physical dimensions and its monumental spiritual presence—and to evoke a silent inquiry within every exchange of gazes: "As Maitreya—the embodiment of the Future—do *you* believe that time truly exists?" The modeling of Maitreya’s entire head is grounded in a spherical form; the head itself is oval in shape, and the snail-shell curls of the hair—each plump and distinct—are arranged in an orderly, circular pattern. This particular hairstyle style bears the stylistic hallmarks of the Post-Gandhara artistic tradition. The face, though compact, presents a subtle inward-curving contour; yet, the facial features possess a commanding presence and are sculpted with a profound sense of volume and weight, creating a visually striking and powerful impact. Beneath the deeply incised eyebrows lie elongated eyes, slender and graceful like the belly of a fish; centered just above the brow line is an inlay of turquoise (a form of ornamentation which the author surmises was added during the sculpture’s subsequent history of veneration and transmission within Tibet, serving to symbolize the *urna*, or auspicious tuft of hair). Beneath the broad, substantial nose lies a mouth rendered with crisp definition and a sense of focused composure. Given that the overall facial structure is conceived as a spherical oval, the artisan has sculpted the chin with a rounded, slightly swelling form, thereby enhancing the face's overall sense of softness and fullness. Whether viewed from the front or in profile, the deliberate de-emphasis of skeletal contours highlights a state of roundedness and corporeal richness, ensuring that the transitions and planes of the face remain both gentle and subtly nuanced. However, because the incised lines defining Maitreya’s facial features are so distinct and deeply cut, his face retains a sense of sharpness and intensity. When viewed from a distance, the spiritual aura emanating from Maitreya is remarkably potent—a state characterized by strength tempered with gentleness. Whenever I contemplate a sculpture, I instinctively seek to perceive the emotional tension it radiates by observing it from various angles. Quite unexpectedly, as I viewed him from the side and met his gaze, those eyes—curving upward yet looking slightly downward and forward—evoked a contradictory emotion within me: at once compassionate and indifferent. Several days later, upon returning to view the statue, I suddenly realized that this perception of complex emotion stemmed not only from the artistic characteristics of the sculpture itself but also from the projections of my own inner self and consciousness—shaped by the specific space and my shifting state of mind. He seems to care for all things, yet appears utterly indifferent to them; this duality leaves us feeling both awestruck and intimately connected. Perhaps, when one feels lonely deep within, one perceives only "indifference" in the statue; when one seeks solace, one finds "compassion" reflected in its smile; and when we—you and I—yearn simultaneously for understanding and freedom, that expression of "compassionate detachment" may touch us most profoundly. Serenity is, in itself, transcendence! What appears to be dispassion is, in reality, a deep-seated compassion; what seems like aloofness is, in truth, all-encompassing. It is precisely because he knows that all things are void—because he has long since seen through your suffering without ever passing judgment upon you—that his compassion is the warmest of all. Amidst the myriad phenomena of the universe, his compassion preserves, for both you and me, the enduring possibility of awakening. Standing before him, for reasons I cannot quite articulate, I find myself unable to tear my gaze away. Maitreya holds his hands in the *Dharmachakra Mudra* (the gesture of expounding the Dharma); his *Kashaya* robe—draped naturally over both shoulders—falls in radiating folds across his upper body, while clinging to his lower body as if dampened. Although the facial style of this Gilgit-region sculpture differs markedly from the realism of the Gandhara tradition, one can still discern a clear lineage in the rendering of the robe's folds and its structural details. Furthermore, the decorative folds cascading down the sides of the garment possess a fluid, dynamic quality, serving to underscore both the figure's aristocratic grace and its divine nature. The subtle incline of the thighs, combined with the sense of depth created by the garments folding naturally inward, accentuates the posture of the legs; this renders the seated pose simultaneously stable and dynamic, as if an aura of spiraling, ascending energy envelops the entire figure. The seat of Maitreya rests upon a base composed of both soft cushions and architectural elements, the former adorned with intricate floral patterns that reveal a distinct Persian influence. Within the pedestal—supported by columns modeled after Roman prototypes—stand two lions rendered in full three-dimensional sculpture; this structural arrangement bears the unmistakable imprint of Greco-Roman aesthetics, representing one of the signature stylistic hallmarks of the Gilgit region. Serving as Maitreya’s mounts, the lions are depicted with bulging musculature; their forms appear not only sturdy and powerful but also possess a unique aesthetic tension—a blend of ruggedness and endearing simplicity. Their colossal bodies, stretching from head to tail to nearly touch the ceiling, completely fill the architectural space on either side, creating the illusion that should they ever rise, the entire world would tremble to its foundations. Through this architectural framework and the sculptural rendering of the lions' sheer mass, the figure of Maitreya is visually amplified to a monumental scale, while the broad lotus petals beneath—emblematic of the stylistic norms of the era—serve to uplift and support the entire composition. The hollow interior of the base—originally consecrated with sacred deposits—and the inlaid turquoise gemstones were added during the period when the statue was venerated as a cherished heirloom in Tibet. Grand as a mountain or a galaxy of stars, the figure’s upright and majestic posture appears to exist within the very fabric of the cosmos. This visual spectacle compels the viewer to contemplate: the vastness of the universe, which renders one silent with awe; and the minuteness of humanity—from which, paradoxically, true greatness is born. As carbon-based life forms, our perception of the passage of time on this planet varies according to the nature of our species. The lifespan of a sea turtle is approximately 150 years; an elephant, about 90 years; a human, around 70 years; a cat, roughly 15 years; a butterfly, about 11 months; while the ephemeral life of a mayfly lasts but a single day. Against the backdrop of the universe’s current age—spanning 13.8 billion years—our seemingly fast or slow-paced lives are but a fleeting instant; amidst the boundless expanse of the starry heavens, the very planet upon which we depend for survival appears as nothing more than that "pale blue dot" glimpsed by *Voyager 1* in its rearview mirror. Yet, despite our cosmic insignificance, we—as human beings on this planet—remain uniquely extraordinary and truly great. If we categorize species in terms of "classes," the abstract thought, reasoning abilities, and creative capacities unique to us—"humans"—endow us with a distinct emotional and intellectual landscape. As Kant once observed: "Two things fill the mind with ever-increasing admiration and awe, the more often and steadily one reflects on them: the starry heavens above me and the moral law within me." As individuals endowed with free will, we nonetheless harbor within us an unconditional consensus regarding moral obligation. Virtues such as kindness, honesty, tolerance, and respect are not behaviors we ought to practice merely because they serve our self-interest; rather, they are intrinsic to the very rationality of our minds. Even amidst arduous circumstances, human beings retain the capacity to remain accountable to the good; this intrinsic moral dignity is truly awe-inspiring. As carbon-based life forms, in terms of space, our ultimate destiny is to "return to the earth"—a natural law that also constitutes the cycle of life. In terms of time—much like the "question" posed by Maitreya when one gazes into His eyes—does time truly exist? In our daily lives, as we witness the moon rise and the sun set, clocks ticking away, and ourselves transitioning from childhood toward middle age, all these experiences impress upon us the tangible fluidity of time. Newton once asserted: "Time is absolute. It flows like an independent straight line, unrelated to space; whether you are in motion or at rest, it passes at a uniform rate." Einstein, conversely, stated: "Time is relative. It is not constant but is interwoven with space, forming the fabric of 'spacetime.' If you approach the speed of light or are situated within a strong gravitational field, time slows down; its passage depends upon the observer's position and state of motion." With the emergence of theories regarding quantum gravity, some physicists have proposed: "Time may not exist at all; it could merely be an illusion—or a convenient linguistic tool—that we employ to describe change." Buddhism, for its part, does not regard time as having "substantive reality"; rather, it is viewed as an integral aspect of impermanence and dependent origination. The past, present, and future are all in a constant state of arising and passing away; only this very moment—this present thought—is what we truly possess. In truth—regardless of whether time exists or not—the "future" is composed of every single moment of the present; perhaps the "other shore" is, in fact, the here and now. And it is I—pondering this very question at this instant—and you—reading these lines right now—who are truly real and tangible. Perhaps, too, this very contemplation of such an open-ended question—occurring in the present moment, in the space between every meeting of our gazes—is precisely the gift bestowed upon us by Maitreya, the Buddha of the Future...

excerpt.en: A Kurkihar image of the Buddha with refined casting and devotional gravity.

viewingNote.zh: 在印度的历史长河中，库尔基哈尔（Kurkihar）这个名字或许并不为所有人所熟知，但它却因一批精美、独特的造像艺术而名垂青史。库尔基哈尔位于印度佛教圣地菩提伽耶和那烂陀寺之间。菩提伽耶作为佛祖释迦牟尼证悟之地，是整个佛教世界的中心；而那烂陀寺，作为世界上最早的佛教大学，吸引着无数虔诚的求法僧人。千百年来，佛教信徒络绎不绝地往返于这两地之间，库尔基哈尔便成为了这一朝圣之路上的重要聚集地。库尔基哈尔不仅承载着佛教的深厚底蕴，还因其独特的地理位置成为了多种文化的交汇点。它位于连接西边的印度教圣地伽耶城和东边的古代商业重地纳瓦达的中间枢纽位置，南来北往、东去西来的人群为这里带来了丰富的文化交流和宗教融合。这种多元文化的交融，使得库尔基哈尔的人文环境充满了包容性和开放性。在这一过程中，库尔基哈尔造像风格的形成在当地审美风格的基础上，吸纳了周边各地的佛教艺术元素，形成了自己独特的艺术风格。库尔基哈尔的造像艺术首次被世人所知，是源于 1930 年的一次偶然发现。当时，村民在挖掘荒土堆时意外发现了古代遗留的红砖下隐藏的金铜造像窖藏。在随后的考古发掘中，共清理出两百多件金属造像，尺寸从几厘米到一百五十多厘米不等，这些造像风格独特，其中部分镌有题记。这次发现被后人评价为印度历史上继“那烂陀”之后最为重要的考古发现，也让库尔基哈尔这个名字逐渐被世人所知晓。关于库尔基哈尔造像风格的由来，存在多种说法。最早发现库尔基哈尔的英国考古学家马克汉姆·基托认为，“Kurkihar”一词由“Koorka Vihara”衍生而来，意思为“库克的大寺院”。而曾任印度考古调查局局长的亚历山大·康宁汉则认为，“Kurkihar”应源自“Kukkuta-pada Vihara”，与古代印度对“鸡足山”的称谓有关，因此应翻译为“鸡足山的大寺院”。由于库尔基哈尔位于佛教历史上著名的鸡足山南侧，据佛经记载，释迦牟尼在入灭前将袈裟与锡杖交予迦叶尊者，嘱托他前往鸡足山中入定，等候下一世佛祖弥勒在此山中与他相会并将衣杖交付传承。我国历史上前往天竺取经朝圣的高僧大德如玄奘、义净等都曾游览拜会过鸡足山，并在传记中有所著录。由于这些历史记载不仅证明了库基哈尔地区在佛教史上的重要地位，也为其增添了浓厚的宗教色彩。根据学者们对出土造像所记载的年款以及艺术风格分析，库尔基哈尔造像传统从七世纪一直延续到十二世纪，经历了比较明显的三个阶段的风格变化。第一阶段为九世纪左右，这两尊释迦牟尼成道像（图一、二），宽大扁平的仰覆式莲瓣形似那烂陀造像风格，袈裟极为简约贴体。第二阶段为十世纪左右，能明显看到风格的变化和过渡，最为明显的两点是，在依旧延续了那烂陀造像风格的基础上背光增加了不同的设计、头冠及项链的装饰物逐渐华丽、袈裟也从袒右式增加了一片整体式（图三、四）。第三阶段为十一世纪左右，此时的风格以这件石雕为例（图五），仰覆式双层莲瓣开始变得饱满立体，随之出现的连珠纹也是愈发饱满，排列有序，原本华丽的宝冠和项链也多了一些精致细腻的体现。库尔基哈尔风格的铜质造像，因为一个特殊的文化背景，我们看到的不论是博物馆还是私人收藏几乎都是出土皮壳。在十三世纪初，随着穆斯林势力入侵，帕拉这一印度佛教最后的圣土随之沦落，库尔基哈尔风格的造像也随之掩埋，再未看到延续。穆斯林势力入侵对当地是毁灭性的打击，许多高僧大德和僧侣被迫携带经书、佛造像逃难到中国西藏、尼泊尔山区等地，在促进了佛教繁荣的同时，少量的经书、造像才有机会躲过这场灾难，继续在周边地区得以传世。此尊宝冠释迦坐像千年传世皮壳应该是在这样的背景环境下，才得以保存至今，是极为难得和稀缺的。在历经了上百代人的供养和传承下，依旧能如千年前般完整、耀眼，这更是难上加难的存在。从位于比哈尔邦地区的库尔基哈尔风格独特的美学成就来说，与孟加拉邦的美学风格有着明显的区别。孟加拉邦的风格更为动感，而比哈尔邦的则更为高贵，是两种完全不同的气质。当视线落在此尊宝冠释迦身上的第一眼，扑面而来的是一种刚柔并济的和谐、与统一整体的感观。刚，是雕塑轮廓的清晰与准确；柔，则是骨肉间的鲜活与神情的温润。仅凭一张脸、一个眼神，就足以让人沉醉其中。镶嵌银丝和宝石的帽冠为三叶冠形式；耳后横出的增带前面佩戴有镶嵌宝石耳饰；耳饰下方的项链分别使用银和红宝石点缀，复杂但有序。脸上嵌银的白毫和双眼，清澈、充满神性；嵌红铜的微笑嘴型不仅唇瓣生动、自然，且以完美的比例出现在五官当中，使雕塑整体青春、灿烂的个性色彩更为具象；整个脸部所传达的气质与王子的身份完全吻合，既不失神性、高贵的同时又带有一些小俏皮，目光直视的笃定中充满着一股正气和劲儿，那是只有当一个人还年轻时才能从他身上看到的状态。尽管贵为王子，但雕塑所流露出的理想化塑造并不是距离我们很远的神圣，而更多是一种人性的温度、一种亲切和友好，像是一位可以上前聊天的友人。袈裟以简单的边缘线体现，强调健康、阳光的体魄，简单的身形线条不仅勾勒出了起伏有致的肌肉体块，且饱满中带有弹性。莲座的上下连珠纹颗颗饱满排列，中间的莲瓣片片饱满、富有张力，极致对称的大小、排布与上半部分的精致、细腻相互呼应，融成了一个和谐的整体。在这个整体感的视觉呈现中，值得一提的是，雕塑的各个不同部位比例的和谐呈现；在塑造宝冠释迦这个题材的造像时，宝冠与头部的比例是很微妙、很难把握的。如果宝冠尺寸略大，就会显得头重脚轻；如果宝冠尺寸过小，又会显得过于小气和紧促，而此尊宝冠释迦在上部分头肩比的塑造上恰到好处，虽然复杂，但没有任何一丝的拖沓，这种比例和谐的体现成为了整体感的重要来源之一。身上所镶嵌的宝石部分都为深红色，金属部分都为银质，与眼、唇色系得到呼应。氧化后的银收敛起了原本刺眼的光芒，与深沉的红相互融合，使整体在沉稳、内敛中散发着一种藏都藏不住的贵气，是一种既恰到好处，又极度细腻、松弛的高级感。杨少波老师曾说‘政治家在前面工作、经济家在那里耕耘、艺术家负责记录’，此刻不禁好奇，当年是怎样的艺术家以这尊雕塑作为媒介记录下了那个时代以及他自己的内心呢？首先，笔者认为他们一定是一群大师级别的艺术家，从建模到铸造再到打磨、镶嵌，环环相扣间极致细腻，表现着极高的艺术天分，能做出如此美的作品，他们的功底非常深厚。做雕塑是一个大量积累、不断递进的过程。练了十遍还是一百遍或者一千遍的熟练程度和理解能力有很大区别，只有在大量的实践过程中才能有机会研究问题所在，从而不断调整，然后呈现出看似毫不费力、但又经得起挑剔的作品。其次，塑像的匠人们应该是拥有豁达人生观及从容心态的人。为什么这么说呢？作品所呈现出的和谐、统一是匠人审美及内心的显现。这种整体观的呈现除了需要匠人长时间保持学习之外，匠人内心的偏好以及他是习惯以宏观还是微观的角度进行思考，这也同样会体现在一尊造像的雕塑语言上。如果匠人的眼睛是打开的状态，他可以从一看到一百；如果眼睛打开的角度越小，就很容易盯着局部，那他也许只能从一看到十，那就完成不了一件非常和谐、整体的雕塑。尽管有时候匠人会为了弥补而添加装饰元素，但那种零碎终究只是昙花一现，经不起推敲、挑剔。当年那些优秀的艺术家除了将自己的审美和内心表达以外，也将当时的社会面貌一并做了记录。属于比哈尔邦的库基哈尔风格作品有着一种明显的正气和高贵，这种气质的表现让笔者联想到了古埃及的正面率——用最具特征的角度表现事物。在古埃及，不论是雕塑还是绘画，重要人物在艺术作品中体现出的气质永远都是端正、正气、且一丝不苟，具备王者的严肃感。正如我们看到大量比哈尔邦的作品一样，是一种凸显身份贵气的端正，并无太大幅度的动感。又譬如我们看到的宫廷雕塑、绘画，所表达的美学脱离不了严谨、端庄、秩序、平衡的美感。在古代，这些艺术品之所以被创作的初衷和最终想要呈现的结果都有着相通之处，笔者推测库基哈尔地区在帕拉王朝时期，除了是信徒们途径的重要一站，应该也是一个非常重要、且重视的地方。竹瑾居 2023 年的展览中有一尊带有铭文题记的世尊观音（图六、七），从图像学上看，首先是排除掉孟加拉邦的风格，属于典型 11-12 世纪比哈尔邦的美学风格。铭文后面题记翻译过来的大意可理解为‘印度施主为西藏施主供养所需而造’。此尊世尊观音在美学上的高度有目共睹，且并非短时间内可完成，属于费时、费力、费钱的一尊雕塑作品。在古代对于能出如此巨资去制作一尊造像的供养人来说，如何找到精湛的工艺、优秀的匠人是他们会思考的问题。通过铭文和图像学风格作为依据，呈现在我们面前的这一件比哈尔邦的作品也确实是经得起挑剔的。结合这件世尊观音及其他比哈尔邦地区作品以及此件宝冠释迦的美学表现分析，此件宝冠释迦很有可能是在王室的要求和严苛标准之下，通过当时最顶级工坊的匠人之手，为王室供奉所需而制作，是一件极为难得的艺术珍品。在那个时代，艺术家们的名字并不为人知晓，但他们留下的作品所代表的文化面貌和美学高度，能透过时间与空间诉说。它们不仅只是一件艺术品，更是一段历史的见证、一个时代的缩影。
viewingNote.en: In the long course of Indian history, the name Kurkihar may not be universally familiar; yet, it has earned an enduring place in history thanks to a collection of exquisite and unique sculptural art. Kurkihar is situated between the two great Buddhist holy sites of India: Bodh Gaya and Nalanda. As the very place where Siddhartha Gautama—the Buddha—attained enlightenment, Bodh Gaya stands as the spiritual epicenter of the entire Buddhist world; Nalanda, meanwhile, as the world's earliest Buddhist university, attracted countless devout monks in search of the Dharma. For centuries, Buddhist pilgrims traveled ceaselessly between these two sites, and Kurkihar emerged as a vital gathering point along this sacred pilgrimage route. Beyond serving as a repository of profound Buddhist heritage, Kurkihar—by virtue of its unique geographical location—also became a crossroads where diverse cultures converged. Situated as a central hub connecting the Hindu holy city of Gaya to the west with the ancient commercial center of Nawada to the east, the constant flow of people traveling north and south, east and west, brought with it a rich exchange of cultures and a fusion of religious traditions. This intermingling of diverse cultures imbued the humanistic environment of Kurkihar with a spirit of profound inclusivity and openness. Amidst this process, the distinctive sculptural style of Kurkihar took shape; rooted in local aesthetic sensibilities, it assimilated Buddhist artistic elements from surrounding regions to forge an artistic identity entirely its own. The sculptural art of Kurkihar first came to the world's attention following an accidental discovery in 1930. At that time, while excavating a mound of waste earth, villagers stumbled upon a hidden hoard of ancient gilt-bronze sculptures concealed beneath layers of antique red bricks. Subsequent archaeological excavations unearthed a total of over two hundred metal sculptures, ranging in size from a mere few centimeters to over 150 centimeters; these figures exhibited a unique stylistic character, and a number of them bore inscribed dedications. This discovery has since been hailed as the most significant archaeological find in Indian history following that of Nalanda, and it was this event that gradually brought the name Kurkihar to the attention of the wider world. Regarding the origins of the Kurkihar sculptural style, various theories and interpretations exist. Markham Kittoe, the British archaeologist who first discovered Kurkihar, believed that the name "Kurkihar" was derived from "Koorka Vihara," meaning "Koorka's Great Monastery." Conversely, Alexander Cunningham—a former Director-General of the Archaeological Survey of India—argued that "Kurkihar" likely originated from "Kukkuta-pada Vihara." This name is linked to the ancient Indian designation for "Kukkuta-pada Hill" (Chicken-Foot Hill); thus, it should be translated as "The Great Monastery of Chicken-Foot Hill." Kurkihar is situated on the southern flank of Kukkuta-pada Hill—a site of great renown in Buddhist history. According to Buddhist scriptures, shortly before entering *Nirvana*, Shakyamuni Buddha entrusted his *kasaya* (monastic robe) and *khakkhara* (staff) to the Venerable Mahakasyapa, instructing him to enter deep meditation within Kukkuta-pada Hill. There, Mahakasyapa was to await the arrival of Maitreya—the Buddha of the next age—who would meet him on the mountain to receive these sacred vestments and thereby inherit the spiritual lineage. Throughout history, eminent Chinese monks and pilgrims—such as Xuanzang and Yijing—who journeyed to India in search of scriptures and enlightenment visited and paid homage to Kukkuta-pada Hill, recording their experiences in their biographies. These historical records not only attest to the pivotal role Kurkihar played in the history of Buddhism but also imbue the site with a profound religious significance. Based on scholarly analyses of the inscribed dates and artistic styles of excavated sculptures, the sculptural tradition of Kurkihar is believed to have flourished from the 7th century through the 12th century, undergoing three distinct phases of stylistic evolution. The first phase dates to approximately the 9th century; exemplified by two statues depicting Shakyamuni's Enlightenment (Figures 1 and 2), this period features broad, flattened, and inverted-superimposed lotus petals—a style reminiscent of the sculptural tradition of Nalanda—while the monastic robes are rendered with extreme simplicity, clinging closely to the body. The second phase, dating to around the 10th century, reveals a palpable shift and transition in style. Two features stand out most prominently: while the influence of the Nalanda sculptural tradition persists, the *mandorlas* (halos) now incorporate more varied designs, the decorative elements—such as crowns and necklaces—become increasingly ornate, and the monastic robes evolve from the traditional "right-shoulder-bared" style to include a more integrated, full-coverage drapery (Figures 3 and 4). The third phase dates to approximately the 11th century. The stylistic characteristics of this period are exemplified by the stone carving shown in Figure 5: the double-tiered lotus petals—arranged in alternating upward- and downward-facing rows—begin to appear fuller and more three-dimensional. Concurrently, the accompanying beaded borders become increasingly plump and are arranged with greater precision; likewise, the once-lavish jeweled crowns and necklaces now exhibit a heightened sense of exquisite refinement. Due to a unique historical context, almost all bronze sculptures in the Kurkihar style—whether found in museums or private collections—bear the distinctive patina of having been excavated from the earth. In the early 13th century, with the invasion of Muslim forces, Pala—the last sanctuary of Indian Buddhism—fell into ruin. Consequently, sculptures in the Kurkihar style were buried beneath the earth, and their artistic lineage was severed forever. The Muslim invasion dealt a devastating blow to the region; many eminent monks and clergy members were forced to flee—carrying scriptures and Buddhist images with them—to places such as Tibet (China) and the mountainous regions of Nepal. While this exodus fostered the subsequent flourishing of Buddhism in those new lands, it also meant that only a precious few scriptures and sculptures managed to escape the catastrophe, thereby surviving to be passed down through the generations in neighboring regions. It is against this historical backdrop that this seated figure of the Crowned Shakyamuni—bearing the patina of a thousand years of continuous transmission—has managed to survive to the present day, making it an object of extreme rarity and scarcity. To have endured through hundreds of generations of veneration and transmission, yet remain as intact and radiant as it was a thousand years ago, is a feat of truly extraordinary magnitude. From an aesthetic perspective, the unique artistic achievements of the Kurkihar style—centered in the Bihar region—stand in distinct contrast to the aesthetic sensibilities of the Bengal region. While the Bengal style tends to be more dynamic, the Bihar style exudes a greater sense of nobility, representing two entirely different artistic temperaments. The very moment one’s gaze falls upon this figure of the Crowned Shakyamuni, one is immediately struck by a harmonious blend of strength and softness, creating a profound sense of aesthetic unity. The "strength" is manifested in the crisp, precise contours of the sculpture; the "softness" lies in the lifelike vitality of the flesh and bone, and the gentle warmth of the facial expression. A mere glance at the face—or even a single look into the eyes—is enough to leave one utterly captivated. The jeweled crown, inlaid with silver wire and gemstones, takes the form of a tripartite diadem; the ribbons extending horizontally behind the ears are adorned at the front with jeweled pendants; and the necklace beneath the ear ornaments—embellished with alternating silver accents and rubies—displays a design that is intricate yet perfectly ordered. The *urna* (tuft of hair) and the eyes—inlaid with silver—appear crystal-clear and imbued with divinity. The smiling mouth, inlaid with red copper, features lips that are not only vivid and lifelike but also positioned in perfect proportion to the other facial features, thereby giving concrete form to the sculpture's overall youthful and radiant character. The temperament conveyed by the face aligns perfectly with the figure's status as a prince: while retaining an air of divinity and nobility, it also possesses a touch of playful charm. The steady, direct gaze is charged with a sense of righteous energy and vitality—a spirit typically seen only in the bloom of youth. Despite his royal status, the idealized form embodied by this sculpture does not project a distant, inaccessible sanctity; rather, it radiates a human warmth—an air of approachability and friendliness, much like a friend one might feel comfortable walking up to and engaging in conversation. The *kasaya* (monastic robe) is delineated by simple contour lines that emphasize a healthy, vibrant physique; these minimalist lines not only outline the well-defined, undulating musculature but also convey a sense of fullness and resilient elasticity. The rows of beaded ornamentation adorning the upper and lower edges of the lotus pedestal are composed of plump, perfectly aligned beads, while the central lotus petals appear full-bodied and taut with energy. The exquisite symmetry of their size and arrangement harmonizes with the refined delicacy of the upper body, fusing the entire piece into a cohesive, unified whole. Within this unified visual presentation, particular mention must be made of the harmonious proportional relationships established between the sculpture's various components. When crafting an image of the "Crowned Shakyamuni"—a specific iconographic subject—the relative proportions of the crown to the head present a subtle and notoriously difficult challenge to master. If the crown is sized even slightly too large, the figure appears top-heavy and unbalanced; conversely, if it is too small, the aesthetic feels petty and cramped. In this particular sculpture of the Crowned Shakyamuni, however, the proportions of the head and shoulders are rendered with absolute precision; despite the complexity of the design, there is not a single trace of visual clutter or superfluity. This masterful execution of harmonious proportion serves as one of the primary sources of the sculpture's profound sense of overall unity. The inlaid gemstones adorning the figure are uniformly deep red, while the metal inlays are rendered in silver—a color palette that harmonizes beautifully with the tones of the eyes and lips. The oxidized silver has tempered its original dazzling brilliance, blending seamlessly with the deep crimson hues to create an aesthetic that is at once poised and understated—yet radiates a nobility so inherent that it simply cannot be concealed. It embodies a sense of high-caliber sophistication that is simultaneously perfectly balanced, exquisitely refined, and effortlessly graceful. As the artist Yang Shaobo once remarked, "Politicians lead the way, economists cultivate the field, and artists are responsible for documenting it all." At this moment, one cannot help but wonder: what kind of artist, back in that era, chose sculpture as the medium to record both the spirit of the times and the landscape of his own inner world? First and foremost, I believe they must have been a collective of master-level artists. From modeling and casting to polishing and inlaying—every step of the intricate process is executed with exquisite precision, demonstrating artistic talent of the highest caliber. To create a work of such beauty, their technical foundation must have been profoundly deep. The creation of sculpture is a process of immense accumulation and continuous progression. There is a vast difference in both proficiency and understanding between practicing ten times, a hundred times, or a thousand times. It is only through extensive practical application that an artist gains the opportunity to identify specific issues, make constant adjustments, and ultimately produce a work that appears effortless yet stands up to the most rigorous scrutiny. Secondly, the artisans behind these statues must have possessed a broad-minded outlook on life and a serene state of mind. Why do I say this? The harmony and unity manifested in the artwork are a direct reflection of the artisan's aesthetic sensibilities and inner landscape. Beyond the necessity for the artisan to maintain a lifelong commitment to learning, the expression of this holistic vision is also shaped by the artisan's personal preferences—specifically, whether they are accustomed to viewing the world from a macro or a micro perspective—which is invariably reflected in the sculptural language of the piece. If an artisan's vision is fully open and expansive, they can perceive the whole—seeing "from one to a hundred." Conversely, if their vision is narrow, they may become fixated on isolated details—seeing only "from one to ten"—and thus fail to create a sculpture that possesses true harmony and wholeness. Although an artisan might occasionally add decorative elements to compensate for perceived deficiencies, such fragmented additions are ultimately fleeting; they cannot withstand close examination or critical analysis. Those exceptional artists of yesteryear did more than merely express their own aesthetics and inner selves; they also simultaneously documented the social landscape of their time. Works belonging to the "Kurkihar style" of Bihar State possess a distinct aura of righteousness and nobility—a quality that reminds me of the "Law of Frontality" found in ancient Egyptian art: the principle of depicting subjects from the most characteristic and representative angles. In ancient Egypt—whether in sculpture or painting—the demeanor of prominent figures in artistic representations was invariably portrayed as upright, dignified, and meticulous, imbued with the solemn gravitas befitting royalty. As is evident in the numerous artworks we observe from the Bihar region, a defining characteristic is a dignified bearing that underscores aristocratic status, largely devoid of dramatic dynamism. Similarly, the court sculptures and paintings we encounter—whether in two or three dimensions—invariably embody an aesthetic rooted in rigor, decorum, order, and balance. In antiquity, the original intent behind the creation of such artworks and the ultimate aesthetic results they sought to achieve shared a common thread. The author posits that during the Pala Dynasty, the Kurkihar region—beyond serving merely as a significant waypoint for pilgrims—must have been a site of immense importance and high esteem. Featured in the 2023 exhibition at Zhujinju is a statue of Avalokiteśvara (the Lord of the World) bearing an inscribed dedication (Figures 6 and 7). From an iconographic perspective, the piece can immediately be distinguished from the stylistic traditions of Bengal; instead, it represents the quintessential aesthetic style of Bihar dating to the 11th or 12th century. The inscription accompanying the dedication may be broadly translated as: "Commissioned by an Indian patron to fulfill the devotional requirements of a Tibetan patron." The aesthetic excellence of this Avalokiteśvara figure is self-evident; moreover, it is a work that could not have been completed in haste, representing a sculptural undertaking that demanded considerable time, labor, and financial resources. In the ancient world, for a patron willing to expend such vast sums to commission a devotional image, the paramount concern would undoubtedly have been how to secure the most exquisite craftsmanship and the most skilled artisans available. Drawing upon the evidence provided by both the inscription and its iconographic style, this artwork from Bihar—now presented before us—is indeed a piece that withstands the most exacting scrutiny. By analyzing the aesthetic characteristics of this Avalokiteśvara figure in conjunction with other artworks from the Bihar region—as well as the *Crowned Shakyamuni* under discussion—it becomes highly probable that this *Crowned Shakyamuni* was commissioned to fulfill royal devotional needs. Created under the strict standards and specific directives of the royal court, and executed by the hands of artisans from the era's most elite workshops, it stands as an exceptionally rare and precious artistic treasure. In that bygone era, the names of individual artists often remained unrecorded; yet, the cultural ethos and aesthetic heights embodied by the works they left behind continue to speak across the boundaries of time and space. These objects are not merely artworks; they serve as enduring witnesses to history and as microcosms of an entire epoch.

excerpt.en: A Swat bronze of Maitreya with a lucid silhouette and inward poise.

viewingNote.zh: 斯瓦特谷地，属古印度的一部分，位于兴都库什山麓以南，处印度次大陆与中亚交汇处的枢纽地带。法 显于《佛国记》中首次记录此地；而玄奘在《大唐西域记》将其记作乌仗那国，并描绘出 7 世纪该地的佛法 兴盛之貌 。斯瓦特地区的佛教艺术起源于贵霜时期，早期亦属犍陀罗文化区的一部分，因其优渥的地理位 置 ，在犍陀罗地区的佛教式微以后，成为新的佛教圣地，并在公元 6 世纪以后逐步发展出自我的美术体系 。 且斯瓦特亦为密教的发源地之一，著名的莲花生大师即出生于此 ，对藏传佛教影响巨大 。 弥勒的信仰在佛教中出现的时间极早，作为拥有“未来佛” 与“现世菩萨”的双重身份，弥勒信仰的起 源据考证克追溯至公元前 2 世纪左右 。据佛教经典所述：弥勒现世为菩萨身份，居于兜率天宫，未来将降 生成佛，度化人间 。在佛教造像之始的犍陀罗与马图拉艺术中，即有弥勒的形象出现，后跟随佛教思想的传 播，其图像广泛流行于印度、尼泊尔 、中国及东亚、南亚等地 。 此尊弥勒圣像为我们展示了典型的斯瓦特地区造像美学观 ，简约的造型 ，饱满精湛 。头戴三叶宝冠，正 面冠叶上的佛塔为弥勒菩萨的身份象征；菩萨发髻高盘 ，两侧发辫自然垂落于肩上 。造像弯目长眉，双眼嵌 银 ，眼神清澈而具备穿透力，当与之对视，好像一眼就能看穿人们的内心；眼睛线条的刻画利落 、果断，呈 现着凛冽 、不怒自威的气质；高鼻，唇部丰满微珉，脸型塑造如鹅蛋般圆润，洋溢着古典优雅的内在气质 。 菩萨右手抬至胸前着说法印，左手轻扶膝盖 ，持一株龙华树叶置于肩头；左腿盘起 ，右腿踏小莲茎，游戏坐 于莲花座上，头部微抬，躯干直立，自在而松弛 。造像比例结构准确，肌肉的塑造壮健结实 、匀称有力，线 条的塑造硬朗 、厚重 ，没有刻意精雕细琢局部肌肉，着重把握整体的体积、块面，只表现体块正侧后面 、空 间关系以及转折，具有鲜明的犍陀罗美学特征遗风；下身所着的长裙质地厚重 ，匠人在衣褶上做了细致的刻 画，宛如湖中涤荡的波浪；莲台上平滑舒展的大叶莲瓣，具有鲜明的斯瓦特地域特征；莲台下方山形的四方 须弥座 ，将菩萨苦修时岩洞的具象事物以几何形状概括，粗旷硬朗的线条给人正气凌然之感，结合上轻松自 在的坐姿 ，使造像整体充满着原始野性的张力和美 ，是秩序与自然的完美统一 。 本尊 7-8 世纪斯瓦特弥勒菩萨在逾千年时光的打磨下，雕塑由内而外透出了温润的光泽，在时光的流逝 中雕塑从神态、举止到装饰，都散发着一种静谧的气质，使观众沉浸于一种平和宁静的精神状态中，莹润的 皮壳诉说着他千年来所接受的虔诚供养，时光成为了最令人惊叹的工匠 ，恰到好处的磨损则给出了最令人惊 喜的独特美感 。
viewingNote.en: The Swat Valley, historically part of ancient India, is situated south of the foothills of the Hindu Kush mountains, occupying a pivotal nexus zone at the convergence of the Indian subcontinent and Central Asia. Faxian first documented this region in his *Record of Buddhist Kingdoms* (Foguo Ji), while Xuanzang, in his *Records of the Western Regions of the Great Tang* (Datang Xiyu Ji), referred to it as the Kingdom of Udyana and vividly portrayed the flourishing state of Buddhism in the area during the 7th century. Buddhist art in the Swat region originated during the Kushan period and was initially part of the broader Gandhara cultural sphere. Due to its advantageous geographical location, Swat emerged as a new Buddhist holy site following the decline of Buddhism in the Gandhara heartland; subsequently—particularly after the 6th century CE—it gradually developed its own distinct artistic system. Moreover, Swat is recognized as one of the birthplaces of Vajrayana Buddhism; the renowned Guru Padmasambhava was born here, exerting a profound influence on the development of Tibetan Buddhism. Devotion to Maitreya appeared very early in the history of Buddhism. Possessing the dual identity of both the "Future Buddha" and a "Present-Day Bodhisattva," the origins of Maitreya worship have been traced by scholars back to approximately the 2nd century BCE. According to Buddhist scriptures, Maitreya currently resides in the Tushita Heaven as a Bodhisattva; in the future, he is destined to descend to the human realm, attain Buddhahood, and bring salvation to humanity. Images of Maitreya were present from the very inception of Buddhist iconography—notably in the art of Gandhara and Mathura—and subsequently, as Buddhist thought spread, his imagery became widely popular across India, Nepal, China, and throughout East and South Asia. This sacred image of Maitreya exemplifies the distinctive aesthetic principles of Swat Valley sculpture, characterized by a simplicity of form that is simultaneously robust and exquisitely refined. The figure wears a tripartite jeweled crown, the central leaf of which features a miniature stupa—a definitive iconographic symbol identifying the subject as Maitreya Bodhisattva. The Bodhisattva's hair is gathered into a high topknot, with braids cascading naturally down over the shoulders on either side. The sculpture features arched eyes and long brows, with the eyes themselves inlaid with silver; the gaze is clear yet penetrating—when meeting its eyes, one feels as though one's very soul is instantly laid bare. The lines defining the eyes are incisive and decisive, conveying an austere aura of inherent authority that commands respect without the need for overt anger. With a high-bridged nose and full, slightly pursed lips, the face is sculpted into a rounded, "goose-egg" shape, exuding an inner essence of classical elegance. The Bodhisattva raises his right hand to chest level to form the *Dharmachakra Mudra* (Gesture of Preaching), while his left hand rests lightly upon his knee, holding a sprig of *Nāgapuṣpa* (Dragon Flower) leaves that rests upon his shoulder. His left leg is folded in a cross-legged position, while his right foot rests upon a small lotus stem; he sits in a posture of "royal ease" (*Lalitasana*) upon a lotus throne. With his head slightly lifted and his torso held upright, the figure conveys a sense of complete freedom and relaxation. The sculpture exhibits precise proportions and structural integrity; the musculature is rendered as robust, solid, and harmoniously powerful, defined by bold, substantial lines. Rather than engaging in the meticulous, hyper-realistic carving of individual muscles, the artist focused on capturing the overall volume and planes of the form—emphasizing the spatial relationships and transitions between the front, side, and rear masses—thereby preserving the distinct aesthetic legacy of the Gandhara style. The long robe draped over the lower body is rendered with a sense of substantial weight; the artisan has meticulously sculpted the folds of the garment to resemble ripples washing across the surface of a lake. The broad, smoothly unfurling lotus petals adorning the throne exhibit the distinctive regional characteristics of the Swat Valley style. Beneath the lotus throne lies a square, mountain-shaped *Sumeru* pedestal, which abstracts the tangible imagery of the Bodhisattva's ascetic retreat within a rocky cave into geometric forms. The pedestal's rugged, bold lines evoke a sense of awe-inspiring righteousness; when combined with the Bodhisattva's relaxed and unconstrained seated posture, the sculpture as a whole radiates a primal, wild tension and beauty—representing a perfect synthesis of order and nature. This figure—a Swat Valley Bodhisattva Maitreya dating to the 7th or 8th century—has been burnished by the passage of over a millennium; consequently, the sculpture now radiates a mellow luster from within. As the centuries have flowed by, every aspect of the piece—from its facial expression and posture to its ornamentation—has come to exude an aura of profound tranquility, drawing the viewer into a state of serene spiritual peace. Its lustrous patina bears silent witness to the centuries of devout offerings it has received, while time itself—acting as the most astonishing of craftsmen—has imparted a perfectly balanced wear that endows the piece with a unique and delightful aesthetic beauty.

excerpt.en: A gilt-bronze image of Indra animated by princely ease and tensile form.

viewingNote.zh: 帝释天，一位佛教里从古印度神话中继承而来的天神之一。佛经里常说，祂会在佛陀出生、成道或涅槃时出现，礼敬佛陀、守护僧团。祂是忉利天的主宰，居住在须弥山顶，所以祂的形象往往象征着威仪、护法和天界的秩序。 须弥山，在佛教、印度教、耆那教等传统里，被看作是宇宙的中心。山顶是忉利天，帝释天的居所就在其中，统领着三十三天神；四面则由四大天王守护人间。须弥山原本并不是现实中的山，而是一种宇宙的象征 。 而在现实里，西藏阿里的冈仁波齐，被认为是须弥山在人间的显现，是佛教、印度教、耆那教和苯教共同尊崇的圣地 。印度教说那是湿婆的居所；藏传佛教认为它是曼荼罗的核心，同样也是帝释天的居所；苯教则称它是宇宙的“九层天柱”。所以，冈仁波齐成了人们可见 、可亲近的“宇宙中心”，朝圣绕山，其实就是在与宇宙的轴心建立身体性的连接。 佛教的世界观里，有三界：欲界、色界和无色界。欲界是我们熟悉的人、阿修罗和欲界天，充满欲望与追逐 。色界是通过禅定才能进入的境界，超越了粗重的欲望，但依然保有“色身”，也就是一种清净的形态 。无色界则是没有形体，只有心识 。而忉利天就属于色界的最高层之一，由帝释天主宰。所谓“色身”，可以理解为一种带着“烟火气”的存在 。天人虽然超越了欲望，但他们依然有宫殿、有花园、有 天乐与清风 ，祂们不是抽象到无法触摸的概念，而是带着气息的生命。这就像一种超脱后的余温，提醒我们：真正的超越，并不是彻底远离，而是以更清澈、更轻盈的方式继续存在 。我们眼前这尊帝释天的造像，正是匠人在对佛教文化理解后赋予的形象化表达，让这种抽象的存在，变得具体可感 。 我们眼前看到的这尊帝释天造像，第一眼会让人觉得特别轻盈，甚至有一点飘逸的味道 。祂以一种很放松的姿态坐在莲台上，一手结说法印，另一手则握着金刚杵撑住莲台。金刚杵在佛教里有很重要的象征意义，它代表着不可摧毁的佛法和神力。换句话说，它既是守护的武器，也是智慧和权威的象征 。 如果仔细观察祂的姿态，你会发现整个人的体态非常挺拔 。那只结印的手臂自然地倚靠在大腿之上，既放松又带着一种空间上的张力。祂并不是紧绷地撑在那里，而是像呼吸一样自然，就像一个人随意坐下，却依然显得有力量、有气度 。这种“不用力”的从容，恰恰传达出帝释天自在的神性 。 这尊造像出自马拉王朝早期，和后期一些厚重大块面的雕塑不同，这件作品的体块并不强调厚重感，而是偏向一种更灵动的塑造方式 。匠人没有用粗犷的体量去堆砌力量，而是通过肌肉的紧实感，表现出一种健康、充盈的生命力。那种力量，不是压迫式的，而是一种由内而外散发的美感 。因为佛教造像的体块感往往会随着题材的不同而调整，帝释天作为天界的主神，祂不需要像护法神那样厚重和威严，而是更强调色界天人的轻灵和自在 。于是，这里我们看到的，不是沉重的压迫，而是一种“若有若无”的体量感，让祂看起来仿佛带着空气般的仙气 。观者的目光在祂的身体周围可以自由游走，不会被某个厚重的部分卡住，这正是“空灵意味”在造型上的体现 。 帝释天头戴高耸 、华丽的宝冠，微微侧首，耳边的带饰和耳环好像随风在飘动，这让静止的雕塑多了一份流动感 。祂的脸庞圆润、柔和，带着马拉王朝时期特有的甜美和亲切。虽然祂是天界的主神，但这种甜美感拉近了与人之间的距离，让祂少了一些高高在上的威严，而多了一份慈和与雅致 。 帝释天身体的塑造同样耐人寻味 。上半身呈倒三角形，肩膀宽阔、结实，从腋下往腰部内收的线条自然，随着微微的侧首，整个身体也出现了一个轻柔的弯曲。这种线条让造像形态显得灵动，而不是僵硬的对称，是一种有节奏、有呼吸的动态 。腰间的衣结立体而细致，胸前的禅修带、腿上的飘带，都柔软地弯曲着，这些细节也都为整体增添了一种灵动的气息 。可以说，这件作品在造型上既写实又有理想化的提升。祂符合人体的姿态规律，看上去非常自然，但同时又通过比例和细节让整个形象超越现实。这种塑造使祂传达出一种“没有被任何东西拘束”的感觉，好像祂真的坐在空中，而不是被固定在石头里 。 我常喜欢用“意味”两个字来形容一尊雕塑所散发的气息 。在雕塑的语境里，意味不是单纯的外表美，而是由形态、姿态、比例、材质、空间关系乃至气质共同营造出来的一种精神氛围。它像空气一样，看不见，但你靠近时就能感觉到 。那是一种超越了物质的精神性和思想性 。你可能会在不知不觉中屏住呼吸，因为你感受到的不仅仅是一个神祇的形象，而是一种被氛围裹挟的体验 。 这尊帝释天的意味 ，是空灵的。祂轻盈，没有压迫感，祂的存在更像是一阵风 、一抹光，自在地停驻在空间里 。这种轻盈不仅仅是形式上的，它还象征着超脱 ，祂超越了世俗的沉重，超越了人间的束缚，展现出天界神祇独有的自由与自在 。 当我们站在祂面前时，这种空灵意味会慢慢感染我们 。你会觉得自己的心也轻了，呼吸也柔和了。祂不是用威严去震慑你，而是用一种若即若离的温柔气息，把你带入一种宁静和自在的境界。这，也是这件帝释天最动人的地方——它不仅仅只是冰冷的金属元素塑成的形象，更是一种能与观者心灵相通的精神空间。
viewingNote.en: Indra (Di Shitian) is one of theistic deities within Buddhism, inherited from ancient Indian mythology. Buddhist scriptures frequently recount that He appears during the Buddha's birth, enlightenment, or *Nirvana* to pay homage to the Buddha and safeguard the monastic community. As the sovereign of the *Trāyastriṃśa* Heaven, He resides atop Mount Sumeru; consequently, His iconography often symbolizes majesty, the protection of the Dharma, and the cosmic order of the celestial realms. In the traditions of Buddhism, Hinduism, Jainism, and others, Mount Sumeru is regarded as the center of the universe. Its summit houses the *Trāyastriṃśa* Heaven—the abode of Indra—where He presides over the thirty-three celestial deities; meanwhile, the four cardinal directions surrounding the mountain are guarded by the Four Heavenly Kings, who watch over the human realm. Fundamentally, Mount Sumeru is not a physical mountain in the empirical world, but rather a symbolic representation of the cosmos. In the physical world, however, Mount Kailash (Gang Rinpoche) in the Ngari Prefecture of Tibet is revered as the earthly manifestation of Mount Sumeru—a sacred site venerated jointly by Buddhism, Hinduism, Jainism, and the Bon religion. Hinduism identifies it as the abode of Lord Shiva; Tibetan Buddhism regards it as the core of the *Mandala* and, likewise, as the dwelling place of Indra; the Bon religion hails it as the universe's "Nine-Story Celestial Pillar." Thus, Mount Kailash has become a tangible and accessible "center of the universe" for humanity; the act of circumambulating the mountain during pilgrimage is, in essence, a means of establishing a physical connection with the very axis of the cosmos. Within the Buddhist cosmology, there exist three realms: the Realm of Desire (*Kāmadhātu*), the Realm of Form (*Rūpadhātu*), and the Realm of Formlessness (*Arūpyadhātu*). The Realm of Desire encompasses the beings familiar to us—humans, *Asuras*, and the celestial beings of the desire realm—and is characterized by an abundance of desires and ceaseless striving. The Realm of Form is a state accessible only through deep meditative absorption (*Dhyāna*); while transcending coarse, material desires, beings in this realm still retain a "form-body"—a refined, ethereal physical manifestation. The Realm of Formlessness, conversely, is entirely devoid of physical form, existing solely as pure consciousness. The *Trāyastriṃśa* Heaven, presided over by Indra, ranks among the highest strata of the Realm of Form. The aforementioned "form-body" may be understood as a mode of existence that still retains a certain "earthly warmth" or tangible presence. Although these celestial beings have transcended the cravings of desire, they nonetheless possess palaces, gardens, heavenly music, and gentle breezes; they are not abstract, intangible concepts, but rather living entities imbued with a palpable vitality. This serves as a kind of lingering warmth following transcendence—a reminder that true transcendence does not entail a complete withdrawal from existence, but rather a continued presence in the world, albeit in a manner that is far more lucid and ethereal. The statue of Indra (帝释天) standing before us represents the artisans' visual interpretation of Buddhist culture—an artistic expression that transforms an abstract entity into a tangible, palpable presence. At first glance, this depiction of Indra strikes the viewer as remarkably light and airy, possessing an almost ethereal grace. He sits upon a lotus pedestal in a deeply relaxed posture; one hand forms the *Dharmachakra Mudra* (the gesture of expounding the Dharma), while the other grasps a *Vajra* (thunderbolt scepter) to support himself against the pedestal. In Buddhism, the *Vajra* holds profound symbolic significance, representing the indestructible nature of the Buddha-Dharma and divine power. In essence, it serves simultaneously as a weapon of protection and a symbol of wisdom and authority. Upon closer observation of his posture, one notices the figure's remarkably upright and poised physique. The arm forming the *Mudra* rests naturally upon his thigh—a gesture that conveys both relaxation and a subtle spatial tension. He does not brace himself rigidly against the pedestal; rather, his stance feels as effortless as breathing—much like a person sitting down casually, yet still exuding an aura of strength and dignity. This sense of "effortless" composure precisely conveys the unconstrained divinity inherent in Indra. Dating back to the early period of the Pala Dynasty, this sculpture stands in contrast to the heavy, monumental forms characteristic of later periods; instead of emphasizing sheer mass and weight, this work favors a more fluid and dynamic sculptural style. The artisan has not relied on brute volume to convey power, but rather utilizes the tautness of the musculature to express a vibrant, robust vitality. This power is not oppressive or overbearing; rather, it manifests as an aesthetic beauty that radiates outward from within. Since the sculptural mass of Buddhist imagery is often modulated according to the specific subject matter, Indra—as the principal deity of the celestial realms—does not require the heavy, imposing gravitas typical of Guardian Deities. Instead, his depiction emphasizes the lightness and freedom characteristic of the celestial beings (*Devas*) inhabiting the Realm of Form. Consequently, what we witness here is not a sense of heavy oppression, but rather a volume that feels "present yet elusive"—imbuing the figure with an ethereal, air-like quality. The viewer's gaze is free to wander unhindered across his form, never snagging on any ponderous mass; this serves as a sculptural embodiment of that very "ethereal spirit." Indra wears a towering, magnificent jeweled crown; his head is tilted ever so slightly to the side, and the ribbons and earrings adorning his ears appear to flutter as if caught in a breeze, infusing the static sculpture with a sense of fluid motion. His face is round and gentle, imbued with the characteristic sweetness and amiability unique to the Malla Dynasty era. Although he is the principal deity of the celestial realm, this sweetness bridges the distance between the divine and the human; it tempers his lofty, imposing majesty, replacing it instead with an air of benevolence and elegance. The sculpting of Indra’s physique is equally intriguing. His upper torso forms an inverted triangle—broad and robust at the shoulders—tapering naturally inward from the armpits toward the waist. Mirroring the slight tilt of his head, his entire body follows suit, assuming a gentle, graceful curve. This interplay of lines renders the figure dynamic rather than rigidly symmetrical, creating a rhythmic, living vitality that seems to breathe. The knot of his sash at the waist is rendered with three-dimensional depth and exquisite detail; likewise, the meditation strap across his chest and the flowing ribbons draped over his legs curve with a soft pliability. These intricate details collectively imbue the entire piece with an ethereal, lively spirit. Indeed, one might say that this work achieves a stylistic balance between realism and idealized elevation. While adhering to the natural mechanics of human posture—appearing utterly lifelike—it simultaneously transcends reality through its refined proportions and meticulous details. This sculptural approach conveys a profound sense of liberation—as if the deity were "unfettered by any constraint"—giving the impression that he is truly seated in mid-air, rather than being fixed immovably within a block of stone. I often find myself using the word "resonance" (*yiwei*) to describe the distinct aura emanating from a sculpture. In the context of sculpture, this "resonance" is not merely a matter of superficial aesthetic beauty; rather, it is a spiritual atmosphere collectively conjured by the interplay of form, posture, proportion, material, spatial relationships, and—above all—temperament. It is like the air itself: invisible to the eye, yet palpable the moment one draws near. It represents a spiritual and intellectual essence that transcends the purely material realm. You may find yourself holding your breath without even realizing it, for what you perceive is not merely the visual image of a deity, but an immersive experience—one in which you are enveloped and swept away by the very atmosphere the sculpture creates. The resonance of this particular Indra figure is one of pure ethereality. He is light and airy, devoid of any oppressive weight; his presence feels less like a solid mass and more like a gentle breeze or a fleeting ray of light—resting effortlessly, in perfect freedom, within the boundless expanse of space. This sense of lightness is not merely formal; it symbolizes transcendence—a state wherein He rises above the weight of the mundane and the constraints of the human realm, manifesting the unique freedom and ease inherent to a celestial deity. As we stand in His presence, this ethereal quality gradually permeates our being. You sense your own heart growing lighter, your breath softening. He does not seek to overawe you with sheer majesty; rather, through an aura of gentle, elusive tenderness, He draws you into a realm of profound tranquility and inner peace. This, indeed, is the most captivating aspect of this depiction of Indra—it is not merely a figure forged from cold metal elements, but a spiritual space capable of forging a deep, resonant connection with the soul of the beholder.

viewingNote.zh: 每次看到那些富有积淀和厚重感的色彩，我都不由自主的被它们所吸引。从 深邃的蓝天到红、白、黑相间的建筑群，自然纯净与艳丽的色彩潜藏着吸引人们 的奥秘，除了是一种感官的享受，心中更是感到一种深深的敬畏之情。这片土地 让人着迷，我们似乎对这片土地一点都不陌生，反而给人们带来一种愉悦和一种 深刻的熟悉感；在原始文明社会，那些充满自然美、色彩美的地方正是能够提高 人类祖先生存机会的地方，人类对于色彩常常是带着求生的内涵，比如，红色常 常被用于象征火和热情，也是对于危险与祭祀的刺激。与此相反，绿色因为与树 木和水源有深刻的联结，被视为和平和生命的色彩。在这片土地上所展现给我 们的色彩、线条正好与人类思维和情感相互关联，让我们与这天地间的一切产生 了联系。那与内心意识深处产生的原始情感共振，也使这里的每一个角落都充 满了神秘与浩瀚。 在中国西藏，由于其特殊的地理环境和气候条件，对植物的生存构成了一定 的挑战。于是生命就在这短短的时间里，努力张扬出更加蓬勃旺盛的力量，生命 借由色彩都努力地绽放，显现出无与伦比的热烈、与奔放。自然风景和深厚的文 化传统造就了独特的西藏艺术，它将自然和文化融合，展现出令人惊叹的美感和 视觉冲击力，在灵性与原始本性的底色上传递着一种精神之美。当这些色彩反照 应到一件件艺术品上时，历史与文化的脉络似乎也变得隐约可见。 公元 841 年，吐蕃赞普朗达玛发起了灭佛运动，导致西藏的佛教艺术历经了 一百多年的空白期，部分僧人纷纷逃到了安多地区（即现在青海一带）融入了当 地的佛教氛围中，在这一百多年间，青海逐渐发展成了一个新的佛教中心。于此 期间吐蕃王室的子孙们也分别去到阿里地区建立了自己的王朝，直到 978 年，佛 教才再次从青海和阿里两路传入卫藏地区，就分别形成了上路弘法和下路弘法的 历史背景。公元 10 世纪，声名显赫的古格王朝统治者崇尚佛教，第三代国王意 希沃尤为突出，他提倡和引进佛教，成为了古格王朝历史上最著名的佛教护持 者。他曾派遣家族中 21 人赴克什米尔等地求法，其中一员名叫仁钦桑布的僧人 学成归来后，成为了西藏佛教后弘初期著名的译经大师。学成归国的仁钦桑布专门邀请了 32 位克什米尔匠人来到古格，帮助建寺和造像，于是藏西早期的艺术 风格以克什米尔为主。11 世纪随着印度高僧达磨波罗和阿底峡入藏途经阿里、及 卫藏地区弘法，帕拉美学元素也因此传入高原腹地。此时随着佛教在西藏的传播 及日渐强盛的影响力，流行于卫藏地区的帕拉风格绘画也被传到以克什米尔风格 为主的西藏西部，并影响和融入到了其艺术创作中。时间发展到 13 世纪，随着 尼泊尔风潮的席卷，不同地区将不同美学元素相融，创作出了独具地方特色的艺 术作品。此幅噶当派上师对坐绘画，则出自十三世纪西藏西部，将帕拉美学元素 及尼泊尔美学元素相融合的典型之作。 上师题材作为藏传佛教中极具特点的艺术门类，不仅只存在于三维雕塑 中，匠人们也同样通过二维平面上的色彩、线条和构图来呈现着那一位位真实存 在过的人物。上师作为佛和众生之间的桥梁，享有崇高的地位。在上师圆寂 后，弟子们会根据其生前模样为其塑像、绘画，以表纪念。此幅以人物为主题的 肖像画，为噶当派上师对坐，唐卡以分段叙事、棋格式布局以及突出主题的构图 形式，描述着两位上师在修行中交流与对谈的画面。 画面缓缓展开，首先映入眼帘的是一片宁静而庄严的氛围。以红色调为主的 画面，在第一眼见时，则被那扑面而的鲜活气息所吸引。画面上段以棋格构图的 方式分别绘有三排神灵和喇嘛，佛、菩萨、瑜伽士、喇嘛、供养人的形象共聚一 堂。这些形象则分别代表着不同的境界和力量，不仅展现了佛教信仰的完整性和 丰富性，也共同编织着一段关于传承、慈悲与智慧的故事。随着视线往下顺 延，半圆形的背光上方岩洞内分别居住着带噶当派僧帽的祖师（或阿底峡尊者）、护 法、佛、菩萨、大成就等十位不同人物。其中具有典型元代风格的胜乐金刚和金 刚手菩萨，形象浑圆壮实，胖乎乎的体态不禁让人升起喜悦之心；其他祖师、菩 萨类形象同样分别手持不同法器、结不同手印，画工细腻间象征着不同的佛教教 义。其中古铜色肌肤的大成就者帕当巴桑杰，以其经典的形象出现在画面右 侧，如铜铃般圆瞪的神情炯炯澄澈、纯真灵动。帕当巴桑杰肖像的描绘与西藏西 部古格帕尔洞窟的一幅 12 世纪壁画上的形象相似构图上，唐卡巧妙地运用了空间分割，将两位上师置于画面的中段位置，以 突出主题。艾米 · 海勒在 2008 的文章《噶举派两位藏族上师的唐卡》中认为此 幅唐卡为噶举派传承，虽然没有铭文可以非常准确的确认其身份，但通过右侧上 师的俗家形象及其在其他绘画中的五官和形象特征分析，笔者认为应该为噶当派 创始人仲敦巴的可能性更大，画面左侧的人物肖像应该为仲敦巴的老师或者上 师。两位上师分别结跏趺坐安坐于带六拏具背光的仰覆式莲台之上。六拏具上 方摩羯的尾部变化成卷草，旋转的卷草细腻、灵动，表现出尼泊尔美学元素的渗 透。尽管上师造像是根据其生前模样、特征进行描绘，但眉眼间的神情、线条和 绘画笔触透着明显的帕拉绘画风格神韵。 上师的衣饰上点缀着模仿金线刺绣的花卉图案，繁复的花卉在线条的穿插 勾勒下繁而不乱、节奏明确，色彩鲜艳且不失庄重，一笔一画间都蕴含着匠人的 虔诚与敬意。上师面容慈祥，对视间，眼神中透露出平和与智慧、眉宇间洋溢着 对知识的渴望与对真理的执着。他们的对话，虽无声却胜有声，每一个眼神的交 换，每一次手势的轻扬，都蕴含着深邃的哲理与无尽的智慧。他们或许在探讨宇 宙的奥秘，或许在传授修行的法门，又或许在分享各自的人生感悟与修行体验。 这份交流，超越了言语的界限，直达观者内心深处。 五彩的双层仰覆式莲台的下装饰着四狮两象，这种布局为典型的帕拉风格元 素（图二）。顺着视线再往下，最下层绘画有十六位手持不同法器，正在舞蹈的天 女，在佛教寓意中，天女们四位一组，共分为四组，分别代表着东南西北四个方 位。唐卡背面绘画有佛塔，佛塔内写有多行藏文，包括以下偈语开头的祈祷 文：Om a hum vajra guru padma siddhi hum，这是莲花生大士的心咒；接下来 是普巴金刚、毗湿奴、文殊菩萨的开光咒；以及观世音菩萨的 Om mani padme hum 六字真言；金刚手菩萨的 Om vajra pani hum ；接下来是“ye dharma hetu...”佛教经文，以及一段《波罗提木叉经》的摘录。随着目光的深入，这幅大尺幅的上师对坐唐卡所营造出的空间感愈发强 烈，如同一幅浓缩的宇宙图卷。它不仅仅局限于画面所展现的物理空间，更通过 两位上师之间的微妙互动，构建了一个超越物质世界的灵性空间。在这个空间 里，时间仿佛失去了意义，外界的喧嚣与纷扰都被隔绝在外，只留下两颗纯净无 染的心灵在相互碰撞、交融。
viewingNote.en: Whenever I encounter colors imbued with such depth and gravitas, I find myself irresistibly drawn to them. From the azure depths of the sky to architectural complexes interwoven with hues of red, white, and black, these colors—at once naturally pure and vividly brilliant—harbor a mysterious allure that captivates the human spirit. Beyond merely offering a feast for the senses, they evoke within the heart a profound sense of awe. This land is utterly mesmerizing; far from feeling alien, it instills in us a sense of pure delight and a deep, abiding familiarity. In the context of primitive human societies, places rich in natural and chromatic beauty were precisely those that enhanced our ancestors' chances of survival. Consequently, humanity has often imbued color with connotations linked to survival: for instance, red frequently symbolizes fire and passion, while also serving as a visceral trigger associated with danger and ritual sacrifice. Conversely, green—owing to its deep-seated connection with trees and water sources—is revered as the color of peace and life itself. The colors and contours revealed to us in this land resonate deeply with the intricacies of human thought and emotion, forging a profound connection between us and all that exists between heaven and earth. This resonance with the primal emotions stirring in the deepest recesses of our consciousness imbues every corner of this place with an aura of mystery and boundless grandeur. In Tibet, China—owing to its unique geographical terrain and climatic conditions—the survival of plant life faces significant challenges. Consequently, within this fleeting window of opportunity, life strives to assert itself with even greater vigor and vitality; through the medium of color, life bursts forth in a magnificent bloom, manifesting an unparalleled intensity and unbridled exuberance. The convergence of natural landscapes and a profound cultural heritage has given rise to the distinctive art of Tibet—an artistic tradition that seamlessly blends nature and culture to create a breathtaking aesthetic and visual impact, conveying a spiritual beauty against a backdrop of deep spirituality and primal nature. As these vibrant colors are reflected and distilled into individual works of art, the intricate threads of history and culture seem to emerge, becoming faintly yet perceptibly visible. In the year 841 AD, Langdarma, the *Tsenpo* (King) of the Tubo Kingdom, launched a campaign to suppress Buddhism. This event plunged Tibetan Buddhist art into a hiatus spanning more than a century. Many monks fled to the Amdo region (roughly corresponding to present-day Qinghai Province), where they integrated into the local Buddhist milieu; over the course of that century, Qinghai gradually evolved into a new, vibrant center of Buddhist culture. During this period, descendants of the Tubo royal family dispersed across the Ngari region to establish their own independent dynasties. It was not until 978 AD that Buddhism was reintroduced into the Ü-Tsang region—arriving via two distinct routes: one from Qinghai and the other from Ngari. This dual influx established the historical context for what became known as the "Upper Propagation" and the "Lower Propagation" of the Dharma. In the 10th century, the rulers of the illustrious Guge Kingdom became ardent patrons of Buddhism; the third monarch, Yeshe-Ö, was particularly prominent in this regard. He actively promoted and introduced Buddhist teachings, earning a reputation as the most renowned patron of Buddhism in the history of the Guge Kingdom. He dispatched a delegation of twenty-one family members to Kashmir and other regions to study the Dharma. Upon his return, one member of this group—a monk named Rinchen Zangpo—emerged as a celebrated translator of Buddhist scriptures during the early phase of the "Later Propagation" in Tibet. Having successfully completed his studies abroad, Rinchen Zangpo invited thirty-two Kashmiri artisans to Guge to assist in the construction of monasteries and the creation of religious imagery; consequently, the early artistic style of Western Tibet was predominantly Kashmiri in character. In the 11th century, as the eminent Indian masters Dharmapala and Atisha traveled through Ngari and Ü-Tsang to propagate the Dharma, aesthetic elements of the Pala style were introduced into the heartland of the Tibetan Plateau. As Buddhism continued to spread throughout Tibet and its influence grew increasingly potent, the Pala-style painting tradition—which had flourished in the Ü-Tsang region—was transmitted to Western Tibet (a region previously dominated by the Kashmiri style), where it influenced and became integrated into local artistic production. By the 13th century, amidst the sweeping influence of Nepalese artistic trends, artists across different regions began to synthesize diverse aesthetic elements, creating artworks that possessed unique local characteristics. The painting featured here—depicting two Kadampa masters seated in dialogue—dates to 13th-century Western Tibet and stands as a quintessential example of this synthesis between Pala and Nepalese aesthetic traditions. As a distinct and significant genre within Tibetan Buddhist art, the depiction of spiritual masters (*lamas*) is not confined solely to three-dimensional sculpture; artisans also employ the two-dimensional mediums of color, line, and composition to render the likenesses of these historical figures who once walked the earth. Serving as a vital bridge between the Buddha and sentient beings, the spiritual master occupies a position of profound reverence. Following a master's passing (*Parinirvana*), disciples would create sculptures or paintings based on his living appearance as a means of commemoration and homage. This portrait-style Thangka, centered on human figures, depicts two Kadampa masters seated opposite one another. Employing a narrative-segmentation approach, a grid-like layout, and a compositional style that emphasizes the central theme, the artwork portrays a scene of dialogue and spiritual exchange between the two masters during their practice. As the painting slowly unfolds before the viewer, the first impression is one of profound tranquility and solemnity. Dominated by a palette of red hues, the image immediately captivates the eye with its vibrant, palpable energy. The upper section of the painting features a grid-like composition comprising three rows of deities and lamas; here, figures of Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, yogis, lamas, and patrons are gathered together in harmonious assembly. Each of these figures represents a distinct spiritual realm or power, collectively demonstrating the richness and comprehensive nature of the Buddhist faith while weaving a narrative of lineage, compassion, and wisdom. As the gaze descends, a semi-circular aureole frames a rocky grotto housing ten distinct figures—including lineage patriarchs (specifically Atisha Dipankara) wearing the distinctive Kadampa monastic hats, Dharma protectors, Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and Mahasiddhas. Among them, the figures of Chakrasamvara and Vajrapani—rendered in a quintessential Yuan Dynasty style—appear robust and rounded; their plump, corpulent forms evoke a sense of pure joy in the beholder. The other patriarchs and Bodhisattvas likewise hold various ritual implements and perform distinct mudras; executed with exquisite detail, these elements serve as symbolic representations of diverse Buddhist doctrines. Notably, the Mahasiddha Phadampa Sangye—distinguished by his bronze-hued skin—appears in his classic iconography on the right side of the composition, his wide, round eyes—resembling copper bells—gazing out with a piercing clarity, innocence, and lively spirit. The depiction of Phadampa Sangye in this Thangka bears a striking compositional resemblance to a 12th-century mural found within the Pal Caves of the Guge Kingdom in Western Tibet. In terms of overall composition, the Thangka skillfully utilizes spatial segmentation, positioning the two central masters in the middle section of the painting to effectively highlight the primary subject. In her 2008 article, *Thangkas of Two Tibetan Kagyu Lamas*, Amy Heller identifies this thangka as belonging to the Kagyu lineage. Although the absence of inscriptions precludes a definitive identification, an analysis of the figure on the right—specifically his appearance as a layperson, as well as a comparison of his facial features and physical characteristics with those depicted in other paintings—leads this author to conclude that he is most likely Dromtönpa, the founder of the Kadampa school. Consequently, the portrait of the figure on the left is presumed to depict Dromtönpa’s own teacher or spiritual master. Both masters are seated in full lotus posture upon double-tiered lotus thrones, each surmounted by a *prabhamandala* (aureole) featuring the "Six Ornaments" (*Shad-anga*). Above the Six Ornaments, the tails of the *makaras* (mythical sea creatures) transform into scrolling vines; these swirling tendrils are rendered with exquisite delicacy and dynamism, clearly demonstrating the pervasive influence of Nepalese aesthetic elements. Although the portraits of the masters were ostensibly modeled after their actual physical appearances and characteristics during their lifetimes, the expressions in their eyes—as well as the specific lines and brushstrokes employed—radiate the distinct artistic spirit of the Pala painting style. The masters' robes are adorned with floral motifs designed to mimic gold-thread embroidery. These intricate floral patterns, delineated through an interplay of interwoven lines, appear lush yet orderly, possessing a clear visual rhythm that is simultaneously vibrant and dignified; indeed, every single stroke embodies the craftsman's profound piety and reverence. The masters wear benevolent expressions; in their mutual gaze, their eyes convey a sense of profound peace and wisdom, while their brows radiate an intense thirst for knowledge and an unwavering dedication to the pursuit of truth. Their dialogue, though silent, speaks volumes; every exchange of glances and every subtle gesture of the hand is imbued with profound philosophical depth and boundless wisdom. Perhaps they are contemplating the mysteries of the universe, imparting methods of spiritual practice, or simply sharing their personal insights into life and their experiences on the spiritual path. This exchange transcends the limitations of language, reaching directly into the deepest recesses of the viewer's heart. The base of the colorful, double-tiered lotus throne is adorned with four lions and two elephants—an arrangement that constitutes a quintessential element of the Pala artistic style (Figure 2). Following the gaze further downward, the lowest tier of the painting depicts sixteen celestial maidens—each holding a distinct ritual implement—engaged in a dance. In Buddhist iconography, these maidens are arranged in four groups of four, collectively representing the four cardinal directions: East, South, West, and North. The reverse side of the Thangka features a painted stupa, within which are inscribed multiple lines of Tibetan text. These include a prayer commencing with the mantra: *Om a hum vajra guru padma siddhi hum*—the heart mantra of Guru Rinpoche (Padmasambhava). This is followed by consecration mantras for Vajrakilaya (Phurba), Vishnu, and Manjushri Bodhisattva; the six-syllable mantra of Avalokiteshvara (Guanyin)—*Om mani padme hum*; and the mantra of Vajrapani Bodhisattva—*Om vajra pani hum*. Next appear the Buddhist scriptural verses beginning with *“ye dharma hetu...”*, along with an excerpt from the *Pratimoksha Sutra*. As one’s gaze delves deeper, the sense of spatial depth evoked by this large-format Thangka—depicting two spiritual masters seated in mutual contemplation—grows increasingly profound, unfolding like a microcosm of the universe itself. Its scope transcends the mere physical space depicted within the frame; through the subtle interplay between the two masters, it constructs a spiritual realm that exists beyond the material world. Within this space, time seems to lose its significance; the clamor and turmoil of the external world are completely shut out, leaving behind only two pure, unblemished souls—meeting, merging, and resonating with one another.

viewingNote.zh: 这是一尊来自西藏中部的佛造像 。乍看之下，祂似乎与其他很多古代造像 无异，但每次凝视 ，内心总被一种无法言说的情绪悄然触动——像雾、像 风，是一种朦胧的辽阔感，像一种“在”，却又“无形”的存在 。后来我才慢慢 意识到，那是一种“虚空”的感觉 。 这是一尊受到帕拉风格影响的造像 。高高的发髻、细长上扬的眉眼、嘴角 一抹耐人寻味的笑意，以及飞扬的衣袖，都带着一种流动的帕拉艺术风格。那 是千年前从东南边境吹入雪域的风 ，停留在了这尊造像上 。
viewingNote.en: This is a Buddhist sculpture hailing from Central Tibet. At first glance, it appears indistinguishable from many other ancient statues; yet, with every lingering gaze, my inner self is quietly stirred by an emotion that defies description—like mist, like wind, a sense of nebulous vastness; a presence that is undeniably "there," yet utterly "formless." Only later did I slowly come to realize that this sensation was, in fact, the feeling of "Emptiness." This sculpture bears the distinct influence of the Pala style. Its towering topknot, slender and upward-sweeping brows and eyes, the enigmatic smile playing upon its lips, and its billowing sleeves all embody the fluid aesthetic of Pala art. It is a wind that drifted into the Land of Snows from the southeastern frontiers a thousand years ago—a breeze that has come to rest upon this very statue.
