excerpt.zh: 色彩作为变幻的媒介，沉醉其中的我们似乎可以获得比“线条 - 构图”更重要的关于美与神圣的本质。
excerpt.en: A Ratnasambhava thangka distinguished by chromatic order and luminous clarity.

viewingNote.zh: 当我们游走在青藏高原时，映入眼帘的大多是纯度极高的绚烂色彩，威严的 蓝、耀眼的红与超脱的白，它们与黄色、绿色构成了藏传文化的五种本源象征色。 在这里色彩不仅如实呈现了由元素构成的大千世界；更重要的是，这背后所阐述 的是一个个有关感性力量和哲学思变的具体情境。色彩作为变幻的媒介，沉醉其 中的我们似乎可以获得比“线条 - 构图”更重要的关于美与神圣的本质。在青藏 高原这片神秘而壮丽的土地上，绘画艺术如同璀璨的花朵，在圣洁的天空下绚烂 绽放，成为连接神圣与美的独特媒介。它不仅让我们领会到了高原的深厚文化底 蕴，更让我们感受到了艺术的力量和魅力。 从历史背景来看，13 世纪是西藏佛教艺术发展的重要时期。这一时期，西 藏在经历了朗达玛灭佛的混乱局面后，迎来了后弘期佛教兴盛与政教合一的时 代，同样也是西藏艺术的辉煌——丹萨替寺造像的开始。 自 11 世纪初，印度高僧阿底峡入藏弘法之后，为西藏带来了印度帕拉艺术 的影响。与此之后，随着 12 世纪末帕拉王朝的覆灭，僧侣与匠人们的纷纷逃 离，以及因十三世纪萨迦政权的繁荣强大，而被吸引过来的尼泊尔匠人，在这样 的背景下，十三世纪的藏传佛教艺术，在不断融合与创新中呈现出了新的美学高 度。这幅带有明显帕拉美学风格的宝生佛唐卡，也正是在这样的历史背景下诞生 了，它充分的展现了当时西藏艺术风格的兼容并蓄。 宝生佛，为佛教密宗崇奉的五方佛之一，这组深奥的神祇共同构成了密宗的 开悟宇宙观。五方佛中的每一尊都通过颜色、手势和方向来识别，宝生佛则住在 南方欢喜世界。唐卡采用分段叙事以及最具特征的表现手法构图，勾勒出了一个 神圣、庄严、梦幻的佛国净土。首先印入眼帘是耀眼的红和灿烂的黄，这两种颜 色作为主色调，充斥着整块画布。唐卡最上方绘画有六位人物形象，其中五位为 佛陀形象，一位为一尊上师像。人物的下一层为一排宝塔，塔顶后方为五彩斑斓 的智慧树，象征着智慧与觉悟的无尽源泉，卡通、抽象的绘画方式简单直接，像 童话世界般纯真、美好。宝塔中间为一座佛塔的塔顶位置，从塔幢形状来看，为 元代风格，这也体现了藏族画师吸收了印度风格后融入了西藏本土的元素。 叙事中段为宝生佛和金刚幢菩萨以及金刚幢菩萨的明妃。宝生佛全身金 色，面带微 笑、眉目柔和；身戴宝冠、耳饰、臂钏、项链、珠宝璎珞，身着裙 裤，佩戴腰带、脚环，华丽、高贵。宝生佛那洋溢着青春、阳光的气质，肌肉体 块明显、硬朗，匠人仅仅使 用了几笔就 将宝生佛的身躯体 现，且 线条流畅柔 软，予人肌肤富有弹性般的视觉观感，这看似简约的线条实，则彰显着匠人深厚的绘画功底。 宝生佛以结全跏趺坐的座姿，端身正坐于莲台之上，莲瓣宽大、舒展，瓣尖 翻卷，其图像风格为典型的元代特征。宝生佛左手于腹前结禅定印，右手掌心向 外，结与愿印。据说此印可以满足众生一切愿望，在佛教信仰中，宝生佛是一位 能满足众生愿求的慈悲大佛。宝生佛身后是由神兽组成的六拏具背光，在佛前虔 诚的神兽们，面容可爱、灵动；柔软的线条、丰富的色彩以及晕染的手法，使神 兽们的形象生动且立体；上方张口龇牙的摩羯，更是把我们拉入了一个梦幻且深 邃的海洋世界。在构图上，中间主尊宝生佛的比例占据整体画面的三分之二，这 种最具特征的表现手法意为凸显主尊的次第与精神威望。此种表现手法也为西 藏早期绘画风格的表现特征。 宝生佛两侧分别站立的金刚幢菩萨及其明妃，与中世纪东北印度艺术的典型 布局如出一辙。金刚幢菩萨和其明妃同样头戴宝冠、身戴珠宝、璎珞，以曼 妙、动感的身姿站立其左右侧。金刚幢菩萨和其明妃的裙裤设计很有特点，这种 以珠宝穿成线来表现薄纱透明、下垂质地的手法，不仅展现了匠人的创造力，更 将人物形象赋予了独特的神性气质。薄纱的轻盈与珠宝的璀璨相互映衬，使得裙 裤仿佛在光线的照耀下轻轻摇曳，既展现了华贵之气，又不失朦胧之美，在仙气 飘飘的气质中，更是将整个画面进一步推向了一个超脱尘世的境界。莲座下方 左右两边分别绘画有供养菩萨和宝生佛的坐骑“马”，匠人运用同系色中不同深浅 的棕色就将马儿优雅灵巧、奔放弛聘的英姿展现。整个叙事中最为特殊的是底 部绘画有藏传佛教的吉祥八宝，八宝又称八瑞相、八吉祥，是藏传佛教中八种表 示吉庆祥瑞之物，象征吉祥、幸福、圆满。吉祥八宝在大多数十三到十四世纪的 早期西藏唐卡绘画里面较为少见，这也是充分的展现了此幅唐卡的印藏融合风 格。 虽然这幅唐卡明显遵循了印度原型，但它也展示了西藏风格的地域性，特别 是人物的开脸、身型、比例以及色彩。画中没有任何废笔之处，线条有劲，轮廓 清晰，动物的绘画也都惟妙惟肖，应该是藏族画师在学习了印度绘画风格后，融 合了藏地元素进行的创作。此幅唐卡在历经了 800 余年，只是有一些轻微的脱 彩，其整体保存状态依旧如此完好、色彩依旧如此鲜艳，可见历代寺庙与藏家对 其的重视，其珍贵程度不亚于一张宫廷品质的宋画。
viewingNote.en: As we traverse the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau, our eyes are met primarily by colors of extraordinary purity and brilliance—majestic blues, dazzling reds, and transcendent whites. Together with yellow and green, these hues constitute the five primordial symbolic colors of Tibetan culture. Here, color serves not merely to faithfully depict the vast material world composed of the elements; more importantly, it articulates specific contexts regarding the power of sensibility and philosophical contemplation. As a medium of flux and transformation, color allows those of us immersed within it to grasp an essence of beauty and the sacred that transcends the mere interplay of "line and composition." On this mysterious and magnificent land of the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau, the art of painting blossoms like a radiant flower beneath the pristine skies, serving as a unique conduit connecting the divine with the beautiful. It enables us not only to appreciate the profound cultural heritage of the plateau but also to experience the sheer power and allure of art itself. From a historical perspective, the 13th century marked a pivotal era in the development of Tibetan Buddhist art. Following the chaotic aftermath of King Langdarma’s suppression of Buddhism, this period ushered in the "Later Propagation"—an era characterized by the resurgence of Buddhism, the unification of religious and political authority, and the dawn of a golden age in Tibetan art, exemplified by the sculptural masterpieces of Densatil Monastery. Beginning in the early 11th century, the arrival of the eminent Indian master Atisha to propagate the Dharma in Tibet introduced the aesthetic influences of India’s Pala Empire. Subsequently—against a backdrop defined by the late 12th-century collapse of the Pala Dynasty (which prompted an exodus of monks and artisans), and the concurrent rise of the powerful Sakya regime in the 13th century (which attracted artisans from Nepal)—Tibetan Buddhist art of the 13th century attained new aesthetic heights through a continuous process of synthesis and innovation. This Thangka painting of Ratnasambhava Buddha—bearing the distinct aesthetic hallmarks of the Pala style—emerged precisely within this historical context, serving as a vivid testament to the eclectic and inclusive nature of Tibetan art during that era. Ratnasambhava Buddha is one of the Five Dhyani Buddhas revered in Vajrayana Buddhism; together, this pantheon of profound deities constitutes the enlightened cosmological framework of the Vajrayana tradition. Each of the Five Dhyani Buddhas is distinguished by specific colors, hand gestures (mudras), and cardinal directions; Ratnasambhava resides in the Southern Realm of Joy. The Thangka employs a compositional style characterized by segmented narratives and highly distinctive artistic techniques, delineating a sacred, majestic, and ethereal Pure Land—a Buddha-realm of dreams. The viewer’s gaze is first captivated by dazzling reds and brilliant yellows; serving as the dominant color palette, these two hues saturate the entire canvas. Depicted across the uppermost section of the Thangka are six figures: five are images of Buddhas, while the sixth represents a spiritual Guru. Situated immediately beneath these figures is a row of stupas; rising behind their finials are resplendent, multicolored Trees of Wisdom—symbols of the inexhaustible wellsprings of wisdom and enlightenment. Rendered in a style that is at once stylized and abstract, the imagery is simple and direct, evoking the innocence and beauty of a fairytale realm. Centered among the stupas is the finial of a central pagoda; judging by the form of its spire, it exhibits a distinct Yuan Dynasty aesthetic—a testament to how Tibetan painters, having assimilated Indian artistic conventions, subsequently integrated indigenous Tibetan elements into their work. The central narrative section features Ratnasambhava, accompanied by the Bodhisattva Vajradhvaja and the Bodhisattva’s consort. Ratnasambhava is depicted with a body of pure gold, his face bearing a gentle smile and his features radiating softness. He is adorned with a jeweled crown, earrings, armbands, necklaces, and elaborate garlands of gems; clad in a skirt-like lower garment, he wears a sash and anklets, presenting an appearance of magnificent nobility. Ratnasambhava exudes an aura of youthful vitality and radiance; his musculature is clearly defined and robust. With just a few strokes, the artisan has masterfully delineated the Buddha’s physique; the lines flow with a fluid softness, creating the visual impression of supple, elastic skin. These seemingly simple lines, in reality, serve to underscore the artisan’s profound mastery of painting technique. Ratnasambhava sits upright and poised upon a lotus throne, assuming the full cross-legged posture (*vajrasana*). The lotus petals are broad and expansive, with their tips curling outward—a stylistic feature characteristic of the Yuan Dynasty period. Ratnasambhava’s left hand rests before his abdomen, forming the Mudra of Meditation (*dhyana mudra*), while his right hand, with its palm facing outward, forms the Mudra of Granting Wishes (*varada mudra*). It is said that this mudra (hand gesture) has the power to fulfill all the wishes of sentient beings; in Buddhist belief, Ratnasambhava—the Jewel-Born Buddha—is a great and compassionate deity capable of granting the prayers of all beings. Behind Ratnasambhava stands a *prabhamandala* (halo) composed of the *Shad-anga* (Six-Limbed) motif, featuring mythical beasts. These beasts, depicted kneeling reverently before the Buddha, possess charming and spirited countenances. Through the use of fluid lines, rich colors, and subtle shading techniques, the figures of these mythical creatures are rendered with vivid realism and three-dimensional depth. Above them, a pair of *Makaras* (mythical sea creatures)—depicted with gaping jaws and bared fangs—draws the viewer into a dreamlike and profound oceanic realm. In terms of composition, the central figure of Ratnasambhava occupies two-thirds of the entire canvas; this distinctive stylistic approach serves to underscore the deity's hierarchical preeminence and spiritual authority—a characteristic feature of early Tibetan painting styles. Flanking Ratnasambhava are the Bodhisattva Vajradhvaja and his consort; their arrangement mirrors the typical compositional layout found in the art of medieval Northeast India. Vajradhvaja and his consort are likewise adorned with jeweled crowns, body ornaments, and *yajnopavitas* (sacred cords); they stand to the Buddha's left and right, depicted in graceful, dynamic postures. The design of their lower garments is particularly distinctive: the technique of using strings of jewels to simulate the transparency and draping quality of sheer fabric not only demonstrates the artisan's ingenuity but also imbues the figures with a unique aura of divine transcendence. The ethereal lightness of the sheer fabric contrasts beautifully with the dazzling brilliance of the jewels, creating the illusion that the garments are gently swaying in the light; this effect conveys an air of opulent grandeur without sacrificing a sense of ethereal beauty, elevating the entire scene to a realm that transcends the mundane world. Beneath the lotus throne, on the left and right sides respectively, are painted images of offering Bodhisattvas and Ratnasambhava's mount—the Horse. Through the skillful application of varying shades of brown within a single color palette, the artisan has vividly captured the horse's elegant agility and its spirited, unbridled vigor. A particularly unique element of the overall narrative composition is found at the very bottom of the painting, where the *Ashtamangala*—the Eight Auspicious Symbols of Tibetan Buddhism—are depicted. Also known as the Eight Auspicious Signs or Eight Good Omens, these eight objects represent good fortune and auspiciousness within the Tibetan Buddhist tradition, symbolizing prosperity, happiness, and spiritual perfection. The Eight Auspicious Symbols are relatively rare in most early Tibetan Thangka paintings dating from the 13th and 14th centuries; their presence here serves as a compelling testament to the Indo-Tibetan fusion style embodied by this particular Thangka. While this painting clearly adheres to Indian prototypes, it simultaneously showcases distinct regional characteristics of the Tibetan style—particularly evident in the facial rendering, physique, proportions, and color palette of the figures. The artwork is executed with absolute precision, devoid of any superfluous strokes; its lines are vigorous, its contours crisp, and its depictions of animals remarkably lifelike. It appears to be the creation of a Tibetan artist who, having mastered Indian painting styles, subsequently integrated indigenous Tibetan elements into the work. Despite having endured for over eight centuries—suffering only minor pigment loss—this Thangka remains in a remarkably pristine state of preservation, with its colors retaining their original vibrancy. This exceptional condition bears witness to the profound reverence accorded to the piece by generations of monasteries and private collectors, rendering it a treasure of a rarity and value comparable to a Song Dynasty court painting of the highest caliber.

excerpt.en: A Nepalese stupa that compresses architectural clarity into a small ritual form.

viewingNote.zh: 佛塔，是印度梵文 Stupa（窣堵波）的音译，也称为浮屠。佛塔作为佛教建 筑的代表，不仅是佛教信仰和文化的重要象征，还承载着丰富的历史、宗教、艺 术和文化意义。佛塔最早起源于释迦牟尼圆寂后，弟子们为了纪念佛陀，而用石 块建塔以埋葬其骨灰。最初的佛塔多为简单的土堆或石堆，用以纪念。随着佛 教的兴盛，佛塔逐渐演变成了复杂的石造建筑，成为了佛教信仰的重要象征。在 印度，阿育王统治时期，佛教被列为国教，佛塔的建立达到了空前的高涨，分建 了八万四千座佛塔，这一时期的佛塔多为覆钵式塔。随着佛教的传播发展和在亚 洲各地的兴起，佛塔历经漫长的历史演变过程后，形成了多种的风格和形式。佛 塔被视为佛陀圣物的安放处，象征着佛陀的身体、言语和心灵。它们也通常建造 和出现在具有宗教意义的地点，作为供奉、祈祷和冥想的中心。 这座九到十世纪的尼泊尔理查维晚期佛塔，为红铜鎏金铸造，它像是一座缩 小的庙宇建筑，在微缩世界中讲述着宏达叙事。佛塔的顶部采用了典型的螺旋形 设计，这种形式在佛教建筑中被称为“相轮”，象征着宇宙的中心与佛陀的智慧之 光。圆形的半球形顶盖，称为“覆钵”，代表了宇宙的无边无际，以及佛教中解脱 轮回的理想。覆钵的形式为早期佛塔形制的延续，同样，整个上半部分也 为尼泊尔常见的早期佛塔形制。衔接着覆钵的覆式莲瓣宽大、舒展，瓣尖微微上 翘，此种莲瓣风格延续了印度那烂陀七到八世纪的早期风格。 佛塔的中段和底座则是多层的方形结构，这些结构代表了佛教宇宙观中的不 同世界。整个塔看上去就像一座完整的缩小版庙宇，塔的四周等分布局，对称的 四扇门楣前分别供奉着四尊佛，因为年代久远已经遗失。平衡对称的布局是宇宙 秩序的镜像，更是对和谐、平衡理念的诠释。在这种对称中，我们仿佛看到了天 地万物间的相互依存与制约。每一面都如同宇宙的一扇窗，具有空间的透视 性，透过它，我们可以窥见不同的风景，却又在根本上保持着一致与统一。塔身 的门廊上装饰有对称的八根立柱，柱体表面的切面塑造写实，装饰有连珠纹和部 分几何形图案。部分立柱从侧面看过去为镂空铸造，体现了当时尼泊尔精湛的铸 造工艺。立柱的上方分别有两只面对面站立的摩羯，摩羯长鼻、利齿，翻卷的尾 翼似能翻江倒海。在古印度神话中，摩羯原本是性恶的海中巨兽，会加害于人。 然而，在佛教的度化后，摩羯的形象像神兽般灵动、温顺且可爱。 随着视线顺延向上，出现在门楣中间的为天福之面。天福之面，源于上古时期的印度，是湿婆神用第三只眼变出的一只面目狰狞、双眼外凸、嘴巴巨大且极 为贪食的怪兽。然而，由于其忠诚，最终被封为专司门户的门神，其兽面常出现 在佛塔、寺庙等宗教建筑物的门楣中央或拱道之上，位置高于其他神祇。天福之 面的塑造具有极强的视觉冲击力和表现力。其面目狰狞、凶猛异常，表现出一种 震慑人心的力量感。它作为门神的象征，守护着佛教的神圣空间，同时也传达着 一种威严和庄重的感觉。在塔基的上层其中一面铸造有心形莲瓣，起到了标注塔 方位的作用，塔基上的此种莲瓣与十世纪印度库尔奇哈尔风格造像的莲瓣如出一 辙。塔基莲台的其他三个面，以折叠的塑造方式层层扩大，如同生命的阶 梯。整个佛塔上中下的结构设计，在圆形与方形两种形状的巧妙结合中，不仅展 现了建筑形式上的变化与丰富，更带有着无限的哲学关系。 试想，如果我们真的能够将自己缩小，当站在这座佛塔面前，那将是一种何 等的体验？那一刻，所有的喧嚣与纷扰都将远去，只留下内心的平静与敬畏。我 们会惊讶于这座微缩庙宇所展现出的对称、均衡与和谐之美，那是一种超越了物 质世界的视觉震撼。在这座雕塑构建的空间里，我们会不由自主地放慢脚步，让 心灵在这份宁静与美好中得到真正的休憩与升华。 这座别致、特殊的佛塔曾经可能供奉在一座重要的寺庙中，承载着信徒们的 信仰和虔诚，见证着无数次的宗教仪式和祈祷活动。尽管经历了千年的传世，这 座佛塔保存完好，这得是无数人代人的接力传承。相较同时期或者更早的类似佛 塔而言，这件佛塔是目前见到的唯一一件几乎完整的作品，大多数都是相轮部分 破损或遗失，不论稀缺性、重要性、艺术性角度而言，这件九到十世纪的尼泊尔 佛塔都是一件不可多得的艺术珍品。
viewingNote.en: The *stupa* (Chinese: *fota* or *futou*) is a transliteration of the Sanskrit term *Stupa*. As the quintessential form of Buddhist architecture, the stupa serves not only as a vital symbol of Buddhist faith and culture but also embodies profound historical, religious, artistic, and cultural significance. The origins of the stupa trace back to the period following the *parinirvana* (passing) of Siddhartha Gautama (the Buddha); to honor his memory, his disciples constructed stone mounds to enshrine his cremated remains. Initially, these stupas were predominantly simple mounds of earth or stone, serving primarily as commemorative monuments. As Buddhism flourished, the stupa gradually evolved into complex stone structures, becoming a central icon of the Buddhist faith. During the reign of Emperor Ashoka in India, when Buddhism was established as the state religion, the construction of stupas reached an unprecedented zenith, with the erection of some 84,000 monuments across the empire; stupas from this era typically adopted the "inverted-bowl" architectural style. As Buddhism spread and took root across the Asian continent, the stupa underwent a long process of historical evolution, giving rise to a diverse array of styles and forms. Stupas are revered as repositories for the Buddha's sacred relics, symbolizing his Body, Speech, and Mind. Furthermore, they are typically constructed—or situated—at sites of religious significance, serving as focal points for worship, prayer, and meditation. This particular stupa, dating to the late Licchavi period in Nepal (9th–10th centuries), is crafted from gilt-bronze. Resembling a miniature temple structure, it conveys a grand narrative within a microcosmic world. The apex of the stupa features a quintessential spiral design—known in Buddhist architecture as the *xianglun* (finial)—which symbolizes the cosmic center and the radiant light of the Buddha's wisdom. The spherical, hemispherical dome—known as the *fubo* (inverted bowl)—represents the boundless nature of the universe and embodies the Buddhist ideal of liberation from the cycle of *samsara* (reincarnation). The form of this "inverted bowl" represents a continuation of early stupa typologies; indeed, the entire upper section of the monument reflects the architectural styles characteristic of early stupas commonly found in Nepal. Adorning the base of the dome is a band of broad, gracefully unfurling lotus petals with tips that curl slightly upward—a stylistic feature that perpetuates the early artistic traditions of India's Nalanda region, dating back to the 7th and 8th centuries. The middle section and base of the stupa consist of multi-tiered square structures, each representing a distinct realm within the Buddhist cosmology. Viewed in its entirety, the stupa resembles a miniature temple; its layout is radially symmetrical, with four symmetrically positioned doorways—each originally surmounted by a lintel and flanked by a statue of the Buddha—though these statues have long since been lost to the passage of time. This balanced and symmetrical arrangement serves as a mirror of cosmic order, as well as an artistic interpretation of the ideals of harmony and equilibrium. Within this symmetry, we seem to perceive the intricate web of interdependence and mutual constraint that binds together all things in heaven and on earth. Each face of the stupa acts as a window onto the cosmos, offering a spatial perspective through which we may glimpse diverse vistas that, nonetheless, remain fundamentally consistent and unified. The porticoes of the stupa’s body are adorned with eight symmetrically arranged columns; the faceted surfaces of these columns are rendered with striking realism and embellished with pearl-bead motifs and geometric patterns. Viewed from the side, some of these columns reveal themselves to be hollow-cast—a testament to the exquisite metalworking craftsmanship prevalent in Nepal during that era. Surmounting each column are a pair of *Makaras* (mythical sea creatures) standing face-to-face; depicted with long snouts and sharp fangs, their curling, fin-like tails appear capable of stirring up the very oceans. In ancient Indian mythology, the *Makara* was originally conceived as a malevolent marine behemoth that preyed upon humans. However, following its spiritual redemption through the teachings of Buddhism, the *Makara* was transformed into a divine beast—depicted as spirited, docile, and endearing. As the gaze ascends further, the "Face of Heavenly Blessings" (*Kirtimukha*) appears centered upon the lintel. Originating in ancient India, this visage—known as the *Kirtimukha*—is said to have been conjured by the god Shiva from his third eye; it manifests as a monstrous entity with a ferocious countenance, bulging eyes, a gaping maw, and an insatiable appetite. Yet, by virtue of its unwavering loyalty, it was ultimately elevated to the status of a guardian deity presiding over thresholds. Consequently, this beast-like visage frequently appears centered upon the lintels or arches of religious structures—such as stupas and temples—occupying a position of prominence situated above all other deities. The sculptural rendering of the *Kirtimukha* possesses immense visual impact and expressive power; its ferocious, exceptionally fierce countenance projects an overwhelming sense of power capable of striking awe into the beholder. Serving as the symbolic guardian of sacred Buddhist spaces, it simultaneously conveys an aura of majesty and solemnity. On one side of the upper tier of the base, heart-shaped lotus petals are cast in relief; these serve to mark the orientation of the stupa. These particular lotus petals on the base are virtually identical to those found on 10th-century Indian sculptures in the Khajuraho style. The remaining three sides of the base’s lotus platform are sculpted in a layered, expanding fashion, resembling a "stairway of life." The structural design of the entire stupa—encompassing its upper, middle, and lower sections—demonstrates a masterful interplay between circular and square forms; this not only showcases a rich variety of architectural shapes but also embodies profound philosophical significance. Imagine, if we could truly shrink ourselves down to a miniature scale and stand before this stupa—what an extraordinary experience that would be! In that moment, all worldly noise and turmoil would fade away, leaving behind only inner peace and reverence. We would marvel at the beauty of symmetry, balance, and harmony displayed by this miniature temple—a visual spectacle that transcends the material world. Within the space defined by this sculptural architecture, we would instinctively slow our pace, allowing our spirits to find true repose and spiritual elevation amidst such tranquility and beauty. This unique and distinctive stupa likely once resided within a prominent temple, serving as a vessel for the faith and piety of believers and bearing witness to countless religious rituals and prayers. Despite having survived for a millennium, the stupa remains remarkably well-preserved—a testament to the continuous, intergenerational stewardship of countless individuals. Compared to similar stupas of the same era or earlier periods, this particular piece is the only known example to survive in an almost entirely intact state; most other surviving examples suffer from damage to, or loss of, their *sōrin* (finial) sections. Whether judged by its rarity, historical significance, or artistic merit, this Nepalese stupa—dating from the 9th or 10th century—stands as an exceptionally rare and invaluable artistic treasure.

viewingNote.zh: 扎堆的家在甘孜新都桥附近 。他家的后山上是四座彼此环绕 、遥遥相对 的雪山。每座雪山的名字都不同，我想，去过的人应该已经猜出地理位置了。 扎堆家屋前两侧，是两座宽阔的牧山，夏季时青草丰盛，牛羊如云。每次 到他家时，总爱坐在门前的长条凳上，静静地眺望对面的山峦，那一坐就是一 下午。因为，对面的山体厚重、沉稳，如同一位沉默、可靠的长兄 。只要看 着，心里便总能慢慢地安静下来 。远古时期，大山、大树、大石是最稳定、最 不易倒塌的庇护，它们能为人类遮风避雨、提供藏身之所。可能正是因为这种 依附与信赖早已写进了我们基因，所以每当目光触及到那些沉默伫立的大山 时，总会感到一种古老的庇护，那是一种无需言语的安慰 。 荣格曾在分析心理学中写道，山象征着“父性、意志与永恒”。它在那里，不 因你崩溃而倒塌，不因你动摇而动摇。我眼前的大山恰好对应了我们这次带来 拍摄的另一尊 14 世纪的上师肖像所散发的精神气质。这是一尊不论陈列在客厅、展厅、或是佛堂，都不会被忽视的存在 。只需一眼，便能感受到内心被安 定下来的力量。 当第一次见到祂时，我惊讶于祂的体量感和神性的散发 。那是一种如山般 的厚重，却毫无臃肿。祂的面庞圆中带方，五官开阔而大气 ，嘴角含笑，自然而 亲切。那双神性化处理的眼睛，沉静慈悲 。宽大的耳形与挺拔厚实的身形相 映，使整尊雕像散发出一种慈祥 、淳朴，且不动如山的庄严和定力。 除了这份沉稳与力量，肖像同样让我动容的，还有匠人所倾注的情感与修 持。首先，我们能直观的看出这件肖像的工艺非常细腻 。嵌银的连珠纹颗颗清 晰、嵌红铜的刻花笔笔明了而有力，并没有因为花纹小而忽视任何造型细节，这 样精细的工艺，需要极大的耐心与专注 。而这份专注，源自信念，是匠人对所 造之“像”所怀有的深切敬意和信仰。不论远近，在视觉上，整体结构呈现的 是复杂且主次分明的感官。显然匠人在塑造前，心中早已有了清晰的构图与信 心。他大概是位既有天赋 、又具深厚修行的雕塑家，是一位内外兼修的人 。 其次，更让我惊喜的是，这尊上师肖像身上，带有一种“绘画感”，仿佛隐约 游走在雕塑与绘画的边界。上师衣袍的层次和褶皱都清晰、明朗，呈现出一种秩 序美：内里坎肩上的几道线条与背部披袍上的线条，有序而节制，衣褶铺在蒲团 上所排列出的那一圈一圈有序的衣褶，如同笔中勾勒出的线条。而垂落在蒲团前 的布料，则令人联想到唐卡中一笔一笔描绘的纹理与流线 。这种绘画感在佛教雕 塑中很是少见，它既考验技艺与匠心，更显露出一种超越形式的精神凝练。 上师姿态挺拔、庄重，手手相传的敬意从温润如玉的皮壳质感上清晰可见 。 祂如从画中走来，静坐于世间。那种感受，就像见到了一位充满智慧的兄长，那 一刻唤起的是心底的一种心安与亲切。 夏天的藏区，一片绿意 。从我坐的位置往山体看去，山上长满了各种植被 。 此时，正值日落时分，山体随着阳光的变化而生出不同的光影与色阶。那种层 层叠叠的色彩流动，很像是一幅原始的画境 。自然的呼吸、时间的流动、生命 的更迭，在这一片山色之间如实呈现 。那是一种返璞归真的心灵觉醒，是一种 与世界交感的唤起 。 当你真正用心地凝视一座山、一阵风 、或一双眼睛，你会发现，它们从来都 不是孤立存在的，它们都像是携带着某种世界的回响 。而你，也不仅是一个旁 观者，也是一名回应者。就像艺术 ，也从不孤立 。真正能打动人的艺术 ，早已 超越了材质和语言，穿过了时间的界限，进入了某种“互感领域”——那是存在 与存在之间的一次真实相遇 。哲学追问秩序，科学探寻原理，美术呈现感 受，而大自然，则像沉默的诗 ... 这些看似不同的呈现方式，其实都指向一个方 向：我们与世界，是可以互感 、互融的。那是一种奇妙的情绪联结。 每当我凝视着一些质朴、纯粹 、又美的雕塑时，我心中就会升起同样的感 觉 。就像此刻，当我看着眼前的上师肖像，觉得祂像眼前的山一样稳时，这不 是偶然——而是基因深处，仍记得你来自哪里 。我们都来自自然，向往安宁。 因为那是一种，比语言更早的信任 。
viewingNote.en: Dadhul’s home is situated near Xinduqiao in Ganzi. Rising behind his house stand four snow-capped mountains—circling one another, yet standing in distant, silent dialogue. Each peak bears a distinct name; I imagine that anyone who has visited the region has likely already guessed its exact location. Flanking the front of Dadhul’s home lie two expansive pastures; in the summer months, the grass grows lush and verdant, and herds of cattle and sheep drift across the slopes like clouds. Whenever I visit, I love to sit on the long wooden bench by the door, gazing quietly across at the distant mountain ranges—often remaining there for an entire afternoon. For those mountains—massive and steadfast—resemble a silent, reliable elder brother. Simply by looking at them, my mind gradually settles into a state of profound tranquility. In ancient times, great mountains, mighty trees, and massive boulders served as humanity’s most stable and enduring sanctuaries, offering shelter from the wind and rain, and providing safe havens in which to hide. Perhaps it is because this deep-seated reliance and trust have long been etched into our very genes that, whenever our gaze falls upon these silently standing mountains, we instinctively sense a primal sense of protection—a form of solace that requires no words. Carl Jung once wrote in his analytical psychology that the mountain symbolizes "the paternal principle, the will, and eternity." It simply *is*—it does not crumble when you collapse, nor does it waver when you falter. The mountains before my eyes perfectly mirror the spiritual aura exuded by another object we brought along for this trip: a 14th-century portrait of a spiritual master. It is a presence that commands attention—whether displayed in a living room, an exhibition hall, or a Buddhist shrine—and one that simply cannot be overlooked. A single glance is enough to feel a profound sense of inner calm taking root within one’s soul. When I first beheld this figure, I was struck by its sheer physical presence and the palpable divinity it radiated. It possessed a monumental solidity—much like a mountain—yet was entirely devoid of any heaviness or bulkiness. The face is a harmonious blend of roundness and angularity, with broad, majestic features; the corners of the mouth curl upward in a gentle smile—natural, warm, and approachable. The eyes—rendered with a transcendent, spiritual quality—are deep, serene, and filled with boundless compassion. The figure’s broad, distinctive ears complement its upright, robust physique, imbuing the entire sculpture with an aura of benevolent kindness, unadorned simplicity, and a steadfast dignity—immovable and unshakable as a mountain. Beyond the sense of composure and strength it conveys, what moves me just as deeply in this portrait is the emotion and spiritual discipline the artisan poured into it. First, one can immediately discern the exquisite craftsmanship of this piece. Each bead in the silver-inlaid pearl-pattern border is distinct, and every stroke of the red-copper inlay work is clear and vigorous; no detail of the form—however minute the pattern—has been overlooked. Such meticulous artistry demands immense patience and concentration. This concentration, in turn, stems from conviction—a profound reverence and faith held by the artisan toward the "image" he was creating. Whether viewed from afar or up close, the visual impression conveyed by the overall structure is one of complexity yet clear hierarchy. Evidently, before he began sculpting, the artisan already held a vivid composition and unwavering confidence within his mind. He was likely a sculptor endowed with both natural talent and deep spiritual cultivation—a man who had refined both his inner spirit and his outward craft. Secondly—and even more delightfully—this portrait of the Guru possesses a distinct "painterly quality," appearing to hover subtly at the very boundary between sculpture and painting. The layers and folds of the Guru’s robes are rendered with striking clarity and definition, manifesting a beauty of order: the lines on the inner vest and those on the draped outer robe are arranged with discipline and restraint; the concentric rings formed by the folds of fabric spreading across the meditation cushion resemble lines sketched with a painter’s brush. Meanwhile, the fabric cascading down in front of the cushion evokes the textures and flowing contours meticulously delineated, stroke by stroke, in traditional Thangka paintings. Such a painterly quality is a rarity in Buddhist sculpture; it not only serves as a testament to technical mastery and artistic ingenuity but also reveals a spiritual essence that transcends mere form. The Guru’s posture is upright and dignified; the reverence passed down through generations of hands is clearly palpable in the smooth, jade-like patina of the surface. He appears as if he has stepped forth from a painting, sitting in quiet repose amidst the world. The sensation is akin to encountering a wise and elder brother—a moment that evokes a profound sense of inner peace and kinship deep within one’s heart. In the Tibetan region during the summer, the landscape is awash with greenery. From where I sit, gazing out toward the mountainside, I see the slopes lush with a rich tapestry of vegetation. At this moment—the hour of sunset—the mountain slopes come alive with shifting patterns of light, shadow, and color gradients, responding to the changing sunlight. This cascading flow of hues resembles a primordial tableau. The very breath of nature, the passage of time, and the ceaseless cycle of life are revealed in their unadorned truth amidst this mountain scenery. It is a spiritual awakening—a return to one’s authentic essence—and a stirring of deep resonance with the world around us. When you truly gaze, with full presence of mind, upon a mountain, a breeze, or a pair of eyes, you discover that they never exist in isolation; rather, they seem to carry within them a certain echo of the world itself. And you, too, are not merely a bystander, but a responder. Art, likewise, never exists in isolation. Art that truly moves the human spirit transcends the boundaries of material and language, piercing through the limits of time to enter a realm of "mutual resonance"—a genuine encounter between one existence and another. Philosophy seeks to understand order; science explores fundamental principles; fine art gives form to human feeling; and Nature—she is like a silent poem. These seemingly disparate modes of expression all, in truth, point toward a single direction: that we and the world are capable of mutual resonance and deep integration. It is a wondrous emotional bond. Whenever I gaze upon sculptures that are at once simple, pure, and beautiful, the very same sensation rises within my heart. Just as in this moment, as I look upon the portrait of the Guru before me—perceiving in Him a steadfastness as unshakeable as the mountain itself—I realize this is no mere coincidence. Rather, it is the deep memory encoded within our very genes, recalling the source from which we came. We all originate from Nature, and we all yearn for tranquility. For this is a form of trust that existed long before the advent of language.

title.en: Portrait of the Fifth Dalai Lama

excerpt.en: A miniature gold portrait carrying remarkable authority at a precious scale.

viewingNote.zh: 五世达赖喇嘛阿旺罗桑嘉措（1617-1682），是藏传佛教格鲁派历史上具有重要地位的一位宗教领袖 。 1642 年，在蒙古和硕特部固始汗的帮助下，他和四世班禅一起建立了格鲁派在藏区的宗教统治权 。1644 年满族政权入关之后，他不断加强与清廷的联系，顺治九年（1652）更亲往北京，进献千件贡礼 。一年 后，顺治帝赐金册金印，封为“西天大善自在佛所领天下释教普通瓦赤喇怛喇达赖喇嘛”称号，自此 ，达赖 喇嘛在蒙藏地区的宗教领袖地位正式得到确认 ，格鲁派的发展进入鼎盛时期 。 此尊造像尺寸虽小却写实生动，尊者颧骨高隆 ，下颏尖凸，呈鹅蛋脸型 ，神情坚毅 ，青春的面庞里充 盈着智者的慈和与睿智，端坐于双层卡垫之上，躯体端正挺直 ，内着僧坎和僧裙，外披袈裟和僧氅，圆鼓 壮硕的肢体在膨胀的袈裟的每个细节上得以体现；袈裟华丽贴体，衣褶处理流畅自然 ，雕刻甚为精美 ，花 纹繁而不乱，錾刻力道深刻均匀，尤能体现工匠在虔诚的宗教感情激发下的深厚功力，以及供养人对尊者 无比崇敬的心态 。底座造型软垫堆栈，别致少见；锦垫錾刻繁密卷草纹及莲花，刀法流畅细腻 ，台座底部 是完好如初的封底 。卡垫背面整齐錾刻两行行藏文铭文 ，汉译为“胜利的王，遍知一切的阿旺 · 罗桑嘉 措，贤德，我们尊敬他 。”为此像的身份提供了可靠的信息 。 五世达赖喇嘛的造像坊间流传颇广，但这是目前已知唯一一尊纯金铸造 ，且明确指出其身份的，其宗 教意义无与伦比 。不仅尺寸小巧，同时艺术手法自然写实，整体雕刻工艺极为精湛，可称为西藏祖师类造 像的巅峰之作 。
viewingNote.en: The Fifth Dalai Lama, Ngawang Lobsang Gyatso (1617–1682), was a religious leader of pivotal importance in the history of the Gelug school of Tibetan Buddhism. In 1642, with the assistance of Gushi Khan of the Khoshut Mongols, he—together with the Fourth Panchen Lama—established the Gelug school's religious authority throughout the Tibetan region. Following the Manchu regime's entry into China Proper in 1644, he consistently strengthened his ties with the Qing court; in the ninth year of the Shunzhi reign (1652), he personally traveled to Beijing to present a tribute of one thousand items. A year later, the Shunzhi Emperor bestowed upon him a golden decree and a golden seal, conferring the title "The Dalai Lama, Vajradhara, Universal Ruler of the Buddhist Faith throughout the World, under the Great Benevolent Self-Existent Buddha of the West." From that moment on, the Dalai Lama's status as the supreme religious leader of the Mongol and Tibetan regions was officially affirmed, and the development of the Gelug school entered its golden age. Although small in scale, this sculpture is rendered with striking realism and vitality. The figure features high cheekbones and a pointed chin, forming an "egg-shaped" facial contour; his expression is resolute, yet his youthful countenance radiates the benevolence and wisdom of a sage. He sits upright upon a double-layered cushion base, clad in the traditional monastic attire: an inner vest and skirt, overlaid by a *kashaya* robe and outer cloak. His rounded, robust physique is palpable beneath the voluminous folds of the robe, evident in every minute detail. The *kashaya* fits elegantly to the body, its drapery rendered with fluid naturalness; the carving is exquisitely refined, featuring intricate patterns that remain orderly and harmonious. The chiseling technique—executed with profound, uniform force—powerfully conveys the artisan's deep mastery, inspired by sincere religious devotion, as well as the patron's boundless reverence for the revered figure. The base is uniquely styled as a stack of soft cushions—a rare and distinctive design—with the brocade cushions intricately chiseled with dense scrolling vines and lotus motifs, executed with fluid, delicate strokes. The underside of the base retains its original, perfectly preserved sealed cover. On the reverse side of the cushion base, two lines of Tibetan inscription are neatly chiseled; translated into Chinese, they read: "The Victorious King, the Omniscient Ngawang Lobsang Gyatso—virtuous and worthy of our reverence." This inscription provides reliable information regarding the identity of the figure depicted in this sculpture. While images of the Fifth Dalai Lama circulate widely, this is currently the only known statue cast entirely in pure gold that explicitly identifies its subject; consequently, its religious significance is unparalleled. Not only is it diminutive in size, but it also features a naturalistic and realistic artistic style; the overall craftsmanship is exceptionally exquisite, making it a veritable masterpiece among Tibetan lineage-master iconography.

excerpt.en: A stone master portrait shaped by weathered surface and inward concentration.

viewingNote.zh: 我走向车旁，打开盒子，拿出那尊迟 迟没有拍摄的上师石雕造像 。说 道：“这次我们还有这件上师像一直没拍照，我想，最适合的时间出现了。那就 是此刻你散发的光 。质朴、鲜活、细腻 、又充满力量 。”扎堆面带羞涩的，双 手接过造像，轻轻举过头顶，低声念了一串经文 。“感觉这位上师的头好圆。” 扎堆笑着说 。我点头：“是啊，上师生前就是这个模样。祂的五官量感很大，特 别是眼睛，画得清晰细致，眼白、瞳孔 、瞳仁分明，给人一种强烈的真实感 。 眉毛纤细修长，嘴唇略施红彩。整张面孔因写实而格外生动，仿佛有血有肉。 同样，也正是因为祂五官在整个头部的量感，所以我们第一眼看上去就会细究 祂的整个表情，就是整个人物细微的这种动态 。”我指着雕像继续道：“你再看 祂的背光，虽然厚重且装饰繁复，但第一眼总是先落在祂脸上——那种神 情，好像一汪泉水 ，干净、清澈，透着喜悦与信念，像是智慧沉淀后自然流露 的通透和自信。” 扎堆凝视着雕像，沉思后缓缓说：“祂看起来很慈悲、很简单，但又有种我 说不清楚的能量包裹着。”“从正面看，平易近人；从侧面看，又很庄严。能感 觉到匠人在挑选石头时，就已经开始在想如何挑选石料才能更好的还原自己对 上师的理解和设想 。在雕凿过程中，匠人有在‘寻石造像’，从上师塑造的体量 和整个背光以及底座的和谐度和贴合度来看，匠人在开凿的过程中，像是极为 克制和小心，想尽量寻石来保留人物的量感和气场。” 我继续介绍：“你看这背光，外圈编织纹理像是麻绳，六拏具上的神兽神态 灵动，底座上刻着宝瓶 ，还有一群像童话中走出的大象，整件作品在繁复中透 出一种庄严与灵性 。六拏具上的神兽和底座上的大象都像童话中走出来般，带 着精灵之气 。底座中间雕刻着宝瓶，两侧为布满花纹的雕刻，使雕像整体在繁 复中凸显着一种华贵、具象的场域 。以红、黄色调为主的绘彩，颜色既明亮又 沉稳，凸显着上师的高贵。所以整体就会给人一种庄严的气场和情绪张力”扎 堆听得入神，忽然认真地说：“这尊雕像，像极了我们藏族人的性格。”我一 愣：“怎么说？”他笑了笑：“石头是粗糙坚硬的，但被雕刻后却能展现出温柔、生 动的神态，就像我们藏族人，看起来粗犷、不精致，嘴巴也不利索，但心里，其 实很柔软 。是一种拙中带细、不拘小节的质朴。”我轻声回应：“是啊，外在豁 达洒脱 ，内心细腻澄明 。你也一样——明亮、美好。” 话匣子被打开的扎堆忽然严肃起来：“姐，你知道吗？我们藏族人不害怕死 亡，因为我们相信轮回。”“曾经在纽约有一个以藏文化为主的博物馆——鲁 宾，博物馆曾经有做过一个展，展的主题——死亡不是终结”我回忆道 。扎堆 点头：“我们修法、念经、供灯、转山，这些看似重复的行为，其实是在不断提 醒自己：保持正念，成为一个善良的人 。因为这个世界太吵闹了，我们需要反 复地修习，才不会迷失 。”他顿了顿，语气缓慢而坚定：“如果一个人一生心念是 善的，哪怕身体消失了，在下一个循环 、轮回中，那这个善根就牵引着你去到美 好的地方。“我补充说：“在物理学中，这叫‘能量守恒定律’。能量不会凭空消 失，它只会转换形态 。从这个角度看，我们从未真正离开，只是以另一种形式 继续存在 。死亡和新生共同循环 、共生共存”扎堆忽然调皮地说：“那说不定 这些雕像里，也藏着某些能量呢？”我看着那尊静默的上师，默默微笑 。 是啊。每一个生命走过的痕迹，都会被这个宇宙悄然记录下。肉体终将归 于尘土，但精神会以另一种形态——思想、记忆 、意志 、或一尊雕塑——继续 存在下去 ... 机舱内传来婴儿尖锐而剧烈的啼哭，像初春突至的惊雷，穿透密闭的空 气 ，在耳边炸开。我忽然从梦境中惊醒，意识从虚浮而沉静的朦胧中挣脱 。眼 前依旧是机舱内柔的灯光和陌生的人，低语与呼吸交错。我花了一些时间，才 将身体与意识重新对齐。哭声依旧在持续 。可不知为什么，刚开始觉得刺耳的 声音，在完全清醒之后，竟开始在内心有了一种不同的回响 。那像是生命初生 的召唤，干净、原始、毫无遮掩，像是某种久违的“开始”。 我们出生时本自具足，没有“匮乏”或“需求”的概念，柔软、澄澈、无所 欠缺 。这是一种存在本身的圆满，就像一滴水 ，它已是水本身，不需成为海洋 才能成全自己 。然而随着成长，我们渐渐失去了这份圆满。我们开始“区 分”，世界被划分为对立的两极：好与坏 、有与无 、成功与失败、我与他人 ... 从一体到分裂，我们在学会表达的同时，也开始误以为语言就是现实，误以为 概念所指的就是“真实的我”。从此，我们不再相信自己原是完整的，而是不断 向外寻找“让自己更完整”的东西。 佛法里说：“迷时众生，觉时即佛。”圆满，其实从未离开过我们 。它不过 是被层层迷雾遮蔽了，我们只是暂时忘了，自己本来是谁 。找回圆满，并不是 “变得更好”，而是“成为那个原本 、真实的自己”。人生，或许正是一场从完整 中出发，在千变万化中穿越破碎，最终照见生命深处那份美好与明亮，重新归 于完整的旅程 。
viewingNote.en: I walked over to the car, opened the box, and took out the stone sculpture of the Guru—the one we had put off photographing for so long. "We still have this Guru statue that hasn't been photographed yet," I said. "I think the perfect moment has finally arrived. And that moment is the light you are radiating right now—simple, vivid, nuanced, and brimming with power." With a shy smile, Zhadui accepted the statue with both hands, gently raised it above his head, and softly recited a string of scriptures. "The Guru's head feels so perfectly round," Zhadui remarked with a smile. I nodded: "Indeed, this is exactly how the Guru looked during his lifetime. His facial features possess a substantial visual weight—particularly his eyes, which are rendered with such clarity and meticulous detail that the whites, irises, and pupils are sharply defined, imparting a powerful sense of realism. His eyebrows are slender and elongated, and his lips are touched with a subtle hint of red pigment. The entire face, thanks to its realistic execution, appears extraordinarily lifelike—as if it were truly flesh and blood. Furthermore, precisely because of the visual weight his features carry within the context of his head, our gaze is instinctively drawn to scrutinize his overall expression at first glance—capturing the subtle, dynamic nuances of the figure as a whole." Pointing to the statue, I continued: "Now, observe his *prabhamandala*—the halo behind him. Although it is substantial in mass and intricately adorned, one’s gaze invariably settles first upon his face. That expression... it resembles a spring of water: pure, crystal-clear, and radiating both joy and unwavering faith—a translucence and self-assurance that flow naturally from the deep sedimentation of wisdom." Zhadui gazed intently at the statue; after a moment of contemplation, he spoke slowly: "He appears so compassionate and simple, yet he seems enveloped by an energy I cannot quite articulate." "Viewed from the front, he appears approachable and accessible; yet from the side, he exudes a profound solemnity. One can sense that, even while selecting the raw stone, the craftsman was already contemplating how best to choose the material to faithfully recreate his own understanding and vision of the Guru. Throughout the carving process, the craftsman engaged in a true act of 'seeking the form within the stone.' Judging by the sculpted volume of the Guru’s figure—as well as the harmony and seamless integration of the halo and the pedestal—it appears the artisan exercised extreme restraint and caution during the carving process, striving to 'follow the stone' as much as possible in order to preserve the figure’s inherent visual weight and spiritual aura." I continued my commentary: "Look at this halo: the woven texture of its outer ring resembles twisted hemp rope, while the mythical beasts adorning the *Prabhamandala* (*Liunaju*) possess a lively, spirited demeanor. The pedestal features carved treasure vases and a procession of elephants that seem to have stepped straight out of a fairy tale; the entire work, amidst its intricate complexity, radiates an air of solemnity and spirituality. Both the mythical beasts on the halo and the elephants on the pedestal appear as if they have emerged from a realm of fantasy, imbued with an ethereal, sprite-like quality. A treasure vase is carved into the center of the pedestal, flanked on either side by panels of intricate ornamentation, lending the entire statue—amidst its complexity..." Within its complexity, a noble and vivid atmosphere emerged. Dominated by hues of red and yellow, the coloring was at once bright and subdued—highlighting the Guru’s inherent nobility. "Consequently," I observed, "the piece as a whole radiates an aura of solemnity and emotional intensity." Zhadui, who had been listening raptly, suddenly spoke with earnestness: "This statue... it captures the very essence of our Tibetan character." I paused, taken aback: "How so?" He smiled: "Stone is rough and hard, yet once carved, it can reveal expressions of tenderness and vivid vitality. It is just like us Tibetans: we may appear rugged and unrefined—perhaps even a bit clumsy with our words—but deep down, our hearts are actually very soft. It is a kind of rustic simplicity—unfussy and unconstrained, yet harboring a subtle delicacy within its roughness." I responded softly: "Yes, exactly. Outwardly open-hearted and free-spirited; inwardly sensitive and clear. You are just the same—bright and beautiful." With the floodgates of conversation now open, Zhadui suddenly grew serious: "Sister, did you know? We Tibetans do not fear death, for we believe in reincarnation." "I remember a museum in New York dedicated primarily to Tibetan culture—the Rubin Museum," I recalled. "They once hosted an exhibition titled: 'Death Is Not the End.'" Zhadui nodded: "We practice our spiritual disciplines, chant mantras, offer butter lamps, and make pilgrimages around sacred mountains. These acts, which may appear repetitive, are actually constant reminders to ourselves: to maintain mindfulness and to strive to be good human beings. For this world is so noisy; we must practice repeatedly lest we lose our way." He paused, his tone slow yet firm: "If a person’s intentions remain good throughout their life—even after their physical body vanishes—that root of goodness will guide them to a beautiful place in the next cycle, the next reincarnation." I added: "In physics, this is known as the 'Law of Conservation of Energy.' Energy does not vanish into thin air; it merely transforms into a different state. Viewed from that perspective, we never truly leave; we simply continue to exist in another form. Death and rebirth cycle together, coexisting in perfect harmony." Zhadui suddenly spoke with a playful twinkle in his eye: "Then perhaps... perhaps there is some kind of energy hidden within these statues, too?" I gazed at the silent figure of the Guru, smiling to myself. Yes. Every trace left by a life’s passage is quietly recorded by the universe. The physical body will eventually return to dust, yet the spirit will continue to exist in another form—as thoughts, memories, will, or perhaps a sculpted figure... From within the cabin came the sharp, violent wailing of an infant—like a sudden clap of thunder in early spring—piercing the confined air and exploding right beside my ears. I was suddenly jolted awake from my dream state, my consciousness breaking free from a hazy realm of weightless tranquility. Before my eyes lay the familiar scene of the cabin: soft lighting, unfamiliar faces, and a tapestry of interwoven whispers and breaths. It took me a moment to realign my body with my consciousness. The crying continued unabated. Yet, for some inexplicable reason, the sound—which had initially struck me as jarring—began to resonate differently within me once I was fully awake. It felt like a summons from the very dawn of life—pure, primal, and utterly unmasked; like a long-lost "beginning." At birth, we are inherently complete, devoid of any concept of "scarcity" or "need"—soft, lucid, and lacking nothing. This is the perfection inherent in existence itself; much like a single drop of water, it is already water in its entirety and need not become the ocean to fulfill its true nature. However, as we grow, we gradually lose this sense of wholeness. We begin to "discriminate," dividing the world into opposing poles: good and bad, presence and absence, success and failure, self and other... Transitioning from unity to fragmentation, we learn to express ourselves through language, yet in doing so, we begin to mistake language for reality—mistaking the concepts it denotes for our "true selves." From that moment on, we cease to believe in our own innate completeness; instead, we constantly look outward, searching for things to make us "more whole." As the Buddha taught: "In delusion, we are sentient beings; in awakening, we are the Buddha." In truth, this wholeness has never truly left us. It has merely been obscured by layers of mist; we have simply, for a time, forgotten who we truly are. Reclaiming this wholeness is not about "becoming better," but rather about "becoming the original, authentic self." Life, perhaps, is precisely this journey: setting out from a place of wholeness, traversing the fragmentation and flux of the world, and ultimately glimpsing the beauty and radiance deep within the core of existence—thereby returning, once again, to a state of wholeness.

excerpt.en: A Densatil-related image of Jnanadakini, rich in ornament yet structurally disciplined.

viewingNote.zh: 在西藏佛教雕塑艺术史上，丹萨替造像无疑是一种最具影响的造像风格，它以 完美的造型、雄健的躯体 、繁缛的装饰 、精致的工艺，不仅展现了西藏佛像艺术史上 空前绝后的壮美艺术风范，而且也见证了一个家族 、一个教派的兴衰历史；曾经雄伟 壮丽的丹萨替寺现已失去了往日的光彩，所以这些精美的造像更显得弥足珍贵 。 此尊智慧空行母三面六臂，束高发髻，发丝盘束有致 ，髻顶装饰金刚杵，佩戴骷 髅宝冠，骷髅嘴里吐出的璎珞垂于空行母额前，华丽精美 ，极具装饰性 。宽额丰 颐 ，面部饱满，鼻梁高挺 ，呲牙咧嘴，三目圆瞪 ，杏仁状的大眼使得表情静穆又慈 悲，神情具有强烈的穿透力 。双耳垂肩，佩戴镶嵌了宝石的圆形耳珰 。上身披十字 瑜伽带，并有长蛇在身前及腰间缠束，蛇在藏传佛教中代表贪婪，以蛇为饰代表对 贪欲的降服 。手脚佩戴的臂钏刻画的极为精细，连珠纹颗颗饱满 、分明，穿插关系 明显 。六臂依次探出，三只右手分别持有法杖、金刚斧钺 、金刚杵；左手持颅碗 、金 刚铃。佛像塑造之时，凡遇多臂形象者，手臂间的位置与角度在造型中美感的体现 极为重要，此处的六只手臂分为三层，错落有致 ，在身侧形成两道优雅的扇形，和谐 巧妙，各手指姿态皆有细微变化，有韵律地带给雕塑一种奋发向上的气势。空母行 盘腿而坐 ，腿上有垂落的璎珞，脚掌刻画写实细腻 。 坐骑雄狮匍匐于莲台之上，造型生动，形态逼真 ，似乎正在咆哮怒吼，颈上有 髦，颈下系铃和璎珞，背上垂挂的璎珞均镶嵌宝石，足显富贵；其体态健壮，尤其四 腿肌肉线条饱满圆润，似蓄力欲起身，颇具动势。狮尾竖向弯曲垂于背上，毛发纤屡 皆细刻而出 。狮子身下为单层覆式莲花座 ，莲瓣饱满秀长 ，层次丰富，周匝环绕 。 此尊气势恢宏的智慧空行母像，材质厚重 ，整像造形完美 ，比例精准，结构复杂，人 物敦实饱满，金色醇厚，镶嵌华丽灿然 ，应为丹萨替寺鼎盛时期的作品 。
viewingNote.en: In the history of Tibetan Buddhist sculptural art, the Densatil style undoubtedly stands as one of the most influential traditions. Characterized by perfect forms, robust physiques, intricate ornamentation, and exquisite craftsmanship, this style not only showcases an artistic grandeur unparalleled in the history of Tibetan Buddhist imagery but also bears witness to the rise and fall of a specific lineage and religious sect. The once-majestic and magnificent Densatil Monastery has now lost its former glory; consequently, these exquisite sculptures have become all the more precious and invaluable. This particular figure—a Wisdom Dakini—is depicted with three faces and six arms. Her hair is gathered into a high topknot, the strands arranged with meticulous order; the apex of the knot is surmounted by a *vajra* (thunderbolt), while she wears a crown adorned with skulls. Garlands of jewels—issuing from the mouths of the skulls—cascade down across the Dakini’s forehead, creating a lavish, exquisite, and highly decorative effect. She possesses a broad forehead and full cheeks; her face is plump and rounded, featuring a high-bridged nose, bared fangs, and three wide-staring eyes. Yet, her large, almond-shaped eyes lend her expression a sense of profound serenity and compassion, imbuing her gaze with an intense, penetrating power. Her earlobes hang low to her shoulders, adorned with circular earrings inlaid with gemstones. Her upper torso is draped with a crossed yogic sash, while long serpents coil around her front and waist—in Tibetan Buddhism, the serpent symbolizes greed, and its use as an adornment signifies the subjugation of covetous desires. The armbands and anklets adorning her limbs are rendered with exceptional precision; the "bead-chain" patterns are depicted as full, distinct, and intricately interwoven. Her six arms extend outward in a rhythmic sequence: the three right hands hold, respectively, a staff, a *vajra* axe, and a *vajra*; the left hands hold a skull cup and a *vajra* bell. In the creation of multi-armed Buddhist sculptures, the positioning and angles of the arms are crucial to the aesthetic harmony of the overall composition. Here, the six arms are arranged in three distinct tiers, staggered with elegant balance to form two graceful, fan-like arcs on either side of the body—a design both harmonious and ingenious. The gestures of her individual fingers exhibit subtle variations, collectively imparting to the sculpture a dynamic, upward-soaring energy. The Dakini sits cross-legged; garlands of jewels cascade over her legs, while her feet are rendered with a realism and delicacy that is truly lifelike. The mount—a majestic lion—crouches upon a lotus pedestal. Its modeling is vivid and lifelike, appearing as though it is in the very act of roaring furiously. A flowing mane adorns its neck, beneath which hang a bell and elaborate necklaces (*yingluo*); the necklaces draped across its back are richly inlaid with gemstones, underscoring an air of opulence. The lion’s physique is robust and muscular—particularly its four legs, which feature full, rounded contours—suggesting a coiled energy as if poised to spring to its feet, thereby imbuing the piece with a strong sense of dynamic motion. The lion’s tail curves upward before cascading down over its back, with every individual strand of hair meticulously and finely carved. Beneath the lion lies a single-tiered, inverted lotus pedestal featuring full, slender petals arranged in rich, concentric layers that encircle the base. This magnificent statue of the Wisdom Dakini is crafted from substantial material; the figure as a whole boasts perfect form, precise proportions, and intricate structural complexity. The deity is rendered with a solid, full-bodied presence; the gilding possesses a mellow, rich luster; and the gemstone inlay is resplendent and lavish. This masterpiece is almost certainly a creation dating from the zenith of the Densatil Monastery.
