viewingNote.zh:
石头很硬，匠人却偏要用它表现世上最薄的东西——贴在颧骨上的皮肤，眼窝里的一点暗影，还有额上浮起的血管。这是一张被饥饿慢慢改变的脸。双颊已经凹陷，下颌的轮廓几乎无处遮藏，只有头顶的肉髻在告诉着人们，祂是苦修中的悉达多——后来被称为佛陀的人。

在距离祂生活时代的两千多年后，祂的智慧依旧在被后世敬仰、学习。祂并非生来知道中道。中道，是他走到另一条路的尽头以后，才找到的。

悉达多生活的时代，北印度有很多离开家庭的修行者。他们舍弃财产，独自走入山林，以禁欲、节食、静坐和忍受痛苦来寻找解脱。这些人被称为沙门。他们相信欲望把人系在生死之中；身体有多少要求，人便会有多少牵挂。若能克制它，甚至战胜它，人也许就能获得一种不再受制于身体的自由。苦修在当时并不属于一种古怪行为。相反，它是一条受人尊敬的路。因为一个人能忍受常人不能忍受的饥饿、寒冷和孤独，人们便就相信，他也许拥有了更坚定的心和更高的精神力量。悉达多也走进了这条路。

宫廷生活优渥，却无法回答衰老、疾病和死亡的问题。既然享乐不能使人自由，于是悉达多便转向了享乐的反面。祂曾经相信，快乐不能通过快乐获得，只有经过痛苦，才能抵达真正的快乐。于是悉达多约束心念，控制呼吸，最后把每天的食物减到最少。早期佛典形容，那时祂的脊柱像一串珠子，肋骨像旧屋上裸露的椽木；用手摸腹部，仿佛可以隔着薄薄的皮肤触到自己的背脊。这些文字中记录的形象到了犍陀罗匠人的手中，变成了石头上的眼窝、颧骨、血管和肌肉。那位匠人像是了解剖学般，将瘦骨嶙峋的皮肤下结构呈现得如此清晰、明了。苦修中的悉达多，脸虽然消瘦，但神情却没有散乱。充满信念的实践，使其充满力量。

悉达多后来回忆，世上那些苦行者所能体验的剧烈痛苦，祂已经体验过了；但这样的痛苦并没有使其获得更高的智慧。而是开始了反思：如果已经付出这么多，这条路可能走错了？这时，他想起少年时的一件小事。那一年，他坐在树荫下，周围没有喧闹，也没有人要求他克服什么。心自然而然安静下来，进入一种清明而带有喜悦的禅定。他忽然问自己：为什么要害怕这样的快乐？

那不是感官满足带来的兴奋，也不是对某件东西的占有。它很平静、清醒，也不使人沉迷。也许，真正的觉悟并不需要把身体毁坏；也许，一个奄奄一息的人，已经没有足够的气力去看清自己的心了。

于是，在苦修的尽头，他开始重新进食。后来的佛传把这顿食物写成一碗乳粥，由一位名叫苏阇多的女子送来。但当悉达多开始进食时，五位一起共同苦修的同伴却失望地离开了。他们以为悉达多贪图安逸，已经放弃求道。林中重新安静下来。那碗食物没有使祂立即觉悟，只让其身体逐渐恢复，也让祂有力气重新思考。

“中道”便从这样的转身中萌发了出来，它也成为了悟道的重要转折。

过去，人们容易用承受了多少痛苦，来判断一个人离真理有多近。佛陀则开始追问：这样的修行，究竟是会使人更加清醒、自由，还是只是制造了另一种执着？后来，极端的断食被转化成了对饮食分量的觉察；强行压制的心念，被转化成了辨认念头如何生起，又如何消失的机缘。身体不再是必须击败的敌人，而是成为了理解生命的地方。可以感受快乐，但却不被快乐掌控；可以承受痛苦，但却不把痛苦奉为真理。所以，中道不是站在两个极端的正中，而是不再被任何一个极端占有。

许多年后，犍陀罗人将苦修中的悉达多刻像怀念。他们并没有遮掩这段看似走错的路。反而这张消瘦的脸却在告诉我们：人真正的改变，始于不再执着于快乐，也不再执着于痛苦的时候。
viewingNote.en:
Stone is hard, yet the sculptor chose to render with it the thinnest thing in the world: skin drawn tight over the cheekbones, a faint shadow pooling in the eye sockets, veins rising along the brow. This is a face gradually reshaped by hunger. The cheeks have hollowed, the line of the jaw left almost nowhere to hide, and only the uṣṇīṣa at the crown of the head tells us who this is — Siddhartha in the midst of ascetic practice, the man who would later be known as the Buddha.

More than two thousand years after his lifetime, his wisdom is still revered and studied. He was not born already knowing the Middle Way. He found it only after walking another path to its very end.

In Siddhartha's time, northern India had no shortage of renunciants who had left their households behind. They gave up their possessions and went alone into the forests and mountains, seeking liberation through celibacy, fasting, meditation, and the endurance of hardship. These practitioners were known as shramanas. They held that desire binds a person to the cycle of birth and death, and that whatever the body demanded, the mind would remain attached to. If desire could be restrained, even overcome, a person might attain a freedom no longer bound to the body. Ascetic practice was not, at the time, regarded as strange behavior. On the contrary, it was a respected path: because a person could endure hunger, cold, and solitude beyond what ordinary people could bear, others came to believe that he possessed a firmer mind and a higher spiritual strength. Siddhartha, too, set out on this path.

Palace life was comfortable, but it offered no answer to old age, illness, and death. Since pleasure could not set a person free, Siddhartha turned toward its opposite. He came to believe that happiness could not be reached through happiness, that only through suffering could one arrive at true happiness. He disciplined his thoughts, controlled his breath, and eventually reduced his daily food to almost nothing. Early Buddhist texts describe his spine as resembling a string of beads, and his ribs as bare as the exposed rafters of an old house; pressing a hand to his stomach, he could feel, through the thin layer of skin, the bones of his own back. These images, recorded in scripture, passed into the hands of Gandhara's sculptors and became, in stone, eye sockets, cheekbones, veins, and muscle. The sculptor worked as though he understood anatomy itself, rendering the structure beneath the emaciated skin with striking clarity. Siddhartha's face, in the depths of ascetic practice, is gaunt, yet his expression remains gathered, not scattered. A practice sustained by conviction gave him strength even in this state.

Siddhartha later recalled that he had already experienced the most extreme suffering any ascetic in the world could undergo, and that this suffering had not brought him any higher wisdom. Instead, it prompted him to reflect: having given so much already, might this path be the wrong one? At this point, he remembered a small moment from his youth. That year, sitting in the shade of a tree, with no commotion around him and no one asking him to overcome anything, his mind had settled on its own into a state of clear, joyful meditative absorption. He suddenly asked himself: why should this kind of happiness be something to fear?

That happiness was not the excitement of sensory gratification, nor the possession of some object. It was calm, lucid, and did not draw the mind into indulgence. Perhaps true awakening did not require the destruction of the body. Perhaps someone on the verge of death simply no longer had the strength left to see his own mind clearly.

So, at the end of his ascetic practice, he began to eat again. Later accounts of the Buddha's life describe this meal as a bowl of milk-rice, offered by a woman named Sujata. But when Siddhartha began eating, the five companions who had practiced austerities alongside him left in disappointment, believing he had succumbed to comfort and abandoned his search for awakening. The forest fell quiet again. That bowl of food did not bring him immediate enlightenment; it only allowed his body to gradually recover, and gave him the strength to think again.

The Middle Way emerged from this very turn, and it became a crucial turning point on the road to awakening.

In the past, people tended to judge how close a person stood to the truth by how much suffering they could endure. The Buddha began instead to ask a different question: does this kind of practice actually bring greater clarity and freedom, or does it simply create another form of attachment? In time, extreme fasting gave way to a mindful awareness of how much one eats; the forceful suppression of thought gave way to the practice of observing how thoughts arise and pass away. The body was no longer an enemy to be defeated, but became instead a place through which life could be understood. One could feel pleasure without being ruled by it, and bear pain without enshrining it as truth. The Middle Way, then, is not a position exactly midway between two extremes — it is the state of no longer being possessed by either one.

Many years later, the people of Gandhara carved images of Siddhartha in ascetic practice to hold this memory. They made no attempt to conceal what might look, in hindsight, like a wrong turn. If anything, this gaunt face tells us something else entirely: real change in a person begins only when one stops clinging to all that is fleeting.

subtitle.zh: 光没有形状，可人类却一次次在试图寻找光的边界。

excerpt.en: Standing Buddha

viewingNote.zh:
光原本没有形状。

它抓不住、摸不到。可人类却一次次在试图寻找光的边界：一轮圆盘、一圈放射线、一层包围全身的光晕。我们为什么如此执着？

或许因为，人类一直共同面对着一个古老的难题：越重要的东西，往往越看不见。智慧没有轮廓，觉悟没有颜色，尊严、希望和安全感也无法被直接雕刻出来。既然如此，那一种只存在于个人内心的感受，要怎样进入共同体？它要怎样被讲述，被记住，被一代代人反复辨认？人类给出的答案之一，就是让光拥有形状。于是，人们用太阳、火焰、圆环和向外散开的线条等这些原本属于自然现象的形式，来表现那些自然中看不见，却被认为值得共同相信的价值。

我们眼前这尊佛陀雕塑，正是这样一件作品。

这件作品出自大约5世纪左右的大犍陀罗文化区。佛陀优雅站立，身披覆式僧衣，右手举起，作无畏印，左手拎着衣角向外伸出。佛陀身后，头光、身光和放射状外缘层层展开，构成了一套完整的复合背光。那一圈圈向外伸展的光，像火焰，又像花苞，也像不断向四周生长的能量边界。它使这尊原本尺寸不算大的雕塑，突然拥有了一种超出自身尺度的精神体量。

那这种精神体量究竟从何而来？

如果只从佛教内部解释，答案似乎很简单：佛经文本里本来就有佛陀放光的传统。文本中的光，它可以照耀世界，可以象征智慧，也可以标示某种超越性的出现。可问题是，文本提供的是“光的意义”，而不是“光的形状”。但到了雕塑里，匠人必须解决另一个问题：

光究竟应该长什么样？

一个问题将我们带回了作品的诞生地——犍陀罗。

大犍陀罗位于今天巴基斯坦西北部和阿富汗东部的广大区域之间。它连接着白沙瓦盆地、塔克西拉、斯瓦特、喀布尔河谷，并进一步通向中亚与印度平原。由于这里长期处在南亚、中亚和地中海世界之间的交通来往中。希腊化传统、伊朗元素、印度宗教图像、贵霜时期的政治与货币网络，都曾在这里发生交汇；不同政治力量，也带来了各自的图像、材料与制作传统。所以，真正把无形变成有形的，是匠人，也是匠人所处的文明环境。

于是，当站在这尊雕塑面前，我们看到的是多层不同时间的形式在这里沉积。

肉髻、白毫、长耳垂、僧衣、无畏印以及正面礼拜关系，则来自佛教关于佛身、身份、智慧与救护能力的理解。双肩覆盖的僧衣、胸前层层下垂的弧形衣褶，以及优雅的站姿、卷曲的头发、建筑结构式的台座和用线条暗示身体体积的方式，都能追溯到犍陀罗早期对希腊化和罗马古典披衣传统的吸收。它经过贵霜时期石雕、寺院、工坊的反复使用，已经成为了犍陀罗辨认佛陀的一种地方语言。佛陀较为圆润的面部、柔和的五官和清澈的神情，又让人联想到晚期犍陀罗与阿富汗灰泥造像中越来越柔软、内向的面容处理。至于镶银的双眼，更重要的作用或许不是证明某一种地域来源，而是让目光真正从金属中亮起来。眼睛不再只是被铸出的凹凸。它开始回应观看者。

真正复杂的，还是佛陀身后的光。

在当时的视觉世界里，人们早已熟悉太阳神的放射冠、君王与神祇周围的光辉，以及伊朗传统中关于荣耀和权力合法性的观念。贵霜钱币也不断让王者、神祇、火坛和放射性图像在流通中被人看见。但与此同时，佛教文本也早已用光来说明佛陀的智慧、显现和超越。所以，这圈背光不是某个外来符号被原样搬进佛教。更准确地说，是佛教在一片早已充满光辉图像的文化环境中，找到了适合表达自身的形式，然后重新解释了它。虽然形式的经历很复杂，但它最终要说的话，已经改变了。

如果把时间往前推，以大都会博物馆收藏的这件公元1—2世纪左右的犍陀罗铜造像为例。我们会看到犍陀罗当地很早便开始了用金属塑造独立的佛陀形象。早期造像的光，往往仍集中在头部周围。锯齿状放射状的光环表面还保留着金箔痕迹。这件作品非常关键，因为它告诉我们，犍陀罗艺术家很早就已经在做两件事：一是用锯齿边缘把“光正在向外散射”这件事表现出来，二是用金属和金箔让光真的在现实中反射。也就是说，光不再只是被说出来，而是被做出来了。

到了本次展览的这件作品，事情又向前走了一步。

这时的光，已经不满足于停留在佛陀头部后面。它扩大了，从头部扩展到整个身体，从人物背后的一个小圆形，发展成了包围全身的完整结构。光不再只是“身份标记”，而变成了“空间边界”。佛陀被包裹其中，造像也因此获得了一个相对完整、自足的视觉场域。即使离开大型佛塔、石窟或寺院建筑，这尊小型金属佛仍然能够凭借自身的轮廓，制造出一个与周围空间不同的中心。我们不能因此断言它一定会随身被携带，也不能把它直接称为一座“随身寺院”，但至少在形式上，它已经具备了一种新的能力：

它不再完全依靠建筑来证明自己处在中心。

它把中心带在了自己身上。

但这件事发生在一个并不平静的时代。约4世纪末至5世纪初，犍陀罗地区礼拜性造像的尺度和图像结构变得更加复杂；到了5世纪末，传统核心地区的寺院赞助开始衰退，而阿富汗地区的艺术生产仍持续发展。政权变化、交通路线的调整以及赞助结构的改变，共同塑造了这个阶段。

在大型纪念性建筑和小型金属造像并存、寺院往来和交通路线不断变化的环境里，一种能让佛身自身形成完整视觉空间的形式，则获得了更强的凸显。于是，当一尊造像离开了宏大的建筑，它又仍然需要一种方式，告诉观者中心在哪里？那圈光，就承担了这个使命。

写到这里，我们也很容易落入另一种过于轻松的叙述：仿佛文明只要相遇，就一定会诞生更美的艺术。事实并不是这样。文明之间的接触，从来不只有友善的互鉴。它也伴随着扩张、竞争、迁徙、征服、误读与暴力。犍陀罗之所以复杂，恰恰因为这里的边界从来不温柔。形式能够越过边界，但形式穿越边界的过程，并不总是和平的。所以，一种文化真正值得讨论的地方，不只是它吸收了多少外来形式，而是它能不能把这些形式转化为表达自身问题的语言。

这或许比“纯粹”更重要。

所谓文化自信，如果只是不断证明自己不需要任何外部影响，那种自信其实非常脆弱。它必须不停划分边界，也必须把所有相似视为威胁。更可靠的自信，是一种转化能力，因为它知道什么是自己真正不能放弃的东西。就像光环的前史和演变，当它进入佛陀图像之后，它已经被重新解释。它不再只说明太阳、火焰、王权或神祇身份。它开始说明一种觉醒如何超脱肉身、一种不可见的智慧如何获得可见的边界。

犍陀罗真正留下来的，也正是这种能力。

一千六百多年过去了，当现代的我们面对着这尊雕塑时，尽管它的铸造者已经无名、它最初所在的空间也可能永远无法恢复，但那圈被塑成了形状的光，想传达给我们的思索，仍然越过了地理、语言、宗教和时间的边界。最终，我们会发现，这件作品最终想说的不只是文明交流，也不只是佛陀身后的背光。它真正触及的是一个更古老的问题：人类为什么始终相信，那些看不见的价值，值得被一次次赋予形状？
viewingNote.en:
Light is without shape.

It cannot be held or touched, and yet people have gone to considerable lengths to give it an outline— a disc, a ring, a halo. Why does this pursuit persist?

Perhaps because the things that matter most are usually the hardest to see. Wisdom has no outline of its own; enlightenment has no color; ideas like dignity or hope resist direct representation. So how does something that exists only in a person's mind become part of a shared world — something that can be passed down, recognized, and remembered by people who never knew each other?

One solution people arrived at, again and again, was to borrow shapes that light puts on in nature — the sun, flame, a ring of radiance — and use them to give visible form to values that have none of their own.

The Buddha sculpture before us is one such work.

Dated to around the 5th century and produced somewhere within greater Gandhāra, the sculpture shows the Buddha standing, robed in a monastic garment that falls loosely over both shoulders, right hand raised in abhaya mudra, the left holding a fold of his robe. Behind him, a head halo, a body halo, and an outer radiating rim stack in layers to form a single continuous mandorla. The bands of light ripple outward like flame, like petals opening, like the edge of something still expanding. This halo gives a fairly modest object a sense of scale well beyond its actual size.

Where does that sense of scale come from?

The answer is easy enough if explained through Buddhism: Buddhist texts describe the Buddha as radiating light — light that illuminates the world, stands in for wisdom, and signals that something beyond the ordinary is present. But a text can tell you what light means; it can't tell you what it looks like. That was left to the sculptor to work out.

Greater Gandhāra covered a wide swath of what is now northwestern Pakistan and eastern Afghanistan — the Peshawar basin, Taxila, Swat, the Kabul river valley — with connections reaching further into Central Asia and the Indian plains. For centuries it sat at a genuine crossroads: Hellenistic sculptural habits, Iranian visual conventions, Indian religious imagery, and the trade and political networks of the Kushan empire all passed through here, each wave of rulers bringing its own images, materials, and workshops along with it. Therefore, light was given shape not only by the craftsmen but also by the cosmopolitan environment surrounding them.

So it's no surprise the sculpture reads as a stack of different periods.

The ushnisha, the urna, the elongated earlobes, the robe, the abhaya mudra, the frontal pose meant for worship — all of that comes out of Buddhist ideas about the Buddha's body, his identity, his wisdom, his power to save. The way the robe falls over both shoulders in cascading, arced folds, the relaxed stance, the waved hair, the architectural base, even the way carved lines suggest a body underneath the drapery, all trace back to Gandhāra's early borrowing of Hellenistic and Roman drapery conventions, filtered again and again through generations of Kushan-period stone carvers until it became simply the local way of representing the Buddha. The rounded face, the softened features, the calm expression echo the increasingly gentle, inward mood of later Gandhāran and Afghan stucco figures. As for the silver-inlaid eyes, they probably say less about where the piece was made than about how alive the face was meant to look.

The halo is the more complicated part.

People at the time were already familiar with visual arts such as the sun god's radiate crown, the radiance surrounding kings and deities, and the old Iranian idea that legitimate rule comes wrapped in visible glory. Kushan coins put rulers, gods, fire altars, and haloed figures into everyday circulation. Buddhist texts, meanwhile, had their own long-standing habit of using light to talk about wisdom and transcendence. So the halo wasn't some foreign motif bolted onto Buddhism from outside. It's closer to say that Buddhism arrived in a world already full of radiant imagery, recognized a form that suited what it was trying to say, and made that form its own — even if the form's earlier history was more complicated than that.

Go back a little further and you can watch this happen. A Gandhāran bronze Buddha from around the 1st–2nd century, now in the Metropolitan Museum of Art, shows the region already casting independent Buddha images in metal at a very early date. Here the light stays close to the head, and traces of gold leaf still cling to the jagged points of the halo. What's notable is that Gandhāran artists were already doing two separate things this early: cutting a serrated edge to suggest radiating light, and using actual metal and gold leaf to make that light physically catch and throw back real light. Light wasn't just being described anymore. It was being built.

By the time we reach the piece under discussion, the idea has developed further still.

Light no longer stops at the head. It has spread down to cover the whole body, growing from a small disc into a full enclosure around the figure. It has stopped being simply a marker of identity and become something closer to a boundary of space. This creates a self-contained visual field that generate its own center of gravity, regardless of where it originally stood. That doesn't mean it was made to be carried or worn, and it isn't quite right to call it a "portable shrine" either. However, one thing we are sure of is that the sculpture stands well alone without the need for subsidiary elements.

It is its own center.

None of this happened in especially settled times. Between the late 4th and early 5th centuries, devotional images in Gandhāra grew larger and iconographically more elaborate; by the late 5th century, monastic patronage in the historic core of the region was already declining, even as production in Afghanistan kept going strong. Political upheaval, shifting trade routes, and changing patterns of patronage all left their mark on this period.

In a world where enormous commemorative monuments existed alongside small portable brasses, and where monastic and trade networks kept reshaping themselves, an image that could generate its own complete visual space, independent of any building, became genuinely useful. Once a figure left the monument behind, it still needed some way of telling a viewer where to look. The halo did that job.

It would be easy, at this point, to slide into a comforting story: civilizations meet, and beautiful art results. That is not the case. Contact between cultures has never been simply a matter of friendly borrowing — it has come bundled with expansion, rivalry, migration, conquest, misunderstanding, and violence. Gandhāra's art is complicated precisely because its borders never were gentle. Forms travel across those borders, but rarely peacefully. Which is why the more interesting question about any culture isn't how much it borrowed from outside, but what it did with what it borrowed — whether it could turn foreign material into a language of its own.

That is what may matter more.

A culture that defines its own confidence purely by insisting it owes nothing to anyone else is, in practice, not very confident at all — it has to keep defending its borders and treating every resemblance as an accusation. A more durable kind of confidence comes from the ability to absorb and transform while keeping the things that are worth holding onto. The halo's history makes the point: once it entered Buddhist art, it started to be understood in more ways. It stopped standing simply for the sun, or fire, or royal authority, or divine status, and started expressing — how enlightenment moves beyond the body, how an invisible thing like wisdom may take on a visible edge.

In the end, Gandhāra teaches us the power of transformation.More than sixteen hundred years later, we stand in front of this sculpture without knowing who made it or where it originally stood, and the idea behind that ring of light still persists — across geography, language, religion, time. What this piece entails , in the end, isn't only the meeting of civilizations or the halo behind the Buddha. It makes us wonder:

Why does humanity insist on giving shape to things that have none?

subtitle.zh: 当世界仍在运动，我心却已不再动摇。

excerpt.en: Seated Buddha

viewingNote.zh:
八月的成都，气温一度超过四十摄氏度。人在室外站上几分钟，衣服便贴在身上，连空气都像有了重量。

在这样的天气里，再看这尊来自摩揭陀文化核心区的佛陀像，那件薄得几乎消失的僧衣，忽然变得具体起来。

南比哈尔本就有漫长的炎热季节。季风抵达之前，恒河平原与伽耶丘陵持续处于酷热之中；季风到来以后，高温又与湿气、暴雨和上涨的河水交织在一起。十世纪生活在这里的人，同样要面对这样的气候。于是，佛陀身上那件轻薄的僧衣，也有了可以被感知的现实背景。但气候只能帮助我们理解，人为什么需要轻薄的衣服。它无法单独回答，匠人为什么偏偏要把衣服雕刻成这样。一尊造像的形成，从来不是某个单一因素的结果。材料、工匠传统、图像规范、交通路线、寺院制度，以及一个时代如何想象“佛陀”，都在其中发挥作用。

这件僧衣不仅薄，还被有意识地“隐去”了。衣料紧贴身体，几乎没有打断胸腹与四肢的轮廓。它看似在表现衣服，最后凸显出来的，却是衣服下面那具完整、稳定而理想化的佛身。这种近乎透明的袈裟，并不是十世纪摩揭陀突然出现的创造。它延续了笈多时期萨尔纳特造像所形成的视觉传统：尽量减少衣纹对身体的切割，让衣服的物质感退到后面，使佛陀的精神状态直接通过身体显现出来。

炎热只是进入这件雕塑的第一条线索。答案显然还在更深的地方。

再看佛陀的面容。弯弓般的眉形，内敛的双眼，紧闭而饱满的双唇，以及略显修长的脸型，都带有摩揭陀地区造像鲜明的审美特征。佛陀的体态挺拔而充实，身体没有被繁复的珠宝和细节淹没。整件作品因此保留着一种强烈的古典气息：克制、宁静，不靠装饰堆砌的佛身本身充盈着神圣感。

不过，这种“古典”并不是对过去的简单复制。

十世纪的摩揭陀也不是地图上一个孤立的造像中心。它连接着菩提伽耶、那烂陀、王舍城、库尔基哈尔、欧丹多富梨和毗讫罗摩尸罗，也沿着恒河通向孟格尔、跋伽尔布尔等区域。寺院经济、石材开采与运输、朝圣活动、文本翻译、僧侣迁徙和私人捐献，共同维持着这个庞大的文化网络。佛造像正是在这样的网络中被制作、供奉和观看，又沿着人员与信仰流动的路线，去往更远的地方。我们也因此能在这件作品里看到不同传统留下的回响：贵霜时期马图拉造像强健、充盈的身体感；五世纪萨尔纳特造像内敛、精神化的佛身；以及十世纪前后，摩揭陀对圣地、建筑与图像布局的重新组织。

但如果只把它称作“多种风格的混合”，仍然不够。

摩揭陀的匠人并没有机械式地复制或拼凑原有的风格样本。他们把这些传统拆开、吸收，再转化成自己的语言。他们保留了完整的佛身，又在佛身周围加入石柱、横梁、莲瓣、瑞兽、菩提树和铭文。一个原本独立的人物形象，由此向外扩展，逐渐变成了一处可以被观看的圣地。

把视线从佛陀身上稍稍移开，整件作品的结构便开始显现。

佛陀盘坐于菩提树下。莲瓣向外展开，瑞兽分踞背光中段两侧以及底座两侧，石柱与横梁层层叠起，“缘起法颂”沿着头光展开。这些元素将佛陀的神性身份凸显，它们共同搭建出了一座完整的圣地建筑。整件作品上圆下方，外轮廓近似碑形，又像一座被压缩进石头里的佛龛。匠人没有把菩提伽耶原样缩小，而是提取出最能确认圣地身份的元素，再将它们重新组合。

于是，这件作品既是一尊佛陀造像，也是一座微缩的菩提道场。

它不只让人看见佛陀，还试图让那些无法亲临菩提伽耶的人，在一块石头前抵达圣地。

有意思的是，周围的结构越丰富，雕塑的中心反而越安静。

佛陀稳坐中央，右手越过膝部，触及大地。这一触，是以大地作为无数世修行与布施的见证，也是成道之前最关键的时刻。按照佛教叙事，此时魔王及其军队尚未真正离场。诱惑、恐惧和攻击仍然存在。但匠人没有表现奔袭的军队，没有雕刻夸张的搏斗，也没有用激烈的动作制造戏剧冲突。

他甚至有意把冲突拿掉了。

我们看到的只有佛陀：身体稳固，面容平静，右手触地。那些攻击并非没有发生，只是已经无法真正抵达他。外部世界依旧充满力量和变化，佛陀却不再被它左右。正是在这种“不动”之中，匠人手里的刻刀完成了一次重要的转化。“降魔”不再只是一场神与魔之间的战争。它被转化为一个更内在的瞬间：恐惧依旧存在，欲望和怀疑也没有凭空消失，但心识已经不再受它们支配。

真正被战胜的，不是外部某个具体的敌人，而是内心不断被外界牵动的状态。

头光两侧，燃灯佛与弥勒佛分别构成过去与未来的坐标。作为现在佛的释迦牟尼端坐中央，三者共同把一次具体的证悟拉入更长的时间尺度：在释迦牟尼之前，觉悟曾经发生；在他之后，觉悟仍会再次发生。佛陀成道由此不再只是历史中一个孤立的事件，而成为一条跨越过去、现在与未来的精神线索。三世佛的并列也在讲述：个体会离开，时代会更替，但觉悟的可能性，不会随着某一个人的离去而终结。

到了这里，这件雕塑真正想说的话才逐渐显现。

它表面上表现的是佛陀坐在菩提树下，实际上却在一块深色的千枚岩中，建立了一个关于内心秩序的命题。莲瓣仍在展开，瑞兽依旧分踞两侧，铭文依旧沿着头光延伸，石柱和横梁也依旧在不断向外张开。世界并没有因为佛陀成道而停止运动。恰恰相反，一切仍在发生。

改变的不是世界，而是中心与世界的关系。

中心不再被变化裹挟，周围的变化便不再只是混乱。它们开始获得方向，彼此建立关系，最终形成秩序。这里所说的“中心”，并不是控制一切，更不是要求世界按照自己的意愿运行。它只是意味着：当变化再次到来时，人不再轻易被变化带走。

这或许也是为什么，在一个酷热的成都午后，我们仍会被一尊千年前的摩揭陀石雕击中。

最初吸引我们的是那件薄衣，随后是佛陀的身体、面容、手势，以及周围那座被压缩进石头里的圣地。可看到最后才会发现，这件作品最终雕刻的，并不只是线条，也不只是佛陀。它雕刻的是一种状态：当世界仍然喧闹、炎热、潮湿，充满无法预料的变化时，一个人如何不再被世界推着走。

真正的稳定，从来不是让世界停止。

而是世界仍在运动，我心却已不再动摇。
viewingNote.en:
In August, Chengdu's temperature once climbed past forty degrees Celsius. Stand outside for a few minutes and your clothes begin to cling to your skin; even the air felt heavy.

Standing in such weather and looking at this Buddha image from the heartland of Magadha, everything suddenly becomes concrete. The monastic robe appears so thin one might think it could vanish at any moment.

Southern Bihar has always had a long hot season. Before the monsoon arrives, the Gangetic plain and the hills around Gaya endure sustained heat; once the monsoon comes, that heat intertwines with humidity, downpours, and rising rivers. People living here in the tenth century were facing the same climate. The Buddha's thin, light robe thus has a tangible, real-world backdrop. But climate alone can only help us understand why people needed lightweight clothing—it cannot by itself explain why the craftsman chose to carve the robe this way. No single image ever results from one factor alone. Materials, craft traditions, iconographic conventions, trade routes, monastic institutions, and how an era imagined ‘the Buddha’ all played a part.

This robe is not only thin—it has also been deliberately made almost to disappear. The fabric clings to the body, scarcely interrupting the contours of chest, torso, and limbs. Though it appears to depict clothing, what ultimately stands out is the complete, stable, idealized body of the Buddha beneath it. This nearly transparent robe was not a sudden invention of tenth-century Magadha. It continues the visual tradition established by Gupta-period Sarnath sculpture: minimizing how drapery folds cut across the body, letting the material presence of the robe recede, so that the Buddha's spiritual state can emerge directly through the body itself.

The heat is only the first thread leading into this sculpture. The real answer clearly lies deeper.

Look again at the Buddha's face. The bow-shaped eyebrows, the introspective eyes, the closed and full lips, and the slightly elongated shape of the face all carry the distinctive aesthetic of Magadha-region sculpture. The Buddha's posture is upright and full-bodied, unburdened by elaborate jewelry or ornamental detail. The whole work therefore retains a strong classical quality: restrained, serene, a sacredness that fills the Buddha's form without relying on decoration.

Yet this ‘classicism’ is not a simple repetition of the past.

Tenth-century Magadha was not an isolated center of image-making on the map. It was connected to Bodh Gaya, Nalanda, Rajgir, Kurkihar, Odantapuri, and Vikramashila, and linked along the Ganges to regions such as Monghyr and Bhagalpur. Monastic economies, stone quarrying and transport, pilgrimage, textual translation, the movement of monks, and private donations together sustained this vast cultural network. Buddha images were made, venerated, and viewed within this network, then carried further afield along the routes traveled by people and by faith. In this piece we can therefore hear echoes of different traditions: the robust, full-bodied physicality of Kushan-period Mathura sculpture; the restrained, spiritualized Buddha form of fifth-century Sarnath sculpture; and, around the tenth century, Magadha's reorganization of sacred sites, architecture, and pictorial composition.

But to call it merely a ‘mixture of styles’ still falls short.

The craftsmen of Magadha did not mechanically copy or splice together existing stylistic templates. They took these traditions apart, absorbed them, and transformed them into a language of their own. They kept the Buddha's body whole, while adding pillars, lintels, lotus petals, guardian beasts, the Bodhi tree, and inscriptions around it. A figure that was once a self-contained image thus expanded outward, gradually becoming a sacred site to be beheld.

Shift your gaze slightly away from the Buddha, and the structure of the whole work begins to reveal itself.

The Buddha sits cross-legged beneath the Bodhi tree. Lotus petals unfurl outward, guardian beasts flank the midsection of the halo and both sides of the base, pillars and lintels rise in tiers, and the ‘Ye Dharma Hetu’ verse runs along the halo. Together these elements underscore the Buddha's divine identity, jointly constructing a complete sacred architecture. Rounded above and rectangular below, the work's outer silhouette resembles a stele—or a shrine compressed into stone. The craftsman did not simply shrink down Bodh Gaya; instead, he extracted the elements that most confirm the site's sacred identity and recombined them.

The work is thus both an image of the Buddha and a miniature site of enlightenment.

It does more than let people see the Buddha—it tries to let those who cannot travel to Bodh Gaya in person arrive at the sacred site before a single stone.

Interestingly, the richer the surrounding structure becomes, the quieter the sculpture's center feels.

The Buddha sits firmly at the center, his right hand reaching past his knee to touch the earth. This gesture calls the earth to witness countless lifetimes of practice and generosity, and marks the most critical moment before enlightenment. According to Buddhist narrative, Mara and his armies had not yet truly departed at this point—temptation, fear, and attack were still present. But the craftsman did not depict charging armies, did not carve exaggerated combat, and did not use violent motion to stage dramatic conflict.

He even deliberately removed the conflict altogether.

What we see is only the Buddha: body steady, face calm, right hand touching the earth. Those attacks did not fail to happen—they simply could no longer reach him. The outer world remains full of force and change, yet the Buddha is no longer swayed by it. It is precisely within this ‘stillness’ that the carver's chisel accomplishes an essential transformation. ‘Defeating Mara’ is no longer merely a war between god and demon. It becomes a more inward moment instead: fear still exists, desire and doubt have not vanished into thin air, but the mind is no longer ruled by them.

What is truly overcome is not some specific enemy outside, but the inner state of being constantly pulled by the external world.

On either side of the halo, Dipankara Buddha and Maitreya Buddha mark the coordinates of past and future. Shakyamuni, the Buddha of the present, sits enthroned at the center; together the three draw a single act of awakening into a far longer span of time: before Shakyamuni, enlightenment had already occurred; after him, it will occur again. The Buddha's attainment of enlightenment thus becomes more than an isolated event in history—it becomes a spiritual thread running across past, present, and future. The juxtaposition of the Buddhas of the three times also tells us: individuals depart, eras change, but the possibility of awakening does not end with the passing of any one person.

It is only here that what this sculpture truly wants to say begins to emerge.

On the surface it depicts the Buddha seated beneath the Bodhi tree; in fact, within a dark slab of phyllite, it establishes a proposition about inner order. The lotus petals still unfurl, the guardian beasts still flank either side, the inscription still runs along the halo, and the pillars and lintels still keep opening outward. The world did not stop moving because the Buddha attained enlightenment. Quite the opposite—everything is still happening.

What changes is not the world, but the relationship between the center and the world.

Once the center is no longer swept along by change, the changes around it stop being mere chaos. They begin to acquire direction, to form relationships with one another, and ultimately to take on order. The ‘center’ spoken of here does not mean controlling everything, still less demanding that the world run according to one's own will. It simply means this: when change comes again, a person is no longer so easily carried away by it.

Perhaps this is also why, on a scorching Chengdu afternoon, we can still be struck by a thousand-year-old Magadha stone carving.

What first draws us in is that thin robe, then the Buddha's body, face, and gesture, and the sacred site compressed into stone around him. But only at the end do we realize that what this work ultimately carves is not just line, and not just the Buddha. It carves a state of being: how a person, amid a world still noisy, hot, humid, and full of unpredictable change, can stop being swept along by it.

Stability does not refer to an unmoving world.

but rather the ability to be still in a world full of restlessness.

excerpt.en: Yellow Jambhala

viewingNote.zh:
第一眼看到这尊造像，我最喜欢的是祂的脸。

眼睛微微低垂，脸颊丰润，嘴角向上提起了一点。于是，我们很容易使用一个熟悉的词——“神秘的微笑”。

但看过足够多南亚雕塑之后，就会发现类似的嘴角、眼睑和面部关系，并不只出现在财神脸上。佛陀、菩萨、天女，甚至同一时代婆罗门教的神祇，都可能拥有这种安静而略带笑意的面孔。我们以为自己看见的是神的情绪，其实首先看见的，可能是一个时代塑造神圣面孔的方法。

这件造像诞生于大约十世纪，属于东印度帕拉艺术体系。今天，我们习惯把他称作“黄财神”。但如果真的沿着历史往回走，“黄财神”这个名字并不是进入这件作品的第一个名称。首先应该认识的，是 Jambhala[1]。

一千年前的印度人面对的，并不是后来藏传佛教中已经分类得十分清晰的一套黄、白、黑、红、绿财神系统。在现存《Sādhanamālā》[2] 传统的早期写本中能够明确见到黄色、二臂、持香橼果和吐宝鼠的Jambhala。所以，想认识眼前这尊财神，我们得先回到《Sādhanamālā》传统的早期写本中去了解一个问题：

Jambhala 究竟从哪里来？

在佛教产生以前，南亚已经存在一个庞大而复杂的Yakṣa[3] 世界。它们和森林、树木、土地、水源、地下宝藏、丰饶和地方保护有关。后来我们熟悉的Kubera[4]、 Vaiśravaṇa[5]（以及Jambhala，都不同程度地和这一古老宗教土壤发生着关系。

由此，我们通常容易把这种关系直接理解成：Yakṣa 变了成Kubera，Kubera 变成了Vaiśravaṇa，再变成Pañcika[6]，最后成为了Jambhala 。真实文化的发展和演变往往没有这么简单和直接。

在《文殊根本仪轨经》这样的印度佛教仪轨文本中，Kubera、Pañcika 和Jambhala 甚至可以作为不同神格分别出现。这意味着他们的功能和身份虽然长期交叠，却在某些佛教传统中仍然可以彼此区分。所以，比“谁变成了谁”更重要的问题其实是：为什么这些神总是围绕财富、丰饶、保护和现实生活而出现？

大约公元二世纪的犍陀罗已经大量出现Pañcika 和Hārītī[7]。Pañcika 是一位Yakṣa，并和财富之神Vaiśravaṇa、Kubera 的系统联系在一起；Hārītī 则和儿童、生育和丰饶有关。今天洛杉矶艺术博物馆保存的一件约公元2-3 世纪的犍陀罗石雕，就是这种组合的典型实例。也就是说，距离眼前这尊十世纪财神还有七八百年时，佛教已经没有回避那些极其现实的问题：孩子能否平安长大，家庭是否丰足，身体是否健康，生活能否得到保护。所以，财富并不是到了密教时代才突然进入佛教。真正变化的，是佛教后来对这些古老神祇的不断重组。

到了八世纪末至九世纪初，情况已经明显不同。这时候印度密教传统中已经保存了专门的财神修法。说明到这一时期，财神已经不只是一个模糊的“财富夜叉”，而成为可以被独立观想、修持和纳入密教仪轨的神格。所以当我们眼前这尊财神造像被铸造出来时，关于财神背后的财富神传统已经走了好几个世纪。

于是，一个新的追问出现：当祂被制作出来的时候，祂的周围是一个怎样的世界呢？

我们通常很容易因为帕拉王朝和佛教关系密切，就把当时的东印度想象成一个统一而纯粹的佛教世界。其实并非如此，虽然帕拉王朝的身份长期和佛教联系在一起，但碑铭材料又告诉我们，同一批统治者可以大量向婆罗门授予土地，也可以支持湿婆教。因此，早期中世纪东印度的王权本身就可能具有多层宗教身份。所以眼前这件财神生活的世界多元且包容。佛教、密教、湿婆传统、婆罗门宗教、地方神灵，以及那些远比宗派分类更古老的夜叉信仰，同时存在，彼此吸收，也彼此竞争。这也让Kubera和Jambhala之间始终模糊的边界变得更容易理解。

有趣的是，同一个时期的现实社会也从来没有因为佛教讲出离，就停止谈论土地和财富。MahīpālaI[8] 第33 年的Rajbhita[9] 石刻记录了一个名为vaṇiggrāma[10] 的商人组织，证明十世纪末前后的孟加拉已经存在着以群体身份出现在铭文中的商人组织。 而对早期中世纪比哈尔与孟加拉造像铭文的研究又显示，佛教造像的供养人并不只有国王和高僧，还包括商人、家庭成员、女性以及其他不同社会背景的人。

“商人”是这里一道非常重要的线索。但我们却不能因为发现了商人，就说“商人需要发财，所以财神流行”。毕竟目前没有这样的直接证据。但这些碑铭真正告诉我们的，有另一件更基础、也更重要的事情：佛教寺院从来没有生活在物质世界之外。

因为寺院需要土地，需要粮食，需要工匠，需要建筑，需要金属，需要人持续不断地供养。修行的终点可以是超越财富，但修行发生的世界，却仍然需要财富。这或许也是理解财神语境最重要的一把钥匙。佛教并不是只回答“人最终如何解脱”。它同样生活在另一个问题里：人在还没解脱以前，怎样生活？

库尔基哈尔出土了两尊十世纪的Vasudhārā[11]。它们刻有Rājyapāla[12]统治第31 或32 年的铭文，大致属于十世纪中叶，由两位女性供养。这个时期与我们眼前这尊财神大致同时期，而一个真实生活在摩揭陀[13] 社会中的人，也完全可能为一尊与财富、丰饶有关的佛教女神出资造像。库尔基哈尔的铭文研究也显示，这座佛教中心直到十一世纪仍持续吸引来自不同社会层面的供养者。这些铭文让我们看见，当时的“财富神”并非抽象神学概念。他们真的被人制造，被人带进寺院，被人供奉。

聊到这里，我们终于可以重新回到雕塑本身了。

这件Jambhala 最醒目的身体特征是丰足。这是一副丰厚、有重量的身体。财神腹部圆鼓，胸膛饱满，姿态闲适，宝冠、项链、臂钏和璎珞层层覆盖在身体上。脚踏宝瓶的莲台下层以形似宝瓶的结构装饰。财富有序显化，凸显着独特的构思。但如果我们把它和十世纪摩揭陀的其他造像放在一起，就会发现，并不是所有东西都应该解释成“财神的特征”。Susan Huntington 在通过有纪年的作品重新建立库尔基哈尔的金属造像序列时发现，这一地区十世纪的铜像经常保留非常明显的蜡模塑形感。人体不是锋利地切割出来的，身体、衣纹和珠宝之间存在连续而柔软的关系，最终的金属表面仍然让人感到工匠当初在蜡上捏塑、划刻和堆叠的痕迹。也许这种塑造经验是匠人们对“蜡”的一种感觉吧。

重新看眼前这件作品，就会发现这种比较很有意思。

祂的眉弓没有留下僵硬的刀痕，眼睑及面颊之间过渡柔和；鼻翼、嘴唇和下颌都由圆润的体积构成；直立、圆润的身形没有任何线条的断裂感；胸前繁复的珠宝也是如此。装饰没有完全脱离身体成为另一层硬质结构，而像从柔软的蜡面上一点一点生长出来。因此，从目前可以看到的风格语言来说，这件作品值得优先放进十世纪摩揭陀，尤其是库尔基哈尔金属雕塑传统中比较。所以，我们认为祂属于“财神”，其实祂可能更先属于东印度的十世纪，属于一套长时间累积的南亚神圣面孔传统，也属于工匠手中的蜡与金属，还有那一身耀眼的金色。Kurt Behrendt[14] 对那烂陀、库尔基哈尔等9—12 世纪佛教图像做过统计。在他整理的那烂陀233 件铜造像中，财神有 10 件；在他能够纳入统计的库尔基哈尔109 件金属造像中，财神只有 1 件。

然而根据在整理1930 年库尔基哈尔发现的一批帕拉时期的窖藏金属造像时，工作人员所留下的详细记录中，被送进印度巴特那的博物馆的约230件金属器物里，属于造像的约150 件，其中105 件带铭文；而又被明确记录为鎏金的造像却只有3 件。因为库尔基哈尔这一批造像跨越了多个世纪，而且在经过了埋藏、腐蚀、清理后，今天是否还能辨认金层也会影响记录的数量。因此“3 件”只是这一窖藏被整理时明确识别出的鎏金数量，并不能代表帕拉时代原始的生产比例。但也可因此记录而推断，财神在帕拉金属图像中未必特别罕见，但早期的鎏金财神可能确实属于非常有限的存在。

寺院需要财富才能存在，供养需要财富才能完成，造像本身也需要铜、金、工匠与赞助者。财富可以成为资具，可以成为布施，也可以进入宗教仪轨。于是我在想：当年是一位什么样身份的供养者发了一个什么样的心愿呢？

大约一千年前，人们已经在用这样一副丰足而安静的身体，回答一个今天仍然没有过时的问题：

我们需要财富，但我们究竟应该怎样与财富相处？

注释

[1]  Jambhala 为藏传佛教中财神的总集与梵文原名。意义为「财宝之主」或「除贫本尊」。

[2] 《Sādhanamālā》意为「成就法鬘」或「修持法集」是一部印度密教（金刚乘）的重要梵文文献总集，大约在公元5世纪至11世纪之间编成。

[3] Yakṣa，中文通常音译为「夜叉」或「药叉」。

[4] Kubera，中文通常音译为俱毗羅、库贝拉，是印度神话和印度教中的財富之神、北方守护神，也是夜叉和紧那罗种族之王。

[5] Vaiśravaṇa，中文常音译为毗沙门，意译为多闻天王。他是佛教中著名的“四大天王”之一，负责镇守北方。

[6] Pañcika 在佛教和印度传统中意指散脂大將（又译半支迦、般闍迦、散支夜叉），是北方多闻天王（毘沙門天）座下的八大夜叉大将之一。

[7] Hārītī 为佛教中的著名女神，中文通常翻译为鬼子母神、訶利帝母或欢喜母。

[8] Mahīpāla中译为摩醯波罗（波罗王朝国王，约公元977–1027年在位，"摩醯"意为"大地"，"波罗"意为"守护者"，合意为"大地的守护者"。

[9] Rajbhita中译为拉杰比塔（孟加拉地区一处村落遗址，因出土"拉杰比塔石刻铭文"而闻名，该铭文纪年为摩醯波罗一世在位第三十三年）。

[10] vaṇiggrāma中译为商人行会或商人聚落部，指古代印度铭文中所记载的商人行会或商人共同体。

[11] Vasudhārā 在佛教中意为“持宝”、“财富之流”或“持世”。她汉译为持世菩萨、财源天母、财源佛母或金度母，是佛教中专司世间财富、福德与丰饶的女性本尊。

[12] Rājyapāla为帕拉王朝君主：罗阇耶波罗。

[13] 摩揭陀是古代中印度的著名王国和地名，意译为“无害国”、“善胜国”或“致甘露处”。它位于今印度比哈尔邦一带，是古代印度十六大国之一，也是佛教发源地与核心弘法区域。

[14] Kurt A. Behrendt 是一位美国艺术史学者和策展人，研究重点是南亚佛教艺术、犍陀罗艺术，以及印度佛教艺术向喜马拉雅地区传播的问题。
viewingNote.en:
What I love most about this sculpture is its face.

The eyes are lowered ever so slightly, the cheeks full, the corners of the mouth lifted just enough to suggest that familiar phrase, the "enigmatic smile."

Spend enough time with South Asian sculpture and you begin to notice that this particular relationship between mouth, eyelids, and cheek is not unique to wealth deities. Buddhas, bodhisattvas, celestial maidens, even Brahmanical gods of the same period wear the same quiet, faintly smiling expression. What looks like a god's emotion may in fact be something simpler: one era's particular way of shaping a sacred face.

This sculpture was made around the tenth century, within the Pāla art tradition of eastern India. Today we are accustomed to calling him "Yellow Jambhala," but tracing the history back, that is not the name by which this work should first be known. It was first simply Jambhala.

What Indians a thousand years ago encountered was not yet the neatly classified system of yellow, white, black, red, and green wealth deities that would later develop within Xizang Buddhism. The surviving early manuscripts of the Sādhanamālā tradition clearly describe a yellow, two-armed Jambhala holding a citron in one hand and, in the other, a mongoose that spits jewels. So to understand the deity before us, we need to return to those early manuscripts and ask a more basic question: Where did Jambhala come from?

Long before Buddhism arose, South Asia already possessed a vast and intricate world of yakṣas — spirits bound up with forests, trees, land, water sources, buried treasure, fertility, and local protection. Kubera, Vaiśravaṇa, and Jambhala, figures we know well today, are all connected, to varying degrees, with this ancient religious soil.

From this we tend to construct a tidy narrative: the yakṣa became Kubera, Kubera became Vaiśravaṇa, who became Pañcika, who then became Jambhala. The real development of a culture is rarely so simple, or so direct.

In Indian Buddhist ritual texts such as the Mañjuśrīmūlakalpa, Kubera, Pañcika, and Jambhala can even appear as three separate deities. Even though their functions and identities have long overlapped, certain Buddhist traditions still keep them distinct. So the more important question is not "who became whom," but why these deities revolve around wealth, abundance, protection, and the practicalities of daily life.

By around the second century CE, Pañcika and Hārītī appear in large numbers in Gandhāran art. Pañcika was a yakṣa linked to the same system of wealth deities as Vaiśravaṇa and Kubera; Hārītī was associated with children, fertility, and abundance. A Gandhāran stone carving of roughly the second to third century, now in the Los Angeles County Museum of Art, is a classic example of the pairing. In other words, seven or eight centuries before this tenth-century wealth deity came into being, Buddhism was already unwilling to look away from the most pressing practical concerns: whether children would grow up safely, whether a household would prosper, whether the body would stay healthy, whether life itself could be protected. Wealth, then, did not suddenly enter Buddhism with the age of Esoteric Buddhism. What changed, over the centuries, was how Buddhism kept reorganizing these ancient deities.

By the late eighth or early ninth century, the situation had changed: the Indian Esoteric tradition now preserved dedicated sādhanas for wealth deities. This tells us that the wealth deity was no longer a vague "yakṣa of riches" but had become a deity in its own right, one that could be independently visualized, practiced, and incorporated into Esoteric ritual. So by the time the sculpture before us was cast, the tradition behind it had already traveled several centuries.

And so a new question arises: In what surroundings was this image made?

Because the Pāla dynasty was so closely tied to Buddhism, it is tempting to picture early medieval eastern India as a unified, purely Buddhist world. It was not. Although the identity of the Pāla rulers was long bound up with Buddhism, epigraphic evidence shows that the same rulers also granted large tracts of land to Brahmins and supported Śaivism. Royal authority in early medieval eastern India, then, likely carried more than one religious identity at once, and the world this wealth deity inhabited was plural and inclusive. Buddhism, Esoteric Buddhism, Śaiva traditions, Brahmanical religion, local deities, and yakṣa beliefs far older than any sectarian classification all coexisted, absorbing and competing with one another at the same time. This also makes the persistently blurred boundary between Kubera and Jambhala much easier to understand.

Interestingly, that same society never stopped talking about land and wealth simply because Buddhism preached renunciation.

The Rajbhita stone inscription, dated to the thirty-third regnal year of Mahīpāla I, records a merchant organization called a vaṇiggrāma — evidence that by the late tenth century, merchant organizations were already appearing in Bengal's inscriptions as recognized collective bodies. Studies of early medieval image inscriptions from Bihar and Bengal further show that the donors of Buddhist images were not only kings and eminent monks, but also merchants, family members, women, and people from other walks of life.

Merchants are an important clue here, but it doesn’t mean the worship of the wealth deity arose because of them. There is no direct evidence for that. These inscriptions tells us something more basic, and more important: Buddhist monasteries are not separated from the material world.

A monastery needs land, grain, craftsmen, buildings, metal, and a steady stream of people making offerings. The endpoint of spiritual practice may be transcendence of wealth, but the world in which that practice unfolds still needs wealth. This may be the single most important key to understanding the context of the wealth deity. Buddhism does not only answer the question of how a person is ultimately liberated; it also tries to answer the question of how a person lives before liberation?

Two images of Vasudhārā excavated at Kurkihār date to the tenth century. An inscription places them in the thirty-first or thirty-second regnal year of Rājyapāla, roughly the mid-tenth century, and records that they were donated by two women. This is roughly contemporary with the wealth deity before us, and it shows that an ordinary member of Magadhan society could just as well fund the casting of a Buddhist goddess associated with wealth and abundance. Research on the Kurkihār inscriptions also shows that this Buddhist center continued to draw donors from across the social spectrum well into the eleventh century. These inscriptions show us that the "wealth deity" of that era wasn’t an abstract theological concept. These deities were made by, carried by, and worshipped by the people.

Having come this far, we can finally return to our sculpture here.

The most striking physical trait of this Jambhala may be described by the word ‘abundance’. He is a full-bodied, weighty figure, with a rounded belly, an ample chest, and a relaxed posture, layered over with a crown, necklace, armlets, and strings of beads. His feet rest on a treasure vase beneath the lotus throne, and the base itself is decorated with a vase-like form. Wealth, here, has been given an order, a distinct visual logic. But set this piece beside other tenth-century sculpture from Magadha, and it becomes clear that not everything about it should be read as a "feature of the wealth deity."

Susan Huntington observed that the metal sculpture of Kurkihar often preserves a distinctive smoothness in the modeling of its details. In contrast to Nalanda, where jewelry, headdresses, and other details were often made from “small balls or beads of wax,” she noted that at Kurkihar such elements were frequently formed from “a single strand of wax, so that a smoother effect is achieved.”

The difference may seem subtle, but it reveals something of the craftsman’s hand at the very beginning of the casting process: the way the figure was shaped in wax continued to influence the character of the finished bronze. Perhaps this is what it means for an artisan to have a feeling for wax.

Looking again at the work before us, this comparison proves illuminating.

His brow ridge has no stiff, blade-cut edge; the transition from eyelid to cheek is soft. The nostrils, lips, and jaw are all formed from rounded volumes, and neither the upright, rounded body nor the elaborate jewelry across his chest shows any break or fracture of line. The ornamentation never fully detaches from the body into a separate, hardened layer; it seems, instead, to have grown, bit by bit, out of a soft wax surface. Judged by this stylistic vocabulary, the piece deserves to be compared first against tenth-century Magadha, and especially against the Kurkihār metal-sculpture tradition. We think of him as belonging to "the wealth deity," but he may, in fact, belong first to tenth-century eastern India, to a long-accumulated South Asian tradition of the sacred face, to the wax and metal that once passed through a craftsman's hands, and to that one dazzling coat of gold.

Kurt Behrendt compiled statistics on Buddhist imagery from Nālandā, Kurkihār, and other sites of the ninth through twelfth centuries. Of the 233 bronze images from Nālandā he catalogued, ten are wealth deities; of the 109 metal images from Kurkihār he was able to include, only one is a wealth deity.

However, the detailed records left by the team that catalogued the Pāla-period hoard of metal images discovered at Kurkihār in 1930 tell a further story. Of the roughly 230 metal objects sent to the museum in Patna, about 150 were images, and 105 of those bore inscriptions — yet only three were explicitly recorded as gilt. Because the hoard spans several centuries, and because burial, corrosion, and later cleaning all affect whether gilding can still be identified today, that count is inevitably shaped by those conditions. "Three," then, is only the number of gilt images that could be clearly identified at the time of cataloguing; it cannot represent the original production ratio of the Pāla period. Still, the record does suggest that the wealth deity was not necessarily rare among Pāla metal images overall, even if early gilt examples were genuinely scarce.

A monastery needs wealth to exist. An act of devotion needs wealth to be carried out. A sculpture needs copper, gold, craftsmen, and a patron. Wealth can become a ritual implement, an act of giving, a part of religious rite. And so I find myself wondering: what kind of person, in what kind of position, made this donation, and what vow did they make in doing so?

A thousand years ago, artists were already using the robust human form to give shape to questions that we still ask today.

It is true that we need material wealth—but how, exactly, are we meant to live with it?

excerpt.en: Hand of a Buddha

viewingNote.zh:
那天傍晚，碰了一下它的指尖。只是很轻的一下，心却突然跳了一下。

这种感觉很难解释。

这甚至不是一尊完整的造像，只剩下一只左手。原来的身体已经消失，面容、姿态、莲座，甚至它曾经处在怎样的空间里，都无法再看见。留下来的，只是几根手指和一小段手掌。

铜是冷的。

可它看起来很柔软。

手指从掌部缓慢地展开，指节的起伏被处理得很轻，到了末端，又一点点收细。那几根线条不是停在指尖，而像还在继续往前走。

眼睛也会跟着走。

于是很奇怪，明明只是二十几厘米长的一只手，思绪却忽然被带得很远。

由于《奥德赛》的上映，刚好又重新看了一遍《星际穿越》。电影里那些关于时间、宇宙和人类尺度的想象还留在脑子里。所以触碰到它的那一刻，我突然产生了一种很难言说的错位感：眼前是一件一千多年前的人造之物，可指尖之间的距离，却仿佛把两个完全不同的时间折叠到了一起。

人活在地面上太久，很容易把眼前的世界当成全部。

每天面对的是具体的人事物和具体的焦虑。可偶尔有那么一个瞬间，尺度突然被拉开，才会重新意识到：关于时间、意识、宇宙，甚至关于生命为什么会存在，人类知道的其实仍然很少。

世界背后究竟有没有某种更高的秩序？有没有创世之神？有没有某种我们尚且无法感知的空间存在？虽然佛教并不以一个创造世界的唯一神来解释宇宙。但这并不妨碍一件佛教雕塑，让人重新感受到未知。面对这只手，而我真正开始好奇的是：

一种原本不可见的神圣，究竟怎样被注入了一只手里？

如果暂时忘掉宗教，这首先是一件很好的雕塑。

它最迷人的地方，就是柔软。

这是一个很有意思的矛盾。铜本身没有柔软可言。它坚硬、冰冷，需要火、模具和工具才能获得形状。可当古代工匠把它塑造成手以后，材料原来的性格反而退了下去。我们看到的不是铜，而像是皮肤。这种感觉并不来自某个复杂的装饰，而主要来自线条。

手指从掌部向外延伸，没有突然的转折，骨骼的存在感变得很轻；几根手指之间保持着一种舒缓的节奏。它不像一只正在抓取东西的手，也没有现实身体的紧张和用力。正因为如此，当视线沿着它移动时，会产生一种身体的重量似乎被减轻了的特殊感受。

雕塑没有动，观看却发生了运动。这可能正是线条最难被说清楚的力量。

一条线本身不存在任何内容，可当人的目光开始沿着它走，它就拥有了方向、速度，甚至情绪。急促的线条会使人紧张，断裂的线条会造成阻碍，而这只手上的线条却异常连贯，像把人慢慢从现实里的重量牵了出去。可如果再靠近一点，就会发现，这只如此自然、柔软的手，其实并不完全属于我们熟悉的身体。

它的手指之间，有蹼。

而且“蹼”不只是简单地把五指连接起来。在那些细薄的连接处，还能看到一道道交叉刻线，形成近似网状的纹理。在佛教关于佛陀身体的“三十二大人相”传统中，手足缦网是其中之一。“缦网”描述的是一种不同于普通人的手足特征。而这些细节，也让这只残手慢慢靠近了一个更具体的时代。

我目前更倾向于把它放在约公元6—7 世纪的尼泊尔早期金属造像传统中理解。这个判断当然不能只建立在“蹼手”之上。但当几个线索放在一起时，它们开始彼此支持。

6 世纪末，尼泊尔谷地和北印度之间已经存在着非常具体的联系。公元591 年的一尊北印度铜佛，铭文记录的供养者便来自尼泊尔。它至少说明，在那个时代，尼泊尔与北印度之间并不存在我们今天地图意义上的隔绝。宗教、工匠、物品和审美，都在不断流动。

到了7 世纪，尼泊尔自身的金工传统已经留下更加明确的作品。与此同时，关于理查维艺术的研究也注意到，明显的指间蹼膜正是这一时期延续时间较长的一种身体特征，而它背后又可以继续追溯到更早的印度古典传统。所以眼前这只手真正让我感兴趣的，并不是它能不能被简单地贴上“6 世纪或7 世纪”的标签。而是它站在了一条很长的线上。

印度关于神圣身体的想象，经由佛教经典、图像、工艺不断传播；尼泊尔匠人又把这些观念转化成了自己的金属语言。

最后，一些原本宏大的宗教观念，被压缩进了一只手。

这很奇妙。

文明传播在历史书里经常显得很巨大，可到了雕塑里，它有时候小得只是手指之间的一根线条、一张网。历史可以解释网格纹从哪里来，可以解释为什么这个时期会出现这样的手，也可以帮助我们判断这件作品大概属于什么时候。但它却无法解释：为什么今天的人还会被它打动？

如果只是因为我知道它代表“三十二相”，那只是知识。可那天傍晚并不是这样。因为，心跳发生在解释之前。那一刻大脑里还没有联想到关于手足缦网的资料，也没有把它放进理查维艺术史里。

只是碰了一下。

感觉比知识先到了。

后知后觉，这可能正是艺术与图像学最不一样的地方。图像学告诉我们这个图像“意味着什么”。而雕塑有时候并不会等我们先去理解一遍比例、转折、弧度、重量等等，而是先作用在眼睛和身体上。

一根手指怎么慢慢弯曲，一条轮廓怎样从掌缘绕向指尖，这些甚至没有明确的意义，可它们会改变人的呼吸和注意力。

所以神圣并不只存在于符号里。它也可能存在于一种形式关系中。经典为它提供了观念。匠人给它线条，而线条最后抵达人的身体。

这条路走了一千多年。

我们当然已经不可能成为当年的观看者。曾经供奉这尊造像的空间也许消失了，面对它礼拜的人消失了，完整的身体也消失了。可有时候，残缺反而让某些东西变得更突出。

线条变成了全部。

再次回想那天傍晚，当指尖碰到它时，我想到了宇宙，想到时间，也想到人类对于世界那些远远没有获得答案的问题。也许我们永远无法知道世界的尽头在哪里，更不知道所谓神圣是否真的存在于某个超越我们感知的维度。

但至少在那一刻，我又一次很具体地感受到了：艺术为什么能够让不可见的东西暂时获得形状。

一千多年前，一个匠人把那些无法直接看见的东西，留进了几根线里。然而，一千多年后，我碰到了它。那一刻，时间没有真的倒流，宇宙也没有真的向我打开。

只是指尖碰到指尖。

然而，心跳了一下。
viewingNote.en:
The evening I touched its fingertip, my heart skipped a beat.

I felt an inexplicable sense of dislocation.

This isn't even a complete sculpture — only a left hand survives. The original body is gone; the face, the posture, the lotus base, even the kind of space it once occupied, none of it can be seen anymore. What's left is just a hand.

There is something wondrous about seeing a hard material like copper take on the softness of flesh.

The fingers unfold slowly from the palm; the rise and fall of the knuckles is handled with a very light touch, and toward the tips, they taper gradually. Those lines don't stop at the fingertips — they seem to keep moving forward.

Your eyes end up following along.

This hand, approximately 20 centimeters long, carries your thoughts far away.

Because The Odyssey had just come out, I happened to rewatch Interstellar recently, and its vision of time, the universe, and the vastness of human existence was still lingering in my mind. So when I touched it, I felt a strange feeling of displacement. Here was an object made by human hands more than a thousand years ago, and yet, in the small distance between our two fingertips, it felt as though two entirely different spans of time had folded into one.

Live on the ground long enough, and it is easy to mistake the world immediately around us for the whole of existence.

Every day, we deal with specific people, specific things, and specific anxieties. But every once in a while, something pulls the scale wide open and reminds us how little we really know—not only about time, consciousness, and the universe, but even about why we exist at all.

Is there some order behind the world? A creator god? Some dimension of existence that we simply cannot perceive? Buddhism, of course, does not explain the universe through a single creator god. But a Buddhist sculpture can still make us feel the unknown all over again. Standing before this hand, the question that came to me was a strangely simple one:

How does something sacred and invisible find its way into a single hand?

Set religion aside for a moment, and this is, first and foremost, a remarkable piece of sculpture.

What makes it so captivating is its softness.

There is something almost contradictory about it. Copper is not soft. It is hard and cold, and it takes fire, molds, and tools before it can take on any recognizable form. Yet once a craftsman shapes it, the material seems to recede. What we see is no longer copper. It looks almost like skin. And that impression comes not from elaborate ornament, but from something much simpler: the lines.

The fingers extend from the palm without abrupt turns; the suggestion of bone beneath the surface is subdued; and a relaxed rhythm flows from one finger to the next. It does not look like a hand grasping at anything, nor does it carry the tension or effort of an ordinary physical body. As the eye follows its contours, there is an odd sensation that the weight of the body has somehow been lifted.

The sculpture itself does not move, but the act of looking does. Perhaps this is one of the hardest things to put into words about the power of a line.

A line, by itself, is only a mark. But once the eye begins to follow it, it acquires direction, speed, even emotion. A hurried line can make us tense; a broken line can make us stumble. The lines of this hand, however, are unusually continuous. They seem to draw the eye gently outward, loosening it from the weight of the everyday world. Look a little closer, though, and you notice that this hand, for all its natural softness, does not quite belong to the body we know.

Between its fingers, there is webbing.

And that webbing does more than connect the fingers. Within those thin membranes, faint incised lines cross one another, forming a delicate, net-like pattern. In the Buddhist tradition, the “thirty-two marks of a great being” describe a series of bodily features that distinguish the Buddha and other great beings from ordinary human beings; webbed hands and feet are among them. Such details also begin to place this fragmentary hand within a particular historical and artistic context.

My own inclination, for now, is to place it within Nepal’s early metal-casting tradition, roughly in the 6th–7th century CE. That judgment, of course, cannot rest on the webbed fingers alone. But when several clues are considered together, they begin to reinforce one another.

By the late 6th century, there were already concrete connections between the Kathmandu Valley and North India. A North Indian bronze Buddha, dated by inscription to 591 CE, records a donor from Nepal. At the very least, it reminds us that Nepal and North India were not separated in the way our modern maps might suggest. Religious ideas, craftsmen, objects, and artistic tastes were moving across the region.

By the 7th century, Nepal’s own metalworking tradition had produced works that can be dated with greater confidence. Scholarship on Licchavi-period art has also noted the persistence of visibly webbed fingers over a considerable span of the period, a feature with roots extending further back into the classical Indian tradition. So what interests me most about the hand before us is not whether it can simply be labeled “6th” or “7th century.” It is that it stands within a much longer line of transmission.

India’s imagination of the sacred body traveled outward through Buddhist scriptures, images, and techniques of making; Nepalese craftsmen then translated those ideas into their own language of metal. In the end, something vast—a religious conception of the sacred body—was compressed into something as small and intimate as a single hand.

It is a strange and wonderful thing.

In history books, the movement of civilizations can seem enormous. In a sculpture, however, that vast history can sometimes shrink to a single line, a small web between two fingers. History can help us understand where that pattern came from, why such hands appeared in this period, and how the object might be dated. What it cannot fully explain is something more difficult: why does it still move us today?

If I were moved only because I knew that the hand represented one of the thirty-two marks, that would be knowledge. But that was not what happened that evening. Something in the sculpture moved me before I had any explanation for it. My mind had not yet reached for anything about webbed hands and feet, nor had it placed the fragment within the history of Licchavi art.

It was simply a touch.

The feeling came first. The knowledge followed.

Looking back, perhaps this is where art and iconography begin to part ways. Iconography tells us what an image means. Sculpture, however, does not always wait for us to work through proportion, gesture, curve, and weight before it reaches us. Sometimes it acts on the eye and the body first.

The way a finger slowly curves, the way a line sweeps from the edge of the palm toward the fingertip—these things have no fixed meaning of their own, and yet they can alter our breathing and redirect our attention.

So the sacred does not exist only in symbols. It may also exist in relationships between forms. The scriptures provide the idea. The craftsman gives it form, and that form ultimately becomes something the viewer can feel.

This took more than a thousand years.

We can never become the viewers this piece was originally made for. The space where it was once enshrined may be gone. The people who once stood before it are gone. Even the rest of the body is gone. And yet sometimes, what is missing makes what remains more visible.

In the end, the lines were all that remained.

Thinking back to that evening, when my fingertip touched it, I found myself thinking about the universe, about time, and about all the questions humanity still cannot answer about the world. We may never know where the universe truly ends, let alone whether the sacred exists in some dimension beyond what we can perceive.

But perhaps, for a moment, I understood something more concrete. Art can give shape to things that cannot be seen in nature.

More than a thousand years ago, a craftsman folded something invisible into a few lines of metal. More than a thousand years later, I touched those lines. Time did not reverse, and the universe did not suddenly open itself to me.

It was only a fingertip meeting another fingertip.

And yet, I am still in awe.

subtitle.zh: 古典从未过时。

excerpt.en: Akshobhya Buddha

viewingNote.zh:
我们常常把古代艺术想得太简单。

一件作品年代越早，似乎就越应该显得质朴、遥远，甚至带着某种尚未成熟的笨拙。至于几何、材质对比和简约、清晰的视觉结构，我们更习惯把它们归入现代设计。可眼前这尊九世纪尼泊尔的石雕，偏偏让这种判断失效。

第一眼看去，它无疑属于一个古典时代。祂端坐在石座上，身体饱满而克制，面容沉静，袈裟轻薄贴体。没有炫目的珠宝，也没有复杂的动势，整尊造像依靠比例、体量和文本秩序建立起了尊贵。

但当视线移向台座，另一种感觉出现了。

层层折转的山石被处理成锐利而内凹的几何切面，一枚金刚杵嵌在中央的最深处。它像一颗被安放在岩层内部的核心区，它连接着台座，对应着腹部、面部和肉髻，完成了整件作品的垂直中轴。这样的构造，即使放在今天，仍然会让人联想到宝石切割、建筑退台，甚至某种极简而成熟的当代设计。问题也从这里开始：

一千多年前的匠人，为什么会采用如此清晰、甚至让今天的观者感到熟悉的视觉方法？

要回答这个问题，我们得先了解这尊造像。佛陀右手越过膝盖，指尖垂向大地。这是佛教艺术中最著名的姿态之一。释迦牟尼在菩提树下成道之前，面对魔罗的质疑，以手触地，请大地作证。因此，看到触地印，人们通常会立刻想到释迦牟尼。但这一次，答案藏在他的身体之外。

佛座中央有一枚竖立的金刚杵。结合九世纪左右李查维晚期加德满都谷地的宗教环境，这尊造像更应被理解为五方佛体系中的东方阿閦佛。到了这一时期，五方佛信仰及其方位体系，已经成为谷地佛教视觉文化中的重要结构。阿閦佛位于东方，属于金刚部，触地印、金刚杵都共同构成了他的身份线索。

九世纪属于李查维晚期，但“晚期”不等于“过渡”。

我们很容易受线性历史观影响，把一个王朝的后期完全理解为旧秩序逐渐衰弱、新风格尚未完成的阶段。于是，只要作品出现新的形式，就会被解释为下一时代的预兆。这件作品并不适合这种叙述。它给人的整体感受不是犹疑，也不是风格尚未确定。恰恰相反，它表现出一种成熟传统才有的自信：匠人清楚什么需要突出，也清楚什么应该退后；知道如何控制身体的比例，也懂得让材质、光线和图像为其共同服务。

佛陀双肩宽阔，腰部自然收束，双腿向两侧稳定展开。身体并不追求现实肌肉的起伏，而像从内部均匀生长出来，虽紧实，但没有多余的紧张。袈裟袒露右肩，以清晰的平行线从左肩斜过胸前。衣纹存在，却没有切断身体的连贯感。使得衣服既有覆盖，又不妨碍身躯的体量显现。这种处理延续了尼泊尔李查维艺术与北印度笈多古典传统之间的深厚关系。李查维时期的加德满都谷地并非封闭的山间社会。它依靠农业，也处在印度平原和喜马拉雅高地之间的交通网络上。商人、僧侣和使节的往来不仅带来了财富，也带来经典、图像和新的宗教观念。

然而，这件石雕之所以能吸引住我们，还有另一个重要的成因，那就是匠人的审美与巧思。

在表面的处理上，匠人将背光和台座保留了相对粗粝的哑光质感。阿閦佛的面部、胸膛、手臂和双腿则被反复研磨、抛光，呈现出深沉而柔润的光泽。同一块石料，由此产生了两种完全不同的视觉属性。当光落在佛陀身上，它会沿着额头、鼻梁、肩膀、胸腹和双腿缓慢移动。连续的反光使身体轮廓显得格外清楚，也让坚硬的石材获得一种近似肌肤的细腻感。当光线流动到背光和台座，情况却又变了。细密的纹饰、凿刻痕迹和哑光表面迅速打散了光，背景因此自然后退。

这不是简单的“主体精雕，背景略雕”。

匠人利用同一种材料的不同完成度，重新安排了观看的次序。观者甚至不需要了解图像学，也会在第一眼知道哪里是主尊，哪里是属于承托祂的空间。更准确地说，主次并不是再靠尺寸和位置而建立的，而是由光决定了。背光和山石仍然保留着石头的粗粝，佛身却像经过提炼，从岩石中获得了另一层质地。神圣与凡俗之间没有更换材料，也没有依靠鲜艳色彩区分。区别发生在石头的表面。这种工艺上的克制，比过度装饰更难。当然，今天的光泽可能叠加了后来的擦拭和维护。但主尊和背景之间的差别，很难完全靠后期就会造成。它的基础，仍然应当来自匠人最初有意识的选择性打磨。

再向下看，匠人的精彩创作再次现形。

山石式基座在尼泊尔早期雕塑中并不陌生。大约从七世纪前后开始，这类山石结构已经成为一种颇具辨识度的图像语言。匠人并不写实地模拟天然岩壁，而是把山体压缩成层层折线、凹面、台阶和彼此咬合的几何结构。到了这件九世纪作品中，这一传统并没有被简单沿用。它被重新编排了。

左右山石向中央逐级收拢，原本起伏不定的自然岩层，被整理成接近对称的秩序。中央刻出一个明显内陷的空间，周围石面如同宝石切面般向内折转，金刚杵就嵌在这个凹陷的核心之中。开口的金刚杵，尤如笔直的线条，锋利且充满张力。它像一个被打开的内部空间，将阿閦佛所属的金刚部藏在最核心的位置。信仰不是被写在外面，而是被嵌入结构。

面对这样的台座，人很容易产生一种“现代感”。

内凹的切面、清晰的折线、哑光和抛光的对比，这些都和今天的建筑、珠宝、产品设计和视觉展示一定的亲缘性。但若据此说九世纪匠人“超越时代”或“预见了现代设计”，仍然有些轻率了。因为古代艺术的价值，并不需要通过现代审美来认证。而真正值得讨论的是：

为什么有些形式跨越一千多年，回响依旧？

答案可能没有那么神秘。

因为清晰的层次不会过时、准确的比例不会过时、对材料特性的理解也不会过时。匠人并没有努力追求一种未来感，他只是把眼前的问题解决得足够准确、具体。如何让佛陀从背景中突出？他使用不同的抛光程度；如何让一个体量很小的金刚杵成为视觉中心？他让山石向内折叠，用凹陷与阴影集中视线；如何保留传统的山石图像，又不让它显得像是照搬？他将自然形态转化成清晰的几何秩序。所以，这件作品的“新”，并不来自它摆脱了传统。恰恰相反，匠人对七世纪以来的山石图像非常熟悉，也深知李查维古典身体的塑造原则。正因为熟悉，他才有能力在传统内部作出新的安排。我们今天常常会把创造力理解成打破规则，仿佛只有反对过去，才能得到新的突破。今天的我们似乎认为一件作品的颜色一定要强、尺寸要大、信息要多，发声才够响亮，才不会被忽略。这尊石雕却提供了另一种答案。创造也可以发生在传统内部。旧图像并不必然意味着旧思维。真正僵硬的应该从来不是传统，而是失去判断之后的重复。

当一个时代真正掌握自己的语言，它不仅能保存传统，也能从传统内部生长出新的形式。甚至在一千多年之后，那些线条、切面和光泽仍然会使我们停下来。

不是因为它像现代。

而是因为真正落实到具体的形式，很难被时间淘汰。
viewingNote.en:
We often think of ancient art too simply. The older a work is, the more we tend to expect it to look primitive, remote, even a little unrefined. We tend to think of modern design in terms of geometric forms, sharply defined material contrasts, and a clean, legible visual structure. However, this ninth-century Nepalese stone carving does not fit that assumption.

This sculpture belongs unmistakably to a classical age from the first glance. The Buddha sits enthroned on a stone base, his body full yet restrained, his expression serene, his robe thin and close to the skin. There is no dazzling jewelry, no elaborate movement — the figure’s dignity rests entirely on proportion, physical presence, and adherence to canonical convention.

But as we move our gaze to the base, a different sensation takes over.

Tiers of folded, rocky forms are rendered as sharp, inward-cutting geometric facets, with a vajra set into the deepest point at the center. It sits like a core embedded within the layers of rock, anchoring the base and aligning with the belly, the face, and the crown protrusion (ushnisha) to complete the vertical axis running through the entire work. A structure like this, even today, brings to mind gem-cutting, architectural setbacks, even a kind of mature, minimalist contemporary design. And this is where the real question begins: How did a craftsman from a thousand years ago arrive at a visual language this clear — one that feels familiar to viewers to this day.

To answer this, we first need to understand the image itself. The Buddha’s right hand passes over his knee, fingers pointing down toward the earth — one of the most famous gestures in Buddhist art. Before his awakening beneath the Bodhi tree, Shakyamuni, when challenged by Mara, touches the earth, calling it to bear witness. So, one might immedaitely think of Shakyamuni upon seeing the earth-touching gesture (bhumisparsha mudrā) but a closer inspection is called for.

At the center of the throne stands an upright vajra. Read against the religious context of the late Licchavi-period Kathmandu Valley around the ninth century, this image is better understood as Akshobhya, the Buddha of the East, one of the Five Dhyani Buddhas. By this period, belief in the Five Buddhas and their directional scheme were a major structuring principle in the Valley’s Buddhist visual culture. Akshobhya belongs to the east and to the Vajra family, and both the earth-touching gesture and the vajra together supply the clues to his identity.

The ninth century falls within the late Licchavi period, but “late” does not mean “transitional.”

We are easily influenced by a linear view of history, one that treats the later years of any dynasty as a period of a fading old order and an incomplete new style. Under this logic, any new formal feature gets read as a sign of the coming era. This work resists that narrative entirely. What it conveys is not hesitation, nor a style still finding its footing. Quite contrarily, it displays the kind of confidence that only comes from a fully mature tradition: the maker knew exactly what needed to be brought forward and what should recede; he knew how to govern the body’s proportions, and how to make material, light, and image work together in service of a single image.

The Buddha’s shoulders are broad, the waist naturally drawn in, the legs settled evenly to either side. The body does not aim for realistic musculature; it seems instead to grow evenly from within, firm but without excess tension. The robe bares the right shoulder and crosses the chest in clean, parallel lines running down from the left shoulder. The drapery folds are present, yet they never break the continuity of the body beneath — the robe both covers the figure and lets its volume come through. This treatment carries forward the deep relationship between Nepalese Licchavi art and the classical Gupta tradition of northern India. The Kathmandu Valley of the Licchavi period was never a closed, mountain-bound society. It depended on agriculture, but it also sat along the trade routes linking the plains of India with the Himalayan highlands. The movement of merchants, monks, and envoys brought not only wealth, but scriptures, images, and new religious ideas.

Yet there is another, equally important reason this stone carving holds our attention: the maker’s aesthetic judgment and ingenuity.

In treating the surface, the maker left the halo and the base with a comparatively rough, matte texture, while the face, chest, arms, and legs of Akshobhya were polished again and again, until they took on a deep, soft sheen. From a single block of stone come two different visual qualities. As light falls across the Buddha, it moves slowly along the forehead, the bridge of the nose, the shoulders, the torso and abdomen, the legs. The continuous play of reflected light makes the body’s contours especially clear, giving hard stone a delicacy that approaches the texture of skin. When that same light reaches the halo and base, however, everything changes. The fine ornamental patterning, the visible chisel marks, and the matte surface scatter the light at once, and the background recedes naturally as a result.

This cannot be described simply as a ‘finely carved subject with a roughly carved background.’

The maker used differing degrees of finish on the very same material to reorder how the piece is meant to be seen. Even a viewer with no knowledge of iconography would know, at a single glance, where the main deity is and where the space supporting him lies. More precisely, the hierarchy between the two is established not by size or position, but by light. The halo and the rocky base retain the roughness of stone, while the Buddha’s body seems refined, drawn out of the rock as though it had acquired an entirely different texture. There is no change of material between the sacred and the mundane, no reliance on bright color to tell them apart. The distinction happens on the surface of the stone itself. This kind of restraint in craftsmanship is, in its way, harder to achieve than lavish ornament. Of course, some of today’s sheen may be the result of later handling and polishing over the centuries. But the difference between the main figure and its background could hardly have been produced by later wear alone; its foundation must still lie in the maker’s original, deliberate, selective polishing.

Looking further down, the maker’s brilliance is seen once again.

A rocky, mountain-form base is nothing unfamiliar in early Nepalese sculpture. From roughly the seventh century onward, this kind of rock formation had become a recognizable visual language. Instead of imitating a natural cliff face, he compressed the mountain into tiers of folded lines, recessed planes, steps, and interlocking geometric forms. This ninth-century work carries this tradition but not without some slight changes.

The rock forms on either side draw inward toward the center in graduated steps, and what would naturally be an uneven, irregular formation is arranged instead into something close to symmetry. A clearly recessed space is carved at the center, its surrounding stone faces folding inward like the facets of a cut gem, with the vajra set into the very core of that hollow. The open form of the vajra, straight and sharp as a ruled line, is full of tension. It reads like an interior space thrown open, concealing at its deepest point the Vajra family to which Akshobhya belongs. Belief here is built into the structure itself.

A base like this can easily be seen as modern.

The recessed facets, the crisp folded lines, the contrast between matte and polished surfaces — all of this shares a certain kinship with today’s architecture, jewelry, product design, and visual display. But to say, on that basis, that this ninth-century maker was ‘ahead of his time’ or ‘anticipated modern design’ would still be a bit too glib. The value of ancient art does not need modern taste to validate it. What is truly worth asking is: why do certain forms still resonate, more than a thousand years later?

The answer is simple.

Clear hierarchy and accurate proportion do not go out of date. Neither does a real understanding of a material’s properties. The maker was not striving for a futuristic sense— he was simply solving the problems in front of him with enough precision and specificity. To make the Buddha stand out from the background, he varied the degree of polish. To make a small vajra the visual center of the whole piece, he folded the rock inward and used recess and shadow to draw the eye. To preserve a traditional mountain-form image without it looking merely copied, he translated natural form into a clear geometric order.

So what feels ‘new’ about this piece did not come from breaking free of tradition. Quite the opposite: the maker was deeply familiar with mountain-form imagery going back to the seventh century, and equally versed in the classical Licchavi principles for shaping the body. This familiarity enabled him to make new arrangements from within the tradition. Today we tend to equate creativity with breaking rules, as though it were its only way. We seem to assume that a work needs bold color, large scale, and dense information to not be dismissed. This stone carving provides a different answer; creation does not necessarily mean something entirely new. An old image does not necessarily mean old thinking. Rigid is but the repetition that has lost judgement.

When an age truly commands its own visual language, it can do more than preserve tradition — it can grow new forms. Even now, more than a thousand years later, the lines, facets, and the sheen on this stone still stop us in our tracks.

Because inherent in it is a beauty that is timeless.

title.en: Ulrich von Schroeder, Nepalese Stone Sculptures
Aṣṭasāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā on a Palm-Leaf Manuscript

subtitle.zh: 在贝叶上留下一个愿望。
subtitle.en: Wishes on a Palm Leaf — A Twelfth-Century Nepalese Perfection of Wisdom in Eight Thousand Lines
