subtitle.zh: 我愿意走近你的处境，而不带着我固有的形状。

excerpt.en: A doe nursing her fawn

viewingNote.zh:
今天的人很会谈“爱”。谈理解、共情、温柔、善良。可再往深处问一步，真正稀缺的，往往不是这些动人的词，而是：当它落在一个具体生命上时，究竟是什么样子。

一只母鹿，站立，低首，正在哺乳双膝下跪的幼鹿。二者共同立于双层莲瓣台座之上。这件雕塑出自古代尼泊尔尼瓦尔工匠之手。尼瓦尔人长久以来以铸造铜质雕塑著称，但让这件作品灵动的，不只是技术，更是观察。工匠一定见过鹿，见过母鹿低首的弧度，也见过幼鹿跪地时前腿的姿态。他把那真实的一瞬，永久停留在了金属里。

如果要真正读懂这件雕塑，我们需要先回到它的源头。

释迦牟尼最初传法的地方叫鹿野苑。从那时起，鹿便不只是动物，而成为教法本身的象征。传说大梵天敬献法轮时，林中出现了一对克里希那萨拉羚羊，目不转睛地凝视着法轮。释迦牟尼随后将心识被八正道所感化的男女众生，比作这一对小鹿。所以，当我们走进任何一座寺院，屋顶最高处往往是一对小鹿簇拥着八辐法轮。

母鹿头顶细小的角状突起，也是理解这件雕塑的关键细节。通常雌鹿不长角，但现实中的克里希那萨拉羚羊（印度黑羚）却具有明显的两性差异：雄性生有修长的螺旋角，而雌性通常无角。不过，印度自然史记录中也偶见雌性生有短小、退化的羚角。佛教艺术则沿用了这一天然地、模糊了性别边界的特征，将雌雄两鹿都描绘为带角的形态，并非混淆性别，而是以此标示它们已超越普通生物的范畴，同时也宣告着这是法的化身。

这件雕塑同时承载着两个故事——一个关于教法的象征，一个关于慈悲的本质。慈悲的本质，藏在《本生经》里。

一只怀孕的母鹿在抽签中被选中送往屠场。她向鹿王哀求。鹿王只说了一句话：“安心去吧。”然后他自己走向屠夫的刀俎，献出了自己金色的脖颈。波罗奈王目睹这一幕，说：“即便在人类之中，我也从未见过像您这样的存在。”他从此下令，永远保护所有鹿。

让人在雕塑旁久久停留的，不是牺牲的结果，而是“安心去吧”这四个字背后的状态。那不是勇气压制了恐惧，而是某种更深的东西，让恐惧根本没有落脚之地。鹿王走向刀俎，就像走向他本来就应该在的位置。

《本生经》里，释迦牟尼在无数前世化身为国王、商人、兔、象、鹿——不是因为他伟大，而是因为他愿意进入每一种处境，去经验恐惧、饥饿、母性的牵挂、弱小者的无助。他不是以觉者的身份俯视众生的苦，而是以众生的身份，从内部认识那个苦。这，才是慈悲真正的结构：不是“我理解你的苦”，而是“我愿意进入你的处境，而不带着我固有的形状”。

现在，这种能力是非常稀缺的，为什么会如此呢？

不是因为人冷漠，而是因为真正的慈悲需要一个前提：那就是离开自己站的地方，走进另一个人站的地方。不是从自己的位置伸出手，而是真正挪动脚步。一个人需要被无条件地接住过、爱过，才能在身体层面知道那是一种什么感觉，才有可能将它给予出去。很多人从未经历过那个时刻。于是谈共情、谈善良，只是在用头脑描述一种从未用身体经历过的感觉。语言是准确的，但内里是空的。

法国哲学家列维纳斯说，伦理始于对他者脆弱的回应——不是因为规则，而是因为那个脆弱本身对你产生了召唤。鹿王走向刀俎，是因为他真正看见了那只母鹿的处境。母鹿低下头颅，是因为她看见了幼鹿的饥饿。慈悲不是意志力的产物，而是感知力抵达某个深度之后，自然发生的事。当你真的看见，行动不需要说服自己。

这也同样是“境随心变”真正的含义——不是调整心态，而是当一个人内在的感知结构真正改变了，他所能触及的世界深度就变了。慈悲不是道德要求，它是一种感知能力。拥有它的人，与周围人事物的相处也会随之而变——不是因为更努力地去爱，而是因为看见的东西已经不同了。

这件雕塑安静地立在这里。母鹿低着头，幼鹿跪在地上。两个生命，以各自的俯身，完成了一个穿越几百年的动作。它不试图说服你任何事情，它只是把慈悲的形状呈现。

那么此刻，正在看着它的你——上一次真正看见另一个人的处境，是什么时候？
viewingNote.en:
People today are fluent in “love.” They speak of understanding, empathy, tenderness, kindness. But probe one layer deeper, and you find the emptiness of it. What happens when they’re actually put to the test?

Here is a mother deer standing with her head lowered, nursing a fawn kneeling on both forelegs beneath her. The two figures rise together from a double lotus-petal pedestal. This sculpture was cast by a Newar craftsman. The Newar people have long been renowned for their bronze casting, but what animates this piece is more than technical skill — it is observation. The exact curve of a doe’s lowered head, the particular set of a fawn’s forelegs as it kneels all points to the craftsman’s observation of real deer. He then preserved that fleeting moment of reality forever in metal.

To understand this sculpture, we first need to return to its source.

Śākyamuni first turned the Wheel of Dharma at Deer Park in Sarnath. From that moment onward, the deer was no longer simply an animal; it became a symbol of the Buddha’s teaching. According to legend, when Great Brahmā offered the Dharma Wheel, a pair of kṛṣṇa-sāra antelope appeared in the grove and gazed upon it without blinking. Śākyamuni likened the pair to the men and women whose minds had been transformed by the Noble Eightfold Path. This is why, crowning Buddhist temples, one so often finds a pair of deer flanking an eight-spoked Dharma Wheel at the highest point of the roof.

The small, horn-like projections atop the female deer’s head offer another clue to the sculpture’s meaning. Female deer do not ordinarily grow horns, and the kṛṣṇa-sāra antelope—the Indian blackbuck—exhibits a striking difference between the sexes: males bear long, spiraling horns, while females are generally hornless. Yet Indian natural-history records occasionally note females with short, vestigial horns. In Buddhist art, the boundary between male and female antelope could likewise become less fixed, with horns sometimes appearing on both. Here, the unusual feature need not be understood as an attempt at naturalistic accuracy. Rather, it may signal that these deer belong to a realm beyond the ordinary distinctions of the animal world. Their altered forms make them not merely deer, but bearers of the Dharma.

There are two stories to this sculpture: one is a symbol of the Buddha's teaching; the other is the true nature of compassion, revealed by the Jātaka tales.

A pregnant doe was chosen by lot to be sent to slaughter. She begged the Deer King for mercy. Telling the doe to "Go in peace," the deer king walks to the block to offer his own golden throat. Witnessing this, the King of Benares said, "I have never encountered a being like you." From that day on, he decreed that all deer be protected forever.

What makes visitors linger before this sculpture may not be the sacrifice itself, but the state of mind behind the words, "go in peace." This was not courage overpowering fear; it was something deeper — a state in which fear simply had nowhere to take hold. The Deer King walked toward the block the way one walks toward a place one was always meant to.

In the Jātaka tales, Śākyamuni is reborn, life after life, as a king, a merchant, a hare, an elephant, a deer — not as a show of greatness but to show his willingness to experience every condition of existence: to feel fear, hunger, a mother's anxious devotion, the helplessness of the weak. Rather than look down on the suffering of sentient beings from the vantage point of an awakened being, he took on their very form and came to know that suffering from within. True compassion is not merely “understanding” the suffering of others but willing to leave the place you stand to actually experience their suffering.

Why is it so rare to witness such selflessness in today’s world? It is not because people are indifferent but because it requires one to leave the place they stand. It is not a matter of reaching out a hand from where one stands— it requires one to actually move their position. Only someone who has been loved and has been received without condition truly knows that feeling, and only then can they transfer it to someone else. Many people have never experienced it, and so when they speak of empathy, of kindness, they are only describing, with the mind, a feeling they have never experienced themselves. The words are precise but hollow.

The French philosopher Emmanuel Levinas wrote that ethics begins with a response to the vulnerability of the other — not because of any rule, but because that vulnerability itself makes a claim on you, calls out to you. The Deer King walked toward the block because he saw through the doe's situation. The mother deer lowers her head because she sees her fawn's hunger. Compassion is not a product of willpower; it is what happens naturally once perception reaches a certain depth. When you truly see, action needs no persuading.

This, too, is the true meaning of the saying "as the mind changes, so does the world" — not a matter of adjusting one's attitude, but of the fact that once a person's inner structure of perception genuinely changes, so does the depth of the world they are able to reach. Compassion is not a moral obligation; it is a capacity for perception. In those who possess it, the way they relate to the people and things around them shifts accordingly — not because they are trying harder to love, but because what they see has already become something different.

This sculpture stands here in silence. The mother deer's head is lowered; the fawn kneels at her feet. Two lives, each bowed low in its own way, complete a single gesture that has traveled across several hundred years. It does not try to persuade you of anything — it simply presents a shape of compassion.

So a question to the reader, when was the last time you truly saw things from another person’s perspective?

subtitle.zh: 她在边缘，中心才成立。

excerpt.en: Vajra Dakini

viewingNote.zh:
在藏传佛教美术中我们常常会看到女性题材是一个向内收拢的姿势。

怀抱、遮护、容纳。她将双臂围成一个安全的空间，把危险挡在外面，把生命留在里面。即便到了今天，人们谈论女性和母亲时，最常使用的词依然是温柔、照顾和牺牲。

但眼前这尊十三世纪尼泊尔的空行母，是推翻这种固定印象的存在。

她没有把任何人抱在怀里。她右手高举金刚杵，左手托着嘎巴拉，散发垂落在背后，身体以右展立姿向外打开。她的双足没有停在莲台上，而是分别踩住一男一女两位姿态夸张的神祇。头顶是五骷髅冠，胸前垂下一串由十七颗断首组成的人头鬘。

她将危险展示，把死亡穿在了身上。

从图像特征来看，这尊造像很可能表现的是胜乐金刚坛城眷属中的金刚空行母。她一面、二臂、三目，右手持金刚杵，左手持嘎巴拉，而非其他眷属空行母常见的金刚柄钺刀。她也没有以左臂环抱卡杖嘎，因此和独尊形式的金刚瑜伽母和金刚亥母有所区别。胜乐金刚体系中的主尊及其眷属，常常以骷髅冠、骨饰、颅器、忿怒姿态及足踏怖畏和黑时母等元素，共同构成一套彼此关联的图像。当然，在缺少铭文和原始坛城组合的情况下，这一身份仍应保留谨慎。但至少可以确定的是，她并非一位脱离体系、凭空出现的女性神祇。

她原本属于一个更大的世界。

在那个世界里，胜乐金刚和金刚亥母位于坛城中央，空行母则分布在中央之外。按照我们熟悉的空间逻辑，中央似乎天然意味着重要，外围则意味着次要；主尊拥有完整的名称和地位，眷属仿佛只是为了证明主尊的尊贵而存在。

可当这尊空行母被单独铸造，并被我们独立观看到时，原来的空间关系突然就发生了变化。中央本尊已经不在眼前，她却没有因此变得残缺。相反，她自己形成了一个中心。

这个中心，首先是由身体制造出来的。

她的右臂高高举起，金刚杵将力量推向上方；左臂向前侧展开，嘎巴拉又把视线带向外部。与此同时，两腿分别压向左右两侧，使整个身体不再沿着一条稳定、封闭的垂直线站立。她身上带着一种向外迸发的力。从肩部，到手臂；从腰部，到双腿；从散落的头发，到垂悬的人头鬘。几乎每一条线都试图离开身体的中心，向周围的空间伸展。

我们通常也会看到一些相似题材的造像虽然抬高了手臂、迈开了双腿，却仍然只是“摆出”了一个动态姿势。动作存在于外形，身体内部却没有真正的流动。眼前这件作品不同。匠人并不是简单地让她做出一个动作，而是让力量穿过了她的身体。

但更高明的是，这种向外迸发并没有使她失去控制。

她的上半身不断打开，下半身却被牢牢固定。脚下的两位神祇的体积，形成了两个体量饱满的支点，他们使所有向外扩张的线条，都有了可以承受重量的根基。所以在她的动态中既有重量，也有阻力。

她脚下所踩的，是怖畏和黑时母。

怖畏为男性形象，与湿婆信仰中的忿怒形态有关；黑时母则是与之相对的女性形象。在胜乐金刚体系的降伏叙事中，这一男一女被置于本尊足下，不仅可以被理解为烦恼、幻象和我执受到降伏，也保留了佛教密续与湿婆密教彼此竞争、吸收和重新解释的宗教史痕迹。

他们不是台座上一眼就会被忽略的符号，两人的身体向后翻折，头部夸张地后仰，手中仍然握着弯刀、嘎巴拉、达玛鲁鼓与卡杖嘎。他们有清楚的身体，有醒目的体积，也仍然保留着自身的力量与身份。

匠人没有通过缩小对手来抬高空行母。恰恰相反，他强化了对手。这使她的踩踏真正变成了一场正在发生的降伏。脚下之物越有重量，双腿便越显得坚定；他们越无法被忽视，她就越显得强大。因为，一个人战胜毫无抵抗力的东西，并不会使我们感到勇敢。真正令人敬畏的，是她所面对的对象本身就足够强大，而她依然没有后退。因此，脚下两位神祇并不是为了陪衬主尊而存在的多余形象。他们正是她的力量得以显现的条件。

也正因如此，这件空行母和它原本所属的坛城结构就发生了一种呼应。

我们总以为中心必须通过削弱边缘来证明自己。主角越突出，配角就应当越安静，但这件造像不是这样。脚下人物并没有因为她是主尊而消失。头冠、耳环、骨饰、人头鬘和法器也没有因为身体需要突出而被简化。相反，雕塑周围的信息非常密集，每个部分都拥有自己的形态和重量。可这些复杂元素最终也并没有争夺她的位置。而是共同把她推向了中心。

所谓中心，原来并不一定是通过清空周围才能建立起来的。有时，正是因为周围存在着足够复杂、强烈，甚至危险的事物，中心才获得了真正的分量。

她胸前的十七颗断首，也有相似的意味。

我们很容易把人头鬘当成忿怒神祇的标准装饰。看久了，它甚至可能变成一种熟悉的图像符号，不会再令人感到不安。但只要重新想象一下，就会发现这件饰物有多么激烈。

头颅不是普通的骨骼。是一个人的面孔、姓名、表情和社会身份，都集中在了头部。我们通过面孔认出别人，也通过别人的注视确认自己。头颅一旦离开身体，生命不只是短暂结束了，那个曾经稳定、完整的“我”，同时也失去了依托。而她把这些头颅串在一起，佩戴在自己的身体上。这或许也是她令人感到勇敢的原因。

在我们的社会想象中，常常把女性安排在远离死亡、血腥和危险的位置。女性可以美丽，可以照料生命，却不应该靠近那些令人恐惧、失控和不洁的事物。黑暗似乎只属于英雄需要征服的世界，而女性则是被等待保护的对象。但这位空行母没有站在黑暗的对面。她也没有等待谁来替她战胜黑暗。她将黑暗穿在身上。这并不是对杀戮的赞美，也不是因为她感受不到恐惧。恰恰相反，真正的勇敢从来不是不知道恐惧，而是当恐惧靠近后，我们可以不被其掌控。

可是，如果这尊造像只有恐怖，她不会如此动人。

她的脸上仍然保留着一种属于女性的温和。这种温和不是毫无力量的平静。三只眼睛、扬起的眉线和面部微妙的张力，使她的神情仿佛正处在爆发的前一刻。她不是完全愤怒，也不是完全安静；她的脸上同时存在着克制与冲动、温度与威慑。

匠人没有把力量理解成粗暴。

他也没有为了塑造一位强大的女性，而取消她身上所有细腻的部分。她的头冠精致，两侧耳环甚至采用了不同的样式。不同的耳饰给她带来了一点偶然性和个人感，使她像一个有选择、有性格的具体存在。骨饰、腰间的绳状璎珞带和人头鬘层层展开，却没有吞没身体。每一根线条都清晰地又保留各自的节奏。

她让人想到现实中那些真正有力量的女性。

她们未必声量很大，也不一定要变得强硬或粗糙。她们可以依然在意自己的穿着、情绪和感受，也依然保有温柔与细腻，但这并不妨碍她们在关键时刻做出决定、承担重量，甚至直面冲突。真正的力量，从来不是把自己变成“更像男人”，而是依然做自己，同时不被任何一种单一的形象定义。

这尊空行母最动人的地方，正是她拒绝了这种二选一。

她可以佩戴精美的耳环，也可以把人头挂在胸前；她的脸上可以保留温度，她的手中也可以高举金刚杵；她的身体可以柔软而优美，同时又有能力压住脚下两个体量饱满的对手。不是所谓简单的“刚柔并济”，因为“刚”与“柔”在这里并不是两种被勉强拼在一起的性质。它们原本就属于同一个人。

写到这里，我又想到一个社会中常常会产生的偏见。提到“眷属”会容易联想到附属。但“眷属”从来就不等于附属。

在坛城中，外围并不是中心之外无关紧要的剩余空间。每一个方向、每一位眷属、每一种法器和姿态，都参与界定了中央的性质。倘若抽走这些关系，只保留一个孤立的主尊，中心也就失去了它原本的完整意义。中心从来不是一个位置。中心是一组关系共同产生的结果。这尊空行母原本或许位于胜乐金刚坛城的外围，但当她被独立铸造成像时，我们才更清楚地看见：她并没有从中央借来全部意义。她自身就拥有行动、智慧与转化的能力。

我们今天依然生活在一种崇拜中心的秩序里。

我们记住的是最醒目的名字，追随的是最响亮的声音，也习惯了用职位、地位和可见度判断一个人的重要性。一个家庭、一种传统、一个机构乃至一个时代，似乎总要选出少数代表人物，然后把全部成就集中在他们身上。

但真正让一种秩序延续下去的，往往并不只是这些被看见的人。还有无数人在边缘传递知识，维系关系，处理危险，承受混乱，把即将破碎的事物重新连接起来。

她们未必拥有中心的位置，却承担着中心的功能。

同样，她不是因为靠近中心才重要。相反，是因为她在，中心才能成立。
viewingNote.en:
In Tibetan Buddhist art, female figures are often depicted in yab-yum, embracing, sheltering and encompassing their male counterpart.

Her arms curve around to form a safe enclosure, holding danger at bay and cradling life within. Even today, the words we reach for most often when speaking of women and mothers remain tenderness, care, and sacrifice.

However, this thirteenth-century Nepalese dakini before us overturns that fixed image.

She holds no one in her arms. Her right hand raises a vajra high overhead; her left cradles a kapala. Her loose hair streams down her back, and her body opens outward in a striding pose to the right. Her feet rest not on a lotus pedestal but on two deities, one male and one female, both caught in exaggerated, contorted postures. A crown of five skulls sits atop her head, and a garland of seventeen severed heads hangs across her chest.

She puts danger on display and wears death upon her body.

Iconographically, this figure most likely represents Vajradakini, one of the retinue deities of the Chakrasamvara mandala. She has one face, two arms, and three eyes; her right hand holds a vajra and her left a kapala, rather than the vajra-hilted chopper (kartrika) more commonly seen among the other attendant dakinis. The absence of a khaṭvāṅga staff in the crook of her left arm further distinguishes her from the independent forms of Vajrayoginī and Vajravārāhī.

Within the Chakrasamvara system, the central deity and the surrounding retinue typically share a coherent set of visual elements — skull crowns, bone ornaments, skull cups, wrathful postures, and feet trampling Bhairava and Kalaratri. Admittedly, in the absence of an inscription or the original mandala grouping, this identification should be held with appropriate caution. But at the very least, we can be confident that she is not some isolated female deity conjured out of nowhere, detached from any larger system.

She once belonged to a larger world.

In that world, Chakrasamvara and Vajravarahi occupied the center of the mandala, while the dakinis were arrayed around its periphery. By the spatial logic we know so well, the center seems naturally to signify importance and the periphery to signify the secondary; the central deity holds a full name and full status, while the retinue seems to exist only to affirm the central deity's eminence.

But once this dakini is cast as a standalone figure, and once we view her on her own, that original spatial relationship shifts abruptly. The central deity is no longer seen — and yet she is not diminished for it. On the contrary, she becomes a center in her own right.

She is the center first and foremost because of how she stands.

Her right arm rises high, the vajra driving force upward; her left arm extends outward to the side, the kapala pulling the eye further out. At the same time, her two legs press toward opposite sides, so that the body no longer stands along one stable, self-contained vertical axis. Her whole figure carries an outward-bursting energy — from shoulder to arm, from waist to legs, from loosened hair to the hanging garland of skulls. Nearly every line seems to strain away from the body's center, reaching out into the surrounding space.

We often see comparable images that raise an arm or stride a leg and yet still merely “strike” a dynamic pose — the motion exists on the surface, without any real current running through the body. This work is different. The sculptor did not simply place her into a gesture; he let force pass through her entire body.

What is more accomplished still is that this outward burst of energy never costs her control.

Her upper body continually opens outward, while her lower body remains firmly anchored. The substantial bulk of the two deities beneath her feet forms two solid points of support, giving every outward-radiating line a base capable of bearing weight. Her movement therefore carries both mass and resistance.

Trampled under her foot, there lay Bhairava and Kalaratri.

Bhairava is a male figure associated with the wrathful forms of Shaivism, while Kalaratri is his female counterpart. In the subjugation narrative of the Chakrasamvara system, this male-female pair placed beneath the central deity's feet can be read as the taming of affliction, illusion, and ego-clinging — and it also preserves a trace of religious history, the record of Buddhist tantra and Shaiva tantra competing with, absorbing, and reinterpreting one another.

They are no mere symbols to be glanced over and forgotten on the pedestal. Their bodies arch backward, their heads thrown back at an exaggerated angle, and their hands still grip a chopper, a kapala, a damaru drum, and a khatvanga. They possess clearly articulated bodies, a striking physical presence, and they retain their own power and identity.

The sculptor did not elevate the dakini by diminishing her opponents. Quite the opposite — he made them stronger.

This makes her act of trampling look like a subjugation genuinely in progress. The heavier what lies beneath her feet, the more resolute her stance appears; the harder they are to ignore, the more powerful she becomes. After all, overcoming something with no capacity to resist never strikes us as courageous. What truly commands our awe is that the forces she confronts are formidable in their own right, and still she does not retreat. The two deities underfoot, then, are not superfluous figures included merely to set off the central deity. They are precisely the condition through which her power becomes visible.

And it is precisely for this reason that this dakini resonates with the very mandala structure to which she originally belonged.

We tend to assume the center must prove itself by diminishing the margins — the more prominent the protagonist, the quieter the supporting figures ought to be. This sculpture refuses that logic. The figures beneath her feet do not vanish simply because she is the principal deity. Her crown, earrings, bone ornaments, skull garland, and ritual implements are not simplified merely to make her body stand out. On the contrary, the imagery surrounding her is densely packed, and every element carries its own form and weight. Yet none of this complexity competes for her position. Instead, all of it works together to push her toward the center.

The center, it turns out, need not be built by clearing everything around it. Sometimes it is precisely because its surroundings are complex, intense, even dangerous, that the center acquires its true weight.

The seventeen severed heads across her chest carry a similar meaning.

It is easy to treat a garland of skulls as standard iconographic dress for a wrathful deity. Seen often enough, it can even settle into a familiar visual symbol that no longer unsettles us. But imagine it afresh, and its sheer violence becomes apparent again.

A skull is not merely a bone. A person's face, name, expression, and social identity are all concentrated in the head. We recognize others by their faces, and we confirm ourselves through the way others look at us. Once the head is severed from the body, life does not simply end — the once-stable, once-whole ‘self’ loses its foundation as well. And she has strung these heads together and worn them on her own body. This, perhaps, is part of why she strikes us as courageous.

In our social imagination, women are so often positioned far from death, bloodshed, and danger. A woman may be beautiful, may tend to life, but she is not supposed to draw near to what is frightening, uncontrolled, or impure. Darkness seems to belong only to the world that heroes must conquer, while women are cast as those awaiting protection. But this dakini does not stand opposite the darkness. Nor does she wait for anyone to conquer it on her behalf. She wears the darkness on her own body. This is not a celebration of killing, nor does it mean she feels no fear. Quite the opposite: true courage has never meant not knowing fear — it means that when fear draws near, we are not ruled by it.

And yet, if this figure held only terror, she would not move us the way she does.

Her face still retains a gentleness that feels distinctly feminine — though this is not the gentleness of powerless calm. Her three eyes, the arch of her brows, and the subtle tension across her features give her expression the quality of a moment poised just before eruption. She is neither fully wrathful nor fully at peace; her face holds restraint and impulse, warmth and menace, all at once.

The sculptor did not mistake power for brutality.

Nor, in shaping a powerful woman, did he strip away every trace of delicacy. Her crown is finely wrought, and her two earrings are even rendered in different designs — a mismatch that lends her a touch of contingency and individuality, as though she were a specific being capable of choice, possessed of her own character. Her bone ornaments, the corded girdle at her waist, and the garland of heads unfold layer upon layer, yet never overwhelm her body. Every line remains distinct, each keeping its own rhythm. She calls to mind the truly powerful women we encounter in real life.

They need not be loud, nor need they be rough. They can still care about how they dress, how they feel, what moves them; they can still hold on to tenderness and nuance — none of which keeps them from making decisions, bearing weight, or facing conflict head-on when it matters most. True strength has never meant becoming ‘more like a man.’ It means being true to oneself and not defined by a single image.

What makes this dakini so moving is that she does not conform to either category.

She can wear exquisite earrings and still hang severed heads across her chest; her face can hold warmth even as her hand raises a vajra aloft; her body can be soft and graceful while still bearing down on two substantial adversaries beneath her feet. This is not some simple case of ‘strength balanced with softness,’ because strength and softness here are not two qualities forced awkwardly together. They belong, from the start, to one and the same person.

Writing this, I am reminded of a bias our society so often produces. The word ‘retinue’ too easily calls to mind ‘subordinate.’ But a retinue has never been the same thing as a subordinate.

Within a mandala, the periphery is not some inconsequential leftover space outside the center. Every direction, every attendant deity, every ritual implement and posture takes part in defining the nature of the center. Strip away these relationships and leave only an isolated central deity, and the center loses its original, complete meaning. The center was never a position. The center is the outcome produced by a whole set of relationships. This dakini may originally have stood at the edge of the Chakrasamvara mandala, but once cast as an independent figure, we can see all the more clearly: she did not borrow her entire meaning from the center. She herself possesses the capacity for action, wisdom, and transformation.

We still live today within an order that worships the center.

We remember the most conspicuous names, follow the loudest voices, and have grown accustomed to measuring a person's importance by title, status, and visibility. A family, a tradition, an institution, even an entire era, always seems to single out a handful of representative figures and pile every achievement onto them.

But what truly allows an order to endure is rarely just these visible few. Countless others work at the margins, passing on knowledge, sustaining relationships, managing danger, absorbing chaos, and mending what is on the verge of breaking apart.

They may not hold a position at the center, yet they carry out the center's function.

In the same way, her importance is not defined by her proximity to the center. Rather, the center finds its meaning through her presence.

subtitle.zh: 这种魅惑般的迷离感，让人忍不住去反复观看。

excerpt.en: Vajravarahi

viewingNote.zh:
如果遮住她手里的钺刀、头顶的骷髅，还有脚下被踩踏的身体，只看这张脸，真的很难立刻把她和“恐怖”联系在一起。

她有三只眼睛，右侧发间探出一颗蓝色猪首，嘴角微微向上。她的目光凝聚性很强，脸上那种笑意不是温顺的笑，似乎也夹带着一丝忿怒。而舒展、舞动的身姿，以及那鲜红的皮肤、披散的头发、骨饰、珠饰和断首璎珞都叠在一起，使祂看上去既危险，又异常鲜活，充满着一种很难言明的魅惑和迷离感。

这是一幅大约十二世纪的西夏金刚亥母唐卡。

黑水城出土的一份《金刚亥母修习仪》，在描述本尊时，同时用了两个看似冲突的词：一边是“忿怒”，另一边却说她“作窈窕相”。所以我们站在画前感受到的那种吸引力，未必只是现代人的主观投射。至少在这套修法所要求的神圣中，忿怒和迷人原本就能够同时成立。至于画师最终怎样把这种“窈窕”具体画成眼前这双眼睛、这道嘴角，则也已经进入艺术本身的选择。而就是这样一个明显来自印度晚期密宗世界的姿态，为什么会在十二世纪出现在中国西北的黑水城？

今天的黑水城，是一片被风沙包围的废墟。一说到西北，很容易让人想到大漠孤烟直中的戈壁和荒凉。但十二世纪的黑水城并不只是我们今天看到的沙中废城。它建立在黑河下游的绿洲，河流、灌溉系统、农田和人口共同维持着军镇、寺院和城市的运转。‌更重要的是它的位置：向南可以接入河西走廊，向西联系敦煌与西域，向北进入蒙古高原，向东则是西夏腹地；向西南，经青海东部、安多等区域，又可以继续进入藏地。所以黑水城不只是丝绸之路上一个普通的停靠点，更像河西走廊与蒙古高原南北交通之间的一个灵活的转轴点。商人、僧侣、军队、使者、译师、经卷和图像，都可能沿不同方向抵达这里。如果只按今天的国界看地图，黑水城距离印度非常遥远；但如果换成古代道路和人群流动去看，它的位置就完全不同了。

这也牵涉到一个经常被提起、却并不容易真正理解的概念：内亚。“内亚”本身是历史学和区域研究中的一种分析概念，不同学者使用时范围并不完全一致。大体而言是指：蒙古高原、河西走廊、塔里木盆地、青藏高原以及更广阔的欧亚内陆区域，这里长期通过草原、荒漠、绿洲、高原与山地彼此联系。这样重新看地图以后，一尊带有明显印度与藏地视觉语言的金刚亥母出现在黑水城，也就没有最初那么不可思议了。

十一世纪前期，李德明时期的党项政权已经多次主动向北宋求取汉文佛典。宫廷在取得汉文佛教大藏经后，并逐渐建立以佛典翻译为重要任务的机构。1032 年李元昊继位，约1036 年前后西夏文字完成创制并开始推行，1038 年元昊称帝。

然而回看历史，一个国祚不到两百年的政权，却留下了自己的文字、规模庞大的西夏文佛典体系和成熟的翻译机制；佛教僧官体系中出现国师等高级僧职，到了西夏晚期的材料里，还能够看到“帝师”这一特殊称号。

从国祚时间和文明建设的尺度来看，这显然形成一种强烈的反差。

文字首先意味着它有一种明确的国家意识。一个新政权需要行政、教育和法律来建立身份和国家秩序。而对西夏来说，文字还有另一层更实际的象征和意义：它重视文化，它让外来的知识开始被重新组织并内部吸收。佛经可以从汉文译成西夏文，后来藏文佛教文本也进入新的翻译体系。僧侣、译师、官员和抄写者共同参与其中。所以西夏真正特别的，也许并不只是“融合了很多文化”，而是它很早就学会了如何把原本属于别人的知识，转化成自己能够理解、使用，甚至变成持续为王朝产生价值的存在。到了十二世纪，尤其十二世纪后半，这套文化机制已经积累了一个多世纪，而西夏面对的佛教世界也发生了明显变化。

西夏早期接受佛教与汉地、辽以及中国北方佛教传统关系很深。因此黑水城留下的绘画中，有不少熟悉的汉地面貌：阿弥陀净土、水月观音、佛经扉画，一些空间与人物处理也延续着宋、辽和河西长期形成的视觉传统。但可能藏传佛教并不是十二世纪才进入西夏，因为河西一带更早已经存在吐蕃时代延续下来的藏文佛教传统。据记载，只是进入十二世纪，尤其后半叶以后，来自藏地后弘期的新译密教传统、上师以及文本在西夏的影响明显增强。

由于十二世纪的藏地，并不是一个封闭的地方佛教世界。阿底峡在十一世纪已经进入藏地；大量藏地僧人继续前往印度学习，印度东北部与克什米尔等地的学者也不断进入高原。晚期印度密续、灌顶、修法和图像，就在这样的往返中持续传播。西夏南缘与安多、宗喀一带又直接相接，所以这很可能就构成了西夏接入藏地佛教网络的重要通道之一，但它并不是唯一道路。河西、敦煌以及宫廷僧侣之间的跨区域往来，同样属于这张传播网的一部分。因此，十二世纪西夏面对的“藏地佛教”，背后其实还连接着一个仍然活跃的印度晚期佛教世界。

这条路也不是后人或者学者们根据地图想象出来的。克什米尔学者阇耶难陀先进入藏中活动，后来又前往党项宫廷，并获得国师称号；同时也有和弥药党项文化圈1 关系密切的译师传记，保存着进入藏地乃至印度求法的记忆。上师、弟子和译师，用真正的人的移动，把这些地区连在了一起。金刚亥母的修法与视觉体系，正是在这样的跨区域的佛教文化交流中进入了西夏。而黑水城绘画最有意思的一点，也在这里逐渐显现。

西夏并没有把来自不同地区的视觉语言搅拌成一种均匀的“混合风”。与汉地佛教知识传统联系紧密的阿弥陀净土、水月观音和部分佛经扉画，往往以宋、辽、河西已经成熟的汉地绘画语言作为主要视觉基础；而金刚亥母、胜乐等与十二世纪藏印新译密教密切相关的题材，则更明显地保存着东北印度帕拉经藏地和喜马拉雅地区转译后的图像结构和视觉传统。很有意思的是，不同宗教的知识往往会为图像提供不同的主导视觉语法，而西夏的画师却并不愿意受到一种语法的束缚。同一件黑水城绘画内部，也可能同时出现宋式构图、藏式神祇、中国传统符号以及本地化处理。

所以西夏艺术的样貌，未必是建立在“没有外来影响”之上。它的身份，恰恰形成于如何选择和重构这些语言，从而让它们变成我们想说的话。因此，风格在这里也就不再只是一种形式判断。它同时成为了历史留下来的证据：当我们看见一尊神祇怎么画时，也就代表着十二世纪的西夏正在向哪一个知识方向伸手。

所以，重新再次面对眼前这张唐卡时，这种时代背景一下就开始变得非常具体了。

在黑水城出土的《金刚亥母修习仪》中，对本尊如何被观想描述得很细致：赤红的身体，三只眼睛，头侧蓝黑色猪面，右手把弯曲的钺刀举到耳侧附近，左手持颅器，腋下夹卡章嘎，头戴五骷髅冠，披散长发，佩戴断首璎珞，一腿扬起，一腿踩踏，同时呈现忿怒而又“窈窕”的状态。这张唐卡，几乎每一项都能找到对应。

《金刚亥母修习仪》中的记录很重要，因为它说明眼前的金刚亥母并不是一张偶然流入黑水城的“异域宗教图像”。黑水城还保存了和金刚亥母有关的禅定、寝定、施食、集轮、灌顶等不同修习文本。虽然这些文本并不能让我们还原每一个十二世纪修行者真实的日常行为，但却足以说明：金刚亥母在黑水城并不是只存在于图像层面，而已经进入一套非常具体的仪轨实践中。

这也让我重新理解这张脸为什么如此特别。

现代人看一张画，首先会先观察颜色、构图和技法，这是一种站在画外的观看方式。密教观想却并不满足于这种距离。修行者需要在意识中一步步重建本尊：她是什么颜色，身体怎样转动，手中拿什么，眼睛怎样睁开、然后显现出什么，这些在修习过程中都会有清楚的变化。虽然目前我们已经无法证明八百年前的画师刻意把她画得如此迷人，就是为了帮助观想。但这张画形成的视觉效果，确实与这样的宗教功能高度契合。

祂占据中央，几乎把整个画面撑满。红色的身体和红色的火焰不断纠缠，背景也被大片红色吞没；白色的骨饰、黑色的秀发和蓝绿色飘带穿插其中。头部的动势明显前倾，圆睁的眼睛似乎能把人的视线钉住。钺刀逼近画面边缘，斜穿身体的卡章嘎加强了运动感。断首、骷髅、尸体这些关于死亡的符号全部存在，可她没有因此变得沉重。恰好相反，祂轻盈、灵动，太有生命力了。尤其是那一点似笑非笑的神情，让整张画产生一种很奇怪的关系：祂不像安静地在等待我们观看，反而我们像是被祂观看的。

也许所谓“入境”，首先不是靠复杂解释发生的。很多时候，是一个足够鲜明的形体、一双无法回避的眼睛、一点不确定的笑意，先把人的注意力从画外拉进去。对一件和观想实践密切相关的图像而言，这种鲜明、稳定而具有吸引力的画面，与修行中需要持续记忆和重新建立本尊形象的过程，至少形成了一种高度契合。

而这里恰恰也是我们常说的“艺术性”真正展开的地方。

仪轨虽然可以规定金刚亥母必须是红色、三目、有猪首、持钺刀，但却不会完全规定眼睛必须画多大，脸必须多圆，鼻梁到底多长，人物究竟占据多少画面。仪轨规定了本尊的样貌，却无法完全规定画师心中祂的具体模样。而脸型、比例、线条、色彩、构图与身体尺度，也正是艺术传统和画师技艺得到凸显的地方。

在十二世纪东北印度帕拉塞纳体系2 及相关密教艺术中，已经可以看到红色女性神祇、舞姿、火焰、尸体和复杂饰物形成的视觉母体。当这样的语言进入到藏地，在经历了一次重新组织后；到了西夏，图像又继续发生了变化。因此，我们可以在这张金刚亥母身上追溯到印度和藏地的来源，但却不能再把她简单称作为“一张帕拉风格的西夏画”。尽管西夏画师并没有重新发明金刚亥母，但他重新决定了，我们怎么呈现属于他们语言中的金刚亥母。

这其实和西夏此前一个多世纪一直在进行的事情非常相似。

西夏文字使用外来的经典和知识重新译写内容；译经把不同语言中的佛教思想转化成本地能够使用的知识；上师和弟子在不同地区之间传递修法；而绘画，则在重新组织一个带有神圣性的身体。

一个国祚不到两百年的政权，却留下了自己的文字和西夏文的佛典体系、复杂的翻译系统、国师等高级僧职，以及晚期材料中出现的帝师称号；同时还留下了这样一批一眼看去既像印度、又像西藏，却又不是西藏；既有汉地气息，又无法简单归入宋画的佛教图像。

或许它真正吸引人和令人惊讶的，也许从来不是身处交通交汇地带所造成的“混合”。而是在强烈的文化意识的驱动下所做出的选择和所体现的能力，那是一种让不同视觉语言服务于不同知识与信仰的能力。

所以今天面对西夏时，我们总喜欢说它“神秘”。

一个存在不到两百年的王朝，一套后来长期无人识读的文字，一座被荒漠包围的废城，确实很容易让它显得遥远。可真正走近这张画之后，我反而觉得，神秘更多是今天的我们回望一个失落王朝时产生的感觉。对于十二世纪生活在这个世界中的人而言，很多事情其实非常具体。于是再看眼前这张金刚亥母，那张带着忿怒、魅惑和鲜活生命感的脸，也不再只是一个无法理解的“神秘表情”了，反而只会惊叹于它们所留下的艺术魅力。因为当这一切真正落到西夏画师的笔下，历史已经不再只是道路和传播。它变成了颜色，变成了线条，也变成那一张让人忍不住去反复观看的笑意。

此刻我反而想到了一句题外话：为什么我们总觉得这些古代艺术品如此珍贵？因为它真正留下来的，不只是金刚亥母的形象。而是把印度、藏地、安多、河西与黑水城之间曾经真实发生过的人群移动、知识交换与视觉转换，压缩进了一张画面。

八百多年了，当我们重新站到祂面前，那个十二世纪，也就从这具鲜红的身姿中，一点一点开始了重新展开。

1 、“弥药”（也作“弭药”或“木雅”）是藏族对古代党项族（党项羌）及其建立的西夏政权的称谓。“弥药党项文化圈”指的是以党项/弥药族群的历史记忆、语言文字、宗教信仰及独特的地域文化为纽带，在我国西北、西南（如川西藏区、青海、甘肃、宁夏及河西走廊一带）交汇形成的特定历史与文化区域。

2 、“帕拉塞纳”并不是指一个统一的王朝，或一个严格成立的艺术流派。它更像艺术史研究里的一个便利称呼，用来描述大约8—13世纪东北印度，特别是比哈尔、孟加拉一带，从帕拉王朝延续到塞纳王朝时期形成并持续发展的佛教视觉传统。
viewingNote.en:
Before looking at the flaying knife, the skull crown, and the body trampled beneath her feet, look only at her face: she hardly looks terrifying.

With three eyes, and a small blue boar's head emerging from the hair above her right temple; the corners of her mouth curl faintly upward. Her gaze is intensely focused, her smile not quite gentle — something like wrath flickers at its edges. Her limbs open in a dancing pose, and crimson skin, loose flowing hair, bone ornaments, strings of beads, and a garland of severed heads all layer into one figure — dangerous and startlingly alive, with a hazy, dreamlike allure that resists description.

This is a Vajravarahi thangka from Western Xia, dating to around the twelfth century.

A Vajravarahi sadhana excavated at Khara-Khoto describes the deity using two seemingly contradictory terms in the same breath: on one hand “wrathful,” and on the other, it says she takes “a graceful, alluring form.” So the pull we feel standing before this painting may not be merely a modern viewer's projection. At least within the sanctity this practice calls for, wrathfulness and allure were always meant to coexist.

How the painter translated that "gracefulness" into this particular pair of eyes, this curve of the mouth, was his own to decide. The more interesting question is how a figure so rooted in the visual world of late Indian tantric Buddhism came to appear at Khara-Khoto, in northwestern China, in the twelfth century.

Today Khara-Khoto is a ruin swallowed by wind and sand. Mention the northwest and most people picture the vast, solitary desert of popular imagination — the gobi, the emptiness. But twelfth-century Khara-Khoto was more than the sand-buried ruin we see today. It stood on an oasis fed by the lower reaches of the Ejin River, where waterways, irrigation systems, farmland, and population together sustained a garrison town, its monasteries, and its urban life. Just as important was its location: to the south it connected to the Hexi Corridor; to the west it linked to Dunhuang and the Western Regions; to the north it opened onto the Mongolian plateau; to the east lay the Tangut heartland; and to the southwest, by way of eastern Qinghai and the Amdo region, it continued on into Tibet. Khara-Khoto thus functioned more like a flexible pivot point where the north–south routes of the Hexi Corridor and the Mongolian plateau met. Merchants, monks, armies, envoys, translators, scriptures, and images could all converge here from different directions. On a map drawn to today's borders, Khara-Khoto looks impossibly far from India. Measured instead by the ancient roads and the movement of peoples, its position looks entirely different.

This brings us to a term often invoked but rarely well understood: Inner Asia.

“Inner Asia” is an analytical term from historical and regional studies, and its precise scope varies from scholar to scholar; broadly speaking, it refers to the Mongolian plateau, the Hexi Corridor, the Tarim Basin, the Xizang Plateau, and the wider interior of the Eurasian landmass — a world long connected through steppe, desert, oasis, plateau, and mountain. Seen this way, a Vajravarahi so visibly speaking the visual language of India and Tibet no longer seems so improbable an arrival at Khara-Khoto.

In the early eleventh century, under Li Deming, the Tangut regime had repeatedly petitioned the Northern Song court for Chinese Buddhist scriptures. Once the court had obtained the Chinese Buddhist canon, it gradually established institutions devoted to the translation of Buddhist texts. Li Yuanhao succeeded to power in 1032; the Tangut script was completed and began to be promulgated around 1036; and in 1038 Yuanhao proclaimed himself emperor.

And yet, looking back, this was a state that lasted less than two centuries — and still it left behind its own script, an extensive body of Buddhist scripture in the Tangut language, and a mature system of translation. Its Buddhist clergy developed a hierarchy of official ranks that included the title of State Preceptor, and in materials from the late Western Xia we even find the distinct title of Imperial Preceptor.

Set against the brevity of its reign, the scale of this cultural achievement forms a striking contrast.

A script, first of all, signals a clear sense of statehood: a new regime needs administration, education, and law to establish its identity and its order. For Western Xia, the script carried a further, more practical significance as well — it reflected a regime that valued culture, one able to take knowledge from outside and reorganize it for its own use. Buddhist scriptures could be translated from Chinese into Tangut, and later Xizang Buddhist texts entered this same translation system, with monks, translators, officials, and scribes all taking part. What made Western Xia truly distinctive, then, was perhaps not simply that it “blended many cultures,” but that it learned, remarkably early, how to take knowledge that had originally belonged to others and turn it into something it could understand, use, and even draw on as an enduring source of value for the dynasty. By the twelfth century — especially its second half — this cultural mechanism had been building for more than a hundred years, even as the Buddhist world Western Xia now faced was itself changing.

In its early stages, Western Xia's Buddhism was closely tied to the traditions of the Chinese heartland, the Liao, and northern China more broadly. This is why so much of the painting surviving from Khara-Khoto has a familiar Chinese cast to it — Amitabha's Pure Land, Water-Moon Avalokiteshvara, sutra frontispieces — and why its handling of space and figures often continues visual conventions long established under the Song, the Liao, and in the Hexi region. Xizang Buddhism, however, likely did not arrive in Western Xia only in the twelfth century, since the Hexi region carried Xizang Buddhist traditions inherited from the Xizang Empire period. What the records suggest, rather, is that entering the twelfth century — and especially after its midpoint — the influence of the newly translated tantric traditions, teachers, and texts from Tibet's Later Diffusion of the Dharma grew markedly stronger in Western Xia.

Twelfth-century Tibet, after all, was hardly a closed, self-contained Buddhist world. Atisha had entered Tibet in the eleventh century; large numbers of Xizang monks continued travelling to India to study, while scholars from northeastern India and Kashmir kept making their way onto the plateau in turn. Late Indian tantras, empowerments, sadhanas, and iconography spread continuously through this back-and-forth traffic. Because the southern edge of Western Xia bordered directly on Amdo and the Tsongkha region, this was very likely one of the principal channels through which Western Xia connected to Tibet's Buddhist network — though not the only one. The cross-regional traffic among monks in Hexi, Dunhuang, and the court belonged to this same web of transmission. So the “Xizang Buddhism” that twelfth-century Western Xia encountered was, behind the scenes, still tied to a very much living world of late Indian Buddhism.

Nor is this route merely something later scholars have inferred from maps. The Kashmiri scholar Jayananda first worked in central Tibet before travelling on to the Tangut court, where he received the title of State Preceptor. Alongside him, the biographies of translators closely tied to the Minyak-Tangut cultural sphere1 preserve memories of journeys made into Tibet and even India in search of the Dharma. Teachers, disciples, and translators — through the movement of real people — linked these regions together. It was through exactly this kind of cross-regional exchange in Buddhist culture that the practice and visual system of Vajravarahi entered Western Xia. And this is also where the most interesting aspect of Khara-Khoto painting gradually comes into view.

Western Xia did not simply stir the visual languages arriving from different regions into one uniform “hybrid style.” Subjects closely tied to the Chinese Buddhist knowledge tradition — Amitabha's Pure Land, Water-Moon Avalokiteshvara, and some sutra frontispieces — most often took the mature pictorial language of Song, Liao, and Hexi painting as their primary visual foundation; while subjects such as Vajravarahi and Chakrasamvara, closely tied to the newly translated tantric traditions of twelfth-century Tibet and India, more clearly preserved the iconographic structures and visual conventions transmitted through northeastern India's Pala tradition and onward through Tibet and the Himalayan region. What is particularly interesting is that different religious traditions of knowledge tend to impose different dominant visual grammars on an image — yet the painters of Western Xia were unwilling to be bound by any single one. Within a single work of Khara-Khoto painting, one may find Song-style composition, Xizang-style deities, traditional Chinese motifs, and local adaptations all appearing together.

Western Xia art, therefore, is not built on the absence of outside influence. Its identity took shape precisely in how these languages were selected and recombined — how they were made to say what the Tangut wished to say. Style here therefore becomes more than a matter of form: it also stands as evidence left behind by history. To see how a particular deity was painted is to see which direction of knowledge twelfth-century Western Xia was reaching toward.

So when we turn to face this thangka again, that broad historical background becomes concrete.

The Vajravarahi sadhana unearthed at Khara-Khoto describes in careful detail how the deity is to be visualized: a body of deep red, three eyes, a dark blue boar's head at the temple, the right hand raising a curved flaying knife close to the ear, the left hand holding a skull cup, a khatvanga staff tucked beneath the arm, a crown of five skulls, hair falling loose, a garland of severed heads, one leg raised and the other trampling underfoot — wrathful and yet “graceful” all atonce. Almost every one of these details finds its match in this thangka.

This record shows that the Vajravarahi before us is not some “foreign religious image” that simply happened to drift into Khara-Khoto. The site has preserved a whole range of other practice texts related to Vajravarahi as well — on meditative absorption, on the sleeping practice, on the feast offering, on empowerment, and more. These texts cannot, of course, let us reconstruct the actual daily life of any single twelfth-century practitioner, but they are enough to show that Vajravarahi at Khara-Khoto existed not merely as an image, but had entered a fully developed ritual practice.

This also gives a new way of understanding why this face is so distinctive.

A modern viewer looking at a painting will typically begin by observing its color, composition, and technique — a way of looking that stands outside the picture. Tantric visualization, however, closes that gap. The practitioner must rebuild the deity within their own mind, step by step: what color she is, how her body turns, what she holds in each hand, how her eyes open and what then appears — all of this changes in clearly defined stages through the course of practice. We cannot, after eight centuries, prove that the painter deliberately made her captivating in order to aid visualization. But the visual effect this painting produces is, in fact, remarkably well suited to that religious function.

She occupies the center, filling nearly the entire picture plane. Her crimson body and the crimson flames around her twist continuously together, and the background, too, is swallowed by an expanse of red; white bone ornaments, black flowing hair, and blue-green streaming ribbons thread through it all. Her head tilts sharply forward, and her wide-open eyes seem to fix the viewer's gaze in place. The flaying knife presses toward the very edge of the painting, and the khatvanga staff, slanting across her body, heightens the sense of motion. Every emblem of death is present — the severed head, the skulls, the corpse beneath her feet — and yet none of it weighs the image down. Quite the opposite: she is light, quick, astonishingly alive. And that half-smile especially gives the whole painting a strange charge: she does not seem to wait quietly for us to look at her — rather, it feels as though we are the ones being watched.

Perhaps what we might call “entering the image” does not happen, in the first instance, through elaborate explanation. Very often it is a sufficiently vivid form, a pair of eyes impossible to avoid, and an ambiguous half-smile that first pull the viewer's attention in from outside the frame. For an image so closely bound up with visualization practice, this kind of vivid, stable, and compelling picture aligns remarkably well, at the very least, with the practice's own need to continually recall and reconstruct the deity's form in the mind.

And this is precisely where what we usually call “artistic quality” truly comes into play.

The sadhana may prescribe that Vajravarahi must be red, three-eyed, boar-headed, and holding a flaying knife — but it will not specify exactly how large the size of the eyes, the face, the bridge of the nose, or how much of the picture the figure should occupy. The sadhana fixes the deity's iconography, but it cannot fully determine the specific form she takes in the painter's own mind — and it is precisely in the facial structure, proportion, line, color, composition, and bodily scale that artistic tradition and the painter's own skill come to the fore.

In the Pala-Sena tradition2 of twelfth-century northeastern India and its related tantric art, we can see the visual vocabulary of red female deities, dancing poses, flames, corpses, and elaborate ornaments taking shape. When this visual language entered Tibet, it was reorganized once again; and by the time it reached Western Xia, the image had continued to change further still. So although we can trace this Vajravarahi back to Indian and Xizang sources, we can no longer simply call her “a Western Xia painting in the Pala style.” Instead of reinventing, the painter determined how she would be rendered in the visual language that was theirs.

This, in fact, closely resembles what Western Xia had been doing for more than a century before this.

The Tangut script took texts and knowledge from outside and rewrote their content; the translation of scripture converted Buddhist thought expressed in different languages into knowledge the region could use directly; teachers and disciples carried practices back and forth between different regions; and painting, in its own way, was reorganizing a body invested with sanctity.

A state that lasted less than two centuries left behind its own script and its Tangut-language canon of Buddhist scripture, a sophisticated translation system, senior clerical titles such as State Preceptor, and, in its later material, the title of Imperial Preceptor. And it left behind, too, a body of Buddhist imagery that, at first glance, looks both Indian and Xizang, and yet is not quite Xizang either; that carries a distinctly Chinese air, and yet cannot simply be filed away as Song painting.

What is genuinely compelling and surprising about it, perhaps, was never simply the “mixing” produced by sitting at a crossroads of trade and travel. It was, rather, the choices made under a strong and deliberate sense of cultural identity, and the capacity those choices reveal — a capacity to make different visual languages serve different bodies of knowledge and belief.

Today, we describe the arts of Western Xia with a single word: mysterious.

A dynasty that lasted less than two centuries, a script that went unread for centuries afterward, a ruined city buried in desert sand — all of this makes Western Xia easy to view as remote and unknowable. But having come this close to the painting, I find myself thinking that “mystery” is largely a feeling we, looking back today, project onto a lost kingdom. For the people who actually lived in this world in the twelfth century, a great deal of it was perfectly concrete. Looking again at this Vajravarahi, then — that face carrying wrath, allure, and such vivid life — she is no longer simply an inscrutable “mysterious expression.” What remains is only wonder at the artistry she embodies. Because once all of this passed through the hand of a Western Xia painter, history stopped being only roads and transmission. It became color. It became line. And it became this smile that we cannot help but keep coming back to look at.

This brings to mind a passing thought: why do we always find works of ancient art so precious? Because what such a work preserves is never only the image of a deity but real movement of people, real exchange of knowledge, and real transformation of vision that once took place among India, Tibet, Amdo, Hexi, and Khara-Khoto — all compressed into a single painted surface.

More than eight hundred years on, standing before this painting, we watch the twelfth century come back to us, little by little, out of one crimson figure.

1.“Minyak” (also rendered “Minyag”or“Mi-nyag”) is the Xizang name for the ancient Tangut people (the Dangxiang Qiang) and the Western Xia state they founded. The “Minyak-Tangut cultural sphere” refers to the specific historical and cultural region formed where the historical memory, language and script, religious beliefs, and distinctive local cultures of the Tangut/Minyak peoples converge across northwestern and southwestern China — including the Xizang areas of western Sichuan, Qinghai, Gansu, Ningxia, and the Hexi Corridor.

2.“Pāla-Sena” does not refer to a single unified dynasty, nor to a strictly defined artistic school. It functions more as a convenient label within art-historical scholarship, used to describe the Buddhist visual tradition that took shape and continued developing across roughly the 8th to 13th centuries in northeastern India — particularly in Bihar and Bengal — spanning the Pāla and, later, the Sena dynasties.

subtitle.zh: 这些外来语言，一进入藏西，就开始说起了同一种地方口音。

viewingNote.zh:
有一次和央美雕塑系的杨老师聊天，他提到了一个词：在地性。

这个词后来一直留在我脑子里。

什么是在地性？

最简单的理解，好像就是“一个地方自己的东西”。尼泊尔有尼泊尔的样子，克什米尔有克什米尔的样子，西藏西部也应该有属于自己的特征。可真去看历史，又会发现事情没有这么简单。一个地方如果几百年来不断有人进来、有人出去，不断接受新的文化、技术和审美，它还谈得上“在地”吗？

眼前这尊被置于13 世纪西藏西部艺术语境中的不动明王，恰好让我重新理解了这个问题。

祂高三十余厘米，以合金铜铸成。右手举剑，左手持索，双腿大幅张开，身体粗壮而有力量。可仔细看，又会发现它并不属于一种“纯粹”的风格：眼睛、手指甲和脚趾甲镶嵌红铜，可以追溯西北印度金工传统留下的技术记忆；帽冠、缯带、大型圆耳饰，也可以与晚期东印度帕拉系造像的视觉语言比较；开脸以及胸腹、四肢圆厚的体积处理，又与13 世纪纽瓦尔雕塑存在明显的形式亲缘。照理说，来源越多，身份应该越模糊。可它偏偏不是。把它和西北印度、东印度、尼泊尔的作品摆在一起，它仍然有一种很明显的西藏西部气质。

为什么越杂糅，反而越容易认出来？

也许问题就在“在地性”这三个字里。

在地性并不是古代工匠自己使用的艺术史概念，而是我们今天理解作品的一种方法。它也不等于“本土风格”。真正的在地性，关心的不是一个地方如何与外界隔绝，而是外来的东西来到这里以后，怎样被变成同一种“地方口音”。地理会塑造它，宗教会塑造它，材料和技术会塑造它，赞助人的需求会塑造它，工匠自己的经验也会塑造它。

所以一件佛教雕塑为什么会这样呈现，好像也从来不只是一个“风格来源”的问题。

尤其是西藏西部。

从现代的地图上看阿里，很容易觉得那里遥远而孤立的存在。但历史上的“西藏西部”不完全等同于今天的行政划分。它曾经属于一个更连续的西喜马拉雅文化空间：向西连接拉达克，并进一步与克什米尔世界发生关系；向南通过河谷和山口与喜马拉雅南麓联系；向东则进入更广阔的藏地。

它当然是一片难以抵达的高地，却并不是文明的尽头。

我们今天谈艺术传播，经常画几条箭头：克什米尔影响西藏西部，印度影响西藏，尼泊尔影响西藏。可真正越过山口将图像风格带过去的是流动的人群，而不是生硬的箭头。译师去印度和克什米尔求学，僧侣往返于不同寺院，工匠被王室或寺院邀请到新的地方工作，商人带着器物、金属和纺织品移动。跟着他们一起走的，还有经书、图像、造像、工艺，以及一个人脑子里已经看过的东西。

于是所谓“文化交流”，其实是一条条非常具体的路径。

10 世纪后半至11 世纪，西藏西部因佛教复兴与克什米尔之间建立了深厚的联系。仁钦桑布等译师前往印度和克什米尔求法，后世文献传统也记载有克什米尔工匠进入古格参与寺院的建设；托林等地保存下来的艺术遗存，则确实显示出了强烈的克什米尔视觉语言。

到了11 至12 世纪，随着阿底峡的到来，东印度帕拉艺术在整个藏地的重要性不断提高，但在西藏西部，它并没有简单替代更早的克什米尔传统。新的图像和装饰方法不断进入，旧的金工和造型记忆却仍然活着。

13 世纪以后，情况更加复杂。12 世纪末到13 世纪初，北印度大型佛教寺院遭受严重破坏，原有的知识和艺术生产体系开始重组；与此同时，尼泊尔谷地成熟的纽瓦尔金属工艺在藏地的重要性逐渐提高。西尼泊尔的卡萨马拉世界，又构成这一时期理解印度、尼泊尔与西藏西部之间关系不可忽略的中间层。

所以13 世纪的西藏西部特别迷人。

它不是一个旧风格消失、新风格接班的时代，更像是一个地层，是一个地方在不同时期不断留下痕迹，后来一层叠一层的印象。很多东西同时存在，而且变化的速度并不一样。

这尊不动明王就像一件被凝固起来的“风格地层”。

先看它的眼睛和手足。

主体是合金铜，眼睛、手指甲和脚趾甲却专门嵌入红铜。异金属镶嵌在西北印度—克什米尔金工中有很深的传统，早期西藏西部也长期使用类似方法。但到了13 世纪，再把这种做法简单叫作“克什米尔工艺”已经不够准确。因为一种外来的技术，如果在一个地方被反复使用两三百年，它早已进入当地工匠自己的技术记忆。

这就是在地化发生的第一步：来源没有消失，但身份已经改变了。

再看它的头冠、巨大的圆形耳饰以及身体上的臂钏、项链等装饰。这些特征可以与晚期东印度帕拉系造像比较，但它们不是任何单一地区的专属标记。经过几百年的流动，这些神圣身体的视觉语汇已经被尼泊尔、西藏等地反复转译。到了这尊造像上，而是都变成了整体结构的一部分了。

身体更加有意思。

它的脸颊圆鼓，胸腔、腹部、手臂和大腿都有明显体积。工匠不是靠轮廓线告诉我们这里有一条腿，而是真正把一条腿从内部“撑”了出来。身体各部分之间的转折也很连续，这种圆润而有肉感的三维塑造，与13 世纪纽瓦尔金属雕塑之间存在值得注意的形式亲缘。但它最终并没有变成一尊尼泊尔造像。

因为到了西藏西部，这个身体又被赋予了更新的理解。胸更挺，腹部更敦厚，四肢粗壮，脚掌宽大。双腿不是为了表现修长和优雅，而是真的把身体重量压向地面。整个雕塑首先给人的不是精巧，而是扎实。

可这件作品最迷人的地方，又偏偏不是一个“粗”字。它是粗中有细。

双腿间垂下的兽皮，形象具体；缠绕在手臂与腿部的蛇，神性具在。浑圆的手臂并不僵硬，从肩到肘、从肘到腕仍然保持柔软的转折；脚掌虽然厚，脚趾却一个个认真塑了出来，并嵌入红铜。尤其是脸，远看是忿怒尊强烈的圆睁双目和獠牙，靠近以后却能看到眼珠、眉中肌、鼻翼弧度以及发际线、络腮胡、嘴部和脸颊处的细微处理，表面打磨也是非常光洁。

所以粗犷和粗糙，是两回事。

细腻的开脸、手足和镶嵌说明工匠完全具有细节控制的能力，而整尊作品仍然保留了粗壮、直接的大形。也正因为这两者同时存在，它才会有一种很特别的气质：身体很重，肢体却软；轮廓很强，局部却细。也许这才是我们真正应该寻找的“西藏西部”。它不是把克什米尔、帕拉和尼泊尔影响全部剔除以后，最后剩下来的那一点“本土成分”。恰恰相反，我们还能看见它从哪里来，却已经无法把它送回任何一个原来的地方。

图像本来就是高度流动的。同一尊文殊、观音、不动明王，可以跨越印度、尼泊尔和西藏传播。经典可以共享，图像规范也可以相互借用，可它们一旦真正落到不同的地方，就会长出不同的样貌。它必须经过当地的工匠、材料、审美、宗教习惯和几代人的观看经验，最后才成为我们今天面对的这一件作品。所以“在地性”对理解佛教雕塑最重要的意义，也许就在：为什么这些外来语言，一进入藏西，就开始说起了同一种地方口音？

一个地方不断遇见外部世界，会接受一些东西，也会拒绝一些东西；有些形式只短暂出现，有些技术却留下几百年；有些外来的语言被完整保留，有些则被改变到最后只剩下一点点遥远的记忆。经过足够长的时间，这些选择本身就形成了风格。而成熟的地方性，也不是拒绝外面的世界。而是见过很多世界以后，终于有能力决定——我有能力把它变成自己的东西。

回过头再看这件西藏西部的不动明王时，忽然意识到，“在地性”好像还会改变我们判断一件雕塑所谓好坏的传统看法。

如果没有在地意识，我们常常很容易拿“中心”去衡量“地方”。比如看到一件西藏西部作品，我们会觉得它怎么不像尼泊尔那么优美；为什么不像帕拉那么肃穆；又或者不像克什米尔那么精细之类的等等。

于是很容易把“不同”理解成“不够”。但如果我们意识到在地性，也许另一个声音就会出现：它是不是本来就没有打算成为尼泊尔、帕拉、克什米尔？它就它自己。
viewingNote.en:
I once spoke with Professor Yang of the Sculpture Department at the Central Academy of Fine Arts, and he mentioned a term: locality. The word has stayed with me ever since.

What is locality?

At its simplest, it seems to mean “a place’s own thing.” Nepal has a look of its own, Kashmir has a look of its own, and western Xizang ought to have features that belong to it alone. But look closely at the history, and the matter turns out to be less simple than that. If a place has, for centuries on end, continually taken people in and sent people out, continually absorbed new cultures, technologies, and aesthetic sensibilities, can it still be said to have a “locality” of its own?

The Achala before us, situated within the artistic context of thirteenth-century western Xizang, offers a way back into this question.

He stands just over thirty centimetres tall, cast in copper alloy. The right hand raises a sword, the left holds a noose; the legs are set wide apart, the body thickset and forceful. Look closely and one finds that the figure does not belong to any single, “pure” style: the eyes, fingernails, and toenails are inlaid with copper, a technique that recalls the metalworking traditions of northwest India and Kashmir; the crown, ribbons, and large circular earrings invite comparison with the visual language of late eastern Indian Pala sculpture; and the modelling of the face, chest, abdomen, and limbs — full, rounded, voluminous — bears a clear formal kinship with thirteenth-century Newar bronzes. By rights, the more sources a work draws on, the more diffuse its identity ought to become. Yet here the opposite holds. Set this figure beside works from northwest India, eastern India, and Nepal, and it still carries an unmistakably western Xizang character.

Why should mixture make a thing easier, not harder, to recognize?

Perhaps the answer lies in the word: “locality.”

Locality was not a term the ancient craftsmen used to describe their art; it is a method by which we understand these works today. Nor is it the same as “indigenous style.” True locality is not concerned with how a place sealed itself off from the outside world, but with how things arriving from elsewhere were transformed, once they got here, into the same “regional accent.” Geography shapes it. Religion shapes it. Materials and technique shape it. The demands of patrons shape it. And the accumulated experience of the craftsmen themselves shapes it too.

So the question of why a Buddhist sculpture takes the form it does was, it seems, never simply a question of “stylistic origin.”

This is especially true of western Xizang.

Looked at on a modern map, Ngari can seem remote and isolated. But historical “western Xizang” was not quite the same territory as today’s administrative region. It once belonged to a more continuous western Himalayan cultural space: linked westward to Ladakh, and through Ladakh to the world of Kashmir; linked southward, through river valleys and mountain passes, to the southern rim of the Himalaya; and linked eastward into the broader expanse of Xizang.

It was, of course, a high plateau difficult to reach — but it was never the edge of civilization.

When we speak today of the transmission of art, we tend to draw a few arrows: Kashmir influencing western Xizang, India influencing Xizang, Nepal influencing Xizang. But what actually carried image and style across the passes were people in motion, not blunt arrows on a map. Translator-monks travelled to India and Kashmir to study; monks moved back and forth between monasteries; craftsmen were invited by courts or monasteries to work in new places; merchants carried objects, metal, and textiles with them as they moved.

Travelling alongside them were scriptures, images, sculptures, techniques — and everything a person had already seen and carried in his mind.

So what we call “cultural exchange” was, in fact, a set of very specific, traceable paths.

From the latter half of the tenth century into the eleventh, western Xizang forged deep ties with Kashmir through a Buddhist revival. Translation masters such as Rinchen Sangpo travelled to India and Kashmir in search of the teachings, and later textual traditions also record Kashmiri craftsmen entering Guge to take part in monastery construction; the surviving art at sites such as Tholing indeed shows a strong Kashmiri visual language.

By the eleventh and twelfth centuries, with the arrival of Atiśa, the importance of eastern Indian Pala art rose steadily across Xizang as a whole. But in western Xizang it did not simply replace the earlier Kashmiri tradition. New iconographic and decorative approaches kept arriving, even as older metalworking and modelling memories remained very much alive.

From the thirteenth century onward, matters grew more complex still. In the years spanning the end of the twelfth century and the start of the thirteenth, the great Buddhist monasteries of north India suffered severe destruction, and the systems of knowledge and artistic production that had sustained them began to reorganize. At the same time, the mature Newar metalworking traditions of the Kathmandu Valley grew steadily more important across Xizang. The Khasa Malla world of western Nepal formed, in turn, an intermediate layer that cannot be overlooked in understanding the relationship between India, Nepal, and western Xizang in this period.

This is why the thirteenth century in western Xizang is so compelling.

Rather than an age in which new styles simply replaced old ones, it is better understood as a kind of stratigraphy—a place continually leaving traces across time, with one layer settling over another. Many different things coexisted, each changing at its own pace.

This Achala is a “stylistic stratigraphy” suspended in a single moment.

Consider first the eyes and the extremities.

The body is cast in copper alloy, yet the eyes, fingernails, and toenails are separately inlaid with copper. Bimetallic inlay has deep roots in the metalworking traditions of northwest India and Kashmir, and early western Xizang, too, made long use of similar methods. But by the thirteenth century, it is no longer quite accurate to call this practice simply “Kashmiri workmanship.” A technique from elsewhere, once used repeatedly in one place for two or three centuries, has already entered the technical memory of the local craftsmen themselves.

This is the first step by which localization occurs: change of identity without the loss of its origin.

Consider next the crown, the great circular earrings, and the armlets and necklace adorning the body. These features invite comparison with late eastern Indian Pala sculpture, yet they belong to no single region exclusively. Over centuries of movement, the visual vocabulary of these sacred bodies had already been translated and retranslated across Nepal, Xizang, and elsewhere. By the time they arrive on this particular image, they have become part of a single, integrated whole.

The body is more interesting.

The cheeks are round and full; the chest, abdomen, arms, and thighs all carry pronounced volume. The craftsman had made it so that the leg stretches outward from within. The transitions between the body’s different parts flow continuously as well; this rounded, fleshy, three-dimensional modelling shows a formal kinship worth noting with thirteenth-century Newar metal sculpture. Yet it never quite becomes a Nepalese image.

On reaching western Xizang, a further, renewed understanding was born. The chest is thrust out more; the abdomen is thicker and heavier; the limbs are stouter; the feet are broad. The wide-set legs are not there to convey slenderness or grace, but to press the body’s full weight down into the ground. What the sculpture first offers the viewer is not refinement, but solidity.

However, what makes this work most compelling is that it cannot be defined by the word “coarse” alone. It is a fine piece as well.

The animal hide hanging between the legs is rendered with specificity; the snakes coiled around the arms and legs carry their own divine presence. The rounded arms — from shoulder to elbow, elbow to wrist, retain a supple articulation; the soles of the feet, though thick, show each toe carefully modelled and inlaid with copper. The face, above all: from a distance it shows the wide, staring eyes and bared fangs typical of a wrathful deity, yet up close one finds careful attention paid to the pupils, the muscle between the brows, the curve of the nostrils, the hairline, the full beard, the mouth, and the fine modelling of the cheeks — the surface polished to a high gloss throughout. So “bold” and “crude” are two different things.

The refinement of the face, hands, feet, and inlay shows that the craftsman was fully capable of controlling fine detail, even as the sculpture as a whole retains a thick-set, direct overall form. It is precisely because both qualities exist together that the work carries such a distinctive character: the body is heavy, yet the limbs are supple; the silhouette is strong, yet the details are fine. Perhaps this is what we should truly be looking for when we speak of “western Xizang.” It is not what remains after Kashmiri, Pala, and Nepalese influences have all been stripped away — some small residue of “native content.” Quite the opposite: we can still see exactly where it came from, and yet we can no longer send it back to any single place of origin.

Images, after all, were always highly mobile. One and the same Mañjuśrī, Avalokiteśvara, or Achala could travel across India, Nepal, and Xizang. Scriptures could be shared, iconographic conventions could be borrowed across borders — yet once these images truly settled in different places, they grew different appearances. Each had to pass through local craftsmen, local materials, local aesthetic sensibilities, local religious custom, and generations of local viewing before it could become the single object we face today. Perhaps this, then, is the deepest significance of “locality” for understanding Buddhist sculpture: why is it that these foreign styles, after entering western Xizang, began to carry new characteristics?

A place, in its continual encounters with the outside world, lets in some things and refuses others; some forms appear only briefly, while some techniques endure for centuries; some foreign languages are preserved whole, while others are altered until only a distant, fading memory remains. Given enough time, these choices themselves come to constitute a style. And a mature locality is not one that refuses the outside world — it is one that, having seen a great many worlds, has finally gained the capacity to decide: I am able to make this my own.

Looking again at this Achala, it occurs to me that “locality” may also change the conventional way we judge whether a sculpture is good or not.

Without an awareness of locality, we easily fall into measuring the “periphery” against the “centre.” Looking at a western Xizang work, we might well think: why isn’t it as graceful as something Nepalese? Why isn’t it as solemn as something Pala? Why isn’t it as refined as something Kashmiri? — and so on.

In that frame, it becomes very easy to read “different” as “not enough.” But once we become aware of locality, another voice may emerge: perhaps this work was never meant to become Nepalese, or Pala, or Kashmiri in the first place. It is — simply itself.

title.zh: 萨迦班智达·贡噶坚赞肖像
title.en: Portrait of Sakya Pandit Kunga Gyaltsen

subtitle.zh: 这尊雕塑，只属于愿意靠近它的人。
subtitle.en: A call for a closer look

material.zh: 红铜鎏金、嵌银、嵌红铜、嵌宝石
material.en: Gilt copper, inlaid with silver, copper, and gemstones

excerpt.zh: 萨迦班智达·贡噶坚赞肖像
excerpt.en: Portrait of Sakya Pandit Kunga Gyaltsen

viewingNote.zh:
眼前的萨迦班智达安坐于莲台之上。眉目低垂，神情温厚，眉间一点白毫，将这张属于历史人物的脸悄然推向觉者的身份。双手在胸前结说法印，衣袍上铺满细密的花朵錾刻。承托他的莲台更为特别：红铜、白银与大颗珠宝被嵌入同一座基座，花蔓环绕其间，中央还有一个微小人物从花苞中显现。最下方的联珠纹和莲瓣线条层层收束，使如此繁复的装饰没有向外散开，而被牢牢收束在九厘米之内。

面对这类作品，我们常用“小而精”一笔带过。但为什么一件只有8.5 厘米的上师像，会被制作得如此丰富？尺寸从来不只是数字。它决定了雕塑怎样进入空间，也决定人和它保持怎样的距离。大型造像依靠体量建立权威。人站在它面前，首先感受到的是自己的渺小。八厘米的小造像却无法迫使人仰望，它会天然的使人想靠近观看。

最初我们看到的是一位人物安坐的轮廓；继续靠近一些，人物的表情、衣袍上的花朵纹以及莲台中央那个从花苞中显现的小人物才一一出现。这种尺寸决定了造像不是一眼观看就能结束的。匠人把意义分布在不同距离里。作品越小，观看反而越慢。

八厘米的尺寸，也让我们不得不考虑它原本的宗教功能。它可能被安置在僧房、贵族宅邸或者个人修持空间中的小型佛龛内，同样也具备进入旅行佛龛或者便携嘎乌的条件。无论具体答案是哪一种，有一点已经相当清楚：这尊肖像不是为远处观看而做。衣袍上的錾花，在几步之外几乎无法辨认；莲瓣上红铜和白银的色彩差异，也只有在近距离和变化的光线中才会显现。匠人显然预设了一个会靠近它的人。这个人可能每天打开佛龛，可能在诵经之前注视上师的面容，也可能在旅途中不断确认，这位早已圆寂的导师仍与自己同在。

然而，小型雕塑绝不是大型造像的机械式缩小。尺寸发生变化以后，所有形式都需要重新安排。倘若头部完全遵循自然比例，面容便难以辨识；双手若过小，说法印就会失去清晰度；莲瓣刻得太浅，底座会在视觉上模糊成一团；珠宝过大，又可能压过人物本身。匠人面对的真正难题，不是能否制造细节，而是如何在有限空间中重新分配视觉重量。

肖像的头部稳定地落在中轴线上，双肩往两侧舒展，搭在双肩的帽檐边在镂空中的处理下，可以清晰的看见人物的全部脸型。交叠的双腿拓宽了下部轮廓，使人物形成安定的三角形结构。双手在胸前相互呼应，将观者的视线从面容引向身体中央。从雕塑角度而言，说法印不仅只是用来辨认身份的图像符号，也是整件雕塑的形式枢纽。如果双手自然垂落，繁复的莲台很可能夺走全部注意。正是这组向内聚合的手势，把分散在衣袍、珠宝和莲瓣之间的视觉力量重新拉回了人物。

发愿者没有留下姓名，却把自己能够付出的财力、技术和心意嵌入了肖像。但华丽不是萨迦班智达性格的写照，而是后人记忆强度的写照。同样这种艺术语言也并非凭空出现。

十三世纪的萨迦和藏中，并不是封闭在高原内部的孤立世界。译师、僧侣、学者、商人、施主以及工匠沿着不同道路往来，印度、克什米尔、尼泊尔和西藏之间的知识以及技术在这里交汇。当时的尼泊尔工匠接受西藏施主委托，在藏地制作雕塑、绘画和寺院装饰；藏地匠人也不断地吸收着纽瓦尔艺术的造型和工艺经验。

眼前这尊像是否出自尼泊尔工匠之手，尚不能仅凭风格断言，它也可能由熟悉纽瓦尔造型语言的藏地匠人制作。尽管纽瓦尔匠人确实非常擅长让三维体量的图像和二维装饰同时成立。但密集的衣袍錾花、多种金属的并置、珠宝化的莲台，以及线条与体量之间的协调，确实表明它来自一个深受尼泊尔美学影响的视觉世界。

这种跨地域性，也存在于萨迦班智达本人的一生。

萨迦班智达· 贡噶坚赞出生于萨迦昆氏家族，是萨迦五祖中的第四位。早年随叔父扎巴坚赞学习，后来又师从克什米尔大师释迦室利跋陀罗及多位印度、尼泊尔学者。他掌握的梵文、因明、量论、语法、诗学、韵律、仪轨以及佛教哲学，深刻改变了西藏知识传统的标准。因此，这件肖像本身便构成了一种意味深长的对应：

一个通过跨地域学习建立知识体系的人，最终也由一种跨地域流动的艺术语言保存了形象。

人物的思想越过边界，塑造他的美学同样越过边界。但这尊像没有把萨迦班智达表现成旅行者，也没有选择他晚年远赴凉州的历史场景。复杂的一生在匠人心里最终被收束成一个动作：说法。

萨迦班智达最重要的历史身份，首先是一位学者和教师。他认为，佛法在语言、文化和世代之间传播时，知识的准确并不是单纯的学术要求。一位教师对经典的误解，可能经由学生继续传递；一个概念上的含糊，也可能在后来变成难以纠正的传统。

因此，他会公开质疑自己认为缺少经典或正理论证的观点，言辞有时相当锋利。这使他在后世记忆中显得自信、严厉，甚至不易亲近。但他所坚持的，并不是以争论证明自己的优越，而是把批判指向教义和论证，而不是把持有不同观点的人直接变成敌人。

现在再看雕塑中的说法印，它便不再只像是一个程式化的手势。

双手在胸前构成一个明确而集中的空间，仿佛所有散布在衣袍、莲瓣与珠宝之间的视觉声音，都在这里汇聚成语言。匠人没有表现萨迦班智达写作，也没有在身侧放置经书，尽管他被视为智慧菩萨文殊师利的化身。匠人而是让祂的身体本身成为了教法发生的场所。似乎说法不再只是肖像上的形式属性，而是这尊身体存在的理由。

莲台中央从花苞中显现的往生者，又使这个动作获得了回应。

上师在说法，莲座下有人正在聆听。没有这个微小人物，萨迦班智达只是一位被纪念的圣者；有了他，雕塑便不再停留在过去。教法从人物胸前向下传递，另一个生命从花苞中显现，仿佛正在因听闻、信仰或愿力而发生改变。眉间的白毫也属于同一种转化。它并非真实容貌，而是佛陀殊胜身相中的一种。白毫和说法印的结合，再次表明着，他已不再只是贡噶坚赞本人，而是智慧、传承和觉悟的承载者。

尽管肖像的脸看上去温和，但却并没有否定他历史性格中的锋利。

萨迦班智达晚年面对蒙古势力的召请时，已经年过六十。他带着年幼的八思巴及恰那多吉踏上了前往凉州的旅程，此后再未返回萨迦。当有人问他是否真能利益蒙古人时，萨迦班智达回答道：

“我已踏上此程，希望能够利益众生，但我并无确切把握自己真能有所利益。”

他明知结果并不确定，却仍愿意前往，这种承认没有削弱他的勇气，反而让责任显得更加真实。眼前的雕塑没有表现那段危险的旅程，却保存了同一种人格结构。

匠人没有依靠巨大的尺寸证明萨迦班智达的重要，而是把这种重要压缩进每一毫米：白毫不能省略，说法印必须清楚，衣袍上的花朵仍要完整，红铜与白银仍需彼此区分，莲台中央那个几乎可能被忽略的往生者也依然要被制作出来。

作品中的某些细节，也许从来不会被远处的人看见。

但它原本就不属于远处。

它属于一个会不断靠近它的人，属于某座小佛龛里反复亮起的灯光，也属于某位愿意了解他的人。
viewingNote.en:
Sitting upon a lotus throne, Sakya Paṇḍita, with his eyes lowered, carries a gentle and warm expression. A single urna between his brows quietly lifts this historical figure toward the status of an enlightened being. His hands form the teaching gesture (dharmachakra mudrā) at his chest, and his robe is covered in a fine, dense chasing of floral motifs. The lotus base that supports him is remarkable in its own right: copper, silver, and large gemstones are set into a single pedestal, wound about with flowering vines, at the center of which a tiny figure emerges from a lotus bud. Below, tiers of pearl-beading and lotus-petal borders draw inward, so that all this intricate ornament, rather than spreading outward, is held tightly within a span of just eight centimeters.

Works such as this are often reduced to the simple phrase “small but exquisite.” Yet why would a teacher’s portrait, just a little more than eight centimeters in height, be fashioned with such extraordinary refinement? Size is never merely a matter of measurement; it determines not only how a sculpture occupies space, but also how the viewer encounters it. Monumental images establish authority through physical magnitude: before them, one becomes immediately aware of one’s own diminutive scale. A figure of eight centimeters, however, cannot command reverence by overwhelming the senses. Its power lies elsewhere — in its ability to draw the viewer inward, encouraging a closer gaze and a more intimate, almost personal encounter.

At first, all one sees is the seated outline of a figure; only on drawing nearer does the face come into focus, along with the floral pattern on the robe, and finally the tiny figure emerging from the lotus bud at the center of the base. This scale ensures that the image can never be taken in at a single glance. The maker distributed meaning across different distances — the smaller the work, the slower it demands to be seen.

Its eight-centimeter size also forces us to consider its original devotional purpose. It may have stood in a small shrine in a monk's cell, in an aristocratic household, or in a private space for practice; it would equally have suited a portable shrine or a traveling gau (amulet box). Whichever the case, one thing is clear: this portrait was never meant to be viewed from a distance. The chased floral pattern on the robe is nearly illegible a few steps away; the difference in color between the copper and silver on the lotus petals only becomes visible up close, and under shifting light. The maker clearly anticipated a viewer who would draw near — someone who might open the shrine every day, gaze upon the master's face before reciting a text, or, on a journey, repeatedly reassure himself that this long-deceased teacher remained at his side.

A small sculpture is never simply a large sculpture reduced in size. A change of scale demands a complete reconsideration of form. A head that followed natural proportions too faithfully would lose its presence; hands diminished beyond a certain point would obscure the meaning of the teaching mudrā; lotus petals carved without sufficient depth would cause the base to collapse into visual ambiguity; gemstones enlarged for the sake of visibility would dominate rather than adorn the figure. The artisan’s true achievement lay not merely in the ability to reproduce detail, but in the delicate balancing of visual weight, hierarchy, and clarity within the limits of a confined space.

The head of the portrait sits firmly on the central axis, the shoulders spread evenly to either side, and the brim of the hat, resting on the shoulders, is rendered in openwork, leaving the whole of the face clearly visible. The crossed legs widen the lower silhouette, giving the figure a stable, triangular structure. At the chest, the two hands echo one another, drawing the viewer's gaze from the face down toward the body's center. Sculpturally speaking, the teaching mudrā is not merely an iconographic marker of identity — it is also the formal pivot of the entire work. Had the hands fallen at the figure's sides, the elaborate lotus throne might well have claimed all of the viewer's attention. It is precisely this inward-gathering gesture that pulls the visual energy, otherwise scattered across the robe, the gemstones, and the lotus petals, back toward the figure himself.

The donor left no name, yet poured into this portrait whatever wealth, skill, and devotion he could offer. But the opulence here is not a portrait of Sakya Paṇḍita's own character — it is a portrait of the intensity with which later generations remembered him. And this artistic language, too, did not arise out of nowhere.

Thirteenth-century Sakya, and central Xizang more broadly, were by no means an isolated world sealed off within the plateau. Translators, monks, scholars, merchants, patrons, and artisans traveled along different routes, and knowledge and technique from India, Kashmir, Nepal, and Xizang converged here. Xizang patrons commissioned Newar artisans to produce sculpture, painting, and monastic ornamentation in Xizang, while Xizang artisans continually absorbed Newar forms and technical practices.

Whether a Newar artisan made this particular image cannot be determined by style alone; it may equally have been produced by a Xizang artisan well versed in the Newar visual idiom. Newar artisans were indeed especially skilled at integrating three-dimensional volume and two-dimensional ornament in a single image. Still, the dense chasing on the robe, the juxtaposition of several metals, the jewel-encrusted lotus throne, and the coordination between line and volume all point to a visual world deeply shaped by Nepalese aesthetics.

This same cross-regional character runs through Sakya Paṇḍita's own life.

Sakya Paṇḍita Kunga Gyaltsen was born into the Khön family of Sakya and was the fourth of the Five Sakya Forefathers. In his early years, he studied under his uncle Drakpa Gyaltsen, and later trained under the Kashmiri master Śākyaśrībhadra as well as numerous Indian and Nepalese scholars. His command of Sanskrit, logic (pramāṇa), epistemology, grammar, poetics, prosody, ritual, and Buddhist philosophy profoundly reshaped the standards of Xizang scholarship. This portrait, then, forms a suggestive parallel of its own:

A man who built his body of knowledge through learning that crossed regions has, in the end, had his likeness preserved by an artistic language that likewise moved across regions. His thought crossed borders; so did the aesthetic that gave him form. Yet this image does not depict Sakya Paṇḍita as a traveler, nor does it choose the historical scene of his late journey to Liangzhou. In the mind of the artisan, a complex life was finally distilled into a single gesture: teaching the Dharma.

Sakya Paṇḍita's most important historical identity was, first and foremost, that of a scholar and teacher. He held that when the Dharma is transmitted across languages, cultures, and generations, precision in knowledge is not merely an academic requirement. A teacher's misreading of a canonical text can be passed on through generations of students; a single ambiguity in a concept can later harden into a tradition that is difficult to correct.

For this reason, he openly challenged positions he felt lacked scriptural or logical support, and his language could at times be quite sharp. This has left him, in later memory, seeming confident, severe, even difficult to approach. But what he insisted upon was never to win an argument to prove his own superiority — his criticism was directed at doctrines and arguments, not turned into personal enmity against those who happened to hold different views.

Seen in this light, the teaching mudrā in the sculpture is no longer merely a conventional gesture.

The two hands form a clear, concentrated space at the chest, as though every visual voice scattered across the robe, the lotus petals, and the gemstones converges here into language. The artisan did not depict Sakya Paṇḍita in the act of writing, nor did he place a scriptural text beside him, even though he was regarded as an emanation of the bodhisattva of wisdom, Mañjuśrī. Instead, the maker allowed the body itself to become the site where the teaching takes place. Teaching, it seems, is no longer simply a formal attribute of the portrait, but the very reason this body exists.

The figure emerging from the lotus bud at the center of the throne, in turn, gives this gesture its response.

The master is teaching; someone beneath the lotus seat is listening. Without this tiny figure, Sakya Paṇḍita would be no more than a venerated saint being commemorated; with him, the sculpture no longer remains fixed in the past. The teaching passes downward from the figure's chest, and another life emerges from the lotus bud, as though being transformed through hearing, faith, or aspiration. The urna between the brows belongs to this same transformation. It is not a literal likeness but one of the auspicious marks of a Buddha's body. Together with the teaching mudrā, the urna again signals that he is no longer simply Kunga Gyaltsen himself, but a vessel carrying wisdom, lineage, and awakening.

Though the portrait's face appears gentle, this does not contradict the sharper edge of his historical character.

When Sakya Paṇḍita, already past sixty, faced the summons of the Mongol authorities in his later years, he set out for Liangzhou together with the young Chögyal Phakpa and Chakna Dorje, and never returned to Sakya. When asked whether he could truly be of benefit to the Mongols, Sakya Paṇḍita replied:

"I have set out on this journey hoping to benefit sentient beings, but I have no certainty that I will truly be able to help them."

He knew full well that the outcome was uncertain, yet he was willing to go regardless; this admission did not diminish his courage — if anything, it made his sense of responsibility feel more real. The sculpture before us does not depict that perilous journey, yet it preserves the same character structure.

The artisan did not rely on great size to demonstrate Sakya Paṇḍita's importance; instead, he compressed that importance into every millimeter: the urna could not be omitted, the teaching mudrā had to remain clear, the floral pattern on the robe still had to be complete, the copper and silver still had to be distinguishable from one another, and even the easily overlooked figure at the center of the lotus throne still had to be rendered.

Certain details in this work may never be seen by anyone standing at a distance.

It was never meant for the eyes of a distant viewer.

It was meant for the one who keeps coming closer, like a lamp lit incessantly, the one who is willing to learn.
