title.zh: 大轮金刚手曼荼罗唐卡

subtitle.zh: 一朵从混沌中绽放的花。

excerpt.zh: 大轮金刚手曼荼罗唐卡
excerpt.en: Mandala of Vajrapāni Mahācakra

viewingNote.zh:
第一眼看去，这座坛城像一朵完全展开的花。

四片宽大的瓣叶从中心延伸向东西南北，红、白、绿、黄诸色彼此承接。外围又生出一重重圆环，像花瓣，也像光晕。它开得很满，只在上下两端留下狭长的空间，安座着传承上师、护法和供养人。但这不是一朵开在明亮天空下的花。整座坛城浮现在近乎黑色的底色上。黑暗始终没有退去，它围绕着宫殿，渗入尸陀林，也留在人物之间的缝隙里。

深暗使人想到未知、混沌和失去方向；坛城却在其中绽放光亮，建立起中心、四方、边界和道路。大片红色从黑暗中燃起，深蓝色的本尊又从红色中显现。画面的力量，首先来自这种冲突：黑暗与光明，混沌与秩序，柔软的花与忿怒的神，同时存在。

为什么一朵花的中心，会站着如此愤怒的大轮金刚手？要了解这个问题，需要先了解曼荼罗在文化体系中的作用。

曼荼罗在密教中首先表达的是“觉悟者所见的世界”。在这个世界里，万物围绕本尊重新获得位置：中央和四方、宫殿和外围、本尊和眷属、不同颜色和不同方向，都在共同组成一个完整秩序。当然，曼荼罗除了是关于觉悟世界的地图，它还是一种需要被使用的宗教工具。在灌顶仪式中，它把修行者引入特定本尊及其法门；在观想中，修行者要在心里建立宫殿，从外围进入，穿过四门，逐渐趋近中央本尊。修行深入以后，人不再只是站在本尊之外观看，而要使自己的身、语、意与本尊所代表的觉悟品质相应。因此，可以说曼荼罗是一套使人逐渐进入觉悟视野的方法。它一边组织着空间和人的注意力，同时它在安排着神祇的位置，也安排着恐惧、欲望、死亡和力量在内心的位置。

在我们的日常生活经验中，人会因为各种原因而感到害怕、愤怒、依赖、自负，却往往不知道这些情绪彼此是如何关联的。而坛城所做的，就是为这种混乱建立结构。它尝试引导着我们去思考哪里是外围，哪里是门槛，什么必须被看见，什么不能被绕过，最后如何走向什么中心，也就是自己的内心。

从这个角度看，曼荼罗确实是一条通向内心的路。但走向内心，不是为了找到一个更真实、更坚固的“我”，而是为了看清恐惧、欲望和执著如何构成了我们以为牢不可破的自己。

画中的坛城像一座从上方俯视的二维寺院建筑。宫殿的平面被摊开，门楼、门神和本尊却又各自显露正面。不同方向和不同高度的空间，被压缩在同一张画布上。

曼荼罗有许多题材，由于中央本尊的不同，于是进入内心的方法也不同。文殊以智慧穿透无明，观音以慈悲改变人与众生的关系，药师佛与疗愈和净化相关；金刚手所显现的，则是觉悟的力量。它们都指向觉悟，却不从同一条路抵达。

大轮金刚手的道路非常直接。祂不以宁静的面貌使人暂时忘记恐惧，而是让死亡、障碍、神力和自我执著全部显形。进入祂的坛城，不是绕开恐惧，而是穿过恐惧。人内心的力量经常会和防卫、控制与伤害纠缠在一起。大轮金刚手所代表的转化则不是把这种力量消灭，而是使它不再为我执服务，不再为破除障碍、不向无明退让的能力。

所以，这条路必须从最外层的尸陀林开始。

八大尸陀林环绕宫殿。那里散落着尸体、断肢、骨骸、野兽、火焰、成就者、方位神、坐骑与龙族。龙王的鳞片仍被一片片画出，坐骑的眼睛、牙齿和蹄爪依然清楚。那些极小的人物各有姿态和表情：有人安坐，有人起舞，有人暴怒，有人仿佛正从幽暗中回头。

社会生活通常会把死亡和腐败回避在视线之外。人们建立礼仪、语言和空间边界，使日常生活看起来洁净、可控。尸陀林却把这些被回避的内容重新放回了精神世界。它不是赞美死亡，而是拒绝用回避制造虚假的安全感。走进坛城的第一步，不是离开死亡，而是承认死亡；不是假装没有恐惧，而是知道恐惧正在怎样支配自己。

越过尸陀林，是一圈宽阔的五色莲瓣。花瓣首尾相接，托住整座宫殿。莲花以内，是巨大的十字金刚杵基座。它的大部分被宫墙遮住，只有弯曲而锐利的枝条从四门两侧伸出。摩羯昂首张口，金刚杵的利刃从口中吐出，像支撑宫殿的骨骼，也像射向四方的雷电。莲花和金刚杵构成了另一组对照。莲花柔软，意味着生长和开放；金刚杵坚固，意味着不可摧坏。精神秩序既需要生长的能力，也需要有能承受冲击的骨架。

再向内，四面层叠的门楼稳稳压住画面。每一道门都有忿怒门神及其佛母守候。

这些门神不是等待修行者击败的敌人，而是神圣空间的边界。他们使人不能毫无准备地闯入中心。人不能跳过恐惧便宣布自己已经平静，也不能绕开欲望便声称自己已经超脱。每一道门都要求人停下来，看见、承受并理解尚未被消化的经验。只有那些曾经支配人的东西不再暗中发号施令，人才能继续向内。

这条道路不仅存在于题材中，也存在于画面的色彩与线条里。红色的宫墙、五色的莲瓣和金色的线条在画布建立起了明确的层次。黑色带来未知和压力；红色带来生命、热度与警觉；深蓝色的本尊则显得沉重而稳定。

穿过尸陀林、莲瓣、金刚杵和四门，终于抵达花心。

深蓝色的大轮金刚手和佛母安住于内殿。整座宫殿为他们展开，四方化现、门神与外围诸尊，也都围绕中央获得位置。

梵文“金刚”具有霹雳和坚不可摧之物的意思。霹雳迅疾，能够破除障碍；金刚石坚固明澈，不受损坏。“金刚手”，就是“手持金刚者”。若文殊显现觉悟的智慧，观音显现觉悟的慈悲，那么金刚手所代表的，便是使智慧和慈悲真正发生作用的力量。

大轮金刚手是这种力量的忿怒显现。他有三面六臂，獠牙显露，身色深蓝近黑；手中持金刚杵、蛇及种种忿怒法器，其中一双手臂拥抱佛母。佛父和佛母的结合，并非世俗情爱的描写，祂们象征着方便和智慧不可分离的象征。没有智慧的力量容易成为暴力；不能行动的智慧，也无法改变现实。完整的觉悟必须同时具有认识和行动的能力。大轮金刚手脚下踏伏着梵天及帝释天。两位都是印度宗教传统中地位极高的天神。把他们置于本尊足下，说明着世俗神力、身份和权威不能高于觉悟。被踏伏的还包括人对力量的迷信，以及依靠权力证明自我重要性的需要。

祂的忿怒也不是嗔恨。怒目、獠牙、火焰、弯刀、蛇与踏伏，表现的是高度集中的行动能力。大轮金刚手不是要人变得愤怒，而是要人看见自己的力量，承担它，又不再被它控制。因此，花心里等待人的不是一个更坚固的自我，而是一种不必再死守自我和打破的力量。如果说坛城主体组织的是空间，那么画面上方的十七位传承上师组织的就是时间。

他们说明，这条通向内心的道路并不是某个人的即兴发明。它经过印度大成就者、译师和藏地上师，一代代被讲授、记忆和修习。每一个人都只是暂时的承接者，却使法脉得以越过个人生命的限度。

画面下方则更接近现实。忿怒诸尊与护法依次排列，吉祥天母骑在骡背上，多闻天王骑于狮上；最右下角，供养人坐在供品旁边，把整座坛城与一个具体的愿望连接了起来。没有供养人的资源，没有画师的劳动，没有颜料、画布和匠人的长期经验，这些抽象的仪轨便无法成为眼前的作品。私人的精神经验也只有进入了传承、仪式和物质制作中，才能成为跨越时间的文化。

这幅绘于十四世纪的西藏作品，人物造型和细密装饰显示出了纽瓦尔美学和藏地绘画的交融。人物身体饱满健硕，肩臂宽阔，腰腹结实。画师以细微的深浅晕染塑造胸膛、手臂和腿部，肌肉仿佛从颜色里慢慢隆起。即使人物只有指甲大小，也有沉甸甸的体量。

人物有重量，线条却不迟滞。四方化现的身体屈伸回旋，手臂、衣带和火焰向外扬起，内外四方的化现与中央主尊共同形成一个个的十字形。它像水波从花心荡开，也像四面的风在同一个地方相遇。

画面被填得极满，却没有失去层次。其美学本身就在执行坛城的功能：把繁多、冲突甚至令人不安的内容，组织成一种可以面对、可以理解的秩序。尺幅如此有限，故事却没有被草率缩写。画师则是把颜料磨细，把笔锋收得极尖，在一小块布面上安放宫殿、山川、神灵、尸体与火焰。许多藏在整体中的细节，只要把画面一放大，就会一一出现。这幅唐卡，可以盯着看上几天。

我们再退后一些，回到原来的观看距离，整座坛城又重新成为一朵花。

花代表自然的生长，宫殿代表人建立的精神秩序。花从中心向外开放，文化则从一代人传向下一代。自然和文明，都不是孤立事物的堆积，而是依赖关系、次序和不断延续的生命。

大轮金刚手曼荼罗没有承诺消灭黑暗。黑暗仍留在画面上，尸陀林也仍然围绕宫殿。它真正提供的，是一种在黑暗中辨认、在混乱中找到方向的方法。人走进坛城，不是为了成为一个没有恐惧的人，而是为了不再把自己交给恐惧支配。

这朵花之所以鲜活，不是因为它远离黑暗，而是因为它从黑暗中生长出来。

作品信息及方位说明：

此处与主尊双运。主尊为大轮金刚手，是金刚手菩萨的忿怒密乘化现。怀抱的佛母为玛玛姬，五方佛部佛母之一。金刚手足下踩踏的两位人物具体指认为梵天（右足所踏）与帝释天（左足所踏），印度教神祇在密教艺术中被吸收、转化，用以表现我执与邪见被踩伏于足下。

此处为四尊大轮金刚手的四臂忿怒化现。颜色各异，对应不同佛部，各自与佛母双运，各持法器。

四门门神，每门驻有一位忿怒明王，与四位分别执掌钩、索、链、铃四种度化之法的女尊之一配对为双运佛母。东方不动明王 ，佛母为金刚钩母。南方阎魔敌，佛母为金刚索母。西方马头明王，佛母为金刚链母。北方甘露旋，佛母为金刚铃母 。

坛城最外一圈绘有八大尸林，分布于八个方位，每处尸林中皆有护方神及其坐骑、龙王、成就者、尸骸、夜叉、罗刹、饿鬼、怖畏、空行、空行母，以及池塘、火焰、佛塔与修行者。从尸林环的顶部起顺时针方向，居于各尸林中的大成就者依次为：毗瓦巴、鲁伊巴、古古日巴、夏瓦日巴、萨惹哈、因扎菩提、冬比嘿鲁嘎、龙树与铃巴。

尸陀林环之外四角分别为金刚手的其他化现，上半段两侧为大轮金刚手及龙族，下半段两侧为：摧破金刚及龙族。

十七位传承上师, 依次为：金刚持（现金刚萨埵相）；狮面空行母 ；夏瓦里巴；嘉瓦里巴；德瓦· 普纳玛谛；却吉桑波；仁钦俄珠；玛尔岗普；却吉杰波（卡布）；普让巴喇嘛；衮却巴；拓囊（拉杰）；珠些（当巴）；岳顿· 白玛；郭隆巴钦波；洛沃译师 ；却嘉· 帕巴。

护法诸尊与供养人。为男性忿怒尊，持颅碗与法器（剑／杖／斧）；女性忿怒尊，与前四尊忿怒尊姿态相配；白色女尊，作舞姿，或为空行母；骑乘本尊，或为吉祥天母；装束相同，未见坐骑，推测同属吉祥天母眷属；骑骡（或骑马）女尊，为吉祥天母；骑狮多闻天王；陈设供器、结转法轮印的僧人，仅凭图像志无法还原其个人姓名；其手印刻意呼应上缘诸位上师，将其出资绘制此画之举，与传承本身相连接。
viewingNote.en:
At first glance, this mandala looks like a fully open flower.

Four wide petals stretch out from the center, toward east, west, south, and north. Red, white, green, and yellow pass into each other. Around them, ring after ring spreads outward, like petals, like a halo. The flower is fully open. Only a narrow strip at the top and bottom is left for the lineage teachers, protectors, and donors. Rather than a flower blooming under an open sky, the whole mandala sits on an almost black background. The dark never fully lifts. It surrounds the palace, seeps into the charnel grounds, and fills the space between the figures.

Deep dark makes us think of the unknown, of chaos, of losing our way. Yet the mandala blooms with light inside that dark. It builds a center, four directions, a boundary, a path. Broad red rises out of the black. A deep blue deity then appears out of the red. The power of the painting starts with this clash: dark and light, chaos and order, a soft flower and a wrathful god, all at once.

Why is a wrathful Mahachakra Vajrapani standing at the center of a flower? To answer this, we need to understand what a mandala is.

In tantric Buddhism, a mandala first shows “the world as an awakened being sees it.” In this world, everything finds a new place around the central deity: center and four directions, palace and outer ring, deity and retinue, different colors and different directions. All of it forms one complete order. A mandala is a map of an awakened world, but it is also a religious tool that people use. In an empowerment ritual, it brings the practitioner into a specific deity and its practice. In visualization, the practitioner builds the palace in their own mind, enters from the outside, passes through the four gates, and moves step by step toward the deity at the center. As the practice deepens, the person no longer just stands outside the deity and looks at it. Their body, speech, and mind start to match the qualities the deity stands for. In this sense, a mandala is a method that leads a person, step by step, into an awakened way of seeing. It organizes space and attention. At the same time, it places the gods, and it also places fear, desire, death, and power inside the mind.

In daily life, people feel fear, anger, dependence, and pride for many reasons. We often do not see how these feelings connect to each other. What a mandala does is give this confusion a structure. It guides us to ask: where is the outer edge, where is the threshold, what must be seen, what cannot be skipped, and how do we finally reach the center — our own mind.

Seen this way, a mandala is a path to the mind. But walking that path is not about finding a truer, stronger “self.” It is about seeing clearly how fear, desire, and attachment build the self we think is solid and unbreakable.

The mandala in the painting looks like a temple seen from above, flattened onto the surface. The palace floor plan is laid open, yet the gate towers, gate guardians, and deities each face forward. Space from different directions and different heights is pressed onto one flat canvas.

There are many kinds of mandalas. Each has a different central deity, and each offers a different way into the mind. Manjushri uses wisdom to cut through ignorance. Avalokiteshvara uses compassion to change how we relate to other beings. The Medicine Buddha is tied to healing and purification. Vajrapani shows the power of awakening. All of them point to awakening, each one a different road.

Mahachakra Vajrapani's road is very direct. He does not use a calm face to make people forget their fears temporarily. Instead, he brings death, obstacles, divine power, and self-attachment all out into the open. Entering his mandala does not mean going around fear. It means going through it. The power inside a person is often tangled up with defense, control, and harm. Mahachakra Vajrapani does not stand for destroying this power. He stands for freeing it from serving the ego, so it can instead break through obstacles and refuse to give ground to ignorance.

This path must begin at the outermost ring: the charnel grounds.

Eight great charnel grounds surround the palace. Bodies, severed limbs, bones, wild animals, flames, adepts, direction guardians, mounts, naga kings and Mahasiddhas are scattered across them. Each scale of the naga kings is painted one by one. The eyes, teeth, and claws of the mounts are sharp and clear. The tiny figures each have their own pose and expression: some sit calmly, some dance, some rage, and some seem to look back from the dark.

Ordinary social life inclines towards keeping death and decay out of sight. People build customs, language, and physical boundaries to make daily life look clean and under control. The charnel grounds brings forth what we avoid. It is not a celebration of death, but a reminder not to mistake ‘out of sight’ for safety. The first step into the mandala is to accept death. It is to see how fear controls you.

Past the charnel grounds is a wide ring of five-colored lotus petals. The petals link end to end and hold up the whole palace. Inside the lotus sits a huge crossed-vajra base. Most of it is hidden by the palace walls. Only its curved, sharp tips reach out on either side of the four gates. Makaras raise their heads and open their mouths, and the vajra's blades shoot out from between their jaws, like the bones holding up the palace, like lightning striking in four directions. The lotus and the vajra form another contrast. While the lotus is soft and stands for growth and opening, the vajra is hard and indestructible. A spiritual order needs both: the ability to grow, and a strong mind to withhold everything.

Further in, the four gate towers rise in stacked layers and hold the composition steady. A wrathful gate guardian and his consort stand watch at each gate.

These gate guardians are not enemies for a practitioner to defeat. They mark the boundary of a sacred space. They stop people from rushing into the center unprepared. A person cannot skip fear and call it peace, and cannot go around desire and call it freedom. Each gate asks a person to stop, to see, to hold, and to understand what has not yet been faced. Only when we confront the things that controls us can we move further.

This path exists not only in the subject matter, but in the painting's own colors and lines. The red palace walls, the five-colored lotus petals, and the gold lines build clear layers on the canvas. Black brings the feeling of the unknown and of pressure. Red brings life, heat, and alertness. The deep blue deity looks heavy and steady.

Passing through the charnel grounds, the lotus petals, the vajra, and the four gates, we finally reach the heart of the flower.

The deep blue Mahachakra Vajrapani and his consort sit in the inner sanctum. The whole palace opens around them. The emanations in the four directions, the gate guardians, and the deities on the outer rings all take their place around this center.

The Sanskrit word vajra means both thunderbolt and diamond, something unbreakable. A thunderbolt strikes fast and clears obstacles. A diamond is hard and clear, and nothing can damage it. “Vajrapani” means “the one who holds the vajra.” If Manjushri shows the wisdom of awakening, and Avalokiteshvara shows its compassion, then Vajrapani shows the power that makes wisdom and compassion actually work.

Mahachakra Vajrapani is the wrathful form of this power. He has three faces and six arms, bared fangs, and a body of deep blue, almost black. He holds a vajra, a snake, and other wrathful implements, and one pair of arms embraces his consort. The union of the male and female deity is not a picture of worldly love. It stands for wisdom and skillful means, which cannot be separated. Power without wisdom easily turns into violence. Wisdom without action cannot change anything. Full awakening needs both understanding and action. Mahachakra Vajrapani tramples Brahma and Indra underfoot. Both are gods of very high standing in Indian religious tradition. Placing them beneath the deity's feet shows that worldly divine power, status, and authority stand below awakening. Also trampled underfoot is people's blind faith in power, and the need to use power to prove one's own importance.

His wrath is not hatred. The glaring eyes, bared fangs, flames, curved knife, snake, and trampled figures all show a power of action at its sharpest point. Mahachakra Vajrapani does not ask people to become angry. He asks people to see their own power, take responsibility for it, and stop letting it control them. So what waits at the heart of the flower is not a stronger self. It is a power that no longer needs to defend the self, or to break it.

If the body of the mandala organizes space, then the seventeen lineage teachers above it organize time.

They show that this path to the mind passed through great Indian adepts, translators, and Xizang teachers, taught, remembered, and practiced one generation after another. Each person was only a temporary carrier, yet together they let the lineage outlast any single life.

The bottom of the painting is closer to everyday life. Wrathful deities and Dharma protectors line up the bottom row. Shri Devi Dorje Rabtenma on her mule; Vaishravana riding a lion and two early forms of Bhagavan Mahakala. The remaining figures, aside from the solitary white female attendant, as written by Shinzo Shiratori in HAR “are retinue deities of the seventeen deity mandala rather than protector or wealth deities”

At the bottom right, a donor sits beside offerings, linking the whole mandala to one specific wish. Without the donor's resources, the painter's labor, and the pigment, cloth, and long experience of the craftsmen, these abstract rituals could never have become the work in front of us. A private spiritual experience only becomes a culture that crosses time once it enters into lineage, ritual, and physical making.

This work, painted in the fourteenth century, shows figures and fine details that blend Newar aesthetics with Xizang painting. The bodies are full and strong, with broad shoulders and arms and firm waists. The painter shaded the chest, arms, and legs with fine gradations of light and dark, so the muscles seem to rise slowly out of the color. Even a figure the size of a fingernail carries real weight and mass.

The figures carry weight, but the lines never feel stiff. The emanated bodies in the four directions bend and turn, arms, sashes, and flames sweeping outward. The inner and outer emanations, together with the central deity, form cross shapes again and again. It looks like ripples spreading out from the heart of the flower, or like winds from four directions meeting at one point. The painting is packed full, yet it never loses its layers. This beauty is doing the mandala's own work: taking content that is crowded, conflicting, even unsettling, and organizing it into an order we can face and understand. The space is small, but the story is never rushed or cut short. The painter ground the pigment fine and brought the brush tip down to a sharp point, fitting a palace, mountains, rivers, gods, corpses, and flames onto one small piece of cloth. Many details

are hidden inside the whole, and they appear one by one as soon as the image is enlarged. We could spend days contemplating this thangka and still feel we had not seen enough.

Step back to a normal viewing distance, and the whole mandala turns into a flower.

The flower stands for natural growth. The palace stands for the spiritual order people build. A flower opens outward from its center; a culture passes outward from one generation to the next. Neither nature nor civilization is a pile of separate things. Both are made of relationships, order, and the continuity of life.

The Mahachakra Vajrapani mandala makes no promise to destroy the dark. The dark stays in the painting. The charnel grounds still surround the palace. What it offers is a way to see clearly in the dark, and to find direction within confusion. A person enters the mandala not to become someone without fear, but to stop handing themselves over to fear's control.

This flower feels alive not because it stays far from the dark, but because it grows out of it.

Work Information

The central deity (shown in union with his consort) Mahachakra Vajrapani, is the wrathful tantric form of the bodhisattva Vajrapani. The consort he embraces is Mamaki, one of the five consorts of the Buddha families. The two figures trampled under his feet are identified as Brahma (under the right foot) and Indra (under the left foot). These Hindu gods are absorbed and transformed in tantric art to show self-attachment and wrong views crushed underfoot.

Four-armed wrathful emanations of Mahachakra Vajrapani. Each with a different color, matching its Buddha family and each in union with a consort and holding ritual implements.

The four gate guardians holds one wrathful protector, paired with one of four female deities who each hold a different tool of guidance — hook, noose, chain, or bell. East: Achala, paired with Vajrankushi, the hook consort. South: Yamantaka, paired with Vajrapashi, the noose consort. West: Hayagriva, paired with Vajrasphota, the chain consort. North: Amritakundalin, paired with Vajraghanta, the bell consort.

The outermost ring of the mandala shows the eight great charnel grounds, one in each direction, each filled with guardian deities, mounts, naga kings, siddhas, corpses, yakshas, rakshas, pretas, bhairavas, dakas, dakinis, ponds, fires, stupas, and sadhakas.

Moving clockwise from the top of the cemetery circle, the Mahasiddas inhabiting each cemetry are Virupa, Luipa, kukkuripa, Saharipa, Saraha, Indrabhuti, Dombi Heruka, Nagarjuna and Ghandapa.

The four corners outside the ring of charnel grounds hold other emanations of Vajrapani. The two upper corners show Mahachakra Vajrapani with naga kings; the two lower corners show Vajravidarana with naga kings.

The seventeen lineage teachers, in order: Vajradhara (shown as Vajrasattva); Simhamukha, the lion-faced dakini; Shavaripa; Jayaripa; Devapurnamati; Chokyi Zangpo; Rinchen Ngödrub; Margangpu; Chokyi Gyalpo (Khabu); Purangwa Lama; Könchökpa; Toknang (Lajé); Druse (Tampa); Yönten Pema; Gorlungpa Chenpo; the Lowo translator; Chögyal Pakpa.

Protector deities and the donor.

Male wrathful deities, holding skull cups and weapons — sword, staff, or axe.

Female wrathful deities, matched in pose to the four male deities above.

A white female deity in a dancing pose, likely a dakini.

A deity on a mount, likely Palden Lhamo.

A figure in matching dress with no visible mount, likely part of Palden Lhamo's retinue.

A female deity riding a mule, Palden Lhamo.

Vaishravana riding a lion.

A monk arranging offerings, hands in the gesture of turning the Wheel of the Dharma. Iconography alone cannot recover his name. His hand gesture deliberately echoes the teachers above, linking his act of funding this painting to the lineage itself.

subtitle.zh: 四种文明，七个文化世界，一把金刚杵。
subtitle.en: Four Civilizations, Seven Traditions, One Vajra

material.en: Iron, inlaid with gold, silver, and copper; gold sheathing

excerpt.en: Five-Pronged Vajra

viewingNote.zh:
一把金刚杵里，能装下多少个世界？

如果把眼前这件铁质五股金刚杵的形制、纹样和工艺逐层拆开，可以看到四种文明、七个文化世界彼此交叠的线索：印度密教；吉尔吉特、斯瓦特；克什米尔；东北印度帕拉；中亚粟特；唐、河西，以及最终完成这件作品的吐蕃、西藏。

如果要在这些用于比较的文化坐标名称中，了解这件五股金刚杵，那我们需要先从材料和工艺开始。

铁是这件作品最直接的物质性。它没有铜的温润，也没有银的明亮；近千年的氧化，又使表面显得粗粝而冷峻。匠人却在这副坚硬的铁骨上，同时调动了金、银和红铜。不同金属并未互相遮蔽，而像是专门为一套颜色系统以及整体质感的呈现而创作。

在作品中段的莲瓣和护法面以及中央圆球部分，可以看见一种金色薄片附着其上的工艺。这种工艺值得注意。它不是后来常见的汞鎏金，也不像鋄金那样依赖密集交叉纹咬住贵金属。从实物表面看，它更接近一张极薄的金片，被反复敲击、压实，最后服帖在胎体之上。这是一种非常古老的技术。学者A. Oddy 甚至把金属上的金箔机械覆盖追溯到了公元前三千年左右。

Amy Heller在研究吐蕃时期金银器时也曾特别讨论到这种“金箔覆盖装饰”。她提到的青海都兰吐蕃墓葬中的一件八世纪中叶、被认为具有粟特工艺背景的鎏金银器，就已经明确使用了这种方法。在吐蕃控制青海以后，并没有切断吐谷浑时期形成的交通体系，反而随着其向河西和西域的扩张，将这一网络进一步纳入自身的政治与物质文化世界。因此，它所反映的并不是一次单向的异域输入，而是八世纪吐蕃和粟特、中亚之间持续发生的器物、工匠以及技术的流动。这件八世纪中叶进入都兰吐蕃墓葬的银器，所呈现的粟特金工因素，应放在青海道延续数百年的中亚交流网络中理解。因此，早在吐蕃时期，金箔包覆这种技术就已经存在于高原周边的金工世界了。

沿着这种技术往西追，会很快进入吉尔吉特、斯瓦特和克什米尔。

在8 世纪左右吉尔吉特的作品中，我们会看到工匠并不满足于一种金属的颜色，而是在同一件作品上同时使用了铜、银、不同铜合金和金属箔的装饰，匠人把金属本身当成一种“颜色系统”。如果再看这件五股金刚杵上的另一种装饰。除了金箔覆盖以外，还能看见匠人将金以另外一种工艺再次呈现在了同一件作品上。

一眼望去，这件作品每根股刃上的金丝尤为耀眼。工匠先在每根铁质的刃面上开槽，再把金嵌进去，锤实、修平。最后表面几乎重新成为一个平面。金还是金，铁还是铁，但它们的边界已经被打磨得极其圆融，形同一体。

除了金的两种表现形式，匠人似乎觉得这种独特还是不够凸显它的重要，于是在中段的莲瓣与护法面以及圆球中间，分别又嵌上了两圈金、银、铜作为装饰。这些包金、嵌贵金属的工艺我们在大约七世纪前后的吉尔吉特和斯瓦特的作品中也能看到。这时银和红铜镶嵌早已不只是用来表现眼睛和嘴唇。它们进入衣褶、刺绣和织物表面。说明匠人已经非常熟悉如何让异质金属真正进入胎体。到了帕拉时期，这种语言变得更加成熟。同样是合金铜嵌银、红铜；匠人却将这些材料继续扩展到冠饰和身体等细节部分。

所以，关于工艺背景它很难被压缩成一条“帕拉技术传入西藏”的直线。它更适合放在多方向交流中观察：北方有粟特、青海与吐蕃世界的金箔包覆经验；西方有吉尔吉特、斯瓦特、克什米尔较早成熟的多金属镶嵌；南方则有东北印度帕拉佛教金属艺术的精饰传统。而在公元一千年前后，这些工艺就已经在西藏重新相遇了。

我们最开始很容易把这件作品称作“帕拉风格五股金刚杵”。但五股、莲花、摩羯，本来就是印度密教金刚杵逐渐形成的一套基本视觉语法，似乎并不属于帕拉独有。以大都会收藏的一件唐代鎏金铜金刚杵为例，唐代这时的金刚杵已经具备了完整的五股结构：中央一股代表中心，四股对应四方；四条外股从摩羯口中伸出；股根之间有莲花，中央还有一圈忿怒面。也就是说，在九世纪以前，这套来自印度密教的器物语言已经跨过喜马拉雅，进入了中国。

而帕拉真正重要的地方，应该是另一个层面。

十至十二世纪的东北印度，是密教视觉体系高度成熟的时期。神祇、坛城、珠宝、莲花和多金属装饰被组织得越来越精密。一件佛教金属作品不只是承担着仪轨功能，也越来越像一个被压缩的小型宇宙。眼前这件铁杵与这种精饰倾向则形成呼应：材质冷硬，细部却层层展开；股刃的力度、护法面的力量感和精密性并没有彼此抵消。所以与其把它笼统叫作“帕拉风格”，不如说：印度密教提供了基础形制，帕拉世界强化了精密、繁复与秩序化的视觉方式；唐、吐蕃与河西的密教传播，又使忿怒面、摩羯和五股结构沿不同路线流动；最后，藏地匠人最终将这些因素重新组合、更新，蜕变成了一抹更具在地性的独特色彩。

而关于中段上下部分这些包金、突眼、卷眉的忿怒面，经过唐代实物已经能看到，虽然这种忿怒面的开脸气息，更具中原特点，但可见忿怒面的形式很早就进入了密教金刚杵的形象中。它究竟还与草原、与河西发生过怎样的关系，当然值得继续研究。比起仓促为每张脸寻找一个“民族来源”更重要的，是理解一种密教观念：凶猛从未被排除在神圣之外。锋利、愤怒与恐怖进入宗教图像，并不是为了赞美失控，而是为了处理人最难处理的力量。

如果只从图像学解释这把杵，中央的圆形握部，是整件器物最稳定的位置。多珠钦· 晋美丹贝尼玛在解释金刚杵时，将这个圆形中心理解为安住于空性、真如之中的本初智慧，是一种不被二元分别轻易牵走的状态。上下股刃则和五智相连。中央和四方五股分别象征着毗卢遮那、不动、宝生、阿弥陀和不空成就五佛；莲瓣又继续向菩萨和觉悟结构展开。在相关藏传解释中，环抱股刃的摩羯也和“大悲的拥抱”意涵相连。于是，这把看似锋利的法器呈现出严格的内在次序：股刃从摩羯口中伸出，摩羯下承莲花，莲花再回到中央。说明力量不是从暴怒中直接冲出。它必须先经过中心、智慧与慈悲，才获得行动的正当性。

所有图像出现的背后几乎都带着一种文化的深意。而这件五股金刚杵最值得带回当代的问题，是“转化”。

日常生活中，我们很习惯评价一个人说：你太敏感；太倔强；太情绪化；又或者太有攻击性了之类等等。这些词听起来都像一种缺陷，仿佛成长就是要不断去掉自己身上“不够好”的部分。但敏感真的只有坏处吗？一个敏感的人，确实容易过度思考。一个眼神、一句话，都可能在心里反复放大，最后变成怀疑和内耗。

可同一种敏感，它也可以意味着敏锐。他可能比别人更早察觉到变化，更容易发现细节，更能感受到语言、颜色和人的情绪。很多时候，敏感、敏锐以及洞察，甚至同理心之间，本来就只有一步之遥。所以问题可能从来不是：怎样把敏感改掉？而是：让敏感负责什么。如果你让它负责怀疑，那它就会不断制造敌人；但如果让它负责感知，它就会变成一种能力。愤怒也是一样。它可以变成攻击，但它也可以让一个人终于知道，只有生于智慧之上的怒气才会变成真正的力量。欲望也一样。它可以滑向占有，也可以成为创造和探索世界的动力；嫉妒可以把人困在比较里，也有可能会暴露一个我们一直不敢承认的愿望。

当然，不是说所有负面情绪都值得浪漫化。伤害仍然是伤害。但金刚杵提供的不是一套“做一个更优秀的人”的训练计划。它反而是不着急把所谓缺点、所谓人性的复杂删除，这同样也是密教最有意思、也最不讨好的一点。金刚杵给出的是另一种可能，是把已经存在的力量重新放回合适的位置。所以，成长不一定是修改性格，也可能是终于学会使用自己的性格。所谓转化，不是把铁伪装成金，而是让铁承担铁的作用，让金承担金的作用。

此刻，再回头看前面的四种文明、七个文化世界，会发现它们其实也一直在说同一件事。在工艺上，铁没有变成金。金也没有变成银。每一种材料仍然保留着自己的颜色、硬度和性格。图像上，印度的摩羯没有消失，帕拉的精饰经验没有消失，唐、吐蕃世界里的忿怒气息也没有消失。它们没有被熔成同一种东西，但却围绕同一条轴线各就其位。完整从来不等于相同，而是差异获得秩序的呈现。同样，这也是“转化”对今天最锋利的提醒：不是把敏感训练成迟钝，把愤怒改造成永远的微笑。经历越多，人变得复杂几乎不可避免。所以，问题或许从来不是怎样回到那个我们认为纯粹、美好，没有被世界打扰过的纯真年代。那个纯真年代中的人已经不存在了。现在的问题是：经历了这一切以后，你是否还能清楚地辨认自己的中轴？

再看这把金刚杵。外面有四种文明留下的记忆，七个文化世界的痕迹，有金、银、红铜和铁，有莲花、摩羯、忿怒面和向外张开的锋刃。可不论外面有多少变化，它始终围绕着同一条轴心成立，相助相生，却不失自我个性。

所以，它留给我们的精神意涵，也许不是一句关于“坚不可摧”的老话。而是，一件作品可以经历多种文化、容纳多种材料，而不失去自己的中轴。一个人，是不是也可以？

千年过去，这道冷冽的光芒，依旧穿透岁月而来。不同文明在它身上留下的痕迹，没有削弱彼此，反而共同汇聚成了一种难以压低的宏大气象。它凝聚的，不只是一件器物的华美，更是一个时代、一群人对于力量和神圣的理解。

面对它，很难不去想象：在漫长的历史中，曾有多少身处权力、信仰和智慧中心的人，在这样的光芒前停驻、凝视，并为其中所显露的力量、庄严和恒久而心生敬畏。

而今天，当我们再次与它相遇，千年已经过去，那道光依旧没有黯淡。

它依旧让人惊叹。
viewingNote.en:
How many worlds can a single vajra hold?

If we look closely at the form, ornament, and techniques used to make this iron five-pronged vajra, we can trace the influence of four civilizations and seven cultural worlds: Indian esoteric Buddhism; Gilgit and Swat; Kashmir; Pala northeastern India; Sogdian Central Asia; Tang China and the Hexi corridor; and finally the Xizang empire and Xizang, where the object itself was made.

To understand this vajra within this complex web of cultural connections, it is best to begin with its material and the way it was made.

Iron is the first thing we notice about the piece. It has none of the warmth of copper or the brightness of silver, and nearly a thousand years of oxidation have left its surface rough and austere. Yet against this hard iron ground, the smith brought gold, silver, and red copper together. The metals do not simply cover or conceal one another. Instead, they appear to have been deliberately combined for their contrasting colors and textures.

Across the lotus petals and guardian faces of the central section, as well as the sphere at its center, a thin layer of gold adheres to the surface. The technique itself deserves attention. It is neither the mercury gilding that became common later nor koftgari, which relies on a densely cross-hatched surface to hold the precious metal in place. From the appearance of the surface, it seems instead to have been made with an exceptionally thin sheet of gold, hammered and compressed repeatedly until it lay flush against the metal beneath. This is a very old technique. A. Oddy has traced the mechanical application of gold foil to metal as far back as the third millennium BCE.

Amy Heller, in her research on gold and silver objects from the Xizang imperial period, drew particular attention to this kind of gold-foil overlay. The gilt-silver vessel she discusses from the Xizang tombs at Dulan in Qinghai, dated to the mid-eighth century and generally understood to reflect a Sogdian technical background, already employs the technique clearly. After the Xizang empire took control of Qinghai, it did not abandon the transport networks established during the Tuyuhun period. Instead, as it expanded toward Hexi and the Western Regions, it drew these networks further into its own political and material sphere. The vessel therefore reflects not simply an imported object, but an ongoing eighth-century movement of objects, craftsmen, and techniques among Xizang, Sogdiana, and Central Asia. The Sogdian metalworking techniques seen in a vessel buried at Dulan in the mid-eighth century belonged to an exchange network along the Qinghai route that had already existed for centuries. Gold sheathing, in other words, was already part of the metalworking tradition around the plateau by the imperial period.

Follow this technique westward, and we soon arrive at Gilgit, Swat, and Kashmir.

In works from Gilgit dating to around the eighth century, craftsmen were already combining different metals rather than relying on a single metallic color. Copper, silver, various copper alloys, and metal foil appear together on the same objects, turning the materials themselves into a system of color. On our vajra, we can see a similar approach in another form: alongside the gold sheathing, the smith used a second technique to introduce gold into the piece.

At first glance, it is the gold wire running along each prong that catches the eye. The smith cut channels into the iron, fitted the gold into them, hammered it firmly into place, and then worked the surface until it was almost flat again. The gold remains gold and the iron remains iron, yet the boundary between them has been smoothed so carefully that they appear to form a single body.

Even these two applications of gold were apparently not enough to convey the importance of the object. Around the lotus petals and guardian faces of the central section, and around the sphere between them, the smith added two further bands inlaid with gold, silver, and copper. Similar combinations of gold sheathing and precious-metal inlay can be seen in works from Gilgit and Swat dating to roughly the seventh century. By this time, silver and red copper inlay had long ceased to be used only for eyes and lips. Craftsmen had begun incorporating these metals into drapery folds, embroidery, and textile surfaces, demonstrating a sophisticated understanding of how different metals could become an integral part of an object. Under the Pala, this approach became more elaborate still. The materials remained the same, with silver and red copper set into copper alloy, but craftsmen extended their use to crowns and other details of the body.

The technical background of this vajra therefore cannot be reduced to a simple story of “Pala technique arriving in Xizang.” It is better understood as part of a network of exchange that moved in several directions at once. From the north came the tradition of gold sheathing shared by Sogdiana, Qinghai, and the Xizang world. From the west came the multi-metal inlay traditions that had developed early in Gilgit, Swat, and Kashmir. From the south came the refined ornamental vocabulary of Pala Buddhist metalwork in northeastern India. Around the year 1000, these different techniques met again in Xizang.

At first, it may be tempting to call the object a “Pala-style five-pronged vajra.” But the five prongs, lotus, and makaras belong to a broader visual vocabulary that had been developing within Indian esoteric Buddhism for centuries, and none of these features is exclusively Pala. The clearest evidence comes from Tang China.

A gilt-bronze vajra of the Tang dynasty in the Metropolitan Museum already displays the complete five-pronged structure: a central prong representing the center and four others corresponding to the four directions; outer prongs emerging from the mouths of makaras; lotus flowers between their bases; and a ring of wrathful faces around the middle. By the ninth century, then, this visual vocabulary of Indian esoteric Buddhism had already crossed the Himalayas and reached China.

What is distinctive about the Pala tradition lies elsewhere.

From the tenth to the twelfth century, northeastern India was where this esoteric visual system reached a high degree of maturity. Deities, mandalas, jewels, lotuses, and multi-metal ornament were arranged with increasing precision. A Buddhist metal object carried not only a ritual function but something closer to a condensed cosmos. Our iron vajra reflects this same concern with refinement. Its material is cold and hard, yet its details unfold layer by layer. Force and precision do not oppose each other; they reinforce one another. Rather than simply calling the piece “Pala style,” it is more accurate to see it as the result of several traditions coming together: Indian esoteric Buddhism provided the fundamental form; the Pala world intensified its precision, density, and visual order; the spread of esoteric Buddhism through Tang China, Xizang, and Hexi carried wrathful faces, makaras, and the five-pronged structure along different routes; and Xizang craftsmen ultimately recombined and renewed these elements in a style distinctly their own.

The gilded wrathful faces above and below the central section, with their bulging eyes and curling brows, also deserve attention. The Tang object shows that such faces had already entered the imagery of the esoteric vajra at an early date. Their possible connections with Hexi, the steppe, and Xixia remain worthy of further study. More important than assigning each face to a particular ethnic origin, however, is understanding the esoteric principle behind them: ferocity was never excluded from the sacred. Sharpness, anger, and terror enter religious imagery not to celebrate a loss of control, but to confront the forces within us that are hardest to master.

Seen through its iconography, the round grip at the center is the most stable point of the entire object. In his explanation of the vajra, Dodrupchen Jigme Tenpe Nyima understood this round center as primordial wisdom abiding in emptiness and suchness, a state that cannot easily be disturbed by dualistic distinctions. The five prongs above and below correspond to the five wisdoms. The center and four directions stand for Vairocana, Akshobhya, Ratnasambhava, Amitabha, and Amoghasiddhi, while the lotus petals extend the scheme toward the bodhisattvas and the structure of awakening. In Xizang commentary, the makaras enclosing the prongs embody the embrace of great compassion. Thus, what appears to be a sharp and forceful implement is governed by a strict inner order. The prongs emerge from the mouths of the makaras, the makaras rest upon the lotus, and the lotus leads back to the center. Force does not simply burst outward in anger. It must first pass through the center, through wisdom and compassion, before it can truly act.

Almost every image carries a cultural depth beneath its surface. The question this vajra most deserves to bring into the present is one of transformation.

In everyday life, we are used to telling people that they are too sensitive, too stubborn, too emotional, or too aggressive. Each of these qualities is easily treated as a defect, as though growing up meant gradually removing everything in ourselves that does not seem good enough. But is sensitivity really only a liability? A sensitive person may indeed overthink. A glance or a passing remark can be replayed inwardly until it grows into suspicion and self-doubt.

Yet that same sensitivity can also become acuity. Such a person may notice changes earlier than others, catch details more readily, and respond more keenly to language, color, and the moods of those around them. Sensitivity, acuity, insight, and even empathy may be separated by only a small step. Perhaps the question was never how to eliminate sensitivity, but what we choose to direct it toward. Turn it toward suspicion, and it can create an endless supply of imagined enemies. Turn it toward perception, and it becomes a capacity. Anger works in much the same way. It can become an impulse to attack, or it can lead us to understand that only anger guided by wisdom can become genuine strength. Desire is no different. It can become possessiveness, or it can become the drive to create and explore the world. Jealousy can trap us in comparison, or it can reveal a desire we have never dared to acknowledge.

None of this is meant to romanticize every negative emotion. Harm remains harm. But the vajra does not offer a program for becoming a better person. Nor is it in any hurry to erase the qualities we regard as flaws, those complications of being human that are perhaps the most interesting and least accommodating aspect of esoteric Buddhism. Instead, the vajra offers another possibility: to put the forces that already exist within us back where they belong. Growth does not necessarily mean changing who we are. It may mean learning, at last, how to use what we already have. Transformation is not a matter of disguising iron as gold. It is allowing iron to do the work of iron, and gold the work of gold.

Look again at those four civilizations and seven cultural worlds, and it becomes clear that they have been expressing the same principle all along. In the making of this vajra, iron did not become gold, and gold did not become silver. Each material retains its own color, hardness, and character. The Indian makara remains, as does the Pala mastery of refinement and the wrathful character of the Tang and Xizang worlds. These elements were not melted into a single substance. Instead, each found its place around a common axis. Wholeness has never meant sameness. It means giving difference an order. This may also be the most important lesson transformation has to offer us today. The goal is not to train sensitivity into dullness or turn anger into a permanent smile. The more we experience, the harder it becomes not to grow complicated. Perhaps the question was never how to return to an imagined age of innocence, pure and untouched by the world. The person who lived in that world no longer exists. The question now is whether, after everything, we can still recognize our own central axis.

Look at the vajra once more. On its surface are the memories of four civilizations and the traces of seven cultural worlds: gold, silver, red copper, and iron; lotus, makara, wrathful face, and blades opening outward. However much these elements differ, they remain held together around a single axis, each supporting the others without losing its own character.

What it leaves us with, then, may not be the familiar idea of indestructibility. It may instead be the understanding that an object can pass through many cultures and incorporate many materials without losing its central axis. Might a person do the same?

A thousand years later, this quiet presence still reaches us through time. The marks left by different civilizations have not diminished one another. Together, they form a grandeur that is difficult to diminish. What this object preserves is not only the splendor of a single ritual implement, but an understanding of power and the sacred shared by a particular age and the people who lived in it.

Standing before it, it is difficult not to imagine how many people at the centers of power, faith, and wisdom must have paused before such an object over the course of history, struck by the strength, gravity, and permanence it seemed to embody.

And now, a thousand years later, we encounter it again. Its presence is still strong as ever.

excerpt.en: Vajrakilaya Phurba

viewingNote.zh:
现代的我们似乎生活在一个情绪很容易被点燃的时间里。

每天打开屏幕，都有新的事情等待我们愤怒、担忧、同情或者立即表态。情绪以极快的速度升起，又在下一条信息到来时迅速转移。我们似乎比以往任何时候都更关心世界，却也比以往更难把注意力长久地停留在一件事情上。

我们时常会说躺平、心脉受损等缺少力量和能量的词汇。但反观这些互联网上的现象，我们现代人似乎并不缺少情绪，也不缺少力量。真正稀缺的，或许是一个能够承接这些力量的方向。

眼前这件金刚橛，恰好对应着这样的问题。

它有三张忿怒的面孔、六条向外伸展的手臂，以及一双几乎横贯身体的巨大羽翼。它圆睁三目，獠牙外露，头戴骷髅冠，第一眼看上去，像一股彻底失控的怒火。可是，当视线顺着它的身体向下移动，另一种秩序开始出现。四只手外展, 各自握持法器，两只主手却回到胸前，执持一枚小型金刚橛。本尊的身体继续向下，经过纽结和摩羯口，最终变成一枚垂直的三棱铁刃。所有扩张，最后都服从一个尖端。

为什么怒火最终要被铸成一枚橛？在密教自身的解释中，金刚橛本尊表现的不是失去理智的暴怒，而是受到智慧、慈悲以及菩提心约束的“忿怒”。

普通愤怒往往围绕一个受伤的自我展开：我被冒犯，我的利益受损。它急于寻找责任人，也急于让对方付出代价。密教忿怒尊所表现的，则是一种更强烈、也更受限制的行动力。它可以锋利，却不能被仇恨支配；可以摧破障碍，却不能把伤害本身当成目的。因此，我们最初把它看成失控，恰好构成观看这件器物的第一个误会。

这是金刚橛给人的第一个提醒：转化必须从看见问题开始。

人们面对愤怒，通常会以压下去，或者发泄出来这两种方法面对。前者否认情绪，后者服从情绪。其实这两种方法都有在回避一个重要的问题：我为什么会如此愤怒？情绪不会主动告诉我们答案。它只负责拉响警报。因此“铸”，成为了改变力量的存在。怒火本身只有强度，没有方向，未经辨识的愤怒，只会寻找敌人。怒火必须经过智慧的辨认、慈悲的约束和对根源的追问，才能改变原来的性质。

金刚橛本尊的六只手臂，正好让这个过程变得可以看见。

在图像中，我们会看到普巴金刚橛的两只右手分别持九股和五股金刚杵，两只左手持智慧火和三叉戟，胸前主手共同握住金刚橛。虽然传统仪轨并没有把这些持物规定成一套现代心理学的固定步骤，但顺着器物的结构，我们仍然可以看到：每一件法器，都在对力量提出不同的要求。

在部分宁玛派解释中，九股金刚杵联系通往解脱的九乘。它首先提出的是道路问题：这股力量究竟服从什么价值？情绪越强烈，人越容易跳过自我审查。九股杵却要求力量先回答：你要去哪里？五股金刚杵则是通常和五佛部及五种智慧产生联系。它提供的不是压抑和宣泄之间的折中，而是第三种可能：保留情绪的能量，但却需要改变用途。愤怒原本是希望对方感到痛苦，转化后的力量则是试图让伤害停止。左上手的智慧火，则也是在进一步处理那些遮蔽判断的东西。

今天，事实很少单独抵达我们。它往往已经被标题、剪辑、评论与群体立场包裹。我们以为自己在回应事实，实际上可能只是在回应一个被设计的算法。智慧火要烧掉的不是不同意见，而是偏见、投射和误认。而左下手的三叉戟。三尖在部分解释中也同样与贪、嗔、痴产生着联系。它要求人思考需转变，从“谁让我愤怒”改成“是什么使我的愤怒被触发”。思考如果不能深入，人就会不断更换敌人。我们以为自己在反抗世界，实际上可能只是在重复自己。

最后，所有持物都在胸前的小型金刚橛上汇合。

四只手向外伸展，两只主手却回到身体中央。这个动作像一道关口：所有准备冲向外部的力量，都必须先经过内在的再次辨认。智慧负责区分事实和解释，慈悲负责限制行动可以走到多远。如果没有经过这道关口的怒火，就无法获得向外迸发的力量。

金刚橛有着楔或钉的意义和作用。虽然它有时会翻译成“仪式匕首”，但橛和刀剑确是有根本区别的。刀剑可以不断挥砍，橛却必须刺入一个明确的位置。因此，“钉住”不只是力量的集中，也是力量的边界。研究早期印度西藏忿怒尊艺术的Rob Linrothe，将自己的著作命名为“无情的慈悲”。这个看似矛盾的标题，揭示了忿怒尊的真正难题：慈悲有时必须停止退让，但“不退让”绝不等于可以任意攻击。历史上，几乎所有暴力都能为自己寻找理由。只要把对方称为敌人、障碍或者邪恶，伤害就很容易获得正当性。因此，越是相信自己站在正确的一边，越不能跳过对动机、事实以及后果的审查。

这件作品除了九股、五股金刚杵、智慧火、三叉戟以外，横向伸展的双翼是最为醒目的特征之一。但“有翼”并不自动意味着“金翅鸟翼”。双翼是部分黑鲁嘎类忿怒尊和金刚橛图像中的组合。双翼也常常强调迅速抵达并摧破障碍的能力。然而，在今天速度本身并不是价值。今天的社会推崇即时回复、即时表态和快速执行。人们很容易把“反应得快”误认为“看得清楚”。可是，当方向没有确定时，速度越快，可能只是更迅速地离开了问题本身而已。

如果仔细看，双翼内部以细密斜线表现羽毛纹理，柔软的鸟羽仿佛被“金刚化”，获得了一种坚硬而迅疾的视觉感受。双翼和下方的铁刃，也构成了两种相反而互补的形态：翼向左右最大限度地展开，三棱刃则向下最大限度地集中。翼让力量抵达，刃让力量不偏离目标。这种张力也存在于材料之中。这件作品的头部由不同成分的铜合金构成，表面依旧保留着鎏金和部分嵌饰；中间身子、手臂及翼羽部分为合金铜的材质；下部刃身则为铁质。实心铸造的体感沉重。带有些许锈蚀的铁刃，表面层层隆起、开裂、剥落，呈现最自然的时间磨合。

铜让力量获得形象，铁让力量进入现实。这件作品的气场、气息让人难忘。

如果说曼荼罗通过中心和秩序，为人建立一条进入内心的道路，那么金刚橛提供的是另一种精神结构。它不负责安排整个世界，而是逼迫一股分散的力量回答一个关于落点的问题。

所以，怒火之所以要被铸成一枚橛，不是为了让它变得更具攻击性，而是让它终于能够准确地回答：我们的力量，该如何被使用？
viewingNote.en:
We live in an age where our emotions are prone to fluctuations.

Every screen we open holds something new to be angry about, to worry over, to pity, or to take a position on at once. Emotion rises at great speed and moves on the moment the next message arrives. We appear to care about the world more than any generation before us, and we find it harder than ever to hold our attention on any one thing.

We reach often for the vocabulary of depletion: lying flat, burnout, a heart worn thin. Yet look at what happens online and it is clear we lack neither feeling nor force. What is scarce is a direction able to carry them.

The phurba before us raises the same question.

It has three wrathful faces and six arms. Four arms fling outward, while a pair of great wings stretches across nearly the full width of the body. The three eyes on each face glare fiercely at the viewer. Fangs are bared, and crowns of skulls rise above each head. At first glance, the figure seems to embody rage in free fall. Yet follow the body downward, and another order begins to emerge. Each of the four outstretched hands holds an implement, while the two principal hands return to the chest, grasping a small phurba. From there, the body continues downward through a knot and the open jaws of a makara, finally ending in a vertical, three-sided iron blade. Every outward expansion ultimately resolves into a single point.

Why must rage end up cast as a peg?

In the tantric tradition's own account, the Vajrakilaya deity embodies a wrath held within wisdom, compassion, and bodhicitta, rather than fury that has lost its reason.

Ordinary anger organizes itself around an injured self: I have been offended, my interests have been harmed. It hurries to find someone responsible and hurries to make that person pay. The wrathful deity of tantric Buddhism embodies a force at once fiercer and more tightly bound. It may be sharp, yet hatred cannot govern it; it may destroy obstacles, yet harm can never be its purpose. Our first reading of the figure as rage out of control is therefore the first misunderstanding this object invites.

This is the first thing the phurba asks us to notice: transformation begins with seeing the problem.

Faced with anger, people usually push it down or let it out. The first denies the feeling, the second obeys it. Both avoid the harder question: why am I this angry? Feeling will not volunteer the answer. Its work is to sound the alarm. Casting is what changes the nature of the force. Rage on its own carries intensity without direction, and anger left unexamined will only go looking for an enemy. Wisdom must identify it, compassion must bind it, and its root must be questioned before it can become something other than what it was.

The six hands of the deity make that process visible.

In the image, the two right hands of Vajrakilaya hold a nine-pronged and a five-pronged vajra, the two left hands a flame of wisdom and a trident, while the principal hands close together on the phurba at the chest. Traditional ritual texts never set these attributes out as a fixed sequence of modern psychological steps, yet the structure of the object still shows each implement making a different demand on power.

In some Nyingma explanations, the nine-pronged vajra is linked to the nine vehicles that lead to liberation. Its first question is one of path: what value does this force serve? The stronger the feeling, the more readily we skip our own scrutiny, and the nine-pronged vajra requires the force to answer first where it is going. The five-pronged vajra is usually associated with the five buddha families and the five wisdoms. It offers a third possibility in place of any compromise between suppression and release: the energy of the emotion is kept and its use is changed. Anger begins by wishing pain on another; transformed, it works to bring the harm to an end. The flame of wisdom in the upper left hand goes further, and deals with whatever clouds judgment.

Facts rarely reach us alone today. They arrive wrapped in headlines, edits, comments, and the positions of a crowd. We believe we are responding to an event when we may be responding to something an algorithm designed. The flame burns away prejudice, projection, and misrecognition, and leaves disagreement standing. The trident in the lower left hand carries three points that some readings connect to desire, hatred, and ignorance. It asks for a change of question, from who made me angry to what set my anger off. Without that depth of inquiry, a person simply replaces one enemy with the next. We imagine we are resisting the world when we may be repeating ourselves.

In the end, every attribute converges on the small phurba at the chest.

Four hands reach outward while the two principal hands return to the center of the body. The gesture works as a gate: any force preparing to rush outward must first pass through a second inner recognition. Wisdom separates fact from interpretation; compassion sets the limit on how far action may go. Rage that has not passed this gate never earns the power to break outward at all.

The phurba carries the sense and the function of a wedge or a nail. It is sometimes translated as a ritual dagger, though a peg and a blade differ at the root. A sword can be swung again and again; a peg must enter one definite place. To pin something down is thus a concentration of force and a boundary upon it. Rob Linrothe, a scholar of early wrathful imagery in India and Xizang, titled his book Ruthless Compassion. The apparent contradiction names the real difficulty of these deities: compassion must sometimes stop yielding, and refusing to yield is never a licence to attack. Almost every violence in history has found its reasons. Call the other side an enemy, an obstacle, or an evil, and harm acquires its justification easily. The more certain we are of standing on the right side, the less we can afford to skip the examination of motive, fact, and consequence.

Beyond the nine- and five-pronged vajras, the flame of wisdom, and the trident, the laterally spread wings are among the most striking features of this work. Wings alone do not make garuda wings. This pair belongs to a combination found in certain heruka-class wrathful deities and in phurba imagery, and such wings often emphasize the ability to arrive swiftly and break through obstruction. Speed carries no value of its own today. Our society prizes the instant reply, the instant position, and the quick execution, and it is easy to mistake reacting fast for seeing clearly. When the direction has not been settled, greater speed may only carry us away from the problem sooner.

Look closely and the interior of the wings is worked with fine diagonal lines for the feathering, soft plumage rendered as though made of vajra, hard and swift to the eye. The wings and the iron blade beneath them form two opposite and complementary shapes: the wings open to their fullest extent left and right, the three-sided blade gathers to its fullest extent downward. The wings let the force arrive; the blade keeps it from straying from its mark. The same tension runs through the materials. The head is made of copper alloys of differing composition, the surface still holding its gilding and part of its inlay; the torso, arms, and wing feathers are of alloyed copper; the blade below is iron. Cast solid, the piece is heavy in the hand. The lightly corroded blade has risen, cracked, and flaked in layers, the most natural record of its passage through time.

Copper gives the force an image; iron brings it into the world. The presence of this piece stays with the viewer.

If the mandala builds a path inward through a center and an order, the phurba offers a different spiritual structure. It does not arrange the whole world. It presses a scattered force to answer a question about where it will land.

Rage is cast into a peg, then, not to sharpen its aggression, but to provide a clear answer:

How should our power be used?

subtitle.zh: 金色的意义，由黑暗共同创造。
subtitle.en: Everything gold shines despite the darkness

excerpt.en: Shakyamuni Buddha

viewingNote.zh:
那天傍晚，室内的光线慢慢暗了下来。

一根蜡烛发散出的光落在这尊释迦牟尼身上。移动的光斑掠过祂的额头、鼻梁、肩部、手臂和衣褶的转折，时而出现，时而重新隐入黑暗。

随着火焰轻微晃动，祂的轮廓反而越来越清晰。金色的身体像是一个微弱的发光体，在昏暗的空间里安静地浮现出来。那一刻，我似乎突然明白了，佛经文本为什么会反复使用金色和光明来描述佛的身体。

但真正吸引我思索很久的，除了光、除了金色，还有这尊造像本身。

这是一尊制作于十四世纪西藏、受到尼泊尔艺术风格影响的释迦牟尼。造像打磨细腻，身体比例和谐，面部带有尼瓦尔艺术中的古典、克制与优雅。祂没有刻意制造出拒人千里的庄严，也没有沉重、紧张或压迫感。五官立体而分明，面部清新又纯粹。饱满的唇部仅微微含笑，却让人感觉祂似乎随时会露出一丝笑意。

看见祂，人的情绪会自然地松下来。

这其实很难得。

在一些人的印象中，宗教艺术往往意味着严肃、古板和难以接近，仿佛一件作品必须让人感到沉重，才能证明它足够深刻。但这尊释迦牟尼完全不是如此。祂没有依靠冷峻建立权威。相反，祂的古典、明亮和轻松，使欣赏变得毫无负担。

这种感受有一点像照镜子。

当然，我们并不是在祂的脸上看到真实的自己，而是看到了一种自己也愿意拥有的状态：平静，却不疲惫；古典，而不复杂；明亮，但又不刺眼。那是一种“对镜的喜悦感”——人面对祂时，不必先懂得复杂的教义，也不必强迫自己进入某种肃穆的情绪，便已经愿意多看一会儿。宗教形象并不一定只能通过威严说服人。它也可以通过美，通过青春，通过一种让人愿意亲近的气质，和客体建立关系。

今天的我们习惯了在均匀而稳定的灯光下观看艺术品。这种稳定的光线让每一个细节都能被看得清楚。于是，我们也很容易把鎏金理解成一种颜色、一项工艺，或者一层用来表现华丽的装饰。可当光线变得不再固定，或者周围的空间真正暗下来时，金色才开始释放出它更古老的功能——在微弱的光线中，把一个形象从黑暗里带出来。

金色之所以能够如此生动，也离不开雕塑家的塑造。额头、眉弓、鼻梁、眼睑、嘴唇、肩部、手臂和双膝，都是承接光线的曲面。经过细致打磨的金属表面，让光不会粗暴地停在某一处，而是沿着身体的起伏缓慢移动。如果比例生硬，面部平板，身体转折粗糙，即使覆盖黄金，火光也很难产生如此细腻的变化。黄金能够反射光，却不能凭空创造一张令人愉快的脸。真正让光有了表情的，仍然是这尊雕塑本身。

如果按照今天的地理概念去理解，我们很容易产生疑问：一件产生于西藏的造像，为什么会带有尼泊尔的美学语言？

十四世纪的喜马拉雅地区，从来不是由一条条清晰国界隔开的封闭世界。印度、尼泊尔、中亚与西藏本土的材料、图像、工匠和技术长期流动，相互吸收。加德满都谷地的尼瓦尔艺术家在继承印度传统的同时，又形成了高度成熟的金属造像语言，并持续影响着西藏艺术。一些尼瓦尔艺术家受到西藏寺院和供养人的邀请，越过山地，在西藏停留数月甚至数年，参与寺院、绘画和造像的制作。有人完成工作后返回故乡，也有一些造型方式、制作技术和审美趣味留了下来，被西藏工匠继续学习、调整和改造。因此，这尊造像不能被简单理解成“西藏作品里掺入了尼泊尔元素”。它更像一件关系的产物。它的产地属于西藏，审美经验却来自一张更广阔的网络，是图像在道路、寺院、工匠、供养人和信仰之间不断移动之后，留下的结果。这种尼泊尔对其的影响，也不仅表现为某一种固定的脸型或衣纹。它更深地进入了造像对人的理解：年轻的面容、柔和的五官、匀称的身体，以及静止中仍然保持的生命感。

其次，在欣赏一尊造像时，真正好的比例，往往不会让人首先意识到“比例正确”。它只会让人感到，每一个部分都恰好停留在合适的位置。我们看得轻松，恰恰说明工匠做得并不轻松。造像高约四十厘米左右，对于一件金铜造像而言已经不小了。在缺乏原始出处的情况下，我们不能断定它最初究竟被供奉在哪一座寺院、哪一个佛龛或哪一种空间中。但从尺度看，它已经足以在室内形成一个明确的视觉中心。尺寸改变的不只是高度，也改变着人与造像之间的关系。小型造像容易被空间包围，而一尊四十厘米左右的金身，却开始反过来组织空间。人需要稍稍退后，才能看见完整的身体；又会不自觉地靠近，观察那张年轻的脸。观看不再只是一次扫视，而成为接近、停留和重新发现的过程。

释迦牟尼的题材，同样也是让这层黄金显得更加意味深长的锚点。

在佛传传统中，悉达多原本生活在王族和财富构成的环境中，后来离开原有身份，成为出家者。可在他离开财富之后，后世的人却又不断使用黄金，为他塑造一副他早已不再依赖的身体。另一个问题被引出：

一个放下身份和财产的人，为什么最终还是拥有了一副金色之身？

最直接的答案来自佛教文本。早期佛典关于“三十二大人相”的叙述，已经将金色皮肤定义为非凡身体的特征。可是，文本只能回答佛经如何描述佛身，却没有完全回答另一个问题：

人类为什么偏偏会选择贵重的黄金，来想象一个原本要放下执念的人？

这确实是一种矛盾。

也许，人类不会用最没有价值的东西来表达放下。恰恰相反，人往往会拿出自己最珍贵、最难割舍的东西，来证明放下究竟有多重。从人类学角度来说，一份礼物是否有分量，不只取决于赠送这个动作，也取决于赠送者究竟让出了什么。若献出的东西无足轻重，供养也就不需要付出真正的代价吧。人无法直接把“重要”铸造成实体，于是只能借助一种所有人都承认的物质，让抽象观念获得形状。即使观看者不识字，也不了解复杂的佛教教义，仍然可以立刻知道什么是重要的。

其实，黄金的意义，也不是由佛教凭空创造的。

在进入宗教以前，人类早已认识到这种材料的罕见、明亮、稳定和不易腐蚀。它可以被储存，可以被交换，也可以成为权力和身份的证明。更重要的是，它对光线十分敏感。在明亮环境中，黄金或许只是贵重；但在黑暗环境里，它却比大多普通的材料能更快地从周围显现出来。

经典为金身提供了文本依据，但经典中的金色，同样无法完全脱离人类对真实黄金的长期经验。人类学家阿帕杜莱和科皮托夫曾提醒我们，物的意义从来不是固定不变的。一件东西在社会中会经历不同的生命阶段：它可以是地下的矿石、市场中的商品、家族的财富、送给他人的礼物、献给宗教的供品，也可以在数百年后成为收藏品或博物馆中的艺术品。它的物质未必发生根本变化，但它的社会身份已经完全不同。

覆盖在佛像表面的黄金，也经历了这样的变化。

它原本可以被占有、储存、交换和继承；当它被交给工匠，覆盖在释迦牟尼身上时，却被暂时从世俗流通中抽离了出来。释迦牟尼放下的是财富对人的控制，而信仰者献出黄金，则是重新改变财富的用途。这不是把一位离开王宫的人重新装扮成国王。恰恰相反，人们把原本用于证明“权力或身份”的材料，覆盖在一个拒绝以占有定义自己的人身上。黄金依然珍贵，却从私人财富转化成一种共同可见的价值。

当然，这种转换并不意味着黄金从此彻底摆脱了权力。

能够委托这样一尊大型鎏金造像的人，需要拥有财富、资源和社会地位；寺院也必须具有足够的能力，才能调动工匠、金属、黄金和燃料。因此，金身既表达了供养，也可能显示了供养人的实力；既改变了财富的用途，也保留着财富留下的痕迹。

这个矛盾或许无法被彻底解决。

而艺术真正有意思的地方，往往就存在于那些不能被轻易解决的矛盾中。

我们常说，人类渴望光明。

但如果从人类学的角度继续追问，就会发现这句话还不够完整。人类不仅渴望光，还一直在学习如何制造光，并把有限的光放在最重要的位置。在漫长的历史中，黑暗并不是一个抽象的哲学概念，而是每天都会重新降临的现实。太阳落下之后，人的视野缩小，边界变得模糊，方向和潜在危险都更难判断。火因此首先意味着温度、安全和可见。可是，火带来的从来不只是照明。人类学家波莉· 维斯纳在研究夜晚的火边谈话时发现，和白天围绕劳动和实际工作的交流相比，人们在夜晚的火堆旁，更容易谈论故事、已故者、远方人物、社会关系和群体记忆。

这项研究当然不能被简单推广为所有社会共同遵循的规律，但它至少提醒我们：火光不仅让人看见物，也让人重新看见彼此。宗教空间继承并重新改造了这种古老的经验。寺院里的灯火不再只是为了驱赶寒冷或野兽。它被献出，被摆放在造像面前，被纳入供养和仪式。于是，火焰照亮的不再只是人的面孔，而是一个群体共同承认的形象。

在酥油灯或烛火下，坚硬的金属被处理成柔和的身体；固定的表面回应着移动的火光；一个原本完全静止的形象，因为亮点与阴影的变化，仿佛进入了时间。而这尊造像年轻、轻松的气质，也在这种微光中被进一步放大。火光从额头滑向鼻梁，又短暂停留在眼睑和嘴角。那张原本已经柔和的脸，在明暗变化中显得更加鲜活。祂没有突然变得威严，也没有因为黑暗而变得神秘莫测。相反，祂仍然亲切，甚至比白昼中更让人感到愉快。

我不是一次看完它，而是在等待中逐渐发现更多。

随着当时自然光的逐渐退去，这尊金身越来越清晰，似乎正在战胜周围的黑暗。正是黑暗隐藏了无关的细节，压低了环境的噪音，才把有限的光集中到祂身上。金色、火光、空间和观看者在那一刻相互作用。我突然意识到，它的美并没有被完全封存在铜和黄金之中。它需要雕塑家的塑造，需要细腻的打磨与和谐的比例，也需要空间、时间、移动的光线，以及一个愿意站在它面前等待的人。但要再停留片刻之后，忽然发现，事情好像也没有这么简单。

金色并没有消灭黑暗。

它的力量恰恰来自黑暗仍然存在。

所以，金色好像也从未真正战胜黑暗。它只是让人知道，即使黑暗仍然存在，某些事物、某些人，依然可以被看见。那天傍晚的一根蜡烛，似乎短暂地打开了这尊造像生命中的另一种可能。

古人在黑暗中寻找光，现代人却生活在一个几乎没有黑暗的世界里。城市、橱窗、手机、广告和屏幕都在发光，每一种信息都试图成为视觉中心。我们获得了前所未有的可见性，却未必因此更清楚什么值得观看。这或许也是越来越多人愿意重新走近古代艺术品的原因。

并不是因为古代一定比今天更好，也不是因为宗教艺术可以直接给出现代生活的答案。而是面对一件真正优秀的作品时，我们的注意力终于不再被迫同时分给无数对象。

那天傍晚，我原以为，只是蜡烛照亮了这尊金身。后知后觉，我竟开始了新的思考：观看一件作品，究竟意味着什么？
viewingNote.en:
That evening, the light in the room slowly faded.

A single candle threw its light across this figure of Shakyamuni. The flame's restless glow moved over his forehead, the bridge of his nose, his shoulders, his arms, the turning folds of his robe — emerging into light, then sinking back into shadow.

As the flame wavered, his outline grew clearer, and the golden body seemed to become its own faint source of light, quietly emerging out of the dim room. In that moment, I felt I finally understood why Buddhist scripture returns again and again to gold and radiance in describing the Buddha's body.

But what held my attention longest wasn't the light, or even the gold. It was the sculpture itself.

This figure of Shakyamuni was made in fourteenth-century Xizang, under the influence of Nepalese artistic style. The finish is fine and delicate, the proportions harmonious, and the face carries the classical restraint and elegance of Newar art. Nothing about it manufactures a distant, forbidding solemnity — no heaviness, no tension, no sense of pressure. The features are crisp and clearly defined, the face fresh and pure. The full lips hold only the faintest hint of a smile, yet you feel he might break into one at any moment.

Looking at him, you feel yourself relax without even trying. That, in fact, is rare.

In many people's minds, religious art tends to mean solemnity, rigidity, and distance, as if a work must feel heavy before it can be trusted as profound. This Shakyamuni is nothing like that. He doesn't build his authority on austerity. On the contrary, it is his classicism, his brightness, his ease, that make him so simply enjoyable to look at.

It is a little like looking in a mirror.

Of course, it isn't our actual selves we see in his face, but a state we wish we had: calm, simple and bright. Standing in front of him, you don't need to understand any complicated doctrine, or force yourself into a solemn mood to keep looking. A religious image doesn't win people over through solemn authority alone. It can also build a relationship with the viewer through beauty, through youth, through qualities that simply invite you closer.

Today we view art under even, stable lighting, which lets every detail be seen clearly. It's easy, as a result, to think of gilding as simply a color, a technique, a layer of decoration meant to look opulent. But once we remove the modern setting, gold is seen in its older appearance. A figure in the dark dimly lit by the faintest available light.

Thanks to the sculptor, gold looks so vibrant here. The forehead, the brow ridge, the bridge of the nose, the eyelids, the lips, the shoulders, the arms, the knees are all curved surfaces built to catch light. A carefully polished metal surface keeps the light from settling crudely in one spot; instead it moves slowly along the contours of the body. If the proportions were awkward, the face flat, the turns of the body clumsy, firelight would struggle to produce changes this subtle, gold or no gold. Gold can reflect light, but it cannot conjure a pleasing face out of nothing. What gives the light its expressiveness is the sculpture itself.

Thinking in terms of today's geography, an obvious question arises: why would a sculpture made in Xizang speak in a Nepalese aesthetic language?

The fourteenth-century Himalayan world was not a set of closed territories divided by clean borders. Materials, imagery, craftsmen, and techniques from India, Nepal, Central Asia, and Xizang moved constantly back and forth, absorbing one another. Newar artists in the Kathmandu Valley inherited the Indian tradition while developing a highly sophisticated language of metal casting of their own, one that went on shaping Xizang art for centuries. Some were invited by Xizang monasteries and patrons to cross the mountains and stay in Xizang for months, even years, working on temples, paintings, and sculpture. Some returned home once the work was done, but certain approaches to form, certain techniques and tastes, stayed behind, to be studied, adjusted, and reworked further by Xizang craftsmen. So this sculpture shouldn't be understood simply as "a Xizang work with some Nepalese elements mixed in." It can be better understood as the product of a relationship. It was made in Xizang, but its aesthetic sensibility comes from a much wider network — the residue left behind as images moved along roads, through monasteries, among craftsmen, patrons, and believers. Nepal's influence here isn't just a matter of one fixed face type or one style of drapery. It runs deeper, into how the sculpture understands a person: a youthful face, soft features, a well-proportioned body, a sense of life that persists even in stillness.

In a well-proportioned sculpture, the proportions themselves are usually the last thing we consciously notice. All we feel is that every part sits exactly where it should. That we can look at it so effortlessly is a sign of how much effort the craftsman put into it. Forty centimeters is a substantial size for a gilt-bronze figure. Without a documented provenance, we cannot say for certain which temple, which shrine, or what kind of space it was originally installed in, but the size is large enough to become a clear visual center in a room. Size changes more than height; it changes the relationship between viewer and sculpture. A small figure tends to get absorbed into its surroundings, while a golden body some forty centimeters tall begins, instead, to organize the space around it. You find yourself stepping back to take in the figure as a whole, only to be drawn once again toward its youthful face. Looking becomes more than a single glance; it becomes a process of approaching, lingering, and discovering the face anew.

The subject of our statue , Shakyamuni, anchors this layer of gold with a deeper meaning.

In the traditional story of the Buddha’s life, Siddhartha grew up amid royal privilege and abundance, then walked away from it all to become a renunciant. Yet centuries after he had left wealth behind, generations continued to use gold to give form to the man who had taught them how to let it go. So another question emerges: Why does someone who renounced status and possessions come to be given, in the end, a body of gold?

The most direct answer comes from scripture. The early accounts of the "thirty-two marks of a great being" list golden skin among the features of an extraordinary body. But scripture can only tell us how the texts describe the Buddha's body; it doesn't answer another question: Why would people choose precisely the most precious material, gold, to imagine a man who was supposed to have let go of attachment?

This is a contradiction.

Perhaps it is not renunciation if you let go of the least valuable thing in your possession. So people tend to offer what is most precious to them, what is hardest to part with, so that what they let go of is most visible. Anthropologically speaking, the significance of a gift lies not only in the act of giving, but in what the giver is willing to part with. An offering that costs nothing carries little meaning. Because ideas such as “importance” cannot be seen or touched, people express them through materials whose value everyone understands. In this way, the abstract takes physical form. Even a viewer unfamiliar with Buddhist doctrine can recognize, at a glance, what has been considered precious.

In fact, Buddhism did not invent the meaning of gold from nothing.

Long before religion used it, people had recognized this material's rarity, its brightness, its stability, its resistance to decay. It could be stored, exchanged, used as proof of power and status. More importantly, it is remarkably responsive to light. In a bright setting, gold would look expensive; in a dark one, it emerges from its surroundings faster than almost any ordinary material.

Scripture provides the textual grounding for a golden body, but even the gold described in scripture can never be fully separated from humanity's long, lived experience of actual gold. Anthropologists Arjun Appadurai and Igor Kopytoff have both reminded us that the meaning of an object is never fixed. A thing passes through different stages of social life: it can be ore in the ground, a commodity in the market, a family's wealth, a gift given to someone else, an offering made to religion, and, centuries later, a collector's piece or a museum artifact. Its physical matter may never change, but its social identity is different at each stage.

The gold covering the surface of this sculpture went through such a transformation.

Gold that could be possessed, stored, exchanged, or inherited was, once applied to the sculpture, temporarily removed from ordinary circulation. Shakyamuni freed himself from wealth’s grip; the believer, by offering gold, redirects its purpose. This is not dressing a man who left the palace as a king once again. It is the opposite: a material once used to display power and status has been placed upon someone who refused to define himself through possession. The gold remains precious, but its role has changed—from private wealth into a shared, visible expression of what a community holds valuable.

This transformation, of course, does not mean that gold has escaped power entirely.

Whoever commissioned a large gilded sculpture like this needed wealth, resources, and social standing, while the monastery needed the capacity to mobilize craftsmen, metal, gold, and fuel. So the golden body expresses devotion, but it may also display the patron’s power. It redirects wealth toward a different purpose while still bearing the fingerprints of wealth itself.

This contradiction may never be fully resolved.

And what is genuinely interesting about art often lies precisely in contradictions that resist easy resolution.

We often say that human beings long for light.

Push that a little further from an anthropological perspective, and the sentence turns out to be incomplete. Humans have not simply longed for light; they have spent a very long time learning how to make it and how to direct a limited supply toward whatever matters most. For most of human history, darkness was not an abstract philosophical idea but a fact that returned every day. Once the sun went down, a person’s field of vision shrank, boundaries blurred, and both direction and danger became harder to judge. Fire, first and foremost, meant warmth, safety, and visibility. But what fire brought was not just illumination. The anthropologist Polly Wiessner, studying conversation around night fires, found that compared with daytime talk centered on labor and practical matters, people gathered around night fires were far more likely to talk about stories, the dead, people far away, social relationships, and shared memory.

That study obviously cannot be stretched into a universal law that applies to every society, but it at least reminds us that firelight allows people to see not only objects, but one another, in a new way. Religious spaces inherited this ancient experience and reshaped it. Lamps in a monastery are no longer there simply to keep out the cold or wild animals; they are offered, placed before a sculpture, and folded into devotion and ritual. What the flame illuminates is therefore no longer only a human face, but an image that an entire community recognizes together.

Under butter lamps or candlelight, hard metal is transformed into a seemingly soft body. A fixed surface responds to a moving flame, and a figure that is entirely still seems to enter time itself as light and shadow shift across it. The youthful, easy quality of this particular sculpture is only heightened in that dim light. Firelight slides from the forehead down the bridge of the nose, lingers briefly at the eyelids and the corners of the mouth. A face so soft becomes even more alive as light and shadow move across it. It does not become stern, neither does darkness make it mysterious or unreadable. If anything, it remains just as approachable—perhaps even more pleasant to look at than in daylight.

I did not take in the sculpture all at once. I came to discover it slowly, in the waiting

As the natural light in the room continued to fade, the golden body grew clearer, as if it were gradually emerging from the surrounding darkness. The darkness hid away every irrelevant detail, quieted the visual noise of the room, and concentrated what little light remained upon him. Gold, firelight, space, and viewer were all acting upon one another in that moment. I realized, suddenly, that its beauty is not something sealed entirely within the bronze and gold. It needs the sculptor’s shaping hand, careful polishing, harmonious proportions—and it also needs space, time, moving light, and someone willing to stand before it and wait. But stay with that thought a moment longer, and things turn out not to be quite so simple after all.

Gold does not overcome darkness. Its power lies in shining despite it.

So gold, it turns out, never really conquers darkness at all. It only shows us that even while darkness remains, certain things, certain people, can still be seen. That single candle, that evening, briefly opened up another way of experiencing the life of this sculpture.

People in the past searched for light within darkness; people today live in a world with almost no darkness. Cities, shop windows, phones, advertisements, screens—everything glows, and every piece of information competes to become the visual center. We have gained a level of visibility no earlier generation ever had, but that has not necessarily made it any clearer what is actually worth looking at. This may be part of why more and more people are drawn back to ancient art.

Not because the past was necessarily better than the present, and not because religious art offers us any direct answer for modern life, but because when we stand before an excellent work, our attention is, for once, no longer forced to divide itself among a thousand competing things.

That evening, I thought I was simply watching a candlelight bring a golden body to life. But afterwards another thought began to take shape. Perhaps looking at art is not simply about seeing what is before us, but about learning how to see. What, then, does it really mean to look at a work of art?

subtitle.zh: 力量可以很强烈，但不能失控。

material.en: Copper alloy and iron, inlaid with silver and copper

excerpt.en: Vajrakīla (Ritual Dagger)

viewingNote.zh:
今天的人很会发现问题。

批评一种制度，拆解一种观念，揭穿一个人，推翻一套叙事。尤其在自媒体的评论区里，一种观念可以在几分钟内被拆解，一个人也可以在几句话里被判完。每个人手中，都像握着一把刀。

只是刀落下以后，事情通常并没有因此变得更好。

有些人始终不敢出手。即使明知哪里需要改变，仍然不断退让；另一些人则相反，只要开始反对，便一定要把对方彻底压倒。前者缺少突破的胆量，后者又把用力过猛误认为坚定。我们并不缺少指出问题的能力。许多社会困局，也并不难被识别。真正困难的是：指出以后，应该怎么办？也许有些看似难以找到答案的问题，并非没有答案。只要我们愿意暂时放下判断，回望历史，重新观看一件作品，就会发现，古人早已用另一种方式思考过同样的困境。

眼前这件金刚橛，恰似一种回应。

金刚橛是仪式与观想体系中的法器。它并不是现实战斗中的武器，却始终保留着“锋刃”的形态。在相关文本和仪轨语境中，它一方面具有刺穿、降伏障碍的力量；另一方面，又承担着“钉住”、划定边界和建立受保护空间的功能。大英博物馆曾将其解释为一种刺穿幻象的“单点觉知”。这意味着，金刚橛的力量从来不只是摧毁。而是在刺破混乱和守住边界之间的平衡、决断。

金刚橛的上端，是三面忿怒尊。怒目圆睁，獠牙外露，神情猛烈，甚至会令人本能地感到畏惧。面对这样的形象，一个现代社会的问题也随之出现：愤怒本身，究竟有没有价值？

今天的社会对愤怒抱有一种矛盾的态度。一方面，人们被要求压制愤怒，仿佛愤怒天然意味着失态、粗暴与不体面；另一方面，网络又不断奖励最极端、最尖锐的情绪。越激烈的判断，越容易获得关注；越彻底的否定，越容易制造立场。于是，我们常常在两个方向之间摇摆：要么不敢愤怒，要么只剩下愤怒。而金刚橛的忿怒相，却提供了第三种可能：力量可以非常强烈，但不能因此失去控制。愤怒也并非就代表失态，关键在于，它究竟服务于什么？

当愤怒只是为了维护自尊、证明自我正确、压倒他人的话，它便会迅速膨胀为暴力；如果当它不再服务于自我扩张，而是指向对障碍的清醒识别时，它就有了一种能转化成保护性的力量。

眼前这件金刚橛，面容虽然极为凶猛，整体却没有一丝松散。三张面孔向外张开，器身却始终收束在一条稳定的垂直中轴之上。它所呈现的，不是野性力量的任意倾泻，而是力量经过约束之后形成的集中——刚而不暴。

这种节制，不仅存在于形制之中，也存在于工艺细节里。

这件金刚橛有两处尤其值得注意的装饰。忿怒尊的眼睛、头冠与獠牙采用嵌银工艺。银色的光泽带有一种冷冽感，使双眼显得更加锐利，也令獠牙和头冠从深色的合金铜中清晰地显现出来。

这种冷光，使忿怒不再只是猛烈，也多出了一层清醒。

在忿怒尊面容下方的扭结与莲瓣处，匠人又嵌入红铜作为装饰。红铜的暖色与银质的冷光彼此映照，使整件器物在深沉的合金铜色泽中，产生极为微妙的变化。红铜没有喧宾夺主，银质也没有被刻意张扬。匠人只是借助不同金属之间的冷暖关系，让橛身在极为稳定的形制中，生出属于自己的气韵。

这正是传统艺术中最值得珍惜的一种创造力。

传统从来不意味着匠人只能重复。恰恰相反，正因为形制、图像和仪轨具有相对稳定的边界，创造才变得更加困难，也更考验匠人的审美、判断和修持。他不能随意改变金刚橛的基本结构，却可以在材料、比例、色彩和细节中，寻找到属于自己的表达。

没有限制的创造，未必困难。真正困难的是，在不能任意改动的地方，仍然做出差异。

匠人不能改变形制，于是便把变化藏在银、红铜与合金铜的冷暖关系之中。这样的变化看似微小，却需要极其准确的判断。多一处，可能显得炫技；少一处，又不足以形成分别。这种创造如同古人的文章。表面不动声色，真正的变化，却藏在字句与分寸之间。

随着视线继续向下，我们会看到一只张口的摩羯。

摩羯是一种复合神兽。它并不完全属于现实世界，形象中常常混合鳄鱼、象鼻、鱼类以及其他动物的特征。它具有水的流动，也带有野兽般危险的力量。而金刚橛最锋利的部分，正是从摩羯口中伸出。关于这一结构，传统中存在不同层面的解释。但在我看来，它还提供了一种很有意思的理解方式：橛刃并没有绕开那股原始、混杂而危险的力量，它恰恰从这股力量之中生长出来。这意味着，危险的力量并不一定只能被消灭。它也可能被驾驭、被转化，并最终成为突破障碍的锋刃。但如果两者失去平衡，力量同样会反过来吞噬掌控它的人。

修行或许也是如此。

它未必意味着把人的欲望和情绪全部清除，而更接近于学习如何辨认、承受并扭转这些力量。人似乎无法仅仅依靠压制来获得想要的结果。因为被压下去的东西，也许并不会因此消失，反而会换一种更加隐蔽的方式重新回来。所以，真正重要的问题并不是：“怎样才能没有欲望、没有愤怒？”

而是当这些力量出现时，我们能否驭其力，而不为力所役？

金刚橛下方的三棱刃，常被解释为对贪、嗔、痴等根本烦恼的刺破。但贪、嗔、痴并不只是古代经典中的抽象概念。“贪”，不只是对财富的喜爱。它是得到以后仍然觉得不够，是不断把下一次获得当成救赎。“嗔”，也不只是发怒。它是必须找到一个敌人，才能证明自己正确；必须否定别人，才能维持自己的位置。“痴”，更不只是认知不足。它是把情绪当作事实，把偏见当作判断，把自己愿意相信的东西误认为真实。

从这个角度看，金刚橛真正刺向的，未必是外部的某个敌人。

它首先刺向的，是人对自己的袒护。

人总能为自己的欲望找到理由，也总能替自己的愤怒制造正当性。我们往往很容易识破别人的虚伪、偏见与执念，却很难承认，自己也在用相同的方式欺骗自己。因此，真正锋利的智慧，并不是更擅长拆穿别人，而是能够走出自身的混沌，不再轻易被自己的情绪、欲望和立场蒙蔽。金刚橛的“锋利”，并不是一种向外炫耀的攻击性。它更像是一种向内的决断：该醒来的时候，不能继续装睡。

这件金刚橛经历了漫长的时间，表面依然光泽温润，器身沉稳而有分量。

我很喜欢它所呈现出来的状态：沉静自持，却不失张力。

它仿佛始终在提醒我们，真正的力量，不会因为畏惧而失去突破的勇气，也不会因为愤怒而越过应有的分寸。

真正的锋芒，必然有所守。

因为一把失去节制的刀，最终伤到的，往往不只是别人，也包括握刀的人。
viewingNote.en:
People today are good at finding fault.

We criticize institutions, take apart ideas, expose people, and overturn entire narratives. Especially on social media. An idea dismantled in minutes, a person judged and dismissed in a few lines. Everyone seems to be carrying a knife in hand.

Things do not necessarily become better even when its done.

Some people never dare to act at all. Even when they know exactly what needs to change, they keep stepping back from the moment of action. Others go to the opposite extreme: the moment they begin to object, they feel compelled to destroy the other side completely. The first lack the courage to break through; the second mistake force for conviction.

We are not short of the ability to point out problems. Many social predicaments are not hard to identify. The difficult question is: once a problem has been pointed out, what then? Perhaps some questions that seem impossible to answer are not, in fact, unanswerable. If we are willing to set judgment aside for a moment, look back into history, and reconsider a single work of art, we may find that people long ago had already worked through the very same predicament.

The vajrakīla before us can stand in as an answer to that question.

Vajrakīla is a ritual implement used in systems of practice and visualization. Although it may resemble a blade, it is not a weapon intended for physical combat. In its ritual and textual contexts, it carries two complementary functions: on the one hand, the power to pierce through and subdue obstacles; on the other, the power to “pin down,” mark boundaries, and establish a protected space. The British Museum has described it as a kind of “single-pointed awareness” that pierces through illusion. This suggests that the power of the vajrakīla is not simply destructive. It lies in the balance between cutting through chaos and holding a boundary firm—in knowing when to break through and when to remain still.

At the top of the vajrakīla is a three-faced wrathful deity, eyes glaring wide, fangs bared, its expression so fierce that it can trigger an instinctive sense of fear. Faced with an image like this, a very contemporary question comes to mind: does anger have any value?

Contemporary society holds a deeply conflicted attitude toward anger. On one hand, people are expected to suppress it, as though anger by nature meant losing composure, being crude, or behaving improperly. On the other hand, the internet keeps rewarding the most extreme, the sharpest emotions — the more heated a judgment, the more attention it draws; the more total a rejection, the more easily it stakes out a position. So we find ourselves swinging between two extremes: either too afraid to feel anger at all, or left with nothing but anger. The wrathful form of the vajrakīla, however, offers a third possibility: restrained strength. Anger need not mean losing composure — what matters is knowing what it serves.

When anger exists only to defend one’s own pride, to prove oneself right, or to overpower someone else, it swells quickly into violence. But when it no longer serves the expansion of the self, and instead points toward a clear-eyed recognition of an obstacle, it becomes capable of transforming into a protective force.

Though the faces on this vajrakīla are ferocious, nothing about the piece as a whole feels loose or unrestrained. The three faces open outward, yet the body of the implement remains gathered along a single, stable vertical axis. What it presents is not wild power poured out at random, but power concentrated after having passed through restraint — forceful, but never violent.

This restraint exists not only in the overall form, but in the details of the craftsmanship as well.

Two details of ornamentation on this piece are especially worth noting. The eyes, crown, and fangs of the wrathful deity are worked in silver inlay. The cool gleam of the silver sharpens the eyes further, and makes the fangs and crown stand out clearly against the dark tone of the copper alloy.

This cool light keeps the wrath from being merely ferocious — it adds a layer of clarity as well.

Below the wrathful faces, in the knotwork and lotus petals, the maker inlaid copper as further ornament. The warm tone of the copper plays off the cool gleam of the silver, producing an extremely subtle shift of color within the dark, dense tone of the copper-alloy body. The copper never upstages the piece, and the silver is never made to show off. The maker simply used the interplay of warm and cool between different metals to let the dagger, within a form of great stability, take on a character entirely its own.

This is precisely the kind of creativity most worth treasuring in traditional art.

Tradition has never meant that a maker can only repeat what came before. Quite the opposite: because form, iconography, and ritual prescription have relatively fixed boundaries, creativity becomes harder, and tests a maker’s aesthetic sense, judgment, and spiritual discipline all the more. He could not freely alter the basic structure of the vajrakīla, but he could still find his own voice within material, proportion, color, and detail.

Creation without any constraint is not necessarily difficult. What is truly difficult is making a real difference in places where nothing may be arbitrarily changed.

Unable to alter the form itself, the maker hid his variation instead in the play of warmth and coolness between silver, copper, and the copper alloy. Such variation may look minor, yet it demands an extremely precise sense of judgment. One touch too many, and it risks looking like showing off; one touch too few, and it fails to make any real distinction. This kind of creation resembles classical prose: outwardly composed and understated, while the true movement lies hidden between the words, in questions of measure and restraint.

As we continue downward, we come to an openmouthed makara.

The makara is a composite mythical creature. It does not belong entirely to the natural world; its form typically blends features of the crocodile, the elephant’s trunk, fish, and other animals. It carries the fluidity of water along with a beast’s dangerous power. From the makara’s open mouth the vajrakīla’s sharpest point emerges. Tradition offers several layers of interpretation for this structure, but to my mind it also suggests a compelling way of understanding it: the blade does not skirt around that primal, chaotic, dangerous force — it grows directly out of it. This implies that a dangerous force need not simply be destroyed. It can also be mastered, transformed, and ultimately turned into the very edge that breaks through obstruction. But should the balance between the two ever be lost, that same force can just as easily turn and consume the one who thought he controlled it.

Spiritual practice may work in much the same way. It need not mean eliminating every desire and emotion a person has; it comes closer to learning how to recognize these forces, bear them, and turn them around.

It seems that suppression alone cannot get a person the result they want. What has been pushed down does not necessarily disappear — it may simply come back in a more hidden form. So the question that matters is not: ‘How can I be rid of desire, rid of anger?’

It is, rather: when these forces arise, can we harness their strength without becoming enslaved to it?

The three-edged blade at the base of the vajrakīla is often explained as piercing through the root afflictions of greed, hatred, and delusion. But greed, hatred, and delusion are not merely abstract concepts confined to ancient texts. ‘Greed’ is not simply the love of wealth — it is feeling that what one has is not enough, and treating the next acquisition, again and again, as a kind of salvation. ‘Hatred’ is not simply flying into a rage — it is the need to find an enemy in order to prove oneself right, the need to negate someone else in order to hold on to one’s position. ‘Delusion’ goes further than a mere lack of understanding — it is mistaking emotion for fact, mistaking prejudice for judgment, mistaking what one wants to believe for what is actually true.

Seen this way, what the vajrakīla strikes at may not be some enemy out in the world at all.

What it strikes first is a person’s own instinct to protect and excuse themselves.

People can always find a reason for their own desires, and always manufacture some justification for their own anger. We tend to see through the hypocrisy, the bias, the fixed attachments of others quite easily, yet find it far harder to admit that we deceive ourselves in exactly the same way. True sharpness of mind, then, is not simply being better at exposing other people — it is the ability to step out of one’s own confusion, no longer so easily blinded by one’s own emotions, desires, and positions. The ‘sharpness’ of the vajrakīla is not an aggression meant to be shown off to the outside world. It is closer to an inward decisiveness: when it is time to wake up, one cannot go on pretending to be asleep.

Having passed through a long span of time, this vajrakīla still has a warm, soft luster on its surface, carrying a settled, substantial weight.

There is something endearing about its calm, self-possessed presence.

It seems to remind us that true strength lies in knowing when to push through fear and when to hold anger in check.

Real strength lies in knowing when to hold back.

A blade that has lost its restraint, in the end, tends to wound not only others, but the one who wields it as well.
