excerpt.en: Drakpa Gyaltsen

viewingNote.zh:
一尊上师像，为什么既是肖像又不仅仅只是肖像？

当在看一尊上师像时，时常会想，一张从未被见过的脸，为什么会让人如此相信？

在这尊上师肖像的呈现上，我们会看他的年龄、神情、发须，甚至试图从皱纹里猜测脾气。但一尊上师像还有另一重的任务：它不仅要让人认出“这是谁”，还要让一个已经离世的人，在数百年后依然显得可信。这里所说的可信，不只是五官上的肖似，而是我们面对他时，会相信这个人确实以这样的方式活过，也确实具有某种值得被记住的精神。

这尊扎巴坚赞肖像，首先让人停下来的，正是他的脸。

短发紧贴头部，微微卷曲，不像经过特意的修饰，更像一个人天然的发质。标志性的络腮胡沿着面颊铺开，额头上的横纹、眼角的细纹、嘴角纹和法令纹都被准确地捕捉下来。匠人没有把年龄抹去，也没有为了制造神圣感，把他塑造成一张光洁、完满而没有时间的脸。

恰恰相反，时间被留在了脸上。

他的慈祥也不是靠笑容表现的。嘴角并没有明显的上扬，神情甚至带着几分肃静；但那双眼睛没有向观看者施压，而像是越过了身边的一切，停留在了更深邃的地方。面部残存的老彩曾使它更接近活人的视觉，经过数百年的摩挲和剥落，银质又从色层之下隐约显露。于是，这张脸既像真人，又不完全属于现实中的某个瞬间。肉身的温度还在，某种超越肉身的东西也已经浮现出来。我们几乎会脱口而出：真像，像见到了本人。

可问题也从这里开始。

扎巴坚赞生活于1147 年至1216 年，这尊肖像却制作于十五世纪左右。两者相隔数百年。匠人没有见过他，今天的我们更没有见过他。那么所谓“像”，究竟是什么意思？

它未必是一种可以考证的相似，却构成了一种难以否认的真实感。匠人要说服我们的，可能不是扎巴坚赞的眉眼必定如此，而是这个人理应具有这样的气质。皱纹使他有了经历，胡须和微卷的短发赋予他不可替代的个人特征，深远的目光又将外貌引向内在。我们认出的不是精准的面部五官，而是一个人的风神。

但仅仅把脸塑造得细腻，就足以让人格变得可信吗？

再往下看，感受也越发深刻、具体。

与头部近乎微观的雕刻相比，身体的处理明显更加概括。衣袍上没有繁密的錾花，也没有繁复堆叠的装饰工艺。衣纹以一道道直接的刻痕展开，利落，清楚，像刀锋在银面上留下的判断。这种处理很容易让人联想到高原环境中的生命感：开阔、直接、有劲，不以繁缛取胜。衣袍紧紧包裹着身体，宽阔的躯干、紧凑的头身比例和向下沉定的坐姿，共同构成近似山形的轮廓。只是稳稳地坐在那里，却让人觉得很难撼动。

如果匠人的技艺仅止于此，衣袍的简略或许只是能力问题。但那张脸已经否定了这种可能。他当然能够做得更细、更满，甚至更炫目。他没有继续下去，只能说明他在不同部位作出了不同的选择。匠人知道何处必须说得具体，何处不能说得太满。他把最细腻的工夫留给了“这个人是谁”，又用最概括的方式回答“这个人怎样存在”。

那么，他想表现的，究竟是怎样一个人？

扎巴坚赞十一岁时失去父亲。十三岁那年，兄长索南孜摩离开萨迦继续游学，管理萨迦事务的实际责任便落到他身上。他直到二十六岁才正式登上法座，却已经提前十余年开始承受一个家族、一套教法和一个宗教共同体的重量。此后，他引导萨迦传统近六十年。

十三岁，本来还是一个需要被保护的年纪，他却已经开始保护一个法脉。

再看雕像那宽厚、下沉的身体，它所呈现的便不只是体量。人物没有英雄式的激昂，也没有高姿态式的压迫感。他的力量不是向外征服，而是向内承重。关于萨迦派核心教法“道果法”，他的上师曾嘱咐他九年之内不要传授，以使领悟真正成熟。扎巴坚赞最终等待的不是九年，而是十三年。这个细节比许多神迹更能说明一个人。

他不是没有东西可以讲，也不是缺少传法的资格。他只是没有急于把得到的知识兑换成声望。在今天，人们习惯迅速表达、迅速证明，也习惯把能力尽快转化成眼见的成绩。扎巴坚赞的选择却是另一种方式：先让知识彻底扎根，再决定它何时应当进入他人的生命。有能力却不急于证明，是一种比表现欲更强的力量。

这种个性魅力也使衣袍上的克制有了更深的意味。匠人没有借助繁复纹饰为人物增加声量，正如扎巴坚赞的权威也不依靠不断显示自己来证明。他的身体宽阔，手持铃杵的姿态却向内收拢；地位崇高，形象却不咄咄逼人。这种克制并不是温吞。扎巴坚赞对于借宗教追逐名声、财富和追随者的行为，有着相当严厉的判断。在他的观念里，闻思、持戒乃至修行，都可能被人的野心所利用。形式越庄严，越需要警惕它是否已经成为欲望的外衣。

所以他的一句话才格外冷峻：“我们整个漫长的人生，都在做准备。”

人总觉得真正的行动还在以后，于是用准备修行代替修行，用准备生活代替生活，直到死亡打断所有尚未兑现的计划。这种对自我欺骗的辨认，使他的沉静并不软弱，反而带着锋芒。雕像上的刻线也是如此：不繁复，却斩截；不张扬，却有力度。然而，承担和克制还不足以解释这张脸为什么显得慈祥。要理解他的皱纹和目光，还必须进入扎巴坚赞一生反复面对的另一件事：失去。

他幼年丧父，后来又陆续失去多位兄弟和亲人。索南孜摩三十六岁早逝，其他家族成员也先他而去。死亡对他而言不是偶尔闯入生活的意外，而是一次次重返的经历。但痛苦本身并不会自动使一个人深刻。它也可能使人封闭、尖锐，甚至对他人的痛苦变得麻木。真正决定人格的，是一个人把自己的失去变成了什么。扎巴坚赞没有只把丧亲留在私人哀痛中。他长期研究死亡、丧葬仪轨和亡者的归宿，撰写了多部相关著作；又通过抄经、建塔和制作肖像，为逝去的亲人与上师建立纪念形式。他把不可挽回的失去，转化成可以被后来者使用的方法。这时再看雕像的面部，那些皱纹当然不能被机械地解释为某一次丧亲的痕迹，深远的目光也不应被视作现代心理分析的例子。但他的生平改变了我们理解这张脸的方式。它的慈祥不再是未经世事的温和，而更像一个经历过失去之后，仍然没有把痛苦转化为尖锐的人。

晚年时，扎巴坚赞写下唯一一部带有自传性质的著作《上师之梦》。耐人寻味的是，他没有用它罗列自己的学术成就、建筑功绩或者主持萨迦的漫长岁月，而是保存了十七岁至六十六岁之间的七个梦。这些梦涉及前世、死亡、已故的上师与亲人。在中世纪西藏的宗教文化里，梦可以是知识和启示的来源，不能简单地被解释为现代心理学意义上的潜意识。但他的选择仍然显露出极为个人的一面：在那位引领萨迦近六十年的背后，始终存在着一个丰富而幽深的内在世界。

同样，扎巴坚赞还记录过从父亲萨钦· 贡嘎宁波和兄长索南孜摩处听闻的口传教法，为前人的著作撰写注疏，将原本依赖少数人记忆的知识转化为可以传承的文本；他建寺、抄经、造塔、塑像，又培养萨迦班智达，使萨迦传统进入一个新的历史阶段。他并不只是一个坐在法脉谱系中的“第三祖”，也不只是萨迦班智达的老师。他真正重要的地方，在于把一个卓越家族仍然脆弱的继承物，转化成能够超越家族、也超越个人生命的传统。

到了这里，我们才能真正理解，这尊造像为什么要以银质制作。

二十余厘米的银质造像，需要可观的材料、工艺和资金投入。我们不知道具体的委托者是谁，但可以确定，到了十四、十五世纪左右，扎巴坚赞仍然值得萨迦传统的继承者以如此郑重的方式加以纪念。

银质首先给到后世的是：这个人非常重要。

但银只能说明他的分量，不能解释他为什么重要。真正回答这个问题的，仍然是匠人。供养者以贵重材料表达敬意，匠人则以气韵表达理解。也正是在这里，这尊像显出一种少见的分寸：材料上不惜成本，表达上却不事张扬。

最后，这尊像还构成了一个意味深长的回环。

扎巴坚赞一生都在为容易消失的事物寻找持久的形式。他把口传写成文字，把零散的教法整理成传统，把悲伤转化为仪轨，把对亲人和上师的记忆安放在经卷、佛塔、肖像与梦境中。

他一直在保存别人。

数百年后，他自己也成为被保存的人。

所以，一张从未被我们见过的脸，为什么仍然让人如此相信？

不是因为我们能够确认扎巴坚赞的眉眼确实如此，而是因为这尊像内部的精神逻辑足够完整。细腻的面部保存了一个人的具体性，山形的身体表现了承担与稳定，节制的衣纹透露着不急于自我展示的力量，贵重的银质则说明后世愿意为纪念这种人格付出真实的代价。

一尊好的上师肖像，不是把慈悲、智慧、威严几个抽象的词语堆砌到人物身上，而是让人看到，这些精神如何从一次次具体选择中生长出来。这些选择日积月累，最终才成为我们所说的人格。

后世以银质告诉我们：这个人值得被记住。

匠人则用一张脸和一个身体告诉了我们：他为什么值得被记住。

这才是所谓“如见其人”。我们未必见到了扎巴坚赞真实的容貌，却隔着数百年的时间，认出了一个人由一生选择所形成的精神。
viewingNote.en:
A portrait of a master, like any portrait, is often more than an image of a person.

When looking at a portrait of a master, one cannot help but wonder: how can a face no one has ever seen inspire such faith?

This portrait draws our attention to his age, his expression, his hair and beard; we may even try to read his temperament in the lines of his face. Yet a master’s portrait has to do more than preserve a likeness. It must somehow close the distance between his world and ours, allowing a man who died centuries ago to feel almost present again. And by “present,” I mean more than a resemblance in his features. It is the feeling of standing before him and believing that this was once a living person—that behind the face was a spirit worthy of remembrance.

The first thing that makes us pause before this portrait of Drakpa Gyaltsen is his face.

His short hair lies close to the head, slightly curled, as though left almost entirely to its natural state. His characteristic full beard spreads across his cheeks, while the horizontal lines of his forehead, the fine creases at the corners of his eyes, the lines around his mouth are all rendered with remarkable precision. The artisan did not erase his age or smooth his features into a flawless, timeless face in order to make him seem more venerable.

He left it there, allowing time to remain on the face.

The master wears no smile, either. The corners of his mouth remain unlifted, and there is a certain gravity to his expression. His eyes seem to look beyond everything nearby, settling somewhere deeper and more distant. Traces of old pigment still clinging to the face once brought it even closer to the appearance of living flesh; after centuries of handling and wear, the silver beneath now faintly emerges through the layers of color. The result is a face that feels at once unmistakably human and somehow unbound from any single moment in time. The warmth of flesh is still there, yet now something beyond flesh has begun to surface. We’re almost tempted to say that it really looks like him—as though we had ever seen him.

Drakpa Gyaltsen lived from 1147 to 1216, yet this portrait was made around the fifteenth century, centuries after his death. The artisan never saw him, and neither have we. So what does it really mean to call this a “likeness”?

We may never be able to verify the likeness historically, yet the face produces a sense of reality that is difficult to dismiss. What the artisan seems to be asking us to believe is probably not that Drakpa Gyaltsen’s brows and eyes looked exactly like this, but that a man such as he ought to have carried this kind of bearing. The wrinkles give him a history; the beard and slightly curled hair give him an unmistakably individual presence; and the deep, distant gaze draws his appearance inward, toward character. The face gives us more than a collection of recognizable features; it gives us the sense of a real person.

But is a finely modeled face enough to make a personality believable?

Look further down, and the impression becomes more specific, more grounded.

Compared with the almost microscopic attention given to the head, the treatment of the body is noticeably more restrained. There is no dense chased ornament on the robe, no accumulation of elaborate decoration. The folds of the fabric unfold in a series of direct, incised lines—clean and decisive, like the mark of a blade left in the silver. The effect readily evokes the life of the high plateau: open, direct, forceful, never seeking to persuade through ornament. The robe wraps closely around the body, while the broad torso, the compact proportion of head to body, and the settled, low-slung posture together create a silhouette reminiscent of a mountain. He sits there, solid and unshaken, as though nothing could move him.

If the artisan’s skill had stopped there, the simplicity of the robe might simply have been a matter of ability. The face rules that out. He was clearly capable of making the rest of the figure more detailed, more elaborate, even more dazzling. The fact that he chose not to tells us that he made deliberate choices about different parts of the sculpture. He knew where to be specific and where to hold back. The artisan devoted his greatest care to telling us who this person was, while using the simplest means to make him feel present.

So, what kind of person was the artisan trying to portray?

Drakpa Gyaltsen lost his father at the age of eleven. At thirteen, when his elder brother Sonam Tsemo left Sakya to continue his studies elsewhere, much of the responsibility for the affairs of Sakya fell upon him. He was not formally enthroned until the age of twenty-six, yet more than a decade earlier he had begun carrying the weight of a family, a body of teachings, and a religious community. He would go on to guide the Sakya tradition for nearly sixty years.

Thirteen is an age when a child still longs for protection. Drakpa Gyaltsen, however, was already beginning to protect a lineage.

Seen again, the statue’s broad, settled body speaks of more than physical weight. There is nothing heroic or dramatic in his bearing, nothing commanding in his posture. His strength lies not in what he can overcome, but in what he can bear. That same quiet strength appears in the story of his relationship to the Lamdré, the central teaching of the Sakya school. His teacher instructed him to wait nine years before transmitting it, so that his understanding might fully mature. Drakpa Gyaltsen did not merely follow that instruction; he waited thirteen years. That single detail tells us more about the man than many stories of miracles ever could.

He had both the knowledge and the authority to transmit what he had learned. What restrained him was not a lack of ability, but the patience to let knowledge take root before passing it on. We live in a time that rewards speed: to express ourselves quickly, to prove ourselves quickly, to turn ability into visible results as quickly as possible. Drakpa Gyaltsen chose otherwise. He allowed knowledge to mature completely before deciding when it was ready to be transmitted. There is a profound strength in possessing the ability to act, yet having no need to prove it at once.

This quality of character gives the restraint of his robe a deeper meaning. The artisan did not rely on elaborate ornament to assert the figure’s presence, just as Drakpa Gyaltsen’s authority did not depend on constant self-assertion. His body is broad, yet the gesture of his hands, holding bell and vajra, draws inward; his status is exalted, yet nothing in his bearing is aggressive. Beneath this restraint lies something firmer than gentleness: discipline. Drakpa Gyaltsen was uncompromising toward those who used religion to pursue fame, wealth, or followers. He understood that even study, the keeping of vows, and meditation could be appropriated by human ambition. The more solemn the outward form, the more vigilant one must be that it does not become a mere costume for desire.

Which is why one of his sayings still lands with a kind of harsh truth: “Our entire life is spent in preparation.”

We tend to imagine that real action lies somewhere in the future. So we replace practice with preparing to practice, and living with preparing to live, until death interrupts all the plans that were meant to begin someday. Drakpa Gyaltsen’s ability to recognize this kind of self-deception gives his stillness an edge; it is quiet, but never soft. The incised lines on the sculpture carry something of the same quality: spare, yet decisive; restrained, yet forceful. Still, endurance and restraint alone cannot explain why this face feels so kind. To understand its wrinkles and its gaze, we must turn to another experience that returned again and again throughout Drakpa Gyaltsen’s life: loss.

He lost his father as a child, and over the years, several brothers and other family members as well. Sonam Tsemo died young, at thirty-six; other relatives preceded him as well. For Drakpa Gyaltsen, death was woven into the fabric of life, returning again and again. Yet suffering in itself does not necessarily deepen a person. It can just as easily close someone off, sharpen them, or make them indifferent to the suffering of others. What shapes a person is what they make of their losses. Drakpa Gyaltsen did not leave his grief as a private matter. He spent years studying death, funerary ritual, and the fate of the deceased, and wrote several works on these subjects. He also created memorials for departed relatives and teachers through the copying of scriptures, the construction of stupas, and the commissioning of portraits. He transformed irreversible loss into forms of practice that later generations could inherit. Looking again at the statue’s face in this light, the wrinkles obviously cannot be read as literal traces of any particular bereavement, nor should the distant gaze be treated as a case study in modern psychology. But knowing his life changes the way we encounter this face. The kindness we see there does not feel like the untested gentleness of someone who has never suffered; it feels more like the face of a man who lived through loss again and again, yet never allowed pain to harden him into something closed.

Late in life, Drakpa Gyaltsen wrote his only autobiographical work, The Guru’s Dreams. What is striking is that he did not use it to enumerate his scholarly achievements, his building projects, or his long years of leadership at Sakya. Instead, he recorded seven dreams spanning the years from seventeen to sixty-six—dreams touching upon past lives, death, and deceased teachers and relatives. In the religious culture of medieval Xizang, dreams could be understood as sources of knowledge and revelation, rather than reduced to the modern psychological notion of the unconscious. Yet his choice still reveals something deeply personal: behind the man who led Sakya for nearly sixty years was always a rich and inward world.

In the same spirit, Drakpa Gyaltsen recorded the oral teachings he had received from his father, Sachen Kunga Nyingpo, and his brother Sonam Tsemo, and wrote commentaries on earlier works—turning knowledge that had once depended upon the memories of a handful of people into texts that could be transmitted with greater certainty. He built temples, copied scriptures, raised stupas, commissioned images, and trained Sakya Paṇḍita, carrying the Sakya tradition into a new historical stage. A lineage chart may call him the “third patriarch,” and history may remember him as Sakya Paṇḍita’s teacher. Yet neither title quite captures what he accomplished. What matters most is that he took what was still a fragile inheritance belonging to one remarkable family and transformed it into a tradition capable of outliving both that family and any single lifetime.

Only now do we begin to understand why this statue was made of silver.

A silver statue more than twenty centimeters tall represents a considerable investment of material, skill, and patronage. We do not know exactly who commissioned it, but we can be certain that, well into the fifteenth century, Drakpa Gyaltsen remained a figure whom the heirs of the Sakya tradition considered worthy of such an extraordinary act of remembrance.

The silver tells later generations, first of all, that this man mattered greatly.

But silver can measure only the weight of the material; it cannot tell us why he mattered. That answer comes from the artisan. The patron expressed reverence through the costliness of the material; the artisan expressed understanding through the figure’s bearing and spirit. And here the statue reveals a rare sense of proportion: extravagant in material, restrained in expression.

Now, the story has almost come full circle.

Drakpa Gyaltsen spent his life searching for lasting forms for things that easily disappear. He turned oral teachings into writing, scattered doctrines into a coherent tradition, sorrow into ritual, and the memory of his family and teachers into scriptures, stupas, portraits, and dreams.

He spent his life preserving what belonged to others.

Centuries later, he himself became someone to be preserved.

So why does a face none of us has ever seen inspire such faith?

We cannot know whether Drakpa Gyaltsen’s brows and eyes really looked this way. Yet the statue convinces us for another reason: its inner logic is completely coherent. The finely detailed face preserves the specificity of an individual; the mountain-like body conveys endurance and stability; the restrained folds of the robe reveal a strength in no hurry to display itself; and the costly silver tells us that later generations were willing to pay a real price to honor a person of his character.

A good portrait of a master gives abstract qualities— compassion, wisdom, authority—a visible life. It allows us to see how those qualities took shape, choice by concrete choice. Accumulated over a lifetime, those choices are what we finally call a person’s character.

Later generations tell us, through silver, that this man was worth remembering.

The artisan, through a face and a body, tells us why.

Perhaps this is what it truly means to say that a portrait makes us feel we have met the man himself. We may never have seen Drakpa Gyaltsen, yet across the centuries, his spirit—shaped by a lifetime of choices—still lives in the image before us.

subtitle.zh: 世界很大，事情很多。先把手里这一笔，安静地写完。
subtitle.en: The world is vast, and there is much to do. Let us first finish the stroke before us.

viewingNote.zh:
现代的我们，每天会看见很多文字。它们从屏幕上出现，停一会儿，就会被新的消息推走。有些话在当时看来可能觉得要紧，但只要一不记录，过几天也就找不到了。

十三世纪的人，面对文字却可能有另一种心情。

在古代，有人会先把纸做得厚而坚韧，涂上深色，再在上面铺出平整的黑色书写区。随后，抄经人研磨黄金和白银，调成可以运笔的金汁、银汁，一笔一画写下佛经。画师又会在文字两端绘出佛与菩萨。这个流程既费时，费工，也费钱。所以，只有当人在认定这件事十分重要时，才会肯这样慢下来去完成它。我们眼前的这页经书，就是那样一件需要慢慢完成的作品。

这页经书属于藏译《圣八千颂般若波罗蜜多经》，它在藏文《大藏经》甘珠尔中属于般若部，在汉传佛教中，则与《小品般若经》一系关系密切。经页上的题记表明，它属于第五函或第五册，并和第一品有关。它不是供人连续阅读的普通正文页，而更接近一函经书的标题页或扉页。它的存在是想告诉读者：这是什么经，到了哪一函、哪一品；同时也让人在尚未开始诵读之前，就先整顿衣冠和心绪。

这页经叶横长，中央是黑色书写区，金字和银字在暗处显得格外明亮。两边各有两组尊像，共同环绕经文。中央下方另开一小龛，里面坐着一尊释迦牟尼佛。画得很小，却处在整张经页的中轴线上，像一枚安静的印记。这似乎在表示着佛陀不必很大。经典既被认作佛语，祂自然已经在文字之中了。

经页左侧两尊，依次为观自在和金刚萨埵；右侧为普贤和般若波罗蜜多母。

观自在代表大悲；般若讲智慧；金刚萨埵代表清净；右侧的普贤则以双运形态出现，便带有密续佛教所说本初清净、法身与觉性圆满的意味；而般若波罗蜜多母，祂则是般若智慧的人格化形态，也被称为“诸佛之母”。这样看，这四组尊像并非随意排在经文两旁。观自在是悲，金刚萨埵是净，普贤指向本初清净与圆满，般若佛母则是智慧本身。中央的小佛说明经典源自佛陀，中央的大字则是佛陀留下的言教。画面很热闹，意思却很明了：人在智慧中看清事物，也在慈悲中返回人间。

经页上的人物带有鲜明的帕拉艺术传统。帕拉王朝统治东印度约从八世纪到十二世纪中叶，其佛教造像和写本绘画随着僧侣、工匠与经典进入尼泊尔、西藏和喜马拉雅地区。

这页画中的三角形的冠叶、飞扬的眉眼、耳侧缯带、细腰长身、椭圆形头光、红色拱龛、铺满卷草的靠垫以及略带紧张感的细线，都能在帕拉及其影响下的早期藏传佛教绘画中找到近似形式。分别将目光聚向经文处的人物神态灵动、笔触细腻。手臂、腰腹和腿部以柔和的弧线相接，毫不僵硬。整个画面华丽，却丝毫没有繁缛的堆叠之感。

萨迦寺保存的早期彩绘经页，以及鲁宾博物馆所藏十三世纪藏文经页，都可为这种风格提供参照。尤其值得比较的是横长形制、尊像在两端分列的方式、深色书写区以及人物造型。而纽瓦克博物馆所藏的十四函《般若经》则是另一组重要参照。那套经书同样使用深色纸面和金银文字，并保存帕拉传统的小型绘画。取自经叶边缘的纸张曾接受放射性碳测定，校正年代范围为1040 至1335 年，研究者通常将其归入十二至十三世纪。因此，综合这些证据，这页《八千颂般若波罗蜜多经》扉页暂定为十三世纪。它既保存了东印度帕拉艺术的余绪，也已经成为了一件真正的西藏作品。在这页经书上我们会看到，风格从来不是一条画完就断掉的线。它更像水，从一个地方流到另一个地方，经过不同人的手，颜色和声音都会稍稍改变。

这页经书的动人之处，不只在于它古老、稀少。更在于七百多年后，文字中回响着的智慧，仍能穿透现代的混沌。《般若经》讲空。制作它的人却使用了最具体的东西：纸、胶、矿物，以及一生中都不能收回的时间。他们用有形的材料，写下了对于“无固定自性”的理解。在AI 极速发展的今天，我们可以看到的文字以及可以了解到的知识越来越多了。在这样的环境下，我们似乎很容易成为一个具有学识的人，却好像非常难成为一个具有智慧的人。因为真正的智慧，从不会来自那些冰冷的文字、算法，而只会来自人的发心、思考和经过人生命的每一次投入。

在现实生活中的很多问题，这些经页可能无法替我们回答。它只是把一个很朴素的尺度留在这里：人认为什么重要，就会把时间放在哪里；愿意保护什么，也就慢慢成为怎样的人。

七百年前，一位抄经人低头蘸取金汁。窗外也许有风，屋里并不明亮。他不会知道这页经书后来去了哪里，也不会知道多年以后，还有人隔着玻璃辨认他的笔画。

他只把眼前这一笔写好。有时，人的安定也就是这样来的。世界很大，事情很多。先把手里这一笔，安静地写完。
viewingNote.en:
Today, we live amid an endless flow of text. Words appear on our screens, linger for a moment, and are quickly swept aside by the next message. Even the words that matter are often left unsaved, until, a few days later, they will have vanished altogether.

For someone in the thirteenth century, the written word held a significance we can scarcely imagine today.

In earlier times, paper was first made thick and durable, coated in a dark pigment, and worked into a smooth black surface for writing. Scribes would then grind gold and silver into a fine paste, thin enough to draw with, and set down the sutra stroke by stroke. Painters added images of buddhas and bodhisattvas at either end of the text. The process demanded time, skilled labor, and considerable expense, so only when something was judged truly important would anyone commit to working at such a deliberate pace. The folio before us is one such work.

This folio belongs to the Tibetan translation of the Āryāṣṭasāhasrikā-prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, the Perfection of Wisdom in Eight Thousand Lines, classified within the Prajñāpāramitā section of the Kangyur, the Tibetan Buddhist canon. In Chinese Buddhism, its closest counterpart is the Xiaopin Bore Jing, the Chinese recension of the same text. The colophon on the page identifies it as belonging to the fifth volume, associated with the first chapter. Rather than a page of continuous running text, it functions more as a title page or frontispiece for the volume: its purpose is to tell the reader which sutra this is, and which volume and chapter follow, while also giving the reader a moment to compose their dress and their mind before the recitation begins.

The folio is long and horizontal, with a black writing field at its center, against which the gold and silver script glows with particular brightness. Two pairs of deities flank the text, framing it on either edge. Below the center, a small niche holds a seated figure of Shakyamuni Buddha. Painted quite small, he nonetheless occupies the folio's central axis, like a quiet seal set into the page. The scale seems almost to suggest that the Buddha need not be large: since the sutra itself is regarded as the Buddha's own word, he is, in a sense, already present within the text.

On the left side of the folio are Avalokiteshvara and Vajrasattva; on the right, Samantabhadra and Prajñāpāramitā.

Avalokiteshvara embodies great compassion; the Prajñāpāramitā teaching itself speaks to wisdom; Vajrasattva represents purity; and Samantabhadra, shown here in union with his consort, carries the tantric meaning of primordial purity and the full perfection of the dharmakāya and awakened awareness. Prajñāpāramitā symbolises the personification of wisdom, revered as the Mother of All Buddhas. Seen this way, the four deities are not placed at random on either side of the text: Avalokiteshvara stands for compassion, Vajrasattva for purity, Samantabhadra for primordial purity and completeness, and the Perfection of Wisdom deity for wisdom itself. The small Buddha at the center marks the sutra's origin in the Buddha's own teaching, and the large central script carries the teaching he left behind. The composition is rich with figures, yet its meaning is clear: wisdom lets a person see things as they are, and compassion carries them back into the world.

The figures on this folio carry the distinctive imprint of Pala artistic tradition. The Pala dynasty ruled eastern India from roughly the eighth century to the mid-twelfth, and its Buddhist sculpture and manuscript painting traveled onward into Nepal, Tibet, and the Himalayan region, carried by monks, craftsmen, and the texts themselves.

The triangular crown leaves, the sweeping brows and eyes, the ribbons at the temples, the slender waists and elongated bodies, the oval halos, the red arched niches, the cushions covered in scrolling foliage, and the fine lines carrying a slight tension all find close parallels in Pala painting and in the early Xizang Buddhist painting it shaped. The figures, each turned toward the text at the center, are rendered with a lively presence and a delicate touch. Arms, waist, and legs meet in soft, unbroken curves, with no trace of stiffness. The whole composition is lavish, yet nowhere does it feel overcrowded or ornate.

Early painted folios preserved at Sakya Monastery, together with a thirteenth-century Xizang folio in the Rubin Museum of Art, offer useful points of comparison, particularly in the horizontal format, the placement of deities at either end, the dark writing field, and the modeling of the figures. A fourteen-volume set of Prajñāpāramitā manuscripts held at the Newark Museum of Art provides another important reference. That set likewise uses dark-toned paper and gold and silver script, and preserves small paintings in the Pala tradition. Paper taken from the edge of one of its folios has undergone radiocarbon dating, yielding a calibrated range of 1040 to 1335, and scholars generally place it in the twelfth to thirteenth century. Taking this evidence together, the present frontispiece from the Perfection of Wisdom in Eight Thousand Lines is provisionally dated to the thirteenth century. It preserves something of the eastern Indian Pala artistic legacy, while standing as a genuinely Xizang work in its own right.

What this folio shows us is that style is never a line that simply ends once drawn. It behaves more like water, flowing from one place to another, taking on a slightly different color and voice as it passes through different hands.

What makes this folio moving is not only its age or its rarity. It is that, more than seven hundred years later, the wisdom echoing through its text still reaches through the noise of the present. The Prajñāpāramitā teaches emptiness, yet the people who made this folio worked with the most tangible of materials: paper, glue, ground minerals, and time that, once spent, could never be recovered. Through physical substance, they set down an understanding of what has no fixed, independent nature. Today, with AI advancing at remarkable speed, the amount of text we encounter and the knowledge available to us keep expanding. In such an environment, it has become easy to become someone knowledgeable, and correspondingly difficult to become someone wise. Wisdom never comes from lone text or algorithms — it comes from a person's own intention, reflection, and the investment of each moment of a lived life.

There are many questions in life that a folio like this cannot answer for us. What it offers instead is a simple revelation: a person spends time on what they consider important, and is thereby shaped by what they choose.

Seven hundred years ago, a scribe bent his head and dipped his brush in gold. It may have been a windy and gloomy day. He could not have known where this folio would eventually go, nor that centuries later, someone would stand before a pane of glass, tracing the strokes of his hand.

He needed only to finish the work at hand.

Sometimes, that is where a person finds their peace of mind.

The world is vast, and there is much to do. Let us first finish the stroke before us.

subtitle.zh: 那些选择，恰恰是对自身需要部分的回应。
subtitle.en: What we choose reveals what we seek

excerpt.en: Shakyamuni Buddha

viewingNote.zh:
我们已经太熟悉释迦牟尼的样子了。

肉髻、袈裟、结跏趺坐，右手触地印。只要几个特征同时出现，我们几乎不需要思考，就知道这是释迦牟尼成道时的形象。也正因为太熟悉，我们常常先认出了“佛”，却忘了去看祂的身体。

但如果暂时把身份放在一边，只看眼前这尊夏鲁风格的释迦牟尼，会发现它首先给人的并不是纤细、轻盈，而是一种非常明确的身体力量。

肩部、胸腔横向展开，腰腹迅速收紧；两条手臂粗壮，尤其右臂从宽阔的肩部垂落，前臂厚实，手掌稳稳触向膝下。素面的袈裟贴着身体而行，没有田格纹，也没有大面积繁复装饰，只以细密的珠状衣缘标出轮廓。衣服没有遮盖身体，反而让肩、胸、腰之间的关系变得更加清楚。再往下，结跏的双腿重新向两侧展开，落在层层饱满的莲座上，于是整个身体形成一种很稳定的结构：上宽，中间收紧，下部再次打开。

奇怪的是，它并没有表现明显的肌肉体块。没有起伏明显的胸肌，也没有夸张的腹肌。脸也是安静的：双目低垂，嘴唇微抿，神情克制。可我们还是会觉得祂很有力量。为什么？因为藏地需要的或许从来就不是肌肉，而是力量的可见性。

这里的“力量”并不是现代意义上的健壮。匠人真正塑造的是几种感觉：宽、满、稳、定。肩部骨架负责撑开空间，胸腔负责建立体量，收紧的腰部让上身显得更加挺拔，双腿以及宽厚莲座则把所有向外扩张的力量重新压回大地。于是我们感受到的不是一个准备行动的人，而是一个根本不需要行动的人。

这可能正是神圣身体与世俗身体最大的区别。

世俗的力量常常需要被证明：奔跑、挥拳、征服、抵抗。可佛陀成道的核心图像恰恰与此相反。面对魔罗的质疑，释迦牟尼没有起身，没有攻击，而只是端坐，右手触地，让大地为自己的觉悟作证。

雕塑真正困难的，不是让一个运动中的身体显得有力量，而是让一个一动不动的人，看起来依然不可撼动。

眼前这尊造像做到了。而且这种身体并不是完全脱离佛教传统文化而成形。佛教关于“大丈夫相”的古老传统，就已经强调了佛身不是普通人的身体。《长部》第三十经中保存的三十二大人相中，已经包括狮子般的胸部、充实的肩背、匀整的躯干以及特殊的身体比例。换句话说，佛教从很早开始就在用身体的圆满、匀称和超常，去表达一个普通肉身无法直接表现的精神身份。

但经典只能告诉工匠：佛身应该不同于凡人。它不会告诉他，肩膀究竟要宽多少，胸部应该鼓到什么程度，腰应该收得多紧。而真正的地方性，往往就藏在这个“程度”里。于是问题也从“这种宽肩厚胸来自哪里”，慢慢变成了另一个更有意思的问题：为什么这种身体如此适合藏地对神圣的想象？

往往当这个问题一出现，我们很容易就会想到一种听起来很顺的答案：因为高原气候严酷，所以藏地崇尚强壮；因为生活环境艰苦，所以人们喜欢有力量的佛。也许这样的理解过于简单。因为自然环境当然会进入人的身体经验，但自然不会直接生产审美，一座山、一种海拔，也不会产生某一种雕塑比例。然而一个社会在长期形成的文化环境和生活经验中，则会共同影响并导向大家如何理解“有力量的身体”。

在传统文化的表述中，当佛教传入吐蕃开始，舍利、经卷、佛像、绘画等物质对象便被理解为能够通过与佛、菩萨、圣者的联系，承载和传递宗教效力；人与这些对象的观看、触碰、供养等感官关系，也被认为能够产生功德、加持乃至各种宗教效验。这类圣物后来也深入了寺院、共同体乃至政治制度当中。虽然这种对于文化的理解，并不意味着我们可以简单断言：“因为佛像具有宗教效力，所以肩膀一定要做宽。”两者之间不存在如此直接的因果证据。但它至少提醒我们：藏地宗教雕塑面对的任务，从来不只是“像不像佛”。它还必须让一个已经无法以肉身被人见到的佛，在现实空间中获得足够强烈的临在感。这一点似乎非常重要。

如果佛像只是肖似，那么比例准确、面貌优美或许已经足够；但如果祂同时承担着礼拜、供养、观想以及神圣临在的物质媒介作用，那么雕塑必须解决另一个问题：

怎样让“看不见的力量”可以真正显现？

外来的风格之所以能够被一个地方接受，并不仅仅因为当地人觉得它好看。而是：一种外来的形式，恰好能帮助这个社会解决一个它原本就在面对的问题。选择代表回应。这或许正是为什么在藏地一些释迦牟尼造像上，我们会看到身体越来越壮实，甚至还会看见一些明显带有夸张意味的塑造。那并不一定意味着工匠不了解自然人体。恰恰相反，夸张往往意味着选择。

而夏鲁，恰好为我们提供了一个观察选择的历史现场。

夏鲁寺建立于11世纪，但它在艺术史上最重要的阶段之一，是14 世纪上半叶的大规模扩建。夏鲁当地由于扎巴坚赞等人与元廷、萨迦的关系密切；1320 年代初布敦· 仁钦珠进入夏鲁，此后这里就迅速地成为了藏地重要的佛学、翻译与艺术中心。现存壁画与历史文献都说明，当时夏鲁并不是一个封闭的地方寺院，而是处在元代政治、宗教以及工匠流动形成的巨大交织网中。纽瓦尔艺术在其中尤其重要。

13 世纪以后，由于来自加德满都谷地的纽瓦尔匠人持续为藏地赞助人绘制绘画并制作造像；到了14 世纪，尼泊尔艺术就成为了藏地佛教美术最重要的视觉来源之一。我们眼前这尊造像仍然可以感受到这种联系。祂没有田格状拼缀袈裟，素面的僧衣贴着身体而行；面部柔和而年轻，眼睛细长，身体虽然健壮，却没有变得粗笨。尤其腰部收束之后形成的流畅轮廓，使力量与优雅同时成立。这种身体绝不是只剩下重量，祂依然保存着尼瓦尔艺术对于人体比例和金属表面的敏感。

可事情恰恰不能停在“尼泊尔影响”四个字上。因为14 世纪的夏鲁能够接触到的视觉资源并不少。纽瓦尔、东印度以及元廷所连接的汉地艺术因素，在这里并置、交错。这就意味着，夏鲁真正值得看的并不是“融合了多少文化”。而是它选择了什么。

如果一种身型只是被原样照搬，我们可以把它叫作模仿；但如果宽肩被继续强调，整个躯体逐渐获得比原型更强的重量感，那么事情已经发生了变化。

因为夸张本身就是选择。工匠把某一个特征“做得更多”，就意味着他认为那一点尤其重要。

这也是为什么观察藏地雕塑时，那些比眼前这尊释迦更加壮硕、更加挺括，甚至比例略显夸张的身体特别值得注意。它们不能简单证明“西藏同胞天生喜欢壮实”，但至少提示我们：强、稳、满、厚，确实曾经成为藏地表达神圣的一种反复出现的视觉选择。

而这种选择和视觉欣赏本身也有关。

今天我们把一尊造像独立放在桌面上，可以走近到几十厘米处观察眉眼、手指、衣纹。但祂原本进入的是寺院、佛龛和礼拜场合。那里存在观看距离，也存在供器、织物以及其他造像与灯光共同构成的复杂环境。在这样的空间中，一条极细的刻线可能很快消失，但宽阔的肩膀不会，饱满的胸腔不会，稳定的坐姿也不会。

所以有些看起来超出自然人体的比例，并不一定意味着工匠“不懂人体”。恰恰可能因为他知道雕塑最终要在哪里出现、在哪里被看见。

神圣必须隔着距离，也依然得成立。再回来看这尊释迦牟尼，就会发现它真正精彩的地方正在于这里。

面孔没有威慑感，身体却有重量；他没有多余动作，整个雕塑却充满了力量。这种力量没有向外爆发，而是被牢牢控制在跏趺而坐的身体里面。这使其带有一种因为足够强，才可以如此安静的视觉感受。

佛教传统给予强健佛身以宗教合法性；尼瓦尔艺术提供了成熟而优雅的人体语言；13-14 世纪夏鲁所处的政治与工匠流动，让这些形式能够大量进入；而藏地自身长期形成的宗教经验、身体感受与观看方式，则决定了什么会被留下，什么会被放大。

所以我们最初问的是：为什么这尊释迦的肩膀会这么宽？

聊到最后，真正的问题却已经变成：一个社会究竟需要怎样的身体，才能让它相信眼前所见就是神圣？

对于藏地历史中这一类造像而言，答案或许不是强壮本身。而是一种更难表现的东西——让不可见的力量，获得可以被看见的身体。而当一种来自别处的身体语言，开始如此准确地回应当地人关于神圣的需要时，它也就不再只是“外来的风格”了。

它已经成为了藏地自己的佛。
viewingNote.en:
Few figures are as familiar to us as Shakyamuni Buddha.

The uṣṇīṣa, the monastic robe, the cross-legged seated posture, the right hand in bhūmisparśa mudrā (the earth-touching gesture) — the moment these features appear together, we recognize, almost without thinking, the image of Shakyamuni at the moment of his enlightenment. Yet it is precisely this familiarity that leads us to recognize “the Buddha” first, and to forget to look at his body.

If, however, one sets that identification aside for a moment and considers only this Shakyamuni in the Shalu style, what strikes the viewer first is not slenderness or lightness, but a distinct and unmistakable physical power.

The shoulders and chest extend broadly outward, while the waist and abdomen draw sharply inward. The arms are thick and muscular, particularly the right arm, which falls from a broad shoulder into a substantial forearm, the hand resting firmly below the knee. The plain monastic robe follows the contours of the body closely — it bears no checkerboard patterning and no extensive surface decoration, its outline marked only by a fine beaded hem. Rather than concealing the body, the robe brings the relationship between shoulders, chest, and waist into sharper definition.

Below the waist, the crossed legs spread outward again, resting upon a lotus base built up in full, layered petals. The body as a whole thus forms a highly stable structure: broad at the top, drawn in at the center, and open again at the base.

Curiously, the figure shows no pronounced musculature — no clearly defined pectorals, no exaggerated abdominal muscles. The face, too, is composed: the eyes are lowered, the lips gently closed, the expression restrained. And yet the impression of power remains.

Why should this be so? Perhaps because what Xizang's tradition required was never muscle as such, but the visibility of power.

“Power” in this context does not correspond to modern notions of muscularity. What the craftsman shaped were several distinct qualities: breadth, fullness, stability, and firmness. The shoulder structure opens out the surrounding space; the chest establishes volume; the drawn-in waist lends the upper body an upright bearing; and the legs, together with the broad, substantial lotus base, gather all outward-reaching force back down into the earth. The impression conveyed is thus not of a figure poised for action, but of one who has no need to act at all.

This may be the most significant distinction between a sacred body and a worldly one. Worldly power must generally be demonstrated — through running, striking, conquest, resistance. Yet the central image of the Buddha’s enlightenment stands in direct contrast to this. Confronted by Māra’s challenge, Shakyamuni neither rose nor struck back; he simply remained seated, his right hand touching the earth, calling the earth itself to bear witness to his awakening.

The true difficulty for a sculptor lies not in making a body in motion appear powerful, but in making a motionless figure appear utterly immovable.

This particular image achieves exactly that.

Nor did this bodily conception emerge in isolation from Buddhist tradition. The ancient doctrine of the mahāpuruṣa-lakṣaṇa, the “marks of a great being,” had already established that the Buddha’s body was not an ordinary one. Among the thirty-two marks of a great being recorded in the thirtieth sutra of the Dīgha Nikāya are a lion-like chest, full shoulders and back, a well-proportioned torso, and distinctive bodily proportions. In other words, Buddhist tradition had, from a very early period, used bodily fullness, symmetry, and exceptionality to express a spiritual identity that an ordinary body could not directly convey.

Scripture, however, could only instruct the craftsman that the Buddha’s body must differ from that of an ordinary person — it could not specify precisely how broad the shoulders should be, how full the chest, or how tightly drawn the waist. It is in this matter of degree that local character truly resides. The question thus shifts from “where did this broad-shouldered, deep-chested form originate” to a more interesting one: Why should this particular body have been so well suited to Xizang's imagination of the sacred?

When this question arises, an easy and seemingly plausible answer often comes to mind: that the harshness of the plateau climate led Xizang people to esteem physical strength, and that difficult living conditions produced a preference for a powerful Buddha. Such an explanation is likely too simple. The natural environment undoubtedly shapes bodily experience, but the environment does not directly generate aesthetic form — a mountain or an altitude does not by itself produce a particular sculptural proportion. Rather, it is the cultural environment and lived experience accumulated by a society over time that together shape how a community comes to understand what a “powerful body” should look like.

According to traditional accounts, from the time Buddhism was introduced into Xizang, material objects such as relics, scriptures, images, and paintings came to be understood as capable of carrying and transmitting religious efficacy through their connection to buddhas, bodhisattvas, and realized beings; and the sensory relationships between people and these objects — seeing, touching, making offerings — were likewise held to generate merit, blessing, and various forms of religious efficacy. Sacred objects of this kind subsequently became deeply embedded in monasteries, communities, and even political institutions. This cultural understanding does not license the simple claim that “because Buddha images possess religious efficacy, the shoulders must therefore be made broad” — no such direct causal evidence exists between the two. It does, however, remind us that the task facing religious sculpture in Xizang was never merely one of resemblance to the Buddha. It also had to grant a Buddha no longer visible in physical form a sufficiently powerful sense of presence within real space. This point appears to be of considerable importance.

If an image needed only to resemble the Buddha, accurate proportion and a handsome countenance might well have sufficed. But if the image was also to serve as a material vehicle for worship, offering, visualization, and sacred presence, then the sculpture had to resolve a further problem: How could an invisible power be made genuinely to appear?

A foreign style is rarely adopted by a place simply because local viewers find it visually appealing. More often, an imported form happens to help a society resolve a problem it was already confronting. Choice, in this sense, constitutes a response. This may explain why, in certain images from Xizang, Shakyamuni's body grows progressively more robust, at times taking on forms that are unmistakably exaggerated. Such exaggeration does not necessarily indicate that the craftsman lacked knowledge of natural anatomy — quite the opposite. Exaggeration is, more often than not, a sign of deliberate choice.

Shalu Monastery, as it happens, offers a historical site at which precisely this process of choice can be observed.

Shalu Monastery was founded in the eleventh century, but one of its most significant periods in art history came with its large-scale expansion in the first half of the fourteenth century. Owing to the close ties that figures such as Drakpa Gyaltsen maintained with the Yuan court and the Sakya school, and the arrival of Butön Rinchen Drup at Shalu in the early 1320s, the monastery rapidly became a major center of Buddhist scholarship, translation, and art in Xizang. Surviving murals and historical documents both indicate that Shalu at this time was by no means an isolated local monastery, but was situated within an extensive network formed by Yuan-dynasty politics, religion, and the movement of craftsmen.

Newar art played a particularly important role within this network.

From the thirteenth century onward, Newar artisans from the Kathmandu Valley continued to produce paintings and images for Xizang's patrons; by the fourteenth century, Nepalese art had become one of the most important visual sources for Buddhist art in Xizang. This connection remains legible in the image before us. It bears no checkerboard-patterned robe; the plain monastic garment follows the body closely. The face is soft and youthful, the eyes elongated, and although the body is robust, it never becomes coarse. The fluid contour formed by the drawn-in waist, in particular, allows power and elegance to coexist. This is by no means a body reduced to mere weight — it still retains the Newar tradition’s sensitivity to bodily proportion and to the treatment of metal surfaces.

Yet the matter cannot simply rest with the phrase “Nepalese influence.” Fourteenth-century Shalu had access to no shortage of visual resources: Newar, eastern Indian, and Chinese artistic elements connected through the Yuan court all converged and intersected here. What is truly worth examining at Shalu, then, is what, specifically, was chosen.

To reproduce a bodily type unchanged is imitation. But when broad shoulders are accentuated and the body takes on greater mass than its prototype, imitation gives way to transformation.

For exaggeration is itself a form of choice.

When a craftsman gives a particular feature greater emphasis, it indicates that he considered that feature especially important.

This is why, in surveying Xizang's sculpture broadly, figures even more powerfully built and more sharply defined than the present Shakyamuni — some with proportions that appear distinctly exaggerated — deserve particular attention. Such works cannot simply be taken as proof that Xizang people possessed an innate preference for robust physiques; but they do suggest that strength, stability, fullness, and solidity became a recurring visual choice for expressing the sacred in Xizang.

And this choice was also bound up with how such images were meant to be seen.

Today, an image such as this may be placed alone on a table, allowing a viewer to approach within a few dozen centimeters to examine the brow, the fingers, the folds of the robe. However, in its earliest days, it would have stood in a monastery or shrine, a place of worship. In such spaces, viewing distance mattered, as did the complex environment formed by ritual implements, textiles, other images, and lighting. Within such a setting, a finely incised line might quickly disappear from view — but broad shoulders, full chest, and a stable seated posture would not.

Proportions that appear to exceed natural anatomy, then, do not necessarily indicate that the craftsman “did not understand the human body.”

It may instead indicate the opposite — that he understood exactly where the sculpture would ultimately stand, and from where it would be seen.

The sacred had to remain, even across a distance.

Returning to this image of Shakyamuni, it becomes clear that this is where its true accomplishment lies.

The face conveys no sense of intimidation, yet the body carries real weight; there is no superfluous gesture, yet the entire sculpture is charged with power. This power does not erupt outward but remains firmly contained within the seated, cross-legged body — producing the visual impression of a figure so strong that it can afford to remain utterly still.

Buddhist tradition granted religious legitimacy to a powerfully built Buddha body; Newar art supplied a mature and elegant visual language of the human form; the political circumstances and the movement of craftsmen at thirteenth- and fourteenth-century Shalu allowed these forms to enter Xizang in considerable volume; and Xizang’s own long-accumulated religious experience, bodily sensibility, and modes of viewing determined what would ultimately be retained, and what would be amplified.

The question with which we began, then, was:

Why are the shoulders of this Shakyamuni so broad?

By the end of this inquiry, however, the real question has become a different one:

What kind of body does a society require, in order to believe that what stands before it is truly sacred?

For images of this type within Xizang's history, the answer may not be physical strength as such, but something considerably harder to achieve: giving an invisible power a body that can be seen. And once a bodily language originating elsewhere begins to answer local conceptions of the sacred with such precision, it ceases to be merely a “foreign style.”

It has become, instead, Xizang’s own Buddha.

subtitle.zh: 从洱海出发，去西藏。
subtitle.en: From a Lake to a Plateau

excerpt.en: Vajrakīlaya Ritual Dagger (Phurba)

viewingNote.zh:
说到普巴金刚，多半第一反应先想到西藏。

那是一种十分鲜明的形象：三面六臂，三目圆睁，獠牙外露，头发向上燃起，主手在胸前执持金刚橛。相应的法器也往往有三颗忿怒头、金刚杵顶饰、摩羯和蛇纹。看过几件，便不容易认错。

眼前这件却有些不同。

它以铜合金铸成。上半部是三目、獠牙、戴骷髅冠而焰发上扬的普巴金刚；双手却没有执橛，而是在胸前合掌。腰下承着一圈莲瓣，再往下，神祇的身体忽然收成一枚细长的三棱橛，这种实心的三棱柱体形制在大理国的杵戒中尤为突出。正因如此，即使它仍是一件普巴金刚橛，但却不像我们熟悉的西藏普巴那样直截了当。也正是这些“不太一样”的地方，值得我们去继续追问。

普巴，本义是橛、楔或钉。密教仪轨借它标定坛城界域，镇伏扰乱修行的力量，也把散乱、执著与恐惧“钉住”，使它们不能再牵动人的心。普巴又被神格化为普巴金刚，也就是金刚橛本尊。因此，本尊和法器并不是两个分开的对象：金刚橛是本尊力量的物质显现，本尊也可以橛的形态出现。这件橛把这种关系做得很清楚。尊像不是附加在手柄上的装饰，它就是手柄；腰部以下也不再延续人的躯体，而是经莲花形构件直接化为三棱橛身。神与法器共用一副身体。

三棱是辨认金刚橛的重要形制。不同传承将它解释为降伏贪、瞋、痴三毒，也可联系欲界、色界、无色界三界。解释不尽相同，指向却都相近：真正需要被制伏的，不是某个外在敌人，而是妨碍觉知的力量。普巴金刚的面容很凶。密教中的忿怒却不是世俗的发怒，而是文化中慈悲和智慧在面对顽固障碍时显现的猛烈形式。有意思的是，这尊普巴金刚正在合掌。合掌通常指向礼敬、专注和归依，它使原本向外迸发的威慑力被收回了胸前。这种“忿怒而合掌”的结构，使作品呈现出了一种醒目的图像张力：面容显出降伏之力，双手却保留内在的安静。

今天我们谈普巴，很少会想到大理。其实937 年到1253 年的大理国，是西南一个重要的佛教中心。王室长期护持佛教，地方阿吒力传统中有灌顶、护国、明王、大黑天和金刚众等密教内容。

大理佛教并不是西藏佛教的支派。现存的仪轨大多都是以汉文书写，属于承继了唐代不空等人的密教传统；但造像和法器却又显露出了东北印度、缅甸和东南亚因素。因为在古代的地界，它处在中国、印度、东南亚和青藏高原几条道路之间，见到的东西多，最后形成的样子也就不同。僧人带来仪轨，商旅带来金属和器物，工匠见过异乡的样式，再依照本地人的信仰重新制作一遍。而地方风格往往就是在这样的环境下来慢慢长成、成型。学者Megan Bryson 在研究大理金刚橛时发现，大理国仪轨中有用到“橛”或“金刚橛”形制；包括在千寻塔等遗址中也保存了实际的普巴式法器。可见金刚橛并不是后来偶然传入云南，而是它本就在大理的密教生活中。

如果要更详实的了解我们眼前这把普巴金刚，那就绕不开大理和西藏的关系，这就要从更早的南诏说起。

八世纪后半叶，南诏处在唐和吐蕃之间，时而结盟，时而转向。766 年的《南诏德化碑》记录了南诏与唐决裂、转而依附吐蕃的背景；吐蕃一度将南诏视为“兄弟之国”。后来形势改变，南诏又重新与唐结盟。这些往来有时是使节和礼物，有时是军队。尽管政治关系也并不总是和气，但由于山路一直有人在走，那衣饰、器物、语言和宗教观念便也可能跟着走过去了。

当然，政治接触并不直接等同于艺术传播。现有研究认为，南诏虽然和吐蕃长期有往来，但能明确到藏文佛典、西藏仪轨以及造像上的证据仍然不多。既然两地的接触是真实的，但为什么清楚呈现西藏与大理风格混合特征的器物却非常少见？所以这样的实物才尤其值得注意。

进入到大理国时期，向北的道路仍然可从洱海出发，经过丽江、中甸、德钦进入康区，再通往西藏腹地。这是后来滇藏茶马交通体系的重要基础。马匹、茶叶和金属器沿路流动，僧侣、商人、工匠及图像母本也可能在这样的背景下随之往来。在当年，可能只是一张图样、一种手印或一种铸造方法，被匠人记在心里。到了另一处，尺寸变了，面容变了，手印也自然就依当地人的理解而产生变化了。我们眼前的这件作品也许就诞生于某一位有创意的匠人之手。1253 年，蒙古军队攻破大理。大理国结束了，此后云南以及西藏先后进入了元朝的版图中。

学者Bryson 在公开材料中统计了八件依据较为可靠的大理国普巴式金刚橛。它们约长十一至十九点一厘米，材质包括铜、青铜、鎏金铜和铁。数量虽少，习惯却很清楚。这些器物通常上部有神祇，下部是橛。神祇有时只露出头部，有时具有完整半身；胸前常结明确手印；尊身与刃部之间多用莲花形构件衔接；背面一般带环，可以套指，也可能穿绳系于衣带。再看本件，联系便不难理解。它以完整半身构成橛柄，手印位于胸前，莲瓣承接尊像和三棱刃，这些都接近大理国“尊像式金刚橛”的结构。与此同时，三目、獠牙、骷髅冠与焰发，又将它明确带回普巴金刚的忿怒图像。它不是标准的大理金刚橛，也没有完全遵循成熟的西藏普巴程式。更准确地说，它以大理式的身体结构，承载了普巴金刚的题材。

市场上的“罕见”有时只是一句话。器物研究所说的少见，应当能够指出它究竟少在哪里。首先是尺度。与公开著录的大理杵比较，大多比例约为十一至十九厘米左右，本件只十二厘米，形体更为紧凑。它可能用于个人护持、随身携带或小型坛场。其次是手印。大理金刚橛重视胸前结印，本件延续了这种构图，却采用了目前公开作品中极为少见的合掌印。更重要的是地域样式的组合：大理式半身尊像、胸前手印和莲花接口，与普巴金刚的三目、獠牙、骷髅冠、焰发及三棱橛身，被收在同一件小型铜合金法器上。就现有公开材料而言，这并不是常见的图像程式。

器物不大，却两种视觉传统相互交叠。有本尊和法器；有大理和西藏，也有走过山路的人和记住异乡样式的匠人身影。它握在掌中，虽然不声不响。但一条从洱海向北，途经丽江、德钦与康区的旧路，却留在了上面。
viewingNote.en:
Most people think of Xizang when they hear the word Phurba.

It has a vivid and instantly recognizable form: three faces, six arms, three round, wide-open eyes, bared fangs, hair rising in flames, and the principal pair of hands holding a ritual dagger before the chest. The implements associated with this form typically bear three wrathful heads, a vajra finial, and motifs of makaras and serpents. Once you have seen a few examples, they are not easily mistaken for anything else.

The piece before us, however, is somewhat different.

Cast in bronze, it presents Vajrakīlaya's upper body in the familiar wrathful mode: three eyes, bared fangs, a crown of skulls, and hair rising like flames. But instead of gripping a dagger, the hands are joined in añjali at the chest. Below the waist, a ring of lotus petals gathers the figure into a single form, beneath which the body tapers abruptly into a slender, three-sided blade, a solid triangular section prominently seen in the ritual daggers of the Dali kingdom. Thus, although the object is, at its core, a Vajrakīlaya dagger, it does not present itself with the straightforward clarity of the Xizang phurba we know so well. It is precisely these departures from the familiar that invite closer inquiry.

Kīla, in its original sense, means a peg, wedge, or stake. In tantric ritual, it is used to mark the boundaries of a mandala and to subdue the forces that disturb practice, driving distraction, attachment, and fear into the ground like nails so that they can no longer unsettle the mind. The peg was, in turn, deified as Vajrakīlaya, the tutelary deity of the ritual dagger. Deity and implement are therefore not two separate things: the dagger is the material manifestation of the deity's power, while the deity may equally take the form of the dagger. This piece makes that relationship unmistakable. The figure is not an ornament attached to a handle; it is the handle itself. Below the waist, the body ceases to be a human torso and passes through a lotus-shaped collar directly into a three-sided blade. Deity and implement share a single body.

The three-sided blade is a defining feature of the vajra dagger. Different lineages interpret it as the subjugation of the three poisons, desire, hatred, and delusion, and also connect it with the three realms of desire, form, and formlessness. The interpretations vary, but they converge on the same point: what must ultimately be subdued is not an external enemy, but the forces that obstruct awareness. Vajrakīlaya's countenance is fierce, yet wrath in tantric practice is not worldly anger. It is the fierce form that compassion and wisdom take when confronting obstacles too stubborn to yield to gentler means. What makes this figure especially compelling is the gesture of its hands, joined in añjali. Ordinarily associated with veneration, concentration, and refuge, the gesture here draws the deity's outward-radiating power back toward the chest. The combination creates a striking visual tension: the face expresses the force of subjugation, while the hands hold an inner stillness.

When we speak of the phurba today, we hardly think of Dali. Yet the Dali kingdom, which lasted from 937 to 1253, was in fact a major Buddhist center in southwest China. Its royal house sustained Buddhism over the long term, while the local Azhali tradition encompassed tantric elements such as consecration rites, rites for the protection of the state, wrathful kings of wisdom, Mahākāla, and vajra deities.

Dali Buddhism was not a branch of Xizang Buddhism. Most of its surviving ritual texts are written in Chinese and descend from the tantric tradition transmitted by Amoghavajra and other masters of the Tang dynasty. Yet its images and ritual implements also bear traces of northeastern India, Myanmar, and Southeast Asia. Situated at the crossroads of routes linking China, India, Southeast Asia, and the Xizang plateau, Dali absorbed influences from many directions, and what emerged there developed a character of its own. Monks carried ritual texts, merchants carried metal objects and finished works, and craftsmen who had encountered distant styles recast them according to local beliefs. Regional styles took shape gradually through precisely this kind of exchange. In her research on Dali vajra daggers, the scholar Megan Bryson has found that ritual texts of the Dali kingdom refer to the kīla, or vajra-dagger form, and that actual phurba-type implements survive at sites such as the Qianxun Pagoda. The vajra dagger, then, was not something that arrived in Yunnan by chance at a later date. It was already part of Dali's tantric life.

A fuller understanding of the piece before us calls for some account of the relationship between Dali and Xizang, and that story begins earlier still, with the kingdom of Nanzhao.

In the second half of the eighth century, Nanzhao stood between the Tang empire and the Xizang Empire, aligning with one and then the other as circumstances shifted. The Nanzhao Stele of Virtue of 766 records the background to Nanzhao's break with the Tang and its turn toward Xizang, which for a time regarded Nanzhao as a “brother state.” Circumstances later changed again, and Nanzhao renewed its alliance with the Tang. These exchanges took the form, at different times, of envoys and gifts, as well as armies. The political relationship was not always cordial, but people continued to travel the mountain roads regardless, and with them, clothing, objects, language, and religious ideas likely traveled as well.

Political contact, of course, is not the same as artistic transmission. Current scholarship holds that although Nanzhao maintained long-term ties with Xizang, clear evidence connecting these ties to Xizang Buddhist texts, ritual practice, or iconography remains limited. Given that contact between the two regions was real, why do objects that clearly combine Xizang and Dali stylistic features remain so rare? It is this rarity that makes a piece like the present one worth close attention.

By the Dali kingdom period, the northern route ran from Lake Erhai through Lijiang, Zhongdian, and Deqin into the Kham region, and onward into the Xizang heartland, along the same corridor that would later become the backbone of the Yunnan–Xizang tea-horse trade network. Horses, tea, and metal objects moved along this road, and monks, merchants, craftsmen, and iconographic models likely traveled with them. In those years, what passed from place to place might have been no more than an image, a hand gesture, or a casting technique, carried in a craftsman's memory. Arriving somewhere new, it might change in proportion, acquire new features, or take on a gesture reinterpreted according to local understanding. The piece before us may well have been born from the hands of one such inventive craftsman. In 1253, Mongol forces conquered Dali. The Dali kingdom came to an end, and Yunnan, followed by Xizang, was in due course absorbed into the territory of the Yuan dynasty.

The scholar Bryson has catalogued, from published material, eight reasonably well-documented phurba-type vajra daggers of the Dali kingdom. They range from roughly eleven to nineteen centimeters in length and are made of materials including copper, bronze, gilt bronze, and iron. Few as they are, their conventions are consistent: a deity above and a blade below. The deity may appear only as a head or as a full bust; a distinct hand gesture is usually formed at the chest; a lotus-shaped element commonly joins the figure to the blade; and a ring is typically set at the back, large enough for a finger or to hold a cord tied to a belt. Seen against this pattern, the present piece falls readily into place. Its bust forms the full handle, its gesture is positioned at the chest, and its lotus petals join the figure to a triangular blade, all features closely aligned with the structure of the Dali “figural vajra dagger.” At the same time, the three eyes, bared fangs, skull crown, and flaming hair firmly place it within the wrathful iconography of Vajrakīlaya. It is neither a standard Dali vajra dagger nor a complete expression of the mature Xizang phurba formula. More precisely, it carries the subject of Vajrakīlaya within a Dali-style body.

On the art market, “rare” is sometimes little more than a simple word. Properly established through the study of an object, however, rarity should tell us exactly where that object stands apart. Here, that begins with scale. The published Dali comparanda range from roughly eleven to nineteen centimeters, and at twelve centimeters, this piece is among the more compact examples, likely suited to personal devotion, to being carried on the body, or to use on a small altar. It is also a matter of gesture. Dali vajra daggers give particular weight to a gesture formed at the chest, and this piece follows that compositional principle, but with joined palms, a gesture not otherwise recorded among the published comparanda. More significant still is the combination of regional idioms: a Dali-style half-length figure, a chest-level gesture, and a lotus junction, brought together with Vajrakīlaya's three eyes, bared fangs, skull crown, flaming hair, and three-sided blade, all within a single small implement of bronze alloy. Against the currently published material, this is not a common iconographic formula.

Small as it is, the object holds two visual traditions in a single form. Deity and implement meet here; so do Dali and Xizang, as do the travelers who once crossed the mountain roads and the craftsmen who carried distant styles home in memory. It rests quietly in the palm of a hand.Yet an old road from Lake Erhai northward, through Lijiang, Deqin, and Kham, remains etched upon it.

title.zh: 成就者唐卡（卡孜拉索风格）

subtitle.zh: 一位身份模糊的画师，一种无法忽视的绘画。

excerpt.zh: 成就者唐卡（卡孜拉索风格）
excerpt.en: Mahasiddha Thangka (Khazi Lhazo style)

viewingNote.zh:
我们是否生活在一个越来越依赖“被看见”来确认自我价值的时代？

是的。

我们今天的生活把存在和可见绑定得越来越紧了。人们的焦虑，往往不是因为自己没有价值，而是价值没有被看见，没被承认。虽然这些困顿听起来像是个人心态的问题，但个人从来不是悬浮于社会之外的孤岛。制度如何分配机会，阶层如何划定边界，文化如何塑造评价，权力如何决定谁能够发声，都会进入和影响到一个人的生活。于是，人需要交流，需要回应，也需要获得合理的社会承认。

承认本身并没有错。

可真正的问题是：我们是不是渐渐把认可从“价值的社会确认”，变成了“价值产生的唯一条件”？

眼前这幅唐卡，恰好把这个问题推到我们面前。

这件作品有一种无法被忽视的绘画气质。画中人物不是同一副面孔的反复复制，而是拥有各自的身体状态、性格和精神强度；山石与树木并非单纯的装饰，而是共同构成了复杂而通透的空间；蛇、鸟、莲花、水禽与草木，也不是被塞入空白处的填充，而像一群拥有自身生命的参与者。我们能够清楚地感受到画师的判断、趣味和创造力，可是，却无法把这些判断准确归还给一个姓名明确、经历完整的人。

“卡孜拉索”风格是一种大约活跃于18 世纪末至19 世纪初的东部西藏绘画风格，这类绘画传统的大致区域位于西藏东部的察雅。现有的学术研究通常将这类作品归入“卡孜拉索”风格。“Khazi Lhazo”大意是“卡孜村的画师”，并非一位已有确切考证的个人姓名。尽管这位画师的真实身份至今仍然是个谜。“卡孜拉索”并不像勉唐、钦孜那样，是一个拥有相对清晰师承谱系与历史叙述的传统大画派名称。由于它更接近一位身份尚未被完全考定的画师，以及与特定村落相关的一种绘画风格。所以眼前这幅作品究竟是画师亲笔、画坊作品，还是同源图式之下的另一绘制版本，在缺少材料检测、画背题记与可靠流传记录的情况下，目前都不能轻率断定。

可真正有趣的地方，也恰恰在这里：

为什么一个身份如此模糊的人，仍然能够通过一幅画，让我们如此清楚地感觉到他的存在？

理解这幅作品，首先要从它不同寻常的叙事结构开始。它描绘的并不是根本上师和弟子之间由上至下延伸的单线传承，也不是一个人物从起点走向终点的完整传记，而是金刚座大成就者系统中的一幅七人组合的图像。

画面中的七位人物分别是：上方中央的月称，上半部左侧的麦杰巴，右侧的迦那巴，画面中央的阿难陀藏，以及下半部由左至右的阿哇度底巴、查拉巴和释迦友。

他们不是同一个故事中的七个阶段，而是七段彼此独立的生命经验。

最初将他们组织在一起的，是同一套赞颂与祈祷系统；而真正使他们成为一幅画的，则是画师赋予七个名字以不同的身体、环境、性格与命运。这个变化看似只是构图方式的不同，实际上却改变了整幅作品的精神轴心。如果它表现的是一条传承脉络，那么它主要回答的问题会是：教法从哪里传来？但当七位成就者以相对独立的场景共同出现时，画面提出的却是另一个更宽阔的问题：

一个人究竟可以通过多少种不同的生命处境与道路，完成对自身的改变？

答案并没有被写成一句教义，而是被拆解在七个人的身体里。

画面上方，月称安坐于大树之间。

树枝弯曲、交错，数条蛇在枝干和树冠间穿行。飞鸟停驻、鸣叫，甚至探身靠近人物。周围的一切都在生长、游动和变化，月称的身体却保持着异常稳定的平衡。金刚座赞颂文将月称描述为能通达龙树密意、具足文殊智慧的成就者。至于画中蛇群究竟是对“龙树”之名的视觉联想、神通瑞相，还是来自某种尚未确定的图像意义，目前无法断言。但可以确认的是，画师没有把月称描绘成一个远离世界、智慧悬空的哲学家。

思想在这里没有脱离生命。

月称被画入了一个枝叶疯长、蛇身缠绕、鸟声交错的现实世界里，而他却不被世界的复杂性扰乱。这使月称代表了第一条道路：理解，也可以成为修行。真正的学识，不只是熟悉经典和论证，更是让人在复杂现实中不被轻易干扰的能力。智慧并不是站在生活之外解释生活，而是在生活内部看清它。

位于月称左下方的麦杰巴，则处在完全不同的生命状态之中。

他身体裸露，披着红色衣物，仰头望向飞鸟；身旁站立着一位正在起舞的伴侣，身披羚羊皮。更远处的左上角云端，白不动明王在火焰中显现。赞颂文称麦杰巴裸身修行，常居尸陀林，并曾亲见不动明王。于是，伴侣、兽皮、裸体与云端中的本尊，共同将一段简短的赞颂转化为具体场景。

一提到尸陀林，人们通常会想到死亡、腐败、恐惧，以及社会最试图排除的禁忌。进入尸陀林修行，意味着不再依靠井然有序的外部环境维持内心的安稳，而是直接面对人最不愿承认的事实：身体终将腐败，身份终会消失，所谓洁净和污秽之间的边界，也远没有想象中那么牢固。因此，麦杰巴所代表的，并不是对规则的任意破坏，更不是把反常行为浪漫化，而是一种更加严酷的训练：当一个人失去熟悉的秩序感后，他还能依靠什么认识自己？我们当然不必模仿尸陀林修行，但这像是给现代生活的一个提问。当职位、安全感、生活惯性和他人的肯定暂时失效之后，我们是否还知道自己是谁？

月称右下方的迦那巴被布帛包裹，肤色呈灰紫色，身体收缩在相对幽暗的山岩与树木之间。

仅从表面看，他很容易被理解为另一位尸陀林苦行者。但赞颂文所讲述的，却是一个完全不同的故事。迦那巴曾经是一位国王。后来，他主动舍弃王位和尊荣，从事了被世俗社会视为卑微的行为，并与一位社会地位低下的修行伴侣共同证得悉地。他的道路具有一种强烈的颠倒性。他不是从贫寒中向权力攀升，而是从权力顶端主动走向社会边缘。他舍弃的，也不只是一个王位，而是一种更深的价值假设：如果人的价值必须依靠阶层、名望和他人的尊重才能得以证明，那么一切所谓“向下走”都会被理解为失败吗？但在迦那巴的圣传中，恰恰只有当王者不再依靠王权确认自己时，他才真正开始面对自己的存在。

他颠倒的并不是修行原则，而是世俗社会习以为常的价值排序：尊贵的身份未必能够带来解脱，卑微的处境也未必会阻断证悟。这并不是否认社会阶层造成的真实差异。贫寒、歧视和权力的失衡绝不能因为一句“众生平等”便被轻描淡写地抹去。它所质疑的还有另一件事：现实处境是否有资格垄断一个人的全部定义？

整幅画中最醒目的，是位于中央的阿难陀藏。其梵文名为Ānandagarbha，藏文名Kun dga’snying po，即贡噶宁波。

他拥有异常魁梧的身躯，形象介于历史人物、瑜伽士和超常密续形象之间。折叠的身体分别由一根手指支撑，立于两朵莲花之上；双脚并合于胸前，形成一种近似说法印的结构。悬空的身体仿佛不受重力制约，保持着极其严密的平衡。这种特殊身姿并非“卡孜拉索”画师凭空创造。它属于阿难陀藏既有的图像传统，是其成就者身份和神通幻变的识别标志。

画师的创造，不在于发明这一身相，而在于如何让既有身相重新鲜活地进入画面。

阿难陀藏体量最大，占据中央，是整幅画的视觉重心。但他没有把其余六位人物变成自己的附属。其他成就者仍然拥有独立的场景、气质和道路。这是一种极为成熟的画面分布：有中心，却不把中心变成唯一；有结构，却没有将其他人物的差异化压平。阿难陀藏虽然是构图的中心，但却不是意义的唯一来源。他位于视觉中心，但并不意味着他是其余六位成就者的根本上师。中心与脉络，也在这里被清楚地区分了开来。

同样，阿难陀藏本人则代表着另一条重要道路。

他与瑜伽续的解释传统密切相关，是一位具备深厚学识的学者与仪轨权威。与麦杰巴的尸陀林修行、迦那巴对王权的舍弃相比，他的成就更多体现为经论理解、仪轨知识与密续实践之间的结合。这提醒了我们在理解一件作品时，思维上的一个常见误解：仿佛大成就者只能是反制度、反知识、骄纵跋扈、冷峻偏执，依靠狂放行为获得解脱的流浪瑜伽士。阿难陀藏的存在表明，深入传统并不必然意味着被传统束缚。理解经论、解释仪轨、掌握复杂的修持系统，同样可能成为转化生命的道路。真正的问题从来不是一个人是否进入规制，而是他在制度中究竟是获得了理解，还是只获得了服从？

画面下半部，三位成就者被安排在更加贴近地面、水岸与日常生活的空间里。

下半部左侧，阿哇度底巴和一位手持嘎巴拉碗的女性伴侣共同出现。阿哇度底巴坐在兽皮之上，左手高举；其上方云气浮动，一尊度母从云中显现，立于空中，和他形成了明确的对视关系。赞颂文提及度母曾给予阿哇度底巴加持，并帮助他超越八种恐惧，因此，高举手臂、仰首对视的姿态，可能暗示某种加持、传授或礼敬关系。值得注意的是，这个场景并没有将修行理解成对身体和关系的排斥，相反，它呈现出密续修持中另一种重要的转化方式：身体、感知以及人与人之间的关系本身，都可以被纳入修行，并成为通向解脱的道途。

下半部中央，为查拉巴和一位女性伴侣。在这幅唐卡中，查拉巴前方的女性伴侣并未在金刚座祈祷文中被明确提及姓名。因此，在缺少题记支持的情况下，不能轻率地将她泛称为“空行母”。她可能是修行伴侣、仪轨明妃，也可能是经典文本中的其他参与者。但画面的基本方向是清楚的。密续修行并没有简单排除身体、关系和恐惧，而是试图把这些最容易使人失去自主性的经验，重新纳入修行之中。这是一种更加困难的转化：不是逃离身体和关系，而是不再被身体和关系盲目支配。

我们现代生活常常在两个极端之间摇摆。一个极端把欲望、亲密和情感视为必须摆脱的负担；另一个极端则把“忠于感受、跟随内心”理解成服从所有冲动。但不压抑，并不等于不辨别；接纳身体，也不意味着向身体的一切惯性投降。真正的自主，不是没有欲望和恐惧，而是在欲望与恐惧出现时，仍然保有观察和选择的能力。

画面右下方，是释迦友与一位蓝衣女性坐在编织棚篷之下。

这里不是渡船，不是救生篮，也不是一场渡河获救的叙事。简陋的棚篷、山岩与水禽，共同构成了一种贫寒、游方或处于社会边缘的生活环境。赞颂文指出，释迦友出身于樵夫阶层，后来证得悉地。但他的故事并不是现代意义上的“底层逆袭”。他不是通过取得更高身份来证明自己，而是直接否定了社会身份衡量精神价值的资格。如果说迦那巴是从王权的顶端主动走下，那么释迦友则是在社会的底层证得成就。两人的道路方向相反，却共同指向一个结论：社会阶层可以决定一个人的生活处境，却不能决定其精神可能性的边界。

当然，这并不意味着贫寒值得歌颂。贫穷会限制教育、健康、时间和选择，会让一个人付出本不必付出的代价。将贫寒浪漫化，往往只是站在安全位置上的人，对他人苦难进行的消费。所以，释迦友的意义不在于赞美贫穷，而在于拒绝把贫穷等同于精神上的低劣。

至此，七位人物的生命方向逐渐显现出来。

有人依靠哲学理解现实，有人进入尸陀林看到自己；有人舍弃王位，有人深入经论和仪轨；有人训练微细的身体感知，有人把恐惧、身体和亲密关系纳入修行；有人则从最贫寒的社会身份中证得成就。因此，这幅画真正提出的问题，并不是：哪一条道路才是唯一正确的？它所展示的是，悉地并不由某一种社会身份、生活方式或修行形式断定。觉醒可以穿过学问、仪轨、尸陀林、王权的放弃、身体训练、亲密关系、恐惧与贫寒生活。但这并不意味着所有道路都同样轻松，更不意味着任何生活状态都可以被浪漫地解释成修行。七位人物之所以被称为成就者，并不是因为他们选择了奇特的生活方式，而是因为他们能够在各自的处境中，完成对自我执著和惯性认知的根本转化。

画面并不赞美反常本身。它真正质疑的是：人是否常常把某一种外在生活形式——出家、苦行、学问、尊贵、贫寒或亲密关系——误认为觉醒的条件？

这幅作品的精神，不只存在于七位人物的生平中，也存在于人物周围那些看似次要的细节里。宗教绘画中的人物身份、主要姿势和修行线索，往往受到文本、仪轨和粉本的约束。真正留给画师更多自由的，反而是那些不直接承担核心教义的部分。

一只鸟如何侧头，一条蛇怎样穿过枝叶，松针如何排列，山石边缘如何晕染，织物纹样怎样随着身体转折——这些细节，往往更接近画师个人的生活感受和判断力。因为，人物是谁，可能由赞颂文决定。但这个世界是否真正活着，要由画师决定。他没有使用整齐的方格布局，将七段故事彼此隔绝，而是借助动物、树木、山石、水面、莲花、芦苇和棚篷，让不同场景既保持边界，又彼此连通。七位人物虽然生活在不同的时间、身份和处境中，却共同存在于一片连续的山水与世界里。

整个画面看似只有一个主角，又仿佛每个人都是主角。

这正是这幅画最值得注意的地方。它没有因为需要秩序，便消灭差异性；也没有因为承认差异，便放弃整体性。因此，所谓风格，从来不只是几种颜色、山石形态与人物造型的固定组合，它是画师反复面对世界之后，留下的内心结构。

现在，我们终于可以回到那位身份模糊的画师。

不能因为他的姓名没有完整保存，便浪漫地想象他不在乎名声。他或许同样需要委托、报酬、尊重和同行的认可。匿名并不一定等于思想高尚，被历史遗忘也绝不值得赞美。一个人的劳动没有被准确记录，贡献没有被归还给他的名字，本身可能就是历史权力分配的结果。是谁被写进史书，谁被保留姓名，谁只能以“某地画师”“某种风格”存在，从来不只是偶然。但这幅作品依然带给现代人一种重要的提醒：

一个人的影响，并不总能被及时、准确地归还给他的姓名；而价值也不会因为命名迟到，便从未发生。

我们不知道这位画师完成作品时，是否相信自己的名字会被后来的人记住。也许他只是面对已有的粉本、赞颂文和图像规范，认真地决定了一根树枝应该怎样弯曲，一只鸟停在哪里，一条蛇从哪一段枝叶间穿过，又该在一位成就者和另一位人物之间保留多少空间。这些选择看似没那么重要的细节，却都共同决定了画面最终会成为怎样的世界。

他的名字后来模糊了，这些决定却没有消失。

画中的七位成就者告诉我们，知识、王权、贫寒、身体、苦行与亲密关系，都无法独占人的精神可能。画外的这位画师，也用自己的命运补充了另一层意义：人的价值，不必等到世界准确地为他命名之后，才开始存在。这并不是说姓名不重要。恰恰相反，正因为姓名重要，我们才更应该追问那些被历史遮蔽的人；也正因为承认重要，我们才不能把“尚未获得承认”误解为“从未创造价值”。

关于在姓名和评价之外，一个人是否仍然能够通过自己完成的事情，和另一个时代的人发生真实联系？眼前这幅唐卡已经给出了答案。

虽然到了今天，我们依旧无法清楚地知道并说出这位画师是谁，但他却留下了一种无法被人忽视的画风。而一个人真正来过的证据，也许不只是他曾经获得过多少认可。更在于，当他的名字逐渐模糊之后，那些被他改写过的部分，是否仍在悄然延续；当我们站在这幅唐卡面前时，我们究竟是在理解他，还是在他的重新塑造之下，重新开始理解这个世界？或许答案并不重要，重要的是，在这样的相遇中，我们是否开始意识到：所谓存在，究竟是被看见之后才成立，还是在尚未被命名之时，就已经悄然发生？
viewingNote.en:
Are we living in an age that increasingly relies on "being seen" to confirm our worth?

In today’s world, our existence is becoming increasingly tied to being seen. People are often anxious not because they lack value, but because their value has gone unnoticed or unrecognized. Although these struggles may sound like matters of personal attitude, no individual exists in isolation from society. The way institutions distribute opportunities, social classes draw boundaries, cultures shape standards of judgment, and power determines who is allowed to speak—all of these enter into and affect a person’s life. People therefore need communication and response from others, as well as fair recognition from society.

There is nothing wrong with wanting to be recognized.

The real question is: have we started to believe that something has value only when society recognizes it?

The thangka before us pushes this question to the fore.

This thangka has a presence that is impossible to overlook. Each of its figures portrays a distinct posture with easily distinguishable faces, temperament, and inner intensity. Even the rocks and trees are not merely decorative; together, they create a space that is intricate yet open. The snakes, birds, lotuses, waterfowl, and plants do not simply fill the empty areas. They seem to inhabit the painting as living participants in its world.

Although the painter’s judgment, taste, and imagination is vividly exhibited, we cannot securely connect these qualities to a person whose name and life are known to us.

Works of this kind are often associated with the painter conventionally known as “Khazi Lhazo,” a name generally understood to mean “the artist of Khazi village” rather than a securely established personal name. Although the painter’s precise identity remains uncertain, the term is now also used as a stylistic designation for works attributed to his hand, his atelier, and later artists working in a closely related manner. This distinctive painting tradition is associated particularly with the Dagyab region of eastern Xizang and appears to have flourished around the late eighteenth and early nineteenth centuries. Unlike the Menri or Khyenri traditions, however, “Khazi Lhazo” is not the name of a major school with a clearly documented lineage and established historical narrative. It is better understood as a designation connected to a particular place, a distinctive style, and a painter whose identity has not yet been fully established. Without material analysis, an inscription on the back of the painting, or reliable records of provenance, we cannot confidently determine whether this work was painted by the master himself, produced by his workshop, or created by another artist working from the same iconographic tradition.

Yet this uncertainty is precisely what makes the painting so compelling.

How can a person whose identity remains so unclear make us feel his presence so vividly through a single work?

To understand the painting, we must begin with its unusual narrative structure. It does not present a single lineage descending from a root teacher to a sequence of disciples. Nor does it tell the complete life story of one person from beginning to end. Instead, it brings together seven figures belonging to the Vajrāsana Mahāsiddha tradition.

At the upper centre is Candrakīrti. Maitrīpa appears to the upper left and Karṇapa to the upper right. Ānandagarbha occupies the centre of the composition. Along the lower section, from left to right, are Avadhūtipāda, Charpa and Śākyamitra.

These are not seven stages within a single story. They represent seven distinct lives and seven different forms of experience.

What originally brought them together was a shared cycle of praises and prayers. What transforms those seven names into a unified painting, however, is the painter’s ability to give each figure a different body, environment, temperament, and destiny. This may initially seem like a matter of composition, but it changes the spiritual centre of the entire work. Had the painting represented a lineage, its main question would have been: Where did this teaching come from? By presenting the seven adepts in relatively independent settings, however, the painting asks a broader question:

Through how many different circumstances and paths can a human being transform himself?

The answer is not stated as a single doctrine. It is distributed across the bodies and lives of seven people.

At the top of the painting, Candrakīrti sits calmly among large trees.

Branches bend and cross above him. Several snakes move through the trunks and foliage. Birds perch nearby, call out, and lean towards the seated figure. Everything around him appears to be growing, moving, and changing. Candrakīrti’s body, by contrast, remains exceptionally composed. The Vajrāsana praise describes him as an adept who understood the profound intention of Nāgārjuna and possessed the wisdom of Mañjuśrī. It is difficult to determine whether the snakes in the painting are a visual allusion to Nāgārjuna, an auspicious sign associated with spiritual power, or part of some other iconographic meaning that has not yet been identified. What is clear is that the painter did not portray Candrakīrti as a philosopher removed from the world, with wisdom existing somewhere above ordinary life.

Here, thought is not separated from life.

Candrakīrti inhabits a world of dense foliage, coiling snakes, and overlapping birdsong. He remains undisturbed not because the world around him is simple, but because he can remain steady within its complexity. He therefore represents the first of the painting’s paths: understanding itself can become a form of practice. True learning is not simply the ability to recall texts and arguments. It is also the ability to remain clear-minded in the middle of a complicated reality. Wisdom is not standing outside life and explaining it from a distance. It is to see life from within life.

Maitrīpa, positioned below and to the left of Candrakīrti, appears in an entirely different state.

His body is bare apart from a red cloth. He raises his head towards a bird in flight. Beside him stands a dancing female companion wearing an antelope skin. In the clouds at the far upper left, White Acala appears surrounded by flames. The praise describes Maitrīpa as practising unclothed, frequently dwelling in charnel grounds, and having directly beheld Acala. The painter turns these brief textual references into a vivid scene through the naked body, the animal skin, the female companion, and the deity appearing in the sky.

Charnel grounds are usually associated with death, decay, fear, and the taboos that society tries hardest to keep out of sight. To practise in such a place is to stop depending on an orderly external environment for one’s inner stability. It means confronting what human beings are most reluctant to acknowledge: the body will decay, social identity will disappear, and the boundary between purity and impurity is far less secure than we like to believe. Maitrīpa’s path should therefore not be understood as arbitrary rule-breaking, still less as a romantic celebration of transgressive behaviour. It represents a more demanding form of training. When the familiar structures that give life a sense of order are removed, what remains through which a person can know himself? We do not, of course, need to imitate charnel-ground practice for the question to remain relevant. What happens when position, security, habit, and the approval of others temporarily lose their power? Would we still know who we are?

Karṇapa, below and to the right of Candrakīrti, is wrapped in cloth. His skin is greyish purple, and his contracted body is placed among dark rocks and trees.

At first glance, he might appear to be another charnel-ground ascetic. The praise, however, tells a very different story. Karṇapa was once a king. He later gave up his throne and royal status, deliberately adopting a way of life that conventional society regarded as degrading. Together with a female companion of low social standing, he eventually attained siddhi. His path is defined by inversion. He did not rise from poverty towards power. He moved willingly from the highest level of social authority to its margins. What he abandoned was not simply a throne. He also rejected a deeper assumption about human worth: if a person’s value must be proven through rank, reputation, and the respect of others, must every movement downwards be regarded as failure? In Karṇapa’s sacred biography, it is only when the king no longer depends on kingship to confirm who he is that he begins to confront his own existence directly.

What he overturns is not the principle of spiritual practice, but the hierarchy of values that ordinary society takes for granted. A respected position does not necessarily lead to liberation, just as a humble condition does not necessarily prevent awakening. This does not mean that the real effects of social class should be denied. Poverty, discrimination, and unequal power cannot be dismissed simply by saying that all beings are equal. The question raised by Karṇapa’s story is different: Should a person’s social circumstances be allowed to define everything that person can be?

The most visually striking figure in the painting is Ānandagarbha (Tib: Kun dga’ snying po) occupying the central space.

His appearance lies somewhere between a historical adept, a yogin, and a visionary tantric figure. Having folded his body, he balances it on one finger of each hand, each supported by a lotus. His feet meet in front of his chest, creating a form that resembles the teaching gesture. Suspended in the air, he appears almost untouched by gravity, yet his posture remains precise and controlled. This extraordinary position was not invented by the Khazi Lhazo painter. It belongs to an established iconographic tradition associated with Ānandagarbha and serves as a sign of his identity and miraculous attainment.

The painter’s originality, however, lies not in creating the posture, but in making an inherited image feel newly alive.

Although Ānandagarbha is the largest figure and occupies the visual centre of the painting, the other six figures are not reduced to supporting roles. Each retains an independent setting, temperament, and path. The distribution of space is remarkably mature. The painting’s centre does not become the only source of meaning. It has a clear structure, but that structure does not erase the differences among the figures. Likewise, Ānandagarbha, being placed at the centre of the composition does not mean that he is the root teacher of the other six adepts. The painting carefully distinguishes visual centrality from spiritual lineage.

Ānandagarbha also represents a different form of practice.

He was closely associated with the interpretation of Yoga Tantra and was known as a scholar and ritual authority of considerable learning. Unlike Maitrīpa’s charnel-ground practice or Karṇapa’s rejection of royal power, Ānandagarbha’s attainment is expressed through the integration of doctrinal understanding, ritual knowledge, and tantric practice. His presence challenges a common misunderstanding: the idea that a mahāsiddha must always be an anti-institutional, anti-intellectual, unruly wandering yogin who reaches liberation through unconventional behaviour. Ānandagarbha shows that entering deeply into a tradition does not necessarily mean becoming trapped by it. The study of scripture, the interpretation of ritual, and the mastery of complex systems of practice can also become paths of transformation. The important question is not whether a person enters an institution or follows a discipline. It is whether that system leads to genuine understanding or merely produces obedience.

In the lower part of the painting, three figures are placed closer to the ground, the water, and the world of everyday life.

On the lower left, Avadhūtipa appears together with a female consort holding a kapāla (skull cup). Avadhūtipa is seated upon an animal skin, with his left hand raised upward. Above him, clouds drift across the sky, from which Tārā emerges, standing in mid-air and engaging him in a direct gaze. The Vajrāsana praise text mentions that Tārā bestowed blessings upon Avadhūtipa and helped him overcome the eight great fears. Thus, his raised arm and upward gaze toward the deity may suggest a relationship of blessing, transmission, or reverence. Notably, this scene does not present spiritual practice as a rejection of the body or human relationships. Rather, it reveals another important mode of transformation within tantric practice: the body, sensory experience, and interpersonal relationships themselves can all be incorporated into the path of cultivation and become means toward liberation.

In the lower centre, Cārāpā appears together with a female consort. In this thangka, the female figure in front of Cārāpā is not explicitly identified by name in the Vajrāsana prayer text. Without supporting inscriptions, it would therefore be inappropriate to simply label her as a “ḍākinī.” She may represent a spiritual consort, a ritual consort (vidyādevī), or another participant described in tantric literature. Nevertheless, the overall meaning of the scene is clear. Tantric practice does not simply reject the body, relationships, or fear; rather, it seeks to reintegrate these very experiences—those most capable of overwhelming human autonomy—into the process of spiritual transformation. This represents a far more difficult path: not an escape from the body and relationships, but the ability to engage with them without being blindly controlled by them.

Modern life often moves between two extremes. One treats desire, intimacy, and emotion as burdens that must be suppressed. The other interprets phrases such as “follow your heart” as permission to obey every impulse. But freedom from repression is not the same as freedom from discernment. Accepting the body does not require surrendering to every habit of the body. Real autonomy is not the complete absence of desire or fear. It is the ability to observe and choose even while desire and fear are present.

At the lower right, Śākyamitra sits with a woman dressed in blue beneath a woven shelter. The scene does not show a ferry, a rescue basket, or a story of being saved while crossing a river. The rough shelter, surrounding rocks, and nearby waterfowl instead suggest poverty, itinerant life, or existence at the margins of society. The praise states that Śākyamitra was born into the social class of woodcutters and later attained siddhi. His story, however, is not a modern tale of rising from poverty to achieve a higher status. He does not prove his worth by entering a more respected social class. Instead, his attainment rejects the assumption that social rank has the authority to measure spiritual value. Karṇapa willingly descended from the height of royal power. Śākyamitra attained realization while beginning from the lowest levels of society. Their paths move in opposite directions, but they point towards the same conclusion: Social class may determine many of the conditions under which a person lives, but it cannot determine the limits of that person’s spiritual potential.

This does not mean that poverty is something to be praised. Poverty restricts access to education, health, time, security, and meaningful choice. It forces people to bear costs that they should never have had to bear. The romanticization of poverty often amounts to people in secure positions turning the suffering of others into an idea they can admire from a distance. Śākyamitra’s importance therefore lies not in presenting poverty as spiritually desirable, but in refusing to treat poverty as evidence of spiritual inferiority.

By this point, the different directions represented by the seven figures have become clear.

One approaches reality through philosophical understanding. Another enters the charnel ground to confront himself. One gives up royal power, while another enters deeply into scripture and ritual. One works with the subtle experiences of the body. Another brings fear, intimacy, and physical existence into the path. The last attains realization from a position of extreme social poverty. The painting’s central question is therefore not: Which of these is the only correct path? Instead, it shows that siddhi cannot be determined by a single social identity, way of life, or method of practice. Awakening may be approached through scholarship, ritual, the charnel ground, the rejection of political power, bodily discipline, intimate relationships, fear, or a life shaped by poverty. This does not mean that all paths are equally easy. Nor does it mean that every form of life can be romantically reinterpreted as spiritual practice. These seven figures are regarded as accomplished adepts not because they chose unusual ways of living, but because each of them achieved a fundamental transformation of attachment and habitual perception within the particular circumstances of his life.

The painting does not celebrate unconventional behaviour simply because it is unconventional. What it questions is the human tendency to mistake a particular outward form of life—monasticism, asceticism, scholarship, nobility, poverty, or intimate partnership—for the necessary condition of awakening.

The spirit of the painting exists not only in the lives of the seven figures, but also in the details that surround them. In religious painting, the identities of the figures, their principal gestures, and the signs of their practices are often determined by texts, rituals, and established visual models. The painter usually has greater freedom in those elements that do not carry the central doctrinal content. How a bird turns its head, how a snake passes through a cluster of leaves, how pine needles are arranged, how the edge of a rock is shaded, and how the pattern of a textile follows the movement of a body—these details may bring us closer to the painter’s own experience and judgment. The praise text may determine who the figures are. But the painter determines whether the world around them feels alive. He does not divide the seven scenes into a rigid grid. Through animals, trees, rocks, water, lotuses, reeds, and shelters, he allows each scene to preserve its own boundaries while remaining connected to the others. The seven figures belong to different times, identities, and circumstances. Yet the painter places them within one continuous landscape and one shared world.

The painting seems to have a single protagonist, yet it also gives the impression that every figure is a protagonist.

This is one of its greatest achievements. It does not eliminate difference for the sake of order, nor does it abandon unity in order to preserve individuality. Style, in this sense, is not simply a fixed combination of colours, rock formations, and figure types. It is the inner structure that a painter leaves behind after repeatedly observing and responding to the world. We may now return to the painter whose identity remains uncertain.

We should not romanticize the loss of his name by imagining that he had no interest in recognition.
