He may have needed commissions, payment, professional respect, and the approval of other painters just as anyone else did. Anonymity is not necessarily evidence of noble indifference, and being forgotten by history is not something to celebrate. When a person’s labour is not properly recorded and his contribution is not attached to his name, this may itself reveal how historical power was distributed. Who enters the written record, whose name is preserved, and who survives only as “a painter from a certain village” or “the originator of a particular style” has never been entirely a matter of chance. Yet the painting still offers an important reminder to the modern viewer:

A person’s influence is not always returned to his name promptly or accurately. Value does not fail to exist simply because recognition arrives late. We do not know whether the painter believed that later generations would remember him. Perhaps he simply worked with the available visual models, praise texts, and iconographic rules, carefully deciding how a branch should bend, where a bird should perch, through which leaves a snake should pass, and how much space should remain between one adept and another. These choices may seem minor. Together, however, they determined the kind of world the painting would become.

The painter’s name gradually became unclear, but his decisions did not disappear.

The seven adepts inside the painting show us that scholarship, political power, poverty, the body, asceticism, and intimate relationships cannot claim exclusive authority over human spiritual possibility. Through his own historical fate, the painter adds another layer to their message: a person’s value does not have to wait for the world to name him correctly before it can begin to exist. This is not an argument that names are unimportant. On the contrary, it is precisely because names matter that we should continue to search for those whose identities have been obscured by history. Recognition also matters. But because it matters, we must not confuse “not yet recognized” with “having created nothing of value.”

Can a person, beyond name and reputation, still form a real connection with people in another age through the work he has made? This Thangka answers that question.

We still cannot say with certainty who the painter was. Yet he left behind a pictorial voice that is impossible to ignore. The proof that a person truly lived may lie not only in the recognition he received during his lifetime, but also in whether the things he changed continue quietly after his name has faded. When we stand before this thangka, are we trying to understand the painter? Or, through the world he created, are we beginning to understand our own world differently? Perhaps the distinction is less important than the encounter itself. What matters is that the painting asks us to consider whether existence begins only when it is seen and recognized—or whether it has already quietly taken place before anyone has found the right name for it.

title.zh: 帕木竹巴·多吉杰布肖像

subtitle.zh: 真正好的老师，究竟是让学生越来越像自己，还是让学生最后能够成为他自己？
subtitle.en: Finding oneself in the Guidance of another

material.en: Copper alloy with copper and silver inlay

excerpt.zh: 帕木竹巴·多吉杰布肖像
excerpt.en: Portrait of Phagmodrupa

viewingNote.zh:
看一尊人物肖像，我们几乎本能地会问一句：像不像？

这个问题听起来再自然不过。摄影出现以后，我们已经习惯把肖像理解成一个人的视觉存档：眼睛多大，鼻子什么形状，胖还是瘦，脸上的皱纹在哪里。于是，一尊古代人物肖像如果五官鲜活、身体比例真实，我们就很容易进一步判断：这个人在生前，大概就是长这个样子。

借由眼前的这尊帕木竹巴· 多吉杰布肖像，也许会为我们更近一步地理清这个问题。

这是一尊合金铜造像，局部嵌红铜、银。帕木竹巴· 多吉杰布结跏趺坐，身体宽厚，稳稳地占据着莲座上方的空间。最吸引人的还是那张脸：双颊饱满，下颌厚实，眼睛微微收起，嘴角明显上扬。银与红铜的嵌饰把眼、唇等部位从整体铜色中提了出来，人的表情一下就活了。

这不是一张抽象的祖师脸庞。你甚至会觉得，他有点胖，有点威严，又有一点笑意。正因为如此，我们很容易说：这尊造像很“写实”。可写实，并不等于写真。这是看上师肖像时，一个很值得分清的问题。

写实，首先是一种塑造方式。它意味着工匠愿意观察一个真实的人体：脸颊有脂肪，嘴唇有厚度，身体有重量，衣服不是简单覆盖在一个抽象躯壳之上，而是随着胸腹、肩膀和双腿发生变化。人物因此不再只是“某类智者”的符号，而开始有了具体的人的感觉。

而写真却是另一回事。

它呈现的是：这张脸，究竟在多大程度上保存了帕木竹巴· 多吉杰布本人真实的相貌？也就是一个人的气质。对于一件距离人物生活年代已经相隔了一段时间的作品，这个问题其实很难轻易回答。工匠依据的可能是更早的肖像范本，可能是某种已经固定下来的祖师形象，也可能是经过一代代传承之后逐渐稳定的视觉记忆。除非存在足够可靠的同时代证据，否则不能仅仅因为一尊雕塑“很像一个真人”，就断定“本人一定长这样”。

可也正是在这里，上师肖像真正有意思的地方出现了。

因为一尊人物肖像想要留下的，也许从来不只是一个人的脸。它还想留下的是：这个人的气韵，以及他究竟是一个怎样的人。

帕木竹巴· 多吉杰布· 多吉杰布生活在十二世纪，1110 年出生于康区南部。他幼年失去双亲，很早便进入僧团。此后的求学生涯极其广泛，从戒律、阿毗达磨、中观、因明，到密续和各种禅修教授，他都曾系统学习。他似乎很少先问“这是谁家的教法”，而更在意“这里有没有值得学习的东西”。

他曾跟随萨钦· 贡噶宁波研习道果，也接触与噶当、萨迦、希解以及早期噶举有关的不同师承。在后来成为冈波巴弟子之前，他早已不是一个初出茅庐的年轻僧人。相反，他已经拥有相当深厚的学养和修行经验。

所以，他四十多岁以后与冈波巴相遇的故事才格外有意思。

传统传记记载，冈波巴曾让帕木竹巴· 多吉杰布讲述自己的修行体验。帕木竹巴· 多吉杰布认为，自己所体验到的乐、空与无分别觉知，已经抵达很高的证悟层次。而冈波巴却不断否定他的判断。最后，冈波巴甚至捏着一团极普通的糌粑，对帕木竹巴· 多吉杰布说，相比他所谓漂亮的“见道”，自己更喜欢眼前这团糌粑。

这当然是一则圣传故事。但传记为什么偏偏要记录这样一个故事？因为它没有把帕木竹巴· 多吉杰布塑造成一个从年轻时代开始就永远正确、永远完美的人。恰恰相反，它选择保存了他的某一次失败，或者更准确地说，是一次关于自己的确信被推翻的时刻。而且那时的帕木竹巴· 多吉杰布已经不年轻了。

一个人什么都没有的时候，重新开始并不困难。真正困难的是，当你已经有了知识、经验、声誉、学生，甚至已经形成了关于“我是谁”的稳定判断之后，还有没有能力承认：

也许我最珍视的理解，仍然值得重新检查，甚至推翻。

这可能是帕木竹巴· 多吉杰布身上最迷人的品质之一。

许多大师因为坚定而被记住，他却还因为能够允许自己的坚定被打破而被记住。面对冈波巴的质疑，他没有用自己的资历、师承和过去的成就进行辩护，而是重新回到修行本身。传统叙事认为，也正是在这种原有的确信被松动之后，他才真正深入大手印的理解，成为冈波巴最重要的弟子之一。他不是“我从来没有错，所以你应该相信我”。而更像是：

我知道一个人可能会误把自己的体验当成真理，因为我自己也曾经如此。

这样的权威，反而多了一层可信。

冈波巴圆寂之后，帕木竹巴· 多吉杰布没有立刻去建立一个庞大的宗派系统。他一度重新寻找独居生活。1158 年前后，他来到帕木竹，在俯瞰雅鲁藏布江的山谷中居住下来。按照传统记载，最初不过是一间简陋的草屋和极其简单的修行生活。

问题是，他想安静，学生却不断找来。于是一个很有意思的矛盾贯穿了他的后半生——他需要独处，却又不断被别人需要。

传记中说，他把时间分给闭关及讲法；也保存了一类类似的叙述：如果继续严格独修，他或许能够延长修行生命、取得更多个人成就，但频繁接见弟子、讲法和赐予加持，则会消耗他的生命。

无论我们是否把这些预言式的内容当成字面事实，其中那种张力是真实的：

一个渴望退回山林的人，最后选择留在人群之中。

而且他教出来的学生，也没有变成一排整整齐齐的“帕木竹巴· 多吉杰布复制品”。吉天颂恭、达隆塘巴、林热巴等弟子，后来分别发展出各具特点的修行群体与传承。后世把这一谱系中的多个传统纳入了噶举“四大八小”的分类体系。其中“八小”的“小”，主要关系到师承代际，并不是说这些传统历史地位较低。止贡、达隆、竹巴等传统后来都产生了非常深远的影响。所以帕木竹巴· 多吉杰布留下来的，不是一个高度统一的模板。他允许不同的人长成不同的样子。

这其实也是一种很少被讨论的老师的能力：真正好的老师，究竟是让学生越来越像自己，还是让学生最后能够成为他自己？

更有意思的是，他当初那间不起眼的草屋，后来逐渐发展成了大名鼎鼎的丹萨梯寺。丹萨梯这个名字也成为了西藏艺术史上最华丽的名字之一。13-15 世纪之间的丹萨梯寺，陆续营造出了规模惊人的纪念塔与扎西果芒体系。层层展开的建筑结构中布满鎏金造像，珍宝，复杂的神祇系统共同构成巨大的立体曼荼罗。今天即使只从那些幸存和散佚到世界各地的雕塑中，我们仍然能够想象它曾经有多么辉煌。

这形成了一种近乎戏剧性的反差。一个只想住进草屋的人，身后却出现了西藏最华丽的雕塑传统之一。一个不断想把自己退到安静处的人，最终却在历史中留下越来越大的回声。再回过头来看眼前这尊帕木竹巴· 多吉杰布，很多细节就变得不一样了。

他的右手向下伸展，左手安置于腹前，整套身体姿态很容易令人联想到佛陀造像中触地与禅定的视觉组合。肖像借用了我们熟悉的佛陀图像语言，使一个真实生活过的历史人物进入了具有觉悟意味的视觉秩序。

这正是上师肖像最微妙的地方。

一方面，肖像在努力告诉你：这是一个人。所以工匠留下他的体重、脸颊、嘴唇、笑意，甚至一种非常具体的身体存在感。另一方面，肖像又在告诉你：他已经不只是一个普通的人。所以莲座、手印、僧衣、端坐的姿态，将这具极其具体的身体慢慢带入祖师、觉悟者与传承的世界。这两者并不冲突。反而正是这种“非常像一个人，却又已经超过普通个人”的状态，构成了上师肖像最动人的部分。

帕木竹巴· 多吉杰布厚重的躯体给人一种不动摇的感觉，微微收起的眼睛和展开的嘴角，又没有把这种稳定变成严厉。他虽然散发着强大的气场，但却不像某种高高在上的权威。尽管我们不知道，十二世纪真实的帕木竹巴· 多吉杰布，是不是就这样微笑。也无法仅凭这尊雕塑就确认，他本人究竟是不是这样的脸形、这样的身材。

可是到了这里，好像又觉得，这已经不是唯一重要的问题了。

因为肖像的“像”，本来就不只有一种。它可以像一个人的五官，像一个人的身体，也可以像一个人的性格。甚至像后世的人，在漫长记忆中逐渐理解出来的那个他。

帕木竹巴· 多吉杰布博学，却没有让知识成为封闭自己的理由；拥有权威，却曾经允许自己的理解被推翻；渴望独居，却最终留在需要他的学生中间；后来他又成为了多个重要传承的源头，却没有要求所有人长成同一种样子。

所以这尊肖像真正保存下来的，也许并不只是“帕木竹巴· 多吉杰布长什么样”。

它保存的是另一种更难被保存的东西：数百年之后，人们仍然希望帕木竹巴· 多吉杰布以怎样的样子，被我们看见。
viewingNote.en:
When we look at a portrait, we almost instinctively wonder if the actual person looked like it.

Nothing could sound more natural. Since the advent of photography, we have grown accustomed to understanding portraiture as a visual record of an individual: the size of the eyes, the shape of the nose, whether the person was heavy or thin, where the wrinkles fell on the face. As a result, when an ancient portrait sculpture presents vivid features and plausible bodily proportions, we readily conclude that the person in question must have looked much as depicted.

This portrait of Phagmodrupa may help clarify the question further.

This is a copper-alloy sculpture with localized inlays of copper and silver. Phagmodrupa sits in the crosslegged posture, his broad, substantial body occupying the space above the lotus base with evident stability. What draws our eye the most, however, is the face: full cheeks, a heavy jaw, eyes slightly narrowed, and the corners of the mouth distinctly raised. The silver and copper inlay set the eyes and lips apart from the surrounding bronze tone, animating the expression at once.

This is not an abstract patriarch’s countenance. One might even say the face appears somewhat stout, somewhat commanding, and touched with a hint of a smile. Hence we are tempted to call the sculpture “realistic.” Yet realism is not the same as likeness — a distinction well worth drawing when examining a teacher’s portrait.

Realism, first of all, is a mode of representation. It indicates that the craftsman was willing to observe an actual human body: flesh on the cheeks, thickness in the lips, weight in the body — the robe not simply draped over an abstract form, but shifting with the chest, abdomen, shoulders, and legs beneath it. The figure thereby ceases to function merely as a symbol of “a certain type of sage” and begins to convey the sense of a specific individual.

Likeness, however, is another matter.

It concerns the question of to what extent this face actually preserves Phagmodrupa’s true appearance — his individual bearing. For a work produced some time after its subject’s lifetime, this question is not easily answered. The craftsman may have relied on an earlier portrait model, on an already established image of the patriarch, or on a visual memory that had gradually stabilized across generations of transmission. Unless there is sufficiently reliable contemporary evidence, we cannot conclude that a person actually looked that way simply because a sculpture “looks very much like a real person.”

Yet it is here that the true interest of the teacher’s portrait emerges.

For what a portrait sculpture seeks to preserve may never have been simply a face. It also seeks to preserve a person’s bearing and character — the kind of person he truly was.

Phagmodrupa Dorje Gyalpo lived in the twelfth century, born in 1110 in the southern Kham region. Orphaned in early childhood, he entered monastic life while still young. His subsequent education was remarkably broad, encompassing systematic study of monastic discipline (Vinaya), Abhidharma, Madhyamaka philosophy, logic (Hetuvidyā), tantric teachings, and various instructions on meditation. He seems rarely to have asked first “whose lineage does this teaching belong to,” concerning himself instead with whether there was something here worth learning.

He studied the Lamdré teachings under Sachen Kunga Nyingpo, and encountered a range of different lineages connected to the Kadam, Sakya, Shijé, and early Kagyu traditions. By the time he became a disciple of Gampopa, he was already far from an inexperienced young monk — he had, by then, accumulated considerable learning and meditative experience.

This is what makes the story of his encounter with Gampopa, after the age of forty, so compelling.

According to traditional biographical accounts, Gampopa once asked Phagmodrupa to describe his own meditative experience. Phagmodrupa believed that the bliss, emptiness, and non-conceptual awareness he had experienced represented a very advanced level of realization. Gampopa, however, repeatedly rejected this assessment. In the end, Gampopa reportedly held up a lump of ordinary tsampa dough and told Phagmodrupa that he preferred this humble ball of barley flour to what Phagmodrupa considered his fine “vision of the path.”

This is, of course, a work of hagiography. But why would such a biography choose to record a story of this kind? Because it does not portray Phagmodrupa as someone who was invariably correct and flawless from his earliest years. Quite the opposite — it deliberately preserves a moment of failure, or, more precisely, a moment in which his own conviction was overturned. And by that point, Phagmodrupa was no longer young.

When a person has nothing to begin with, starting over presents little difficulty. The real difficulty arises once one has already acquired knowledge, experience, reputation, and students — once one has already formed a stable sense of who one is — and must still find the capacity to admit :“Perhaps even my most cherished understanding still deserves to be reexamined, or even overturned.”

This may be one of the most compelling qualities in Phagmodrupa’s character.

Many great masters are remembered for their unwavering conviction. Phagmodrupa is remembered, in addition, for his willingness to let that conviction be broken. Faced with Gampopa’s challenge, he did not defend himself by invoking his seniority, his lineage, or his past accomplishments, but returned instead to the practice itself. Traditional narrative holds that it was only once this prior certainty had been loosened that he came to a genuine understanding of Mahāmudrā, becoming one of Gampopa’s most important disciples. His stance was not “I have never been wrong, so you should trust me,” but something closer to:

“I know that a person can mistake his own experience for truth, because I myself once did.”

An authority grounded in such self-awareness carries, if anything, an added measure of credibility.

After Gampopa’s passing, Phagmodrupa did not immediately set about establishing a large institutional lineage. For a time, he sought a return to solitary life. Around 1158, he arrived at Phagmodru and settled in a valley overlooking the Yarlung Tsangpo River. According to traditional accounts, his dwelling at first amounted to little more than a simple thatched hut and an extremely austere practice.

The difficulty was that, while he sought quiet, students kept seeking him out. An intriguing tension thus ran through the second half of his life: he needed solitude, yet was continually needed by others.

His biography states that he divided his time between solitary retreat and teaching. It also preserves accounts suggesting that, had he continued strict solitary practice, he might have extended his practice-life and achieved still greater personal attainment — but that frequently receiving disciples, teaching, and bestowing blessings would consume his vitality.

Whether or not such prophetic accounts are taken as literal fact, the tension they describe is real:

A man who longed to withdraw into the mountains chose, in the end, to remain among people.

Nor did the students he trained become a uniform row of “Phagmodrupa replicas.” His disciples Jigten Sumgön, Taklung Thangpa, and Lingrepa each went on to develop distinctive practice communities and lineages of their own. Later tradition classified several branches of this lineage within the Kagyu system known as the “Four Major and Eight Minor” schools. The term “minor” in “Eight Minor” schools refers primarily to generational position within the lineage, not to lesser historical importance — the Drikung, Taklung, Drukpa, and other traditions that emerged from it went on to exert profound and lasting influence.

What Phagmodrupa left behind, then, was not a rigidly uniform template. He allowed different individuals to grow into different forms.

This is, in fact, a rarely discussed capacity of a good teacher:

Does a truly good teacher make students increasingly like himself, or enable them, in the end, to become themselves?

More remarkable still, the unassuming thatched hut where he first settled gradually developed into the renowned Densatil Monastery. The name Densatil would go on to become one of the most celebrated names in the history of Xizang art. Between the thirteenth and fifteenth centuries, Densatil produced a series of extraordinary memorial stupas built according to the Tashi Gomang system. Their tiered architectural structures were densely populated with gilt-bronze images and precious materials, their elaborate pantheons together forming vast three-dimensional maṇḍalas. Even today, working only from the sculptures that survive or have been dispersed to collections around the world, one can still imagine how magnificent the complex once was.

This produces an almost dramatic contrast. A man who wished only to live in a simple hut left behind one of the most magnificent sculptural traditions in Xizang. A man who repeatedly sought to withdraw into quiet retreat left, instead, an ever-growing echo in history. Returning once more to the portrait before us, a number of its details take on new significance.

His right hand extends downward, while the left rests before the abdomen — a bodily configuration readily associated with the combined earth-touching and meditation gestures found in images of the Buddha. The portrait borrows this familiar Buddhist visual language, drawing a historically documented individual into a visual order charged with the significance of enlightenment.

This is precisely the most subtle aspect of the teacher’s portrait.

On one hand, the portrait insists: this is a specific person. The craftsman therefore preserves his weight, his cheeks, his lips, the hint of a smile — a highly specific sense of bodily presence. On the other hand, the portrait also insists: he is no longer merely an ordinary person. The lotus base, the hand gestures, the monastic robe, and the composed seated posture gradually draw this highly specific body into the world of the patriarch, the enlightened being, and the lineage. These two impulses are not in conflict. It is precisely this condition — being remarkably like an individual person while having already exceeded the ordinary individual — that constitutes the most moving quality of the teacher’s portrait.

Phagmodrupa’s substantial physique conveys an impression of unshakeable stability, yet the slightly narrowed eyes and the raised corners of the mouth prevent that stability from hardening into severity. He radiates a powerful presence, yet not one resembling remote, elevated authority. We cannot know whether the historical Phagmodrupa of the twelfth century actually smiled in this way, nor can this sculpture alone confirm that he truly possessed this face or this build.

And yet, at this point, it becomes apparent that this is no longer the only question that matters.

For “resemblance” in portraiture was never a single, fixed thing. It can resemble a person’s features, a person’s body, or a person’s character. It can even resemble the figure that later generations, across a long history of memory, gradually came to understand him to be.

Phagmodrupa was learned, yet never allowed his learning to become a reason for closing himself off. He held authority, yet once allowed his own understanding to be overturned. He longed for solitude, yet remained, in the end, among the students who needed him. He later became the source of several major lineages, yet never required that everyone grow into the same shape.

What this portrait truly preserves, then, may not be simply “what Phagmodrupa looked like.”

It preserves something far more difficult, namely the way in which people, centuries later, wished for Phagmodrupa to be seen.

subtitle.zh: 专题展览

description.zh:
我们时常会在展厅中这些静默的雕塑、绘画前驻足。这些或流畅或粗犷的线条，

是一种古老又很真诚的语言，总能直击人心。它们将情绪、思想、记忆、信仰化

作形体。注视着它们的同时，它们也在回望我们。这种观看是一种双向凝视、是

一种打破时空的心灵联结。当图像所想表征的语言折射到内心时，我想那种感受

比任何文字都真实，也更深刻。在某种意义上，它们也是我们在混沌现实中寻找

到的少有的一种清晰。

在我们看来，这些艺术品是一种关乎美、关乎心灵、关乎情绪的存在，这个文化

也更像是一门心理学。每个人在观看的过程中，经由对镜转换而受到的滋养都有

所不同。今年我们展览的主题围绕一尊“说法弥勒”而展开对于时间的思索。弥

勒在文化中象征着未来——时间存在吗？
description.en:
We often find ourselves pausing before the silent sculptures and paintings within the exhibition halls. These lines—whether fluid or rugged—constitute an ancient yet profoundly sincere language that invariably strikes a chord deep within the human heart. They transform emotions, thoughts, memories, and beliefs into tangible forms. As we gaze upon them, they, in turn, gaze back at us. This act of viewing constitutes a mutual gaze—a spiritual connection that transcends the boundaries of time and space. When the language that these images seek to articulate is refracted into our inner selves, I believe the sensation is more authentic—and certainly more profound—than any written word. In a sense, they represent one of the rare moments of clarity we manage to discover amidst the chaos of reality.

To our minds, these artworks exist as entities concerned with beauty, the spirit, and emotion; indeed, this entire cultural sphere resembles a form of psychology. As each individual engages in the act of viewing, the spiritual nourishment they derive—filtered through the lens of their own inner reflection—varies from person to person. The theme of this year’s exhibition revolves around a sculpture of the "Preaching Maitreya," serving as a focal point for our contemplation on the nature of time. Within this cultural context, Maitreya symbolizes the future—prompting us to ask: Does time truly exist?

description.zh:
作为碳基生命的我们，由于物种的不同，在星球上感受到的时间长度也有所不同。

在日常生活中，我们看着日升日落、钟表滴答作响、自己从孩童即将步入到中年，

这一切的体验都让我们感受着时间真实的流动性。牛顿曾说：“时间是绝对的，

时间像一条独立的直线，与空间无关，无论你是否在动，它都匀速流逝。”爱因

斯坦曾说：“时间是相对的，时间并非恒定，它和空间是交织的，组成‘时空’。”

当量子引力的理论出现时，物理学家提出：“时间可能并不存在，它只是我们用

来描述变化的一种幻觉或一种方便表达的语言工具而已。”而佛教则并不认为时

间是实有的，它是无常与缘起的一部分。过去、现在、未来都在不断生灭之中，

当下这一念才是我们真正拥有的。
description.en:
As carbon-based life forms, we perceive the passage of time on this planet differently, a variation stemming from the distinct nature of our respective species.

In our daily lives—watching the sun rise and set, listening to the rhythmic ticking of clocks, and observing our own transition from childhood toward middle age—we experience the tangible, fluid nature of time. Isaac Newton once asserted: "Time is absolute; it resembles an independent straight line, distinct from space, flowing at a constant rate regardless of whether one is in motion." Albert Einstein, conversely, stated: "Time is relative; it is not immutable but rather interwoven with space, together constituting the fabric of 'spacetime'."

With the advent of quantum gravity theory, physicists have posited: "Time may not actually exist at all; it could merely be an illusion—or perhaps a convenient linguistic tool—that we employ to describe the phenomenon of change." Buddhism, for its part, does not regard time as an inherently real entity; rather, it views it as an integral component of impermanence and dependent origination. The past, present, and future are all in a perpetual state of arising and ceasing; it is only this very moment—this single instant of consciousness—that we truly possess.

description.zh:
其实，不论时间存在与否，“未来”也确实由当下的每一刻构成。而此刻正在逛

展的你，也许才是真实可触摸的，对于这一开放性问题的思考，也正是当下、也

正是每个目光碰撞间，象征着未来的弥勒送给我们的礼物吧...
description.en: In truth—regardless of whether time exists or not—the "future" is indeed composed of every single moment of the present. And you—browsing this exhibition right now—are perhaps the only thing that is truly real and tangible. Your contemplation of this open-ended question—occurring right here, in this very moment, amidst the interplay of every passing gaze—is perhaps the gift that Maitreya, the symbol of the future, has bestowed upon us...

description.zh:
2024 年 8 月 15 日，又一个星期四，成都又一个雨天，又一次在雨声中找到了灵感，

又一次为展览图录撰写序言。

从业近十年，每一年都怀着谦卑的心态去学习与体悟；今年是做公众展的第三年，图录也

是第三本了，尽管每年编辑展览作品成册的过程并不容易，但一想到能让更多的人走近，并

感受到西藏艺术及喜马拉雅艺术品所蕴藏的巨大能量，我们却依旧乐此不疲。

于我们而言，西藏艺术及喜马拉雅艺术品不仅是物质的展示，更是精神的体验。它们像

古老的藏经，富含哲思与智慧。每件作品背后都承载着丰富的文化传承和生活哲学，教会我

敬畏自然、尊重生灵，并在喧嚣中寻找平静。

喜马拉雅艺术对许多人来说可能陌生而神秘，如同十年前的我；但这也正是这次展览的

意义所在——打破界限！让更多人了解这一伟大的艺术传统。我们希望通过展览激发大家对

西藏艺术及喜马拉雅艺术的兴趣，并在文化中体悟那些古老的智慧、在匠人精神中感受时间

的从容、在艺术的世界中重塑思辨能力、在精神的世界中寻找到灵魂的慰藉...

此次展览我们甄选了 38 件展品，其中包括了佛像、法器、唐卡、杂项，包含了金铜、木

雕、石雕、陶质、夹竺等不同材质与工艺，在选择展品上面，我们从艺术性和节点性出发，

尽可能选择在同等年份和风格中，具有代表性和稀缺性的展品。展品的年份从公元 2-3 世纪

到 18 世纪,跨越 1700 余年，产地风格分别含盖了印度、尼泊尔、中国西藏、北京、蒙古。

这些艺术品不仅代表了独特的宗教信仰和艺术传统，还讲述了千百年来在那片土地上生生不

息的人文故事。通过这些展品，我们可以感受到来自雪山之巅的精神力量，以及人们在高原

上与自然、神灵和自我之间的和谐对话。

窗外的雨下得酣畅淋漓，就像我酒杯中的威士忌，猛烈而尽兴！雨在浇灭酷署同时也点

燃了生命；酒在刺激着味蕾的瞬间也激发着灵感… 西藏艺术及喜马拉雅艺术品的浩海，召

唤着我们在生命之舟上挂起美的风帆！海阔、天空，我们是如此脆弱却又如此刚毅；山高、

路长，我们是如此细微却又这般宏伟…
description.en:
August 15, 2024—another Thursday, another rainy day in Chengdu, and once again, amidst the sound of falling rain, inspiration has struck; once again, I find myself writing a preface for an exhibition catalog.

Having worked in this field for nearly a decade, I have approached every year with a spirit of humility—eager to learn and to gain deeper insights. This year marks our third year of organizing public exhibitions, and consequently, our third catalog. Although the annual process of curating and compiling these exhibition works into a volume is never an easy task, the thought of enabling more people to draw closer—to experience the immense energy imbued within Tibetan and Himalayan art—keeps us tirelessly devoted to this endeavor.

For us, Tibetan and Himalayan art objects represent far more than mere material displays; they are, above all, spiritual experiences. Much like ancient Buddhist scriptures, they are rich in philosophical depth and profound wisdom. Behind every piece lies a legacy of rich cultural heritage and a distinct philosophy of life—lessons that teach me to revere nature, respect all living beings, and discover a sense of tranquility amidst the clamor of the modern world.

To many, Himalayan art may seem unfamiliar and enigmatic—much as it did to me a decade ago. Yet, this is precisely the significance of this exhibition: to break down barriers and enable a wider audience to discover this magnificent artistic tradition. Through this exhibition, we hope to ignite a passion for Tibetan and Himalayan art, encouraging visitors to discern ancient wisdom within cultural contexts, to perceive the unhurried rhythm of time through the spirit of craftsmanship, to sharpen their critical faculties within the realm of art, and to find solace for the soul within the spiritual dimension.

For this exhibition, we have carefully selected 38 artifacts, encompassing a diverse range of categories—including Buddhist statuary, ritual implements, *thangkas*, and various *objets d'art*. These pieces feature a variety of materials and techniques, such as gilt bronze, wood carving, stone carving, ceramics, and *jiazhu* (lacquer-over-cloth). In making our selections, we prioritized both artistic merit and historical significance, striving to identify pieces that are truly representative and rare within their specific eras and stylistic traditions. The artifacts span a vast chronological range—from the 2nd or 3rd century CE to the 18th century—covering a period of over 1,700 years, and represent stylistic origins from across the region, including India, Nepal, Xizang (China), Beijing, and Mongolia. These artworks not only embody unique religious beliefs and artistic traditions, but also recount the enduring human stories that have thrived upon that land for millennia. Through these exhibits, we can sense the spiritual power emanating from the snow-capped peaks, as well as the harmonious dialogue—played out across the high plateau—between humanity, the divine, and the self.

Outside the window, the rain falls in a torrential downpour—much like the whiskey in my glass: intense, unbridled, and utterly satisfying! As the rain quenches the scorching heat, it simultaneously ignites the spark of life; just as the whiskey stimulates the taste buds, it simultaneously awakens the spirit of inspiration. The vast ocean of Tibetan and Himalayan art beckons us to hoist the sails of beauty upon the vessel of our lives! With the sea stretching wide and the sky soaring high, we appear so fragile—yet possess such indomitable resilience; with mountains towering and roads winding endlessly, we seem so minuscule—yet are, in truth, so magnificent.

description.zh:
原始、野性、韧性、辽阔、苍茫... 顺延着喜马拉雅山脉的那片神奇土地滋养出的人文、艺术让我着迷。每当看到那些纵情奔放

的线条、热烈绚烂的色彩，总能让我想到人类与自然的和谐相处、秩序与自由的平衡。

在那里色彩与线条不仅如实呈现了由元素构成的大千世界，更重要的是，这背后所阐述的是

一个个有关感性力量和哲学思变的具体情境。对这片土地对我而言似乎一点都不陌生，反而

带来的是一种愉悦和一种深刻的熟悉感；那片土地上所展现给我们的色彩、线条正好与人类

思维和情感相互关联，让我们与这天地间的一切产生了联系，它将自然和文化融合，展现出

令人惊叹的美感和视觉冲击力，在灵性与原始本性的底色上传递着一种精神之美，与内心意

识深处产生了原始的情感共振，这一切使得这里的每一个角落都充满了神秘与浩瀚。

文化初始，从象征性的符号到具象人物雕塑的出现，人们探寻着对理想美的表达；随着文明

的碰撞、思想的沉淀、以及文化的自信与笃定，喜马拉雅山脉周边的不同地区尝试着用不同

的雕塑语言、形态表达着他们的情感和故事，丰富的艺术形式无不展示着他们的才华和审美

感知。

每当思绪低落时，走出房间去到大自然中，五感全开，我们被治愈；又或者走进房间对我来

说也是一种不错的选择，当看到那双双一清澈又似乎能洞察世间一切的双眼时，是那么的坚

定又具有力量，好像在讲述着无我的智慧，在烦恼来源的起心动念间，那些被价值观的束缚

和左右，好像慢慢得到转念，在这房间内我也就无意识的慢慢变得轻松、自在起来，被这文

化中的智慧所治愈。

从雕塑角度于我们而言，喜马拉艺术品是理性与感性的完美结合，在柔软与力量间自带一种

超然境界，创作时在有序的风格表达中更多带有一种直觉的迸发，一种感觉的肆意，也正因

为这种‘无知’的可贵，使雕塑散发着一种原始灵性的美感，虽然没有对现实美、肌肉、体

块、光影的着重塑造，但我似乎看到了苍茫大地上迎着光奔走的人们、与这广阔天地为友的

纯朴灵魂、以及把自然视为生命之源的他们尊重自然界一切的生命形式，艰苦的自然环境中

需要面对的种种困难和挑战反而滋养出的是一位位坚韧不拔、具有顽强生命力和生存智慧的

信念、生活的美好表达着，使原本是同一题材的造像有了不同情绪、不同气韵的传达，以及

description.en:
Primal, wild, resilient, vast, boundless... The humanities and arts nurtured by that mystical land, stretching along the majestic Himalayan range, hold me utterly spellbound. Whenever I behold those unbridled, exuberant lines and those vivid, resplendent colors, I am invariably reminded of the harmonious coexistence between humanity and nature—of the delicate balance between order and freedom.
In that realm, colors and lines do not merely offer a faithful depiction of the vast universe composed of elemental forces; more importantly, they articulate specific contexts—narratives woven from the power of human sensibility and profound philosophical contemplation. To me, this land feels not in the least bit alien; rather, it evokes a sense of pure delight and a profound, deep-seated familiarity. The colors and lines revealed by this land resonate intimately with the currents of human thought and emotion, forging a connection between us and all that exists within this universe. It seamlessly fuses nature and culture, manifesting a beauty and visual impact that are truly breathtaking. Against a backdrop of spirituality and primal instinct, it conveys a spiritual beauty that strikes a primal emotional chord deep within our inner consciousness; all of this imbues every corner of this place with an aura of mystery and immensity.
From the dawn of culture—from the earliest symbolic motifs to the emergence of figurative sculpture—humanity has ceaselessly sought to articulate its ideals of beauty. As civilizations converged, ideas matured, and cultural confidence and conviction took root, the diverse regions surrounding the Himalayas began to employ distinct sculptural languages ​​and forms to express their emotions and narratives; these rich artistic expressions stand as enduring testaments to their extraordinary talent and aesthetic sensibility.
Whenever my spirits flag, I find solace in stepping out of my room and immersing myself in the natural world—opening all five senses to its embrace, I am healed. Yet, for me, stepping *into* a room can be an equally restorative choice. When my gaze meets those eyes—eyes at once crystal-clear and seemingly capable of discerning the very essence of the world—I am struck by their unwavering resolve and power; they seem to speak of the wisdom of selflessness. Amidst the restless stirrings of the mind—the very source of our anxieties and afflictions—the constraints and influences imposed by our values ​​and beliefs seem to gently dissolve, giving way to a shift in perspective. Within the sanctuary of this room, I find myself unconsciously relaxing, shedding my burdens, and settling into a state of profound ease—healed by the timeless wisdom embedded within this culture. From a sculptural perspective, Himalayan artworks represent a perfect fusion of rationality and sensibility; they inherently possess a transcendent quality that bridges the realms of softness and strength. The creative process, while grounded in an ordered stylistic expression, is driven even more by intuitive bursts—a free-spirited outpouring of pure sensation. It is precisely this precious "innocence" that imbues these sculptures with a beauty of primal spirituality. Although they do not prioritize the meticulous rendering of realistic aesthetics—such as musculature, mass, or the interplay of light and shadow—I nonetheless perceive within them images of people striding toward the light across a vast and desolate landscape; of pure souls befriending the boundless heavens and earth; and of a people who, regarding nature as the very source of life, hold deep reverence for every living form within the natural world. Far from being stifled by the hardships and challenges of their arduous natural environment, they are instead nurtured into indomitable warriors—individuals endowed with tenacious vitality and profound wisdom for survival. Existing in perfect harmony with the natural order, unburdened by intellectual constraints, they create freely and spontaneously, guided solely by their instincts. Through their work, they give voice to their inner convictions and the beauty of their daily lives, transforming what might otherwise be identical subjects into sculptures that convey distinct emotions, unique spiritual resonances, and penetrating intellectual depth—thereby revealing to us their boundless imagination and creativity regarding sculptural form.

These ancient artworks serve as a silent language, wordlessly narrating the culture and mystique of that distant land. This exhibition spans a vast historical period—from the 3rd to the 18th century—encompassing a diverse array of stylistic works originating from various regions across the Himalayan cultural sphere. As art serves as a medium for beauty, we sincerely hope that this exhibition will likewise serve as a conduit for you to gain a deeper understanding of Himalayan art. Whether you are an expert, a collector, or simply someone who delights in exploring the mysteries of different cultures, we warmly welcome your visit.

title.zh: 为什么我们持续做展览与图录
title.en: Why We Continue to Make Exhibitions and Catalogues

excerpt.zh: 我们持续作展览与图录，并不只是为了呈现艺术品，更是为了保存一种与作品相遇的方式。
excerpt.en: We continue to make exhibitions and catalogues not only to present artworks, but to preserve a way of encountering them.

body.zh: 于我们而言，这些雕塑与绘画从来不仅仅只是历史遗物。它们承载着信仰、情绪、记忆与时间，也在每一次凝视中，与今天的我们重新发生关系。展览让作品回到观看现场，图录则让这种相遇得以被记录、被延续、被反复思考。
body.en: We continue to make exhibitions and catalogues not only to present artworks, but to preserve a way of encountering them.

body.zh: 我们始终相信，真正优秀的艺术作品，不只是被看见，更能让人从纷杂现实中，重新触碰内心的清晰与安定。也正因如此，我们愿意持续以展览与图录为媒介，让古老的精神在今天继续发声，也让每一次观看，都成为一次与自我、与时间、与世界更深的相遇。
body.en: For us, these sculptures and paintings are never merely historical remnants. They carry faith, emotion, memory, and time, and in every sustained gaze they enter into renewed relation with us in the present. Exhibitions return works to the site of viewing, while catalogues allow these encounters to be recorded, extended, and revisited in thought.

content.zh: 于我们而言，这些雕塑与绘画从来不仅仅只是历史遗物。它们承载着信仰、情绪、记忆与时间，也在每一次凝视中，与今天的我们重新发生关系。展览让作品回到观看现场，图录则让这种相遇得以被记录、被延续、被反复思考。
content.en: We continue to make exhibitions and catalogues not only to present artworks, but to preserve a way of encountering them.

excerpt.zh: 当你踏入空间的那一步，你就已经落入了空间的“陷阱”。
excerpt.en: The moment you enter the space, you are already caught within its “trap”.

body.zh: 当你踏入空间的那一步，你就已经落入了空间的“陷阱”。艺术欣赏是从何时开始的，当你的目光落在艺术品的那一刻吗？然而并不是。
body.en: The moment you step into a space, you've already fallen into its "trap." When does art appreciation begin? Is it the moment your gaze falls upon the artwork? Not at all.

body.zh: 你踏入时发现的四周聚集的光线，未察觉到的铺在身上暗暗的暖色调乃至静谧的四周早就在向你提问“准备好了吗？我在等着你。”空间就是这样一个以无数的信息点编织成的巨大“陷阱”，当你身处其中，各个事物相辅相成交汇而成的巨大能量网便轻而易举地将你捕获。
body.en: The light that gathers around you upon entering, the unnoticed warm, subtly colored hues that blanket you, and even the tranquil surroundings—all these are already asking you, "Are you ready? I'm waiting for you." Space is a vast "trap" woven from countless points of information. When you're within it, the immense network of energy formed by the interaction and convergence of various elements easily captures you .

body.zh: 不知你是否注意到，我们身处的空间像一个有生命的整体，它将我们的感受调频，最终与它合为一体。混乱的房间交织成你混沌的思绪，虔诚的佛教氛围造就你心中的圣洁和超脱。海德格尔借荷尔德林之口深情地赞颂“人，诗意的栖居！”于视觉空间中，艺术品一经落成，它便与周围的一切事物建立起了联系，开始吐丝织网。
body.en: Have you noticed that the space we inhabit is like a living whole? It tunes our senses, ultimately uniting us with it. The chaotic room weaves together your confused thoughts, while the devout Buddhist atmosphere cultivates a sense of sanctity and transcendence within you. Heidegger, through Hölderlin, passionately praises, "Man, poetically dwells!" In visual space, once an artwork is created, it establishes a connection with everything around it, beginning to weave its own web.

body.zh: 艺术与空间仅仅产生了视觉的物质联结吗？
body.en: Does art and space merely create a visual, material connection?

body.zh: 不是的。
body.en:
No.
It also forms a spiritual connection with people and space. A sculpture, embodying the countless hammer blows and forgings of artists from hundreds or even thousands of years ago, has witnessed the devout worship and gaze of people throughout history. Enduring the winds of time, it arrives before modern people, its value clearly far exceeding mere visual enjoyment. It is a spiritual connection between the past and present.

body.zh: 它同样与人、与空间形成了一种精神上的联结。一尊造像雕塑，凝结了数百年乃至千年前的艺术家数以万计的捶打锻造，迎接着历史长河中人们的虔诚叩拜与时代凝视，迎着千年风沙，它来到现代人的身前，其所承载的价值显然远远超过单一的视觉享受。它是古今之间的精神联结。
body.en: When it exists in a dwelling for rest, it pierces through the mists of time and collides with your gaze. An indescribable emotion washes away all the negative pressures of worldly life, and the spiritual connection between art and you begins.

body.zh:
当它存在于用以休憩的居所之时，它穿过时间的迷雾与你目光相撞，不可名状的情绪裹走一切世俗带给你的消极压力，艺术与你的精神联结便由此开始。
尼采总说，现代人是日子的奴隶，是悬挂在瞬间之网上永远挨饿的人，不可喘息的分秒必争总是让现代人惶惶不可终日。以实用为价值导向的事物让闪烁着美丽光芒的艺术黯然失色，精神层面无法填补的空隙被物质世界越填越空。
body.en: Nietzsche often said that modern man is a slave to the days, forever starving, suspended in the web of fleeting moments. The relentless struggle for every second leaves modern man constantly anxious. Things valued for practicality dim the brilliance of art, and the void that cannot be filled on the spiritual level is increasingly emptied by the material world.

body.zh: 只有当我们发现了那一些些穿越时空的救赎，我们才停下脚步、暂停时间，领悟到古人的精神智慧与勇气。现代人与经典艺术的对话在这一空间中展开，这种对话没有结尾，没有终结，解释学家伽达默尔将这样的“对话”视为历史视野与现代视野的结合，即是我们带着身处时代的“偏见”与热情，与眼前的历史艺术生发出内心深处的共鸣。而艺术于这一刻的真正价值 也被懂得艺术的参与者所实现。
body.en: Only when we discover those glimpses of redemption that transcend time do we pause, halt time itself, and grasp the spiritual wisdom and courage of the ancients. A dialogue between modern people and classical art unfolds in this space; this dialogue has no end, no conclusion. Hermeneuticist Gadamer views this "dialogue" as a fusion of historical and modern perspectives—a resonance within us, carrying the "prejudice" and passion of our time, with the historical art before us. The true value of art at this moment is realized by those who understand it.

body.zh: 艺术不仅仅与空间有着视觉与氛围的联结，同样在古今相通的人类悲欢中寄寓着现代人以缺失的精神指引。
body.en: Art not only connects with space visually and atmospherically, but also, within the shared joys and sorrows of humanity throughout history, embodies a spiritual guidance that modern people lack.

content.zh: 它同样与人、与空间形成了一种精神上的联结。一尊造像雕塑，凝结了数百年乃至千年前的艺术家数以万计的捶打锻造，迎接着历史长河中人们的虔诚叩拜与时代凝视，迎着千年风沙，它来到现代人的身前，其所承载的价值显然远远超过单一的视觉享受。它是古今之间的精神联结。
content.en: When it exists in a dwelling for rest, it pierces through the mists of time and collides with your gaze. An indescribable emotion washes away all the negative pressures of worldly life, and the spiritual connection between art and you begins.

content.zh:
当它存在于用以休憩的居所之时，它穿过时间的迷雾与你目光相撞，不可名状的情绪裹走一切世俗带给你的消极压力，艺术与你的精神联结便由此开始。
尼采总说，现代人是日子的奴隶，是悬挂在瞬间之网上永远挨饿的人，不可喘息的分秒必争总是让现代人惶惶不可终日。以实用为价值导向的事物让闪烁着美丽光芒的艺术黯然失色，精神层面无法填补的空隙被物质世界越填越空。
content.en: Nietzsche often said that modern man is a slave to the days, forever starving, suspended in the web of fleeting moments. The relentless struggle for every second leaves modern man constantly anxious. Things valued for practicality dim the brilliance of art, and the void that cannot be filled on the spiritual level is increasingly emptied by the material world.

content.zh: 只有当我们发现了那一些些穿越时空的救赎，我们才停下脚步、暂停时间，领悟到古人的精神智慧与勇气。现代人与经典艺术的对话在这一空间中展开，这种对话没有结尾，没有终结，解释学家伽达默尔将这样的“对话”视为历史视野与现代视野的结合，即是我们带着身处时代的“偏见”与热情，与眼前的历史艺术生发出内心深处的共鸣。而艺术于这一刻的真正价值 也被懂得艺术的参与者所实现。
content.en: Only when we discover those glimpses of redemption that transcend time do we pause, halt time itself, and grasp the spiritual wisdom and courage of the ancients. A dialogue between modern people and classical art unfolds in this space; this dialogue has no end, no conclusion. Hermeneuticist Gadamer views this "dialogue" as a fusion of historical and modern perspectives—a resonance within us, carrying the "prejudice" and passion of our time, with the historical art before us. The true value of art at this moment is realized by those who understand it.

content.zh: 艺术不仅仅与空间有着视觉与氛围的联结，同样在古今相通的人类悲欢中寄寓着现代人以缺失的精神指引。
content.en: Art not only connects with space visually and atmospherically, but also, within the shared joys and sorrows of humanity throughout history, embodies a spiritual guidance that modern people lack.

title.en: Alain Bordier, the aesthete of life

excerpt.zh: 一张照片横挂在教堂的梁柱上，他的精神世界也在这里被分成了两个空间——照片之下，是他的生活、照片之上，是他的信仰与灵感。
excerpt.en: A photograph hangs across the church pillars, dividing his spiritual world into two spaces—below the photograph lies his life; above it, his faith and inspirati...

body.zh: 一张照片横挂在教堂的梁柱上，他的精神世界也在这里被分成了两个空间——照片之下，是他的生活、照片之上，是他的信仰与灵感。
body.en: A photograph hangs across the church pillars, dividing his spiritual world into two spaces—below the photograph lies his life; above it, his faith and inspiration.

body.zh: 他温柔地复合着空间，并用他的智慧独特地打破常规，他的家像是一个无界的画布，处处散发着历史的幽光，这是阿兰伯迪的家，与楼下的西藏艺术博物馆一起坐落在瑞士山脚下的格吕耶尔小镇。与一楼供人静穆观赏的佛教造像不同，二楼的艺术品抛去了令人望而生畏的距离感，以极高的参与度进入着他的生活。
body.en: He gently integrates space, uniquely breaking conventions with his wisdom. His home is like a boundless canvas, radiating the subtle glow of history. This is Alain Bordier's home, nestled in the town of Gruyères at the foot of the Swiss mountains, alongside the Tibetan Art Museum downstairs. Unlike the Buddhist statues on the first floor, intended for quiet contemplation, the artworks on the second floor dispel any sense of intimidation, entering his life with a high degree of engagement.

body.zh: 随着视野的上升，藏族的玄妙音乐充斥着耳朵，我被楼梯墙上深绿色的牧场画的搭配方式拖住了脚步，墙上挂起的是锈迹斑斑的剪刀和各类工具、是原始的敲锤、是饱经风霜的痕迹，还有古朴的黑色石雕。我忍不住惊叹阿兰伯德自由的想象力与创造力，这面墙上绝不仅仅是普通物件的排列组合，这更像是将一位平凡藏民的一生浓缩到了这面墙上，从赖以为生的畜牧 到 支撑灵魂的造像，他们出生自死都与高原为伴。
body.en: As the view ascends, the enigmatic music of Tibetan music fills the air. I am captivated by the combination of deep green pastoral paintings on the stairwell walls. Hanging on the walls are rusty scissors and various tools, primitive hammers, weathered marks, and rustic black stone carvings. I couldn't help but marvel at Alan Bird's free imagination and creativity. This wall is far more than just an arrangement of ordinary objects; it's as if it encapsulates the life of an ordinary Tibetan, from herding livestock for survival to creating sculptures that sustain his soul—they were born and died alongside the plateau.

body.zh: 看着和煦日的光透过窗户洒在造像上、看着以青山为背景的佛头造像、看着阿兰在一旁眉飞色舞地讲述着他的最爱，在这个温暖而神秘生活空间中，喜马拉雅艺术品已不仅仅是他的生活装饰，更是他生活哲学、深沉情感和丰富世界观的生动展示，在这生活空间中的每一处都能看到他的趣味和情感。
body.en: Watching the warm sunlight stream through the window onto the sculptures, seeing the Buddha head against the backdrop of green mountains, watching Alan passionately recount his favorites, in this warm and mysterious living space, the Himalayan artworks are not merely decorations, but a vivid display of his philosophy of life, profound emotions, and rich worldview. His taste and feelings are evident in every corner of this space.

body.zh: 表面看起来他是“痴迷”于藏品，但如果我们深入其中，便能窥见他是那样地热爱生活，在这瞬息万变的世界里，他编织出了与冰冷钢筋水泥截然相反的“温度感”，这些“温度”无关乎物质的价值，而是一种独特的情感传递。这些艺术品超越了传统的收藏意义，而像是被赋予生命一样，静静地呼吸在他的世界里，像是一种内心独白，也像是一种深邃的对话，拥有一种无形的渗透力，在启发着人们去思考生与死、缘与灭、因与果的生命奥义。
body.en: On the surface, he appears "obsessed" with his collection, but if we delve deeper, we can glimpse his deep love for life. In this ever-changing world, he has woven a "warmth" completely opposite to cold steel and concrete—a warmth unrelated to material value, but a unique emotional transmission. These artworks transcend the traditional meaning of collecting; they seem imbued with life, quietly breathing in his world, like an inner monologue, a profound dialogue, possessing an invisible, penetrating power, inspiring people to contemplate the mysteries of life and death, cause and effect.

body.zh: 他是一个生活的艺术家，也是亿万生活者中的独一无二。他的生活，充满了对世界、对艺术品、对喜马拉雅的深深敬意和赞叹。对他而言‘生活’宛如一张泛黄的羊皮纸，承载着古老却又永远鲜活的故事，每一笔都是新的启示，他享受着对生活的理解和领悟，也把这种平和喜乐传递给了我们。这就是生活的奇妙之处——短暂 ，却又如此令人着迷。
body.en: He is an artist of life, unique among millions of people. His life is filled with deep respect and admiration for the world, for art, and for the Himalayas. To him, 'life' is like a yellowed parchment, carrying ancient yet eternally vibrant stories; every stroke is a new revelation. He enjoys understanding and comprehending life, and shares this peace and joy with us. This is the wonder of life—brief, yet so captivating.

body.zh: 在你的生活中，是否也有那样一件艺术品，静静的在影像着你、触动着你呢？
body.en: In your life, is there also such an artwork, quietly reflecting and touching you?

title.zh: 永乐之美：端正、克制与大国气象
title.en: The beauty of Yongle: uprightness, restraint, and the grandeur of a great nation.

excerpt.zh: 一说到“永乐造像”，我们首先想到的，当然是明代永乐时期。
excerpt.en: When we talk about "Yongle Buddhist sculptures," we naturally think of the Yongle period of the Ming Dynasty.

body.zh: 一说到“永乐造像”，我们首先想到的，当然是明代永乐时期。
body.en: When we talk about "Yongle Buddhist sculptures," we naturally think of the Yongle period of the Ming Dynasty.

body.zh:
但如果再往前追溯一步，就会发现，这批宫廷佛像的出现，并不是突然发生的。它背后，其实有一条更长的文化线索。元代时，忽必烈邀请西藏萨迦派祖师八思巴入大都，封为国师，并授以玉印。从那一刻开始，藏传佛教正式进入宫廷文化的核心空间，也就是今天的北京。这件事的意义，不只是文化传播，更像是为后来的明代宫廷造像，打开了一扇门。
到了明代，真正成体系的宫廷佛教造像，基本是从永乐时期开始成熟起来的。这一时期的作品，它既不是单纯的汉地造像，也不是直接照搬藏地样式，而是在宫廷语境中，形成了一种极具辨识度的汉藏融合风格。也正因如此，永乐、宣德时期的宫廷造像，在整个喜马拉雅与藏传佛教艺术史里，都占有重要的位置。
很多时候，一说到“宫廷”，第一反应会想到紫禁城、皇家、权威。这种联想其实是准确的。因为宫廷艺术最核心的气质，本来就不是民间那种自然生长的质朴，而是庄严、高贵、严谨、克制。这种气质，放在永乐宫廷造像上，表现得尤其明显。看它的背光、底座、衣纹和整体结构，就会立刻明白：这类作品从来不是为了“随意好看”而做的，它追求的是一种几乎不允许出错的完整。每一个细节都被收拾得干净、周正，一丝不苟，带着非常强的秩序感。
body.en: However, if we trace back further, we find that the appearance of these court Buddhist statues did not happen suddenly. Behind them lies a longer cultural thread. During the Yuan Dynasty, Kublai Khan invited Phagpa, the founder of the Sakya school of Tibetan Buddhism, to Dadu (Beijing), appointing him as the Imperial Preceptor and bestowing upon him a jade seal. From that moment on, Tibetan Buddhism officially entered the core space of court culture—what is now Beijing. The significance of this event was not merely cultural transmission; it was more like opening a door for later Ming Dynasty court Buddhist sculptures.

body.zh: 也正因为如此，宫廷造像和民间造像之间，其实有着非常明显的区别。民间造像有时会更直接、更生动，甚至带一点朴拙的可爱；而宫廷造像则不一样，它更像是被精心校准过的。制作这类作品的匠人，自然也是当时最拔尖的一批人。只是他们不像西方艺术史里那些被反复传颂的名字——比如米开朗基罗、拉斐尔、达·芬奇——那样被后世广泛记住。
body.en: By the Ming Dynasty, truly systematic court Buddhist sculptures had matured primarily from the Yongle period. The works of this period were neither simply Han Chinese sculptures nor direct copies of Tibetan styles, but rather, within the court context, formed a highly distinctive fusion of Han and Tibetan styles. It is precisely for this reason that the court sculptures of the Yongle and Xuande periods occupy an important place in the entire history of Himalayan and Tibetan Buddhist art.

body.zh:
可即便名字没有留下，他们的水准却清清楚楚地留在了作品里。只要看过一尊真正优秀的永乐宫廷造像的人，就会知道，那不是普通工匠靠熟练就能做出来的，它背后一定有极深的训练、审美与经验。
如果把永乐时期放在更大的世界艺术史里看，也会发现一个很有意思的现象。永乐大约对应的是西方文艺复兴发展中的重要阶段。虽然两者属于完全不同的文化系统，不能简单并置，但在“对理想人体与写实比例的高度追求”这一点上，确实能看到某种若有若无的相通。
body.en: Often, the word "court" immediately evokes images of the Forbidden City, royalty, and authority. This association is accurate. The core essence of court art is not the natural simplicity of folk art, but rather solemnity, nobility, rigor, and restraint. This quality is particularly evident in Yongle court sculptures. Looking at the halo, base, drapery, and overall structure, one immediately understands that these works were never made for mere aesthetic appeal; they pursued a near-perfect perfection. Every detail is meticulously crafted, precise, and imbued with a strong sense of order.

body.zh:
永乐宫廷造像的人体比例通常非常准确，主尊的开脸、肢体、手足、肩背结构，都体现出一种高度理想化之后的写实概括。尤其是衣物的处理，常常轻薄贴体，像丝绸、绸缎那样柔软地覆在身上，既能看见身体的转折，也能感到材质本身的贵气。这种宫廷的“理想美”，恰恰是永乐宫廷造像最迷人的地方之一。
当然，也有人会觉得，永乐宫廷造像太规整了，少了一点更直接的情绪张力，甚至会觉得它有些过于制式化。但这恰恰需要放回它的文化背景里去理解。不同地域的造像，本来就有各自不同的精神气质。犍陀罗像一位优雅的王子，尼泊尔造像常常带着甜美、童真与含蓄，西藏造像则充满一种原始而强烈的灵性力量。而宫廷造像所面对的，是皇家的审美和帝国的秩序，它需要体现的，不是个人情绪的丰沛流露，而是端正、稳重、平衡、大气。

所以，它并不追求夸张，也不纵容逸笔草草般的任性，它追求的是“恰到好处”。从比例到细节，从神情到结构，都像是经过反复权衡之后才被允许留下来的。也正因为这种克制，永乐宫廷造像身上会有一种非常特别的气息——它不是“没有情感”，而是把情感收到了更高一级的秩序里。
换句话说，永乐的造像并不是不表达，而是表达得更深、更稳。它不强调某一个匠人的个体情绪，也不让作品落入过度抒情的方向。它所要传达的，是一种超越个人的气度，一种属于大国、属于皇权、也属于礼制文明的精神面貌。所以你看永乐造像时，会很自然地联想到故宫。故宫的美，不是俏皮的，也不是故意取巧的，它讲究的是对称的美、均衡的美、秩序的美。

永乐宫廷造像也是如此。它并不追求“奇”，而是追求“正”；并不刻意求“险”，而是追求“稳”。这种美，乍看未必最热烈，但越看越能体会到它背后那种被文明反复打磨过的力量。
还有一点也很重要，就是材质。永乐宫廷造像所使用的铜，往往带有非常鲜明的识别性。它在色泽、质感和整体呈现上，都与后世许多造像不同，显得格外细润，也更有宫廷器物独有的贵重感。严格来说，我们不宜把这种特质简单说成“只有永乐才有”，但可以肯定的是，永乐宫廷在铜材选择、合金控制和整体铸造标准上，确实形成了很高的规格。这种材料层面的讲究，其实和西方皇室、教堂艺术中对昂贵石材的使用，有某种相似的逻辑：它不仅关乎工艺，更关乎身份。材料本身，就是权力、资源与审美的一部分。
这也是为什么，永乐宫廷造像在整个喜马拉雅艺术史中，始终占据着一种无法替代的位置。因为它不只是作品，它更像是一种标准。
一种关于“庄严”，什么叫“高贵”，什么叫“把理想做到几乎没有多余败笔”的标准。

content.zh: 一说到“永乐造像”，我们首先想到的，当然是明代永乐时期。
content.en: When we talk about "Yongle Buddhist sculptures," we naturally think of the Yongle period of the Ming Dynasty.

content.zh:
但如果再往前追溯一步，就会发现，这批宫廷佛像的出现，并不是突然发生的。它背后，其实有一条更长的文化线索。元代时，忽必烈邀请西藏萨迦派祖师八思巴入大都，封为国师，并授以玉印。从那一刻开始，藏传佛教正式进入宫廷文化的核心空间，也就是今天的北京。这件事的意义，不只是文化传播，更像是为后来的明代宫廷造像，打开了一扇门。
到了明代，真正成体系的宫廷佛教造像，基本是从永乐时期开始成熟起来的。这一时期的作品，它既不是单纯的汉地造像，也不是直接照搬藏地样式，而是在宫廷语境中，形成了一种极具辨识度的汉藏融合风格。也正因如此，永乐、宣德时期的宫廷造像，在整个喜马拉雅与藏传佛教艺术史里，都占有重要的位置。
很多时候，一说到“宫廷”，第一反应会想到紫禁城、皇家、权威。这种联想其实是准确的。因为宫廷艺术最核心的气质，本来就不是民间那种自然生长的质朴，而是庄严、高贵、严谨、克制。这种气质，放在永乐宫廷造像上，表现得尤其明显。看它的背光、底座、衣纹和整体结构，就会立刻明白：这类作品从来不是为了“随意好看”而做的，它追求的是一种几乎不允许出错的完整。每一个细节都被收拾得干净、周正，一丝不苟，带着非常强的秩序感。
content.en: However, if we trace back further, we find that the appearance of these court Buddhist statues did not happen suddenly. Behind them lies a longer cultural thread. During the Yuan Dynasty, Kublai Khan invited Phagpa, the founder of the Sakya school of Tibetan Buddhism, to Dadu (Beijing), appointing him as the Imperial Preceptor and bestowing upon him a jade seal. From that moment on, Tibetan Buddhism officially entered the core space of court culture—what is now Beijing. The significance of this event was not merely cultural transmission; it was more like opening a door for later Ming Dynasty court Buddhist sculptures.

content.zh: 也正因为如此，宫廷造像和民间造像之间，其实有着非常明显的区别。民间造像有时会更直接、更生动，甚至带一点朴拙的可爱；而宫廷造像则不一样，它更像是被精心校准过的。制作这类作品的匠人，自然也是当时最拔尖的一批人。只是他们不像西方艺术史里那些被反复传颂的名字——比如米开朗基罗、拉斐尔、达·芬奇——那样被后世广泛记住。
content.en: By the Ming Dynasty, truly systematic court Buddhist sculptures had matured primarily from the Yongle period. The works of this period were neither simply Han Chinese sculptures nor direct copies of Tibetan styles, but rather, within the court context, formed a highly distinctive fusion of Han and Tibetan styles. It is precisely for this reason that the court sculptures of the Yongle and Xuande periods occupy an important place in the entire history of Himalayan and Tibetan Buddhist art.

caption.zh: 拉斐尔为梵蒂冈宫廷创作的《雅典学院》
caption.en: Raphael's *The School of Athens*, painted for the Vatican court.

content.zh:
可即便名字没有留下，他们的水准却清清楚楚地留在了作品里。只要看过一尊真正优秀的永乐宫廷造像的人，就会知道，那不是普通工匠靠熟练就能做出来的，它背后一定有极深的训练、审美与经验。
如果把永乐时期放在更大的世界艺术史里看，也会发现一个很有意思的现象。永乐大约对应的是西方文艺复兴发展中的重要阶段。虽然两者属于完全不同的文化系统，不能简单并置，但在“对理想人体与写实比例的高度追求”这一点上，确实能看到某种若有若无的相通。
content.en: Often, the word "court" immediately evokes images of the Forbidden City, royalty, and authority. This association is accurate. The core essence of court art is not the natural simplicity of folk art, but rather solemnity, nobility, rigor, and restraint. This quality is particularly evident in Yongle court sculptures. Looking at the halo, base, drapery, and overall structure, one immediately understands that these works were never made for mere aesthetic appeal; they pursued a near-perfect perfection. Every detail is meticulously crafted, precise, and imbued with a strong sense of order.

content.zh:
永乐宫廷造像的人体比例通常非常准确，主尊的开脸、肢体、手足、肩背结构，都体现出一种高度理想化之后的写实概括。尤其是衣物的处理，常常轻薄贴体，像丝绸、绸缎那样柔软地覆在身上，既能看见身体的转折，也能感到材质本身的贵气。这种宫廷的“理想美”，恰恰是永乐宫廷造像最迷人的地方之一。
当然，也有人会觉得，永乐宫廷造像太规整了，少了一点更直接的情绪张力，甚至会觉得它有些过于制式化。但这恰恰需要放回它的文化背景里去理解。不同地域的造像，本来就有各自不同的精神气质。犍陀罗像一位优雅的王子，尼泊尔造像常常带着甜美、童真与含蓄，西藏造像则充满一种原始而强烈的灵性力量。而宫廷造像所面对的，是皇家的审美和帝国的秩序，它需要体现的，不是个人情绪的丰沛流露，而是端正、稳重、平衡、大气。

所以，它并不追求夸张，也不纵容逸笔草草般的任性，它追求的是“恰到好处”。从比例到细节，从神情到结构，都像是经过反复权衡之后才被允许留下来的。也正因为这种克制，永乐宫廷造像身上会有一种非常特别的气息——它不是“没有情感”，而是把情感收到了更高一级的秩序里。
换句话说，永乐的造像并不是不表达，而是表达得更深、更稳。它不强调某一个匠人的个体情绪，也不让作品落入过度抒情的方向。它所要传达的，是一种超越个人的气度，一种属于大国、属于皇权、也属于礼制文明的精神面貌。所以你看永乐造像时，会很自然地联想到故宫。故宫的美，不是俏皮的，也不是故意取巧的，它讲究的是对称的美、均衡的美、秩序的美。

永乐宫廷造像也是如此。它并不追求“奇”，而是追求“正”；并不刻意求“险”，而是追求“稳”。这种美，乍看未必最热烈，但越看越能体会到它背后那种被文明反复打磨过的力量。

excerpt.zh: 一个时代的“精神气候”，究竟怎样渗入造像的面容与身躯？
excerpt.en: How exactly does the "spiritual climate" of an era permeate the face and body of a sculpture?

body.zh: 一个时代的“精神气候”，究竟怎样渗入造像的面容与身躯？
body.en: How exactly does the "spiritual climate" of an era permeate the face and body of a sculpture?

body.zh: 我们以这尊 12 世纪尼泊尔过渡期的造像为例，在那段王朝更迭的历史缝隙里，它映照出了时代的内在张力。
body.en: Let's take this 12th-century Nepalese transitional sculpture as an example. Within the historical gaps of dynastic change, it reflects the inherent tension of the era.

body.zh: 当时的尼泊尔谷地正从理查维走向马拉王朝。旧秩序瓦解了，新秩序还没来。地方小王朝不断更替，但却没有爆裂式的战乱。社会虽松散，却没崩塌。
body.en: At that time, the Nepalese valleys were transitioning from the Richave dynasty to the Malla dynasty. The old order had crumbled, and the new order had not yet arrived. Local minor dynasties rose and fell constantly, but there was no explosive warfare. Society was loose, but not collapsed.

body.zh: 贵族们用建筑、修寺、造塔来维系影响力，工匠在这样的结构里，逐步获得社会地位，同时也获得了更自由的呼吸和创作空间。那是一个生活不算富裕、秩序虽不稳固，但却精神丰盈的时代。商队频繁来往于喜马拉雅南北，使得贸易与文化交织。在这种外在不定、内在安稳的双重结构下，造像展现出一种浓郁而温和的精神密度。
body.en: Nobles maintained their influence through architecture, temple construction, and stupa building. Within this structure, artisans gradually gained social status and, at the same time, more freedom to breathe and create. It was an era of modest wealth and unstable order, but one of spiritual richness. Frequent caravans traveling between the north and south of the Himalayas intertwined trade and culture. Under this dual structure of external uncertainty and internal stability, the sculpture exhibits a rich yet gentle spiritual density.

body.zh: 你看它的面容：五官清朗，眼神沉静，有着古典遗风般间的沉思与高贵，这不是繁荣时期的自信，也不是乱世的紧绷，而是一种似乎正把时代不安慢慢收拢的内观之气。
body.en: Look at its face: clear features, serene eyes, a contemplative nobility reminiscent of classical elegance. This isn't the confidence of a prosperous era, nor the tension of chaos, but rather an introspective aura that seems to be slowly gathering the unease of the times.

body.zh: 身体的比例被理想化处理，带着神性，也带着人的温度。线条柔韧、节奏饱满，像身体里有一条向上的气流，介于脆弱与坚韧之间，充满柔韧的张力。在它身上没有战斗的紧张，也没有帝国的浮华；反而是一种在不确定中仍保持创造力与生机的状态，这种状态让人着迷，着迷于它所散发出的朝气、优雅与澄澈，有一种站在阳光中的明亮与静候。
body.en: The proportions of its body are idealized, imbued with both divinity and human warmth. The lines are supple, the rhythm full, like an upward current flowing within, existing between fragility and resilience, brimming with supple tension. It lacks the tension of battle, nor the extravagance of empire; instead, it possesses a state of creativity and vitality amidst uncertainty. This state is captivating, captivating the vigor, elegance, and clarity it exudes, a brightness and quiet anticipation like standing in the sunlight.

body.zh:
这让我想到：战乱会塑造刚猛，盛世会塑造华丽。
但只有那种“松散而不绝望”的时代，才会出现这样的气质。
不豪华，但细腻。不激烈，但有内力。不悲怆，却极为深沉。
body.en: This reminds me: war forges fierceness, prosperity forges splendor.

body.zh: 这尊造像呈现着一个时代特有的精神气息。是一种在不确定时代中对稳定的渴望，以及依然保有文化韧性、内心并非贫瘠的精神状态。
body.en: But only in an era of "relaxation without despair" can such a temperament emerge.

title.zh: 为什么资产配置中会有古董？
title.en: Why are antiques included in asset allocation?

excerpt.zh: 古代的雕塑、绘画为什么会成为高净值人群的资产配置选择？
excerpt.en: Why have ancient sculptures and paintings become asset allocation choices for high-net-worth individuals?

body.zh: 古代的雕塑、绘画为什么会成为高净值人群的资产配置选择？
body.en: Why have ancient sculptures and paintings become asset allocation choices for high-net-worth individuals?

body.zh: 聊到“古董艺术品”，毫无疑问，首先它得具备某种价值，因此才会让人愿意去珍藏。尽管这其中每个人重视的价值点有所区别。在当今“结构化”的商业逻辑中，一件能产生商业价值的物品，往往集功能价值、情绪价值、符号价值、资产价值于一身，古董收藏也同样如此。
body.en: When discussing "antique art," it's undeniable that it must first possess some form of value to inspire interest in collecting. While the specific value each individual prioritizes may differ, in today's structured business world, an item that generates commercial value often combines functional, emotional, symbolic, and asset value—and antique collecting is no exception .

body.zh: 说到古代艺术品的功能价值、符合价值，大多数人首先想到的是它们作为陈设、装饰的实用功能。但其实，古代艺术品更重要的功能和符号价值是时间赋予的稀缺属性。怎么理解这种稀缺性呢？在此，我们可以借用著名文艺理论家瓦尔特·本雅明对“灵韵”一词的阐释。“灵韵”（Aura）的字面意思即是“艺术的光晕”。
body.en: When discussing the functional and symbolic value of ancient art, most people first think of its practical function as display and decoration. However, the more important function and symbolic value of ancient art lies in the scarcity attribute bestowed by time. How do we understand this scarcity? Here, we can borrow Walter Benjamin's explanation of the term "aura." The literal meaning of "aura" is "the halo of art."

body.zh: 本雅明认为艺术作品的灵韵不在于它的物质形式，而在于它所传递的独特情感、意义、精神内涵以及创造时所处于彼时、彼地的独一无二性和作品所洋溢着的神性。现代性完成了对传统世界的祛魅，消解了一切艺术事物的神性，现在剩下的仅仅只是机械复制时代种失去灵韵的艺术复制品了。值得关注的是，“灵韵”这个稀缺属性中却又还隐藏着一个非常大的功能价值就是——它在很多时候可以帮助我们平衡和规避掉‘现代性’的冲击。正如甘阳先生所说：艺术品拉开了我们对现代社会的距离，让我们的心灵有了更广阔的存在空间。
body.en: Walter Benjamin believed that the spirit of a work of art lies not in its material form, but in the unique emotions, meanings, and spiritual connotations it conveys, as well as the uniqueness of its creation at that time and place, and the divinity it exudes. Modernity has demystified the traditional world, dissolving the divinity of all artistic things; what remains now are merely artistic replicas devoid of spirit in the age of mechanical reproduction. It is noteworthy that this scarce attribute of "spirit" also hides a significant functional value—it can often help us balance and avoid the impact of "modernity." As Mr. Gan Yang said: Artworks have distanced us from modern society, giving our minds a broader space to exist .

body.zh: 那么什么是现代性呢？1863年，波德莱尔首先提出了“现代性”概念，指的是人与过去环境的断裂，由此，人们进入了一个无序、短暂、碎片、且冷漠的生活状态中。人们只按照严格的数字换算方式来行动，人和人之间以前那种个性化的富有特色的交往已荡然无存。于是人们为了生计，就不得不同进行残酷而冷静的斗争，精于算计的我们，越来越表现出克制、冷漠、模式化的状态，个性也随之消失，人们社会便呈现出了“均质化”的景象。
body.en: So what is modernity? In 1863, Baudelaire first proposed the concept of "modernity," referring to the rupture between humanity and its past environment. As a result, people have entered a disordered, transient, fragmented, and indifferent state of life. People act only according to strict numerical calculations; the personalized and distinctive interactions between people that were once prevalent have vanished. Thus, in the struggle for survival, people are forced into a brutal yet ruthless struggle. Our shrewd calculations increasingly manifest as restraint, indifference, and conformity, with individuality disappearing, resulting in a homogenized society .

body.zh:
为了消解现代性的冲击，人们的内心总是会向往一个安稳、持久且具有确定性地方，而文化的深邃和那可触摸到的一眼千年，则是‘快’的对立面，它的从容、优雅则在无声中疗愈着‘现代性’带来的创伤，给予人们整全的思考与觉察。在这独特的文化语境中，它可以将我们的身、心带入一种有别于世俗社会标准与文化秩序的场域中。就像音乐的功能性一样，站在广场上人们，会选择播放一曲适合跳广场舞的曲子，而下雨天独自居家赏雨的你也许会放上一首巴赫。
而‘情绪价值’可以说是近几年一个非常高频的词汇了。一说到情绪价值，就如字面意思一样，它是能产生愉悦感的。不同人由于境遇的不同在遇到这些雕塑、绘画时的情绪联结、内心感受也都不太相同。
body.en: To mitigate the impact of modernity, people yearn for a stable, enduring, and certain place. The profundity of culture, and the tangible connection to millennia, is the antithesis of "fast." Its composure and elegance silently heal the wounds of "modernity," offering holistic reflection and awareness. Within this unique cultural context, it can transport our body and mind to a field distinct from secular social standards and cultural order. Like the function of music, people in a square might choose to play a piece suitable for square dancing, while someone alone at home on a rainy day might play a piece by Bach.

body.zh: 正如德里达所说：“艺术品的意义并不被边框包裹。”有的朋友是因为文化的神秘感而带来的好奇探索；有的朋友是在展厅灯光的照射下被带入了多重时间层叠的场域;有的朋友也许是因为时间再次塑造下的留白与想象，让祂在补全图像的过程中完成了一次自我疗愈；或许还有的朋友是被一代又一代在传承中的愿力所打动，而惊叹到，祂真的是吹过宋代的风？居然保存得如此完好，而在其中所蕴含的温度和美好祝愿中感受到了关怀，在无声的语言中又多了一次跨越时空的对谈。
body.en: And "emotional value" has become a very frequently used term in recent years. When we talk about emotional value, it's literally about generating pleasure. Different people, due to their different circumstances, will have different emotional connections and inner feelings when encountering these sculptures and paintings.

body.zh: 我想，语言能表达的太有限，每个人被其打动，而想开始去收藏的原因也许也都不尽相同。虽然古代艺术品所能带给我们的情绪价值中精神价值肯定是首当其冲的，但是由收藏家这个身份和收藏这个行为而带来的‘彰显性’也是不能忽略的。在这个情绪价值中的‘彰显性’也可以把它理解为‘影响力’。精英阶层往往重视文化与艺术熏习，这是因为除了上述的审美体验外，艺术品还能给人以社会价值及所属的社会荣誉，所以我们会看到一些收藏家会通过捐赠给博物馆或者通过展览的形式，来让更多人能有机会更直观的接触和欣赏到它们。
body.en: As Derrida said, "The meaning of a work of art is not confined by borders." Some are drawn in by the mystery of culture; others are transported to multiple layers of time under the exhibition lights; some may find healing in the blank spaces and imagination created by time, completing the image; still others are moved by the will to pass it down through generations, marveling at how well it has been preserved, truly echoing the winds of the Song Dynasty, feeling the warmth and good wishes within, and engaging in a dialogue across time in silent language.

body.zh: 当然，艺术品的配置同样和商业过程相关，所以这也就是为什么我们会看到很多大的企业都会有自己的博物馆或美术馆，比如：LVMH基金会艺术中心、鸿禧美术馆、Prada在上海的荣宅之类的等等太多了。
body.en: I think language is too limited in its expression; everyone's reasons for being moved and wanting to collect are likely different. While the spiritual value of ancient artworks is undoubtedly paramount in evoking emotions, the "manifestation" derived from the collector's identity and the act of collecting itself cannot be ignored. This "manifestation" within emotional value can also be understood as "influence."

body.zh: 就像刘先生在龙美术的每次展览，以及最近尤为火热的《天地大观》的展览所带来的社会影响力也不仅仅只是我们表面所能看到的。说到这里，突然想到一个朋友说的一句话，他说‘很多重要的项目在我的艺术空间里，谈着谈着就成了’。
body.en: The elite often value cultural and artistic cultivation because, beyond the aesthetic experience mentioned above, artworks also offer social value and associated social prestige. Therefore, we see collectors donating to museums or holding exhibitions to allow more people to directly access and appreciate their works.

body.zh: 就如同开头聊的，在商业逻辑中，既能让人心情甘情愿的掏钱来购买，又能形成一个国际性收藏的门类，那它除了得具备功能价值、情绪价值，还有一点不能缺的那就是——资产价值。资产具有经济价值，它的价值首先由其性质和类型而决定。不同的资产具有不同的价值属性，比如固定资产、无形资产、流动资产等等。
body.en: Of course, the allocation of artworks is also related to commercial processes. This explains why many large corporations have their own museums or art galleries, such as the LVMH Foundation Art Center, the Hongxi Art Museum, and Prada's Rong Zhai in Shanghai, among many others.

body.zh: 资产的价值在本质上由其未来能够产生的经济利益决定的，而这一经济利益的核心载体是获利能力，当然，不论是哪种资产在不同阶段决定其价值起伏的因素也多种多样，比如市场的供需关系、经济环境、市场状况、资产本身的质量等等多方面因素都会影响到其价值。而古董作为兼具历史、文化和经济价值的特殊资产，决定它价值的维度同样也是多面性的。
body.en: The social impact of Mr. Liu's exhibitions at Long Art Museum, and the recent highly popular "Grand View of Heaven and Earth" exhibition, goes beyond what we can superficially perceive. Speaking of which, I'm reminded of a friend's comment: "Many important projects, discussed in my art space, just happened to fall through."

body.zh: 首先是文化、审美、和精神价值所带来的超额溢价；其次是时间赋予的稀缺属性中所蕴含的不可替代性和某些工艺的不可复制性；以及存世量带来的孤品效应，同样也决定了其价值，比如目前统计全球仅有八件的‘鬼谷子下山’青花罐就拍出了2.3亿的价格、永乐宫廷的阎魔敌唐卡3.4亿的成交价之类的等等；另外古代艺术品的价值，还有其可抵税以及规避货币贬值的风险，也就是长期持有的抗通胀属性，根据梅摩指数的分析，1970-2020年，顶级古董年均的回报率超过了10%，远超同期的黄金（约4%）。
body.en: As discussed at the beginning, in commercial logic, for an asset to be both desirable enough to inspire willingness to spend money and to become an internationally recognized collectible category, it must possess not only functional and emotional value, but also, and most importantly, asset value. Assets possess economic value, primarily determined by their nature and type. Different assets have different value attributes, such as fixed assets, intangible assets, and current assets.

body.zh:
尽管古董作为另类资产，但它稳定的市场共识以及文化属性，已经使成为了高净值群体中，大多数人资产配置中5-10%的配比选择。
聊到这里，视频时长好像已经很难完播了。总之，古代艺术品之所以会被收藏的原因是复杂的。现代性的冰冷催生了古董的“救赎价值”——它的稀缺性对抗着焦虑、给予着确定性，它的美学治愈着碎片化，它的资本属性碾压着通胀，收藏家们用它收割着社交影响力，用10%左右的资产配置实现着精神与财富的双重突围。它既是文化救赎、也是理性投资，更是这快时代里最“慢”的赢家。
body.en: The value of an asset is essentially determined by the economic benefits it can generate in the future, and the core vehicle for these benefits is profitability. Of course, regardless of the type of asset, the factors determining its value fluctuations at different stages are diverse, including market supply and demand, the economic environment, market conditions, and the quality of the asset itself. Antiques, as special assets possessing historical, cultural, and economic value, are also subject to multifaceted dimensions in determining their value.

content.zh: 古代的雕塑、绘画为什么会成为高净值人群的资产配置选择？
content.en: Why have ancient sculptures and paintings become asset allocation choices for high-net-worth individuals?

content.zh: 聊到“古董艺术品”，毫无疑问，首先它得具备某种价值，因此才会让人愿意去珍藏。尽管这其中每个人重视的价值点有所区别。在当今“结构化”的商业逻辑中，一件能产生商业价值的物品，往往集功能价值、情绪价值、符号价值、资产价值于一身，古董收藏也同样如此。
content.en: When discussing "antique art," it's undeniable that it must first possess some form of value to inspire interest in collecting. While the specific value each individual prioritizes may differ, in today's structured business world, an item that generates commercial value often combines functional, emotional, symbolic, and asset value—and antique collecting is no exception .

caption.en: Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York

content.en: When discussing the functional and symbolic value of ancient art, most people first think of its practical function as display and decoration. However, the more important function and symbolic value of ancient art lies in the scarcity attribute bestowed by time. How do we understand this scarcity? Here, we can borrow Walter Benjamin's explanation of the term "aura." The literal meaning of "aura" is "the halo of art."

聊到这里，视频时长好像已经很难完播了。总之，古代艺术品之所以会被收藏的原因是复杂的。现代性的冰冷催生了古董的“救赎价值”——它的稀缺性对抗着焦虑、给予着确定性，它的美学治愈着碎片化，它的资本属性碾压着通胀，收藏家们用它收割着社交影响力，用10%左右的资产配置实现着精神与财富的双重突围。它既是文化救赎、也是理性投资，更是这快时代里最“慢”的赢家。
content.en: The value of an asset is essentially determined by the economic benefits it can generate in the future, and the core vehicle for these benefits is profitability. Of course, regardless of the type of asset, the factors determining its value fluctuations at different stages are diverse, including market supply and demand, the economic environment, market conditions, and the quality of the asset itself. Antiques, as special assets possessing historical, cultural, and economic value, are also subject to multifaceted dimensions in determining their value.
